parts.label: a
parts.text: A weather station in Gilgit records the air temperature and rainfall every 10 minutes. A greenhouse near Quetta keeps its temperature between 22 °C and 26 °C. Explain why the weather station is an example of a monitoring system and the greenhouse is an example of a control system.
parts.answer: The weather station only takes/records/displays readings from sensors and does not change anything. The greenhouse system uses the readings to switch devices (heater, fan, window motor) on or off through actuators to change the conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: monitoring = readings recorded/displayed, no action taken. 1 mark: control = computer uses readings to operate actuators/devices to change conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two sensors, other than temperature sensors, that could be used in the greenhouse.
parts.answer: Any two: humidity/moisture sensor; light sensor; soil moisture sensor; pH sensor; CO₂/gas sensor.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept brand names or 'heat sensor'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each application, name the most suitable sensor.
(i) Detecting a person walking past a shop's automatic door.
(ii) Switching on street lights when it gets dark.
(iii) Detecting when a car is waiting at a traffic light.
(iv) Measuring the acidity of water in a fish farm.
parts.answer: (i) infrared/motion sensor (ii) light sensor (iii) pressure sensor (or magnetic field/induction loop sensor) (iv) pH sensor
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A data logger with a temperature sensor is placed in a cold store at a fruit market in Peshawar. It takes one reading every 5 minutes for exactly 2 days. Calculate the number of readings it takes.
parts.answer: 576 readings

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why a data logger is used for this task rather than a worker writing down readings.
parts.answer: Readings are taken at exactly regular intervals day and night; no human errors in reading or recording.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: works 24 hours / at night without breaks; readings taken at precise intervals; more accurate / no misreading or copying errors; worker does not have to enter the cold store; frees staff for other work; readings stored automatically and can be graphed.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each application, state whether it is an example of monitoring or of control.
(i) A smartwatch records a runner's heart rate during a training session.
(ii) A greenhouse window motor opens the window when the air becomes too warm.
(iii) A station beside a busy road in Lahore records the level of fine dust in the air.
(iv) Traffic lights change to green when sensors detect cars waiting on a side road.
parts.answer: (i) monitoring (ii) control (iii) monitoring (iv) control
parts.working: 1 mark each. Monitoring only measures and records/displays; control uses the readings to make an actuator change the conditions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A pH sensor is connected to a computer in a water treatment plant. Explain why an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) is needed.
parts.answer: The sensor produces an analogue signal; the computer can only process digital data, so the ADC converts the signal to digital.
parts.working: B1: sensor output is analogue / continuously varying; B1: computer works with digital (binary) data so it must be converted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The computer opens a valve to add chemicals when the pH is too low. State why a digital-to-analogue converter (DAC) may be needed between the computer and the valve's motor.
parts.answer: The motor/actuator needs an analogue signal, but the computer outputs digital signals.
parts.working: B1: actuator needs analogue signal / computer's digital output must be converted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name the type of device that physically opens the valve.
parts.answer: An actuator (e.g. a motor or solenoid).
parts.working: B1: actuator / motor / solenoid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shop in Saddar, Karachi, has a computer-controlled burglar alarm. Name two sensors the alarm system could use and state what each one detects.
parts.answer: Infrared (motion) sensor – detects the movement/body heat of an intruder in the room; pressure sensor – detects someone stepping on a mat or floor panel inside the door.
parts.working: For each sensor: 1 mark for the sensor, 1 mark for what it detects. Accept: infrared/motion – movement or body heat; pressure – person standing on mat/floor; acoustic/sound – breaking glass or noise; magnetic field (contact) sensor – door or window opened. Do not accept temperature or light sensors without a sensible link to an intruder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hatchery in Punjab uses a microprocessor-controlled incubator to keep eggs at 37.5 °C. Describe how the microprocessor controls the temperature.
parts.answer: A temperature sensor constantly measures the temperature; the analogue reading is converted to digital by an ADC; the microprocessor compares the reading with the preset value (37.5 °C) stored in memory; if it is lower, a signal is sent (through a DAC/actuator) to switch the heater on (and fan off); if it is higher, the heater is switched off/the fan is switched on; this process repeats continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five: sensor measures temperature; ADC converts analogue to digital; compares with preset value; below → heater on; above → heater off/fan on; actuator/DAC used to operate device; process continuous loop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An automatic washing machine is controlled by a microprocessor. Describe how the microprocessor makes sure the drum is filled to the correct level with water at 40 °C.
parts.answer: A water level/pressure sensor sends readings to the microprocessor, which keeps the inlet valve open until the preset level is reached, then closes it. A temperature sensor sends readings; the microprocessor compares them with 40 °C and switches the heater on if lower and off when 40 °C is reached; this repeats continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: water level/pressure sensor used; microprocessor opens inlet valve / keeps it open while level below preset value; closes valve when level reached; temperature sensor used; reading compared with stored value 40 °C; heater switched on if below, off if at/above; ADC needed for sensor readings; process repeats / continuous loop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A central heating system in an office in Murree is set to 21 °C. The heater is switched on when the temperature is below 21 °C and switched off when it is above 21 °C. The microprocessor receives these three temperature readings, one after another: 19.5 °C, 21.6 °C, 20.8 °C. The heater is off before the first reading. Describe what the microprocessor does after each reading.
parts.answer: 19.5 °C: below 21 °C, so it switches the heater on. 21.6 °C: above 21 °C, so it switches the heater off. 20.8 °C: below 21 °C, so it switches the heater on again.
parts.working: 1 mark per reading. Each answer must link the comparison with the stored value 21 °C to the action (on / off / on).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the system uses a continuous loop of readings rather than one reading each hour.
parts.answer: The temperature can change at any time (doors opening, weather); frequent readings let the system react quickly and keep the temperature close to 21 °C.
parts.working: B1: temperature changes between readings; B1: quicker response / keeps temperature steady / avoids large swings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A chemical factory in Sheikhupura must keep a reaction vessel at 70 °C with a pH between 6.5 and 7.0. Describe how a computer control system does this.
parts.answer: Temperature and pH sensors send readings via an ADC to the computer. The computer compares the temperature with 70 °C and switches a heater on or a cooling valve on as needed. It compares the pH with 6.5 and 7.0: if below 6.5 it opens a valve to add alkali; if above 7.0 it opens a valve to add acid. Actuators open/close the valves. The process repeats continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: temperature sensor and pH sensor named; ADC converts readings; readings compared with stored values (70 °C, 6.5–7.0); heater/cooler switched on/off by computer; if pH < 6.5 alkali added; if pH > 7.0 acid added; actuators/valves operated by computer (DAC if needed); loop repeats continuously / until process stopped.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a school science lesson students measure how quickly a beaker of hot water cools. Give three advantages of using a temperature sensor and data logger rather than reading a thermometer by eye.
parts.answer: Readings are more accurate; readings are taken at exact time intervals; results can be graphed automatically.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: more accurate / no misreading; exact time intervals; very frequent readings possible (e.g. every second); no human needed to watch / students can do other work; data saved automatically; graph produced automatically; no transcription errors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The water cools over about 30 minutes. Suggest a suitable time between readings and give a reason.
parts.answer: About every 10–30 seconds, so there are enough points to show the curve without too much data.
parts.working: B1: any interval from about 5 s to 1 min with a reason linked to enough readings / smooth curve.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An environmental agency wants to monitor the pollution level in the River Ravi at 20 points along its length. It is choosing between using computers with sensors and sending staff to take readings by hand. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using computers with sensors.
parts.answer: Advantages: readings can be taken 24 hours a day and at regular, precise intervals; readings are more accurate/no human error; staff do not need to visit dangerous or polluted places; results can be sent automatically and analysed/graphed immediately; sudden pollution events are noticed quickly and alarms can be raised; cheaper in staff costs in the long term. Disadvantages: high initial cost of sensors, computers and communication links; sensors can be damaged, stolen or fouled and need maintenance/calibration; power failure or a fault may lose data; staff may lose jobs or need retraining. Conclusion weighing both sides.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side only. 1 mark per expanded valid point; 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion. Answers must refer to the river scenario for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A busy crossroads in Rawalpindi has traffic lights controlled by a microprocessor. Describe how the sensors and microprocessor control the lights.
parts.answer: Sensors (e.g. induction loops or cameras/infrared) detect vehicles waiting on each road. Readings are sent to the microprocessor, which compares the number of waiting vehicles and how long they have waited with stored values. It decides which road gets green and for how long, and sends signals to change the lights in the correct sequence. A pedestrian button input is also checked. The process repeats continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: sensor type named (induction loop / pressure / infrared / camera / motion); detects vehicles waiting / queue length; data sent to microprocessor (via ADC if analogue); compared with stored values / preset times; microprocessor decides which lights change and timing; sends signals to the lights / outputs to change sequence (red, red+amber, green, amber); pedestrian push button checked; timer ensures each road gets a turn / maximum wait; continuous loop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A valley in northern Pakistan lies below a glacial lake that could burst and flood villages. An automatic system with sensors monitors the lake's water level and sends warnings by siren and mobile phone message. Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of using this computerised system rather than people checking the lake.
parts.answer: Benefits: monitors 24 hours a day in all weather; no one has to travel to a dangerous, remote place; readings are frequent and accurate; warnings are sent instantly to everyone, giving more time to evacuate; data recorded for analysis. Drawbacks: expensive to buy and install; sensors or power supply may fail or be damaged by ice/floods; needs regular maintenance in a remote place; false alarms may make people ignore warnings; people without phones may not receive messages. Conclusion: benefits likely outweigh drawbacks because lives are at risk, provided there is backup power and maintenance.
parts.working: Level marking: up to 4 marks for one side; max 6. Benefits (any): 24/7 monitoring; no human risk; more frequent/accurate readings; instant automatic warnings; reaches many people at once; data can be analysed/trends predicted. Drawbacks (any): high cost; sensor/power/communication failure; maintenance difficult in remote area; false alarms; phone coverage/people without phones; skills needed. Top band needs both sides and a reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An air quality monitor in Karachi takes one reading every 30 seconds for 7 days. Calculate the number of readings taken.
parts.answer: 20 160 readings
parts.working: M1: 2 readings per minute × 60 × 24 × 7; A1: 20 160.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each reading is stored using 4 bytes. Calculate the storage needed for the week's readings in bytes.
parts.answer: 80 640 bytes
parts.working: B1: 20 160 × 4 = 80 640 (follow through from (a)).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why readings every 30 seconds are more useful than one reading every hour for this application.
parts.answer: Pollution can rise and fall quickly (e.g. rush hour, a fire); hourly readings could miss short peaks, so 30-second readings give a more accurate picture.
parts.working: B1: air quality changes quickly / short peaks; B1: hourly readings would miss them / less accurate / trends less clear.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A family in Karachi books cinema tickets online. Give three advantages to the family of booking online rather than at the cinema box office.
parts.answer: Any three: can book at any time of day; no need to travel to the cinema to book/no queuing; can see the seat plan and choose the seats they want; can compare times/prices easily; e-ticket sent to phone so no paper ticket to lose; may get special online offers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for three distinct advantages. Do not accept 'quicker' or 'easier' without a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A passenger books a seat on an intercity train using a railway company's website. State three items of data the passenger must enter.
parts.answer: Departure station; destination station; date of travel.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: departure station; destination; date; time/train; number of passengers; class of seat; passenger name; CNIC/ID number; contact phone/email; payment card details.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two disadvantages to customers of booking a holiday through an online booking system.
parts.answer: Needs internet access and a device; risk of fraud or hacking when card details are entered.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: needs internet connection/device; risk of card fraud/hacking/phishing sites; no face-to-face advice; may be hard for people with poor IT skills; a slow or crashed website; extra booking fees; cannot see the hotel/seat in person; mistakes in booking may be hard to correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After booking online, a spectator receives an e-ticket containing a QR code. Describe how the e-ticket is used at the entrance of the stadium.
parts.answer: The QR code on the phone or printout is scanned at the gate; the system looks up the booking and checks it is valid and not already used; if valid the gate opens and the ticket is marked as used.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: QR code scanned (by a scanner / phone camera); data checked against booking database; checked valid for this event/date and not used before; entry allowed / ticket marked as used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hotel in Swat shows on its booking website which rooms are free on each date. Give two reasons why this information must be updated as soon as a booking is made.
parts.answer: So the same room is not booked twice; so customers see accurate availability when they search.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: prevents double booking; other customers see correct availability; hotel can plan staff/cleaning; customers can be sent confirmation immediately.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An airline's online booking system must make sure the same seat is never sold to two customers. Describe how the system does this.
parts.answer: When a customer selects a seat, the system checks the central database that it is available; the seat is temporarily held/locked for that customer while they complete payment so no one else can select it; when payment is completed the database is updated immediately (real-time processing) so the seat shows as booked; if payment is not completed within a time limit, the seat is released.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: checks availability in database; seat locked/held during transaction; database updated immediately/real-time; other users see seat as unavailable; seat released after timeout.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps a cricket fan goes through to book seats for a match using an online booking system.
parts.answer: Visit the website and log in or create an account; select the match and date; view the seating plan and choose seats (or ticket type); enter number of tickets and any personal details; enter payment details and confirm; receive confirmation email/e-ticket with booking reference.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: log in / register; search for / select match; view available seats; choose seats/stand and quantity; seats held while booking completes; enter personal details; enter/confirm payment details; confirmation / booking reference / e-ticket sent by email or SMS.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an online booking website uses a secure connection (https) when the customer pays.
parts.answer: Data sent is encrypted using SSL/TLS, so if card details are intercepted they cannot be understood by hackers.
parts.working: B1: https uses SSL/TLS / encryption; B1: intercepted data is meaningless / protects card details.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The website also asks for the 3-digit security code from the back of the card. Explain why.
parts.answer: It shows that the customer has the physical card and is not just using a stolen card number, reducing fraud.
parts.working: B1: proves the card is present / in the customer's possession; B1: makes fraud with stolen numbers harder (code should not be stored by the website).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A theatre in Lahore has 12 rows of 18 seats. The online booking system shows that 147 seats have been sold for Friday evening. Calculate how many seats are still available.
parts.answer: 69 seats

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of seats sold. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe how the seating plan on the screen shows the customer which seats can be chosen.
parts.answer: Available and booked seats are shown in different colours (or booked seats are greyed out and cannot be clicked).
parts.working: B1: different colours / symbols for free and taken seats; taken seats cannot be selected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Online booking systems use real-time processing, not batch processing. Explain why batch processing would not be suitable for booking airline seats.
parts.answer: In batch processing bookings would be collected and processed later, so the database would not be updated immediately. Other customers would see seats as available that were already taken, leading to double booking, and customers would not get instant confirmation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: batch processes data later / in groups; database/seat availability not updated immediately; leads to double booking / wrong availability; no instant confirmation to customer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A concert organiser in Lahore is closing its box office and will sell all tickets through an online booking system. Discuss the benefits and drawbacks to the organiser.
parts.answer: Benefits: fewer box-office staff so lower wage costs; tickets sold 24/7 to customers worldwide; real-time seat availability prevents double booking; payments received immediately/electronically; customer data collected for marketing; e-tickets reduce printing costs; sales reports instantly available. Drawbacks: cost of setting up/maintaining the website and booking software; customers without internet access/cards may not buy tickets, losing sales; risk of hacking/data breach and fake websites; system crash on busy release days loses sales/reputation; staff made redundant; fees charged by payment providers. Conclusion.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side only. 1 mark per expanded point; 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare booking a hotel room through an online booking system with booking it by telephoning the hotel.
parts.answer: Both let the customer choose dates and room type and need payment or contact details, and both give a confirmation. Online booking can be done at any time, lets the customer see photos, prices and all available rooms at once and compare hotels, and gives instant written confirmation by email; however it needs internet access and a device and there is no one to answer questions. Telephone booking allows the customer to ask questions and make special requests directly and suits people without internet, but only works when the hotel is open, may involve waiting, and errors can occur when details are written down by staff.
parts.working: Max 6. Must contain at least one similarity and differences written as comparisons. Similarities: both need personal/payment details; both give a booking/confirmation; both can check availability. Differences: 24/7 vs office hours; see photos/seat or room plans vs description only; instant email confirmation vs verbal/later; compare prices across hotels online; human help/special requests by phone; internet and IT skills needed online; risk of mishearing/transcription errors by phone; online may be cheaper/discounts. Two lists without linking max 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When tickets for a big cricket final went on sale online, about 50 000 fans tried to book at the same moment and the website crashed. Explain two problems this caused for the organiser and the fans.
parts.answer: Fans could not book and became frustrated, some may have lost money if payment was taken without a booking; the organiser lost sales and its reputation suffered, and staff had to deal with many complaints.
parts.working: 2 marks per problem (identify + explain). Problems: lost sales/income; damage to reputation; payments taken but no ticket issued; double bookings if database not updated; complaints/extra staff costs; fans turn to touts/fake ticket sites.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways the booking system could be designed to cope with this demand.
parts.answer: Use a virtual queue that lets fans in a few at a time; use more powerful servers / cloud servers that can scale up.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: online queue/waiting room; more or more powerful servers / load balancing / cloud hosting; release tickets at different times for different stands or groups; limit tickets per customer; hold seats for a fixed time while payment is completed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A busy medical clinic in Lahore, where patients used to queue from early morning to get a token, introduces an online appointment booking system. Evaluate this system for the clinic and for its patients.
parts.answer: Patients can book a time slot from home at any time, avoid long queues and receive SMS reminders; the clinic can spread appointments evenly through the day, plan each doctor's time and keep automatic records, and reminders reduce missed appointments. However, patients without a smartphone, internet access or IT skills (often older or poorer people) may find it hard to book; urgent cases may find no free slot; the clinic must pay to set up and maintain the system; some people may book and not attend. Overall the system improves efficiency and comfort for most patients, provided some walk-in or telephone slots are kept for those who cannot book online.
parts.working: Max 6; both the clinic and patients, benefits and drawbacks, plus a judgement. Benefits: book 24/7 from home; no queues/less waiting; reminders; even spread of patients; doctors' time planned; automatic records; fewer no-shows. Drawbacks: digital divide (no device/internet/skills); urgent cases; set-up/maintenance cost; system failure; no-shows/fake bookings; staff training. 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An online booking system for a chain of cinemas stores its data in a database. Describe how the database is used when a customer searches for and books two seats.
parts.answer: The customer's search (film, cinema, date, time) is used to query the database of showings. The system finds seat records for that showing whose status is 'available' and displays them. When the customer selects two seats, those records are locked/flagged as held so no one else can take them. After payment is accepted, the seat records are updated to 'booked' with the booking reference and customer ID, and a booking record is created. If payment fails, the hold is removed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: tables/records for films/showings, seats, customers, bookings; search criteria used to query; only available seats retrieved/displayed; chosen seats held/locked; payment checked; seat status updated to booked; new booking record with reference/customer ID; confirmation generated from the record; hold released if not paid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car factory near Karachi uses robots to weld and spray-paint car bodies. Give three advantages to the factory of using robots for these tasks.
parts.answer: Any three: robots can work 24 hours a day without breaks; every weld/coat of paint is the same/consistent quality; more accurate than humans; no wages to pay/lower running costs; can work in dangerous environments (fumes, sparks) so workers are safer; higher productivity.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage to the factory of using robots.
parts.answer: e.g. very expensive to buy and install; need regular maintenance/specialist technicians; cannot adapt to unexpected situations; a breakdown can stop the production line.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Other than welding and spray painting, name three tasks that robots carry out in factories.
parts.answer: Assembling parts; packing goods into boxes; moving heavy items between machines.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: assembling/fitting parts (e.g. windscreens, circuit boards); packing/palletising; bottling/filling/capping; drilling; cutting/lathing; moving or lifting goods; quality inspection; labelling; sorting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which a factory robot can be programmed to carry out a task.
parts.answer: A programmer writes the instructions in software on a computer and loads them into the robot; or a worker guides the robot arm through the movements once and the robot records them and repeats them.
parts.working: 1 mark each: programmed with software / sequence of instructions; 'teach' method – arm moved through the task (by hand or controller) and movements stored.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by the end-effector of a robot arm and give one example.
parts.answer: The tool fitted to the end of the arm that carries out the task, e.g. a gripper.
parts.working: B1: tool attached to end of arm; B1: example – gripper, welding gun, spray gun, drill, suction cup, screwdriver.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A family in Islamabad buys a robot vacuum cleaner. Name two sensors it uses and state what each is used for.
parts.answer: Infrared/proximity sensor – detects obstacles such as furniture so it can turn; Pressure/touch (bump) sensor – detects when it hits something.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark sensor, 1 mark use. Accept: infrared/ultrasonic/proximity – obstacle avoidance; pressure/touch – detects bump; infrared cliff sensor – detects stairs/edges; light/camera – mapping the room; dirt sensor (acoustic/optical) – detects dirty areas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small furniture workshop in Chiniot is thinking about buying a robot. Give two disadvantages to the workshop.
parts.answer: Robots are expensive to buy; they cannot easily deal with unusual one-off designs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: high purchase/installation cost; maintenance/repair costs; need skilled staff to program/maintain; cannot handle non-standard / custom tasks easily; production stops if the robot breaks down; staff need retraining; uses floor space and power.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A large online shop uses robots in its warehouse to fetch shelves of goods and bring them to human packers. Describe how the robots can move around the warehouse safely and find the correct shelves.
parts.answer: Robots are controlled by a central computer that sends them the location of the required shelf; they navigate using sensors such as cameras/barcodes or markers on the floor (or GPS-like indoor positioning); proximity/infrared/ultrasonic sensors detect obstacles or people so the robot slows or stops; the robot reads the shelf's barcode/RFID tag to confirm it is the correct shelf before lifting it.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four valid points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A robot on a production line puts caps on bottles. Describe how sensors and the robot's microprocessor make sure each cap is fitted correctly.
parts.answer: A sensor (e.g. light/infrared or camera) detects when a bottle is in position and sends a signal to the microprocessor, which stops the conveyor or times the arm. The arm places and turns the cap; a pressure/torque sensor measures how tightly it is turned and the microprocessor stops turning when the stored value is reached. A camera or sensor then checks the cap; faulty bottles are rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: sensor detects bottle in position; data sent to microprocessor; microprocessor activates actuators/arm; pressure/torque sensor checks tightness against stored value; camera/sensor checks cap present/straight; faulty bottles pushed off line; process repeats for each bottle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of actuators in a robot arm.
parts.answer: Actuators (motors, hydraulic or pneumatic cylinders) receive signals from the controller and produce movement of the arm's joints and end-effector.
parts.working: B1: actuators are motors/hydraulics/pneumatics; B1: convert control signals into movement of joints/gripper.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the robot also needs sensors to provide feedback while it moves.
parts.answer: Sensors tell the controller the arm's actual position or grip pressure, so it can correct the movement and stop at the right place without damaging items.
parts.working: B1: feedback on position/pressure; B1: allows corrections / accurate placement / avoids damage or collisions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A juice company in Lahore uses a computer-controlled production line to fill cartons. Describe how computer control makes sure every carton is filled to the correct level and that underfilled cartons are removed.
parts.answer: A sensor detects each carton arriving under the nozzle and the conveyor stops. The computer opens the valve; a level or weight sensor sends readings, which are compared with the stored value, and the valve closes when the correct level is reached. Later a weight sensor checks each carton; if the weight is below the stored minimum, the computer activates an actuator that pushes the carton off the line. The conveyor restarts and the process repeats.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: sensor detects carton in position; conveyor stopped/started by computer; valve opened by actuator; level/weight sensor used; readings compared with stored value; valve closed at correct level; checking sensor/weight later; underfilled carton rejected by actuator/arm; continuous repeat; counts/records rejects.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Farmers in Punjab are starting to use drones (flying robots) on their fields. Describe two ways drones can be used in farming.
parts.answer: Spraying crops with pesticide or fertiliser exactly where needed; taking images of fields to find areas of crop disease or poor growth.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: spraying pesticide/fertiliser; crop monitoring with cameras/infrared images; mapping fields; checking irrigation/water; counting livestock; planting seeds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one drawback of using drones for this work.
parts.answer: They are expensive and need trained operators (and their batteries last only a short time).
parts.working: B1: cost; training/licence; short battery life; affected by wind/rain; may break down / crash; privacy concerns.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A textile factory in Faisalabad plans to replace many of its machine operators with robots. Discuss the effects of this decision on the factory's workers.
parts.answer: Negative: many operators may lose their jobs (unemployment); remaining workers may have to retrain; work may become deskilled/repetitive supervision; fear and lower morale. Positive: new jobs for robot programmers, technicians and maintenance staff; workers removed from noisy, dusty or dangerous tasks so fewer injuries; retrained workers may earn higher wages; more interesting supervisory work; shorter hours possible. Conclusion.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side only. 1 mark per expanded point; 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion. Answers must be about workers, not the factory's profits.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why goods made by robots are usually more consistent in quality than goods made by human workers, and why robots are less suitable for making hand-tailored wedding clothes.
parts.answer: Robots repeat exactly the same programmed movements every time, do not get tired or bored and so make the same quality product throughout a shift. Hand-tailored clothes are different for every customer and need judgement and creativity; a robot only does what it is programmed for, and reprogramming for each one-off item would be too slow and costly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: same movements / precision every time; no tiredness/boredom/loss of concentration; tailored items each unique / need judgement, creativity or fine skills; robots cannot adapt / reprogramming for one-offs is expensive or slow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Robots are used to inspect and repair equipment inside a nuclear power station and to deal with suspected bombs. Evaluate the use of robots for these tasks.
parts.answer: Robots can go into places with radiation or explosives without risking human life, can work in extreme heat or confined spaces, and can be controlled remotely using cameras. They can be precise and do not suffer from fear or fatigue. However, they are expensive, may be damaged or destroyed, can break down in the middle of a task, may lose their radio link, and lack human judgement in unexpected situations; operators need long training. Overall the protection of human life makes robots the better choice, with humans controlling them remotely.
parts.working: Max 6; both sides plus a judgement. Benefits: no risk to human life; can work in radiation/heat/confined spaces; remote control with cameras; precise; work for long periods; can be decontaminated or replaced. Drawbacks: high cost; robot may be destroyed; breakdowns/loss of signal; cannot make human judgements in unexpected situations; operators need training; slower than a skilled person for some tasks. 1 mark for conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A car parts factory compares two ways of making brake discs.
Human workers: 40 discs per hour, two 8-hour shifts per day.
Robot cell: 55 discs per hour, runs 24 hours per day but is stopped for maintenance 5% of the time.
Calculate the number of discs made per day by each method and how many more the robot cell makes.
parts.answer: Humans: 640 discs; robot: 1254 discs; robot makes 614 more.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three factors other than output that the factory should consider before choosing the robot cell.
parts.answer: Cost of buying and installing the robot; cost and skills needed for maintenance and programming; effect on the workers who may lose their jobs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: purchase/installation cost; maintenance/repair cost; need for skilled technicians/programmers; retraining staff; redundancies/morale; quality/accuracy; flexibility to make other products; electricity costs; downtime if it breaks; space needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A port in Karachi plans to use computer-controlled cranes and self-driving vehicles to move shipping containers. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages to the port company.
parts.answer: Advantages: machines can work 24 hours a day so ships are unloaded faster and more ships can use the port; fewer accidents; lower wage costs; containers are tracked and positioned accurately. Disadvantages: very high initial cost; need for skilled engineers and expensive maintenance; a software fault or cyber attack could stop the whole port; possible strikes or bad publicity over job losses. Conclusion: over many years the savings and extra capacity are likely to pay back the cost if backups and security are in place.
parts.working: Max 6, both sides needed. Advantages: 24/7 operation; faster turnaround/more ships; lower labour cost; fewer accidents/injuries; accurate tracking/placement; consistent work. Disadvantages: high set-up cost; maintenance and skilled staff; breakdown or cyber attack stops work; job losses / industrial action / reputation; inflexible in unusual situations. 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name four components of an expert system.
parts.answer: Any four: knowledge base; rules base; inference engine; user interface; explanation system.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State which component of an expert system does each of the following.
(i) Stores the facts about the subject.
(ii) Asks the user questions on the screen and shows the results.
(iii) Applies the rules to the facts and the user's answers to reach a conclusion.
(iv) Tells the user how the conclusion was reached.
parts.answer: (i) knowledge base (ii) user interface (iii) inference engine (iv) explanation system
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car mechanic in Faisalabad uses an expert system to find faults in engines. Give two advantages to the mechanic of using the expert system.
parts.answer: It suggests faults quickly; it contains the knowledge of many experts, so faults the mechanic has not seen before can be found.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: faster diagnosis; consistent answers; knowledge of many experts; can find rare faults; gives probabilities/explanations; less experienced mechanics can use it; available any time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of relying on the expert system.
parts.answer: It can only use the rules it has been given, so it may give a wrong answer for a new type of engine or fault.
parts.working: B1: depends on quality of data/rules; cannot use common sense / hear or see the engine; expensive; needs updating; mechanic may lose skills.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is stored in the knowledge base and in the rules base of an expert system.
parts.answer: Knowledge base: the facts about the subject collected from experts. Rules base: the IF … THEN rules used to link the facts to conclusions.
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of an IF … THEN rule that could be in a plant-identification expert system.
parts.answer: IF leaves are needle-shaped AND the tree bears cones THEN the tree is a conifer.
parts.working: B1: any sensible rule with a condition and a conclusion about a plant.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An expert system used by a hospital doctor shows a diagnosis together with a percentage, for example 'Typhoid – 82% probability'. Give two reasons why the percentage is shown.
parts.answer: It tells the doctor how confident the system is; the doctor can decide whether more tests are needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: shows level of certainty; doctor can compare several possible diagnoses; doctor knows when to do further tests; doctor still makes the final decision; shows the system could be wrong.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the explanation system would show the doctor.
parts.answer: The reasoning / the rules and answers used to reach the diagnosis.
parts.working: B1: how/why the conclusion was reached, e.g. which symptoms led to it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farmer uses an expert system to identify a disease affecting her wheat crop. Describe how the expert system produces a diagnosis.
parts.answer: The user interface asks the farmer questions about the symptoms (e.g. colour of leaves, spots); the farmer answers, often by choosing yes/no or from options; the inference engine uses the rules base to compare the answers with facts in the knowledge base; the inference engine decides which question to ask next based on previous answers; it produces a diagnosis/list of possible diseases with probabilities; the explanation system shows the reasoning behind the conclusion; suggested treatment given.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five valid points in a logical order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mining company uses an expert system to help decide where to drill for copper in Balochistan. Describe how the expert system is used.
parts.answer: Geologists enter data about the area, such as rock types, soil samples and survey results, by answering questions on the user interface. The inference engine compares this data with the knowledge base and rules base. The system outputs the probability of finding copper at each site, with an explanation, so the company can choose the best place to drill.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: user interface asks questions / data entered; data from samples/surveys/rock types; inference engine applies rules; compares with knowledge base; output: likely location / probability of deposit; explanation of reasoning; geologists make final decision.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A garden plant expert system has these rules:
Rule 1: IF leaves are yellow AND soil is wet THEN overwatering
Rule 2: IF leaves are yellow AND soil is dry THEN underwatering
Rule 3: IF leaves have white powder THEN mildew
Rule 4: IF leaves have holes AND insects are seen THEN pest damage
State the conclusion for each user.
(i) Leaves yellow, soil dry, no insects.
(ii) Leaves have holes, insects seen, soil wet.
(iii) Leaves yellow, soil wet, white powder on leaves.
parts.answer: (i) underwatering (ii) pest damage (iii) overwatering and mildew
parts.working: 1 mark each. (iii) needs both conclusions because Rule 1 and Rule 3 both apply.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which component of the expert system uses these rules.
parts.answer: The inference engine.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before an expert system for diagnosing mobile phone faults is used in repair shops, it is tested. Describe how it should be tested.
parts.answer: Experts provide example faults whose causes are already known. These are entered into the system and the system's conclusions are compared with the known answers. Where the system is wrong, the knowledge base or rules are corrected and the tests repeated. Repair staff also try the user interface to check that the questions are clear.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: use cases with known results; enter data/answer questions; compare output with expected/expert answer; correct rules/knowledge base if wrong; repeat tests; experts involved in checking; test user interface with real users; test unusual/extreme cases.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A courier company uses an expert system to plan the routes of its vans each morning. Give two items of data the dispatcher must input.
parts.answer: The delivery addresses; the delivery deadlines/time windows.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: delivery addresses/locations; time windows/deadlines; parcel sizes/weights; number of vans and their capacity; drivers' working hours; starting depot.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two advantages of using the expert system rather than an experienced dispatcher planning the routes by hand.
parts.answer: It can compare far more possible routes in a short time, so shorter routes are found and fuel is saved; it gives consistent plans and is still available if the experienced dispatcher is absent or leaves the company.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two explained: faster planning; considers many more combinations/factors so less distance/fuel/time; consistent results; knowledge not lost when the expert is absent or leaves; explanation system shows why a route was chosen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how an expert system for diagnosing faults in mobile phones would be created.
parts.answer: Information is gathered from human experts (repair technicians) by interviews/questionnaires and from manuals/other sources; the knowledge base is created and populated with facts; a rules base of IF…THEN rules is created; the inference engine is designed/linked to the rules; the user interface is designed to ask questions and show results; an explanation system is included; the system is tested using faults with known solutions and results compared with the experts' diagnoses.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five valid steps.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two other applications of expert systems.
parts.answer: Any two: medical diagnosis; mineral/oil prospecting; car engine fault diagnosis; tax/financial advice; chess games; plant/animal identification; insurance or credit risk assessment.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A rural health worker in a village far from a hospital is given a tablet with a medical expert system. Discuss the use of the expert system in this situation instead of the patient travelling to see a doctor.
parts.answer: Benefits: patients get a quick diagnosis without a long, costly journey; the system holds the knowledge of many doctors and gives consistent results; it can suggest which patients must be sent to hospital urgently. Drawbacks: the system cannot examine the patient or notice things it is not asked about; results depend on the health worker entering accurate answers; errors in the rules could cause a wrong diagnosis; the tablet needs power and may need updating; patients may not trust it. Conclusion: useful for screening and advice, but serious cases still need a doctor.
parts.working: Max 6; both sides and a conclusion. Benefits: no travel/cost/time; faster diagnosis; knowledge of many experts; consistent; helps decide urgent referrals; explanation system helps health worker learn. Drawbacks: no physical examination/empathy; depends on accurate input; wrong rules → wrong diagnosis; who is responsible for errors; needs power/maintenance/updates; patients' trust; health worker training.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An insurance company uses an expert system to decide the yearly premium for car insurance. Describe how the expert system calculates a premium for a new customer.
parts.answer: The customer's details (age, driving experience, past claims, car model and value, city) are input through the user interface. The inference engine applies the company's rules to these facts, using data in the knowledge base about risk, and outputs a premium with the reasons.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: details input via user interface (examples); inference engine applies rules; knowledge base of risk data/previous claims; output premium (and explanation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two drawbacks of using an expert system for this task.
parts.answer: It applies the rules rigidly and cannot consider unusual circumstances; if the rules contain errors or bias, many customers will be charged wrongly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two explained: no human judgement for unusual cases; errors/bias in rules affect everyone; customers may not understand/accept the decision; system must be updated as risks change; cost of developing.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An expert system that identifies mobile phone faults has these rules:
Rule 1: IF phone will not switch on AND charging light does not come on THEN battery or charger fault
Rule 2: IF phone will not switch on AND charging light comes on THEN power button or software fault
Rule 3: IF screen is black AND phone vibrates on call THEN display fault
Rule 4: IF phone gets hot AND battery drains fast THEN battery fault
State all conclusions for each customer.
(i) The phone will not switch on and the charging light comes on.
(ii) The screen is black, the phone vibrates on a call and it gets hot, but the battery lasts well.
(iii) The phone gets hot and the battery drains fast; the screen works normally.
parts.answer: (i) power button or software fault (ii) display fault (iii) battery fault
parts.working: 1 mark each. (ii): Rule 4 does not apply because the battery does not drain fast (both conditions of an AND rule must be true).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the explanation system is useful to a trainee repair technician using this expert system.
parts.answer: It shows which answers and rules led to the conclusion, so the trainee learns how faults are diagnosed and can check the reasoning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bird-watching club in Islamabad is choosing between an expert system app that identifies birds from the user's answers and a printed field guide book. Evaluate the use of the expert system app.
parts.answer: The app asks questions (size, colours, beak shape, habitat) and narrows down the possibilities quickly, giving a probability for each bird and an explanation; it can include photos and calls and can be updated with new species. The book needs no battery or signal, may be easier to browse, and shows many similar birds side by side so members learn to spot differences. The app may give wrong answers if the user answers questions wrongly, and needs a charged phone. Overall the app is quicker and better for beginners, but experienced members may prefer the book; using both is best.
parts.working: Max 6. Points for the app: fast/narrows choices; questions guide beginners; probabilities/explanations; photos/sounds/video; updated easily; portable on phone. Points against: needs battery/possibly internet; wrong answers lead to wrong identification; cost; members may not learn skills; limited to its rules. Book points can support comparison. Conclusion required for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three advantages to customers of buying groceries through the internet.
parts.answer: Any three: no need to travel/saves fuel and time; can shop 24/7; goods are delivered to the home (useful for elderly/disabled people); easy to compare prices on different websites; can see a full range of products/reviews; fewer impulse purchases because a list is used.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage to customers of internet shopping.
parts.answer: e.g. cannot see/feel goods before buying; risk of fraud/fake websites; delivery charges; delays in delivery; needs internet access and a bank card; returns can be difficult.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A supermarket's stock database has one record for each product. State three fields that would be stored in each record.
parts.answer: Barcode number; product description; price.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: barcode/product code; description/name; price; number in stock; reorder level; reorder quantity; supplier ID; shelf/aisle location; weight/size.

parts.label: a
parts.text: At a point-of-sale (POS) terminal in a pharmacy, the cashier scans the barcode on a packet of plasters. Describe how the name and price of the item appear on the screen and on the receipt.
parts.answer: The barcode reader reads the barcode number and sends it to the computer. The number is used to search the stock file for the matching record. The description and price are taken from that record and sent to the POS screen and printed on the receipt.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: barcode number read / sent to computer; matching record searched/found in database using the code; description and price retrieved and displayed/printed (and added to total).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two benefits to a shop of accepting card payments through an EFTPOS terminal rather than only cash.
parts.answer: Less cash on the premises, so less risk of theft; money goes directly into the shop's bank account.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: less cash to store/risk of theft; no need to bank cash; customers can spend more than the cash they carry; faster transactions/no change; fewer counting errors; automatic records of sales.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two methods a customer can use to pay for goods bought from an online shop.
parts.answer: Debit/credit card; mobile wallet.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: credit card; debit card; mobile wallet/digital wallet; online bank transfer; cash on delivery; PayPal-type payment service; gift card/voucher.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one way the customer can check that the shop's website is secure before entering card details.
parts.answer: The web address starts with https (and the browser shows a padlock).
parts.working: B1: https / padlock symbol / valid digital certificate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A supermarket in Islamabad uses an automatic stock control system linked to its checkouts. Describe how the stock level of an item is kept up to date and how new stock is ordered.
parts.answer: The bar code on the item is scanned at the checkout; the product code is used to search the stock database for the item's record; the price and description are sent back to the checkout; the stock level in the record is reduced by one (by the number sold); the new stock level is compared with the reorder level; if it is at or below the reorder level, an order is automatically sent to the supplier/flag set; the record is flagged as 'on order' so it is not reordered again; when new stock arrives, the stock level is increased.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five valid points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps of a chip and PIN payment at a supermarket checkout, from inserting the card to the payment being completed.
parts.answer: The customer inserts the card into the reader, which reads the chip. The customer checks the amount and enters the PIN. The PIN is checked against the data on the chip. The terminal contacts the customer's bank to check the card is valid and not reported stolen, and that there are enough funds. If authorised, the money is deducted from the customer's account and transferred to the shop's account, and a receipt is printed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: card inserted / chip read; amount confirmed; PIN entered; PIN compared with chip; bank contacted; checks card valid/not stolen/expiry; checks funds/credit limit; authorisation code returned; account debited / shop credited; receipt printed / card removed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A customer in Lahore pays for coffee by holding her smartphone near the card reader. Describe how the payment is made using near field communication (NFC).
parts.answer: She unlocks the phone (fingerprint/face/PIN) and holds it within a few centimetres of the reader; the payment data is sent by NFC radio signal to the reader, which sends it to the bank for authorisation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: phone held very close to the reader / NFC chip in phone transmits data by short-range radio; data sent to bank for authorisation / payment confirmed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why paying by phone in this way can be more secure than using a contactless card.
parts.answer: The phone must be unlocked using biometrics or a PIN before paying, so a thief cannot use it easily; the phone sends a one-time token instead of the real card number.
parts.working: 1 mark each: user authentication on phone (biometric/PIN); tokenisation / real card number not sent; card details not visible to others.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An online electronics shop recommends products to customers, for example 'Customers who bought this phone also bought …'. Explain how the shop uses customer data to produce these recommendations.
parts.answer: The shop stores each customer's browsing history and past purchases in a database. Software analyses this data across many customers to find products that are often bought together or that are similar to items the customer viewed. These products are shown when the customer next visits.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: data collected (past purchases/browsing/searches/cookies); data analysed / patterns found across customers; matching items shown / targeted adverts or emails.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one concern customers may have about this.
parts.answer: Their personal data may be shared with or sold to other companies without permission.
parts.working: B1: privacy; data shared/sold; data could be hacked; feeling of being tracked; pressure to overspend.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens from the moment a customer chooses a phone on an online shop's website until it is delivered.
parts.answer: The customer adds the phone to the basket and goes to the checkout. They log in or enter name, address and contact details, choose delivery and enter payment details. The payment is authorised by the bank and the order is confirmed by email with an order number. The shop's stock level is reduced and the order is sent to the warehouse to be packed and dispatched. The customer can track the parcel online until it is delivered.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: add to basket; checkout/log in or register; delivery address/method chosen; payment details entered/authorised; confirmation email/order number; stock database updated; order picked/packed/dispatched; tracking number/updates; delivery (signature/proof).

parts.label: a
parts.text: The owner of a clothing shop in Hyderabad is closing her shop and selling only through her own online store. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages to the owner.
parts.answer: Advantages: no rent or shop running costs (electricity, staff); can sell to customers across the country/abroad 24/7; fewer staff needed; stock can be kept in a cheaper warehouse; customer data collected for targeted marketing; can update prices/offers instantly. Disadvantages: cost of building and maintaining a secure website; must pay for delivery/packaging and handle returns; loses passing customers who browse in person; customers cannot try clothes on so more returns; risk of hacking/fraud; staff may need retraining or lose jobs; strong competition from large online sellers. Conclusion.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side only. 1 mark per expanded point; 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A shop's stock control system has these values for one brand of rice:
Current stock: 240 bags
Average sales: 35 bags per day
Reorder level: 80 bags
Delivery time from supplier: 3 days
Calculate after how many whole days the stock first falls to or below the reorder level, and the stock at that time.
parts.answer: After 5 days; 65 bags.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The system orders new stock at that point. Explain, using a calculation, why the shop will run out before the delivery arrives, and suggest a better reorder level.
parts.answer: During the 3-day delivery time the shop sells 35 × 3 = 105 bags, but only 65 are left, so it runs out on the second day. The reorder level should be at least 105 bags (e.g. about 120 to allow a safety margin).
parts.working: M1: 35 × 3 = 105 bags sold during delivery time; A1: 105 > 65 so stock runs out; B1: new reorder level ≥ 105 (any sensible value 105–140 with reason).

parts.label: a
parts.text: More people in Lahore now buy clothes, groceries and electronics online. Evaluate the effects of this on society.
parts.answer: Positive: people save time and travel costs, can shop at any time, compare prices easily, and people with disabilities or in remote areas get access to more goods; new jobs are created in delivery and warehouses. Negative: some high-street shops close, reducing jobs for shop staff and making town centres less busy; more delivery vans add to traffic and pollution; people may become less active or socially isolated; people without internet or bank cards are excluded; more risk of online fraud. Overall online shopping brings convenience but its costs fall on shop workers and those who are not online.
parts.working: Max 6, positive and negative effects plus a judgement. Positive: convenience 24/7; price comparison; access for disabled/remote; delivery/warehouse jobs; less travel by shoppers. Negative: shop closures/job losses; empty town centres; isolation/less exercise; digital divide/unbanked excluded; fraud/hacking; packaging waste/delivery traffic.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare paying in a shop with a chip and PIN card and paying with a contactless card.
parts.answer: Both use a card linked to the customer's bank account, both need the terminal to contact the bank for authorisation, and both print a receipt. Chip and PIN needs the card inserted and a PIN entered, so it is slower but more secure, because a thief needs the PIN. Contactless only needs the card held near the reader, so it is quicker, but it is limited to small amounts and a stolen card can be used without a PIN up to the limit. Contactless also avoids touching the keypad.
parts.working: Max 5; at least one similarity. Similarities: linked to bank account; bank authorisation; card details encrypted; receipt. Differences: insert vs tap; PIN vs no PIN (for small amounts); speed; spending limit for contactless; security if stolen; risk of skimming with contactless reader; hygiene.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When paying online, a customer is sent a one-time passcode (OTP) by SMS which must be entered on the payment page. Describe how this system works and explain why it reduces fraud.
parts.answer: After the card details are entered, the bank generates a random code that is valid only once and for a short time, and sends it to the phone number registered to the account. The customer types it into the payment page and the bank checks it matches before authorising. A criminal who has stolen only the card details does not have the customer's phone, so cannot complete the payment.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: bank generates code; sent to registered phone; valid once / short time; entered and checked before authorisation; fraudster needs the phone as well as card details (two-factor authentication).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one weakness of this method.
parts.answer: If the phone is stolen or the SIM is swapped by a criminal, the code can be received by the criminal.
parts.working: B1: SIM-swap / stolen phone; no signal delays payment; customer tricked into sharing code (phishing call).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student reads a history textbook as an eBook on a tablet. Give two features of the eBook that are not available in the printed book.
parts.answer: Any two: words can be searched; text size can be changed; hyperlinks to other pages/websites/glossary; embedded video/audio/animations; built-in dictionary; bookmarks and notes that can be removed/edited easily; can be read aloud by text-to-speech; can be read in the dark (backlit).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of the eBook compared with the printed book.
parts.answer: e.g. needs a charged device; screen can cause eye strain; device is expensive/can be stolen or damaged; may be harder to share or lend.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school in Hyderabad is preparing for its open day. Give two features of a multimedia presentation shown on a screen that make it more effective than a printed poster.
parts.answer: It can include video and sound; it can have animations and transitions that catch attention.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: video; sound/narration/music; animation/transitions; many slides of information; hyperlinks/interactivity; can loop automatically; easily updated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of using the multimedia presentation.
parts.answer: It needs a screen/projector and power, so it is more expensive and can only be seen in one place.
parts.working: B1: needs equipment/power; cost; technical failure; visitors cannot take it away; too much information/distracting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by media streaming.
parts.answer: Playing audio or video over the internet as it is received, without first downloading the whole file.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of media streaming.
parts.answer: Watching a cricket match live online; listening to an online radio station.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: live sports/events; video-sharing sites; film/TV services; online radio; music streaming; podcasts played online; live lectures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Apart from making ordinary phone calls, give three ways a smartphone can be used to communicate.
parts.answer: Sending SMS text messages; making video calls; making voice calls over the internet (VoIP).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: SMS/text messages; VoIP calls; video calling; email; instant messaging apps; social media; accessing websites/internet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A residents' association sends its monthly newsletter by email but some members want a printed copy. Give two advantages of a printed newsletter.
parts.answer: Members without internet or email can read it; it can be pinned up on a notice board.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: no device/internet needed; easy for older people; can be kept/pinned up/passed on; no risk of being treated as spam or deleted; no viruses; easier to read for some people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A publisher in Lahore is deciding whether to publish its monthly science magazine as an ePublication instead of on paper. Describe two advantages and two disadvantages to the publisher of the ePublication.
parts.answer: Advantages: no printing, paper or distribution costs; can reach readers worldwide instantly; can include video, animations and hyperlinks; can be updated/corrected after release; data on readers can be collected. Disadvantages: readers without devices or internet access are lost; easier to copy and share illegally; cost of developing for different devices/formats; some readers prefer paper so sales may fall; advertisers may pay less.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two advantages and two disadvantages (expanded).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by buffering when a video is streamed.
parts.answer: Part of the video is downloaded and stored in memory before and while it plays, so playback can continue smoothly if the data arrives unevenly.
parts.working: B1: data stored temporarily in a buffer/memory ahead of playing; B1: allows smooth playback / covers short delays.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student's streamed video keeps pausing. Give one reason why.
parts.answer: The internet connection is too slow so the buffer empties faster than it fills.
parts.working: B1: low bandwidth/slow connection; many users sharing the network; weak Wi-Fi signal; server overloaded; video quality too high for the connection.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A family in Quetta often calls relatives in Dubai. Describe the advantages and disadvantages of using VoIP rather than ordinary international phone calls.
parts.answer: Advantages: calls are free or very cheap because they use the internet; video can be added. Disadvantages: quality depends on the internet connection, so calls may drop or have echo/delays; both people need a device, an app and internet access.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 3 from one side: cheap/free; video; group calls; can share files/messages during call. Disadvantages: needs good internet connection; quality issues/lag/drops; both need app/device; security risks (hacking/eavesdropping); emergency calls may not be possible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A film is streamed in high definition at 5 megabits per second (Mbps). The film is 90 minutes long. Calculate the amount of data used in megabytes (MB). Assume 1 MB = 8 megabits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a person with a small monthly mobile data allowance might download the film over home Wi-Fi before a journey rather than stream it on mobile data.
parts.answer: Streaming would use about 3.4 GB of the mobile allowance; downloading on Wi-Fi uses no mobile data and the film can be watched without signal.
parts.working: B1: saves mobile data / no signal needed on journey.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A community group in Hunza is advertising a spring festival with a printed poster and a website. Describe two features the poster should have and two features the website could have that the poster cannot.
parts.answer: Poster: a large clear heading with the festival name; date, time and venue. Website: a video of last year's festival; a hyperlink to an online booking or map page.
parts.working: 1 mark each, 2 for poster: heading/title; date/time/venue; eye-catching images/colours; contact details; short text readable from a distance. 2 for website: video/sound; hyperlinks; online booking/forms; interactive map; regular updates/news; photo gallery with many images; share on social media.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A provincial health department wants to make people aware of a new polio vaccination drive. It is considering a website, printed posters and a social media campaign. Evaluate the use of these three methods for this purpose.
parts.answer: Website: can hold detailed information, maps of centres and video; can be updated; but people must know about it and have internet access. Posters: seen by everyone passing, including people without internet or phones; good in rural areas/clinics; but limited information, cannot be updated once printed, cost of printing and distribution, can be damaged. Social media: reaches many people quickly, especially young people; can be shared and targeted to areas; cheap; interactive (questions answered); but misinformation and negative comments can spread; does not reach people without smartphones; older people may not use it. Reasoned conclusion, e.g. a combination is best.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid evaluative point (benefit or drawback) about the methods, up to 5; 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion. Max 4 if only one method discussed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The authorities in Karachi want to warn residents about an approaching heatwave. Evaluate sending SMS text messages to all phones compared with posting warnings on social media.
parts.answer: SMS reaches nearly all mobile phones, including basic phones without internet, and arrives immediately with an alert, so it reaches older and poorer residents; but messages are short with no images or links, and cost money to send to millions. Social media is free, allows images, videos and updates, and can be shared widely, but only reaches people who use those platforms and follow the account; false information and rumours can also spread. Conclusion: SMS is better for reaching everyone quickly, with social media used for extra detail and updates.
parts.working: Max 6; both methods and a judgement. SMS: reaches basic phones/no internet needed; immediate notification; reaches almost everyone; short text only; cost; may be ignored as spam. Social media: free; images/video/links; shareable; updates/two-way; needs internet/smartphone/account; misinformation; algorithm may hide posts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A science teacher is making a multimedia presentation to explain how volcanoes erupt to a class of 12-year-olds. Explain how she could use features of presentation software to make it effective, and discuss any drawbacks.
parts.answer: She could use short video clips of real eruptions and animations that show magma rising step by step, with narration so pupils can listen and watch; hyperlinks to a quiz or a further-information slide; consistent master slides with large clear text and images. Drawbacks: too many animations or sound effects can distract; large videos may not play on the school computer; it takes time to create; pupils may watch passively; equipment failure would stop the lesson.
parts.working: Max 6; at least 1 drawback for full marks. Features (with explanation): video; animation/build-up; sound/narration; hyperlinks/interactive quiz; master slide/consistent style; large font/contrast for readability; transitions used sparingly. Drawbacks: distracting effects; file size/compatibility; time to make; technical failure; passive learning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A newspaper publishes an eNewspaper as well as its printed edition. Explain how four features of the eNewspaper help readers, including readers with poor eyesight.
parts.answer: Text can be enlarged without losing quality; a text-to-speech feature can read articles aloud; a search function finds articles quickly; stories are updated during the day as news breaks.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four explained features: zoom/adjustable text size; text-to-speech/screen reader; high-contrast/dark mode; search; hyperlinks to related stories; embedded video/audio; live updates; archives of past editions; comment/share.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In many rural areas of Pakistan, people use a smartphone, not a laptop, as their only way to access the internet. Explain why, and describe the disadvantages of using a smartphone compared with a laptop for school work.
parts.answer: Smartphones are cheaper than laptops, are portable and use mobile data networks, which reach many villages without fixed broadband; they do not need a mains electricity supply all the time. However, the small screen makes reading and editing long documents difficult, typing on a touch screen is slow, many school programs (e.g. full spreadsheet or database software) are not available or are limited, mobile data can be expensive and the battery runs down quickly.
parts.working: Max 5; max 2 for reasons. Reasons: cheaper; mobile network coverage where no broadband; portable; battery-powered; also used as a phone. Disadvantages: small screen; slow touch-screen typing; limited software/features; expensive mobile data; limited storage; battery life; harder to print.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A customer inserts her bank card into an ATM and asks to withdraw Rs 10 000. Describe the processing that takes place after she has entered her PIN.
parts.answer: The PIN entered is compared with the PIN stored on the card chip/bank's records; if it is wrong the customer is asked to try again (card retained after three failed attempts); the bank's computer is contacted to check that the card is valid/not stolen; the account balance is checked to see that there are enough funds; the daily withdrawal limit is checked; if all checks are passed, the cash is dispensed and the account is debited by Rs 10 000; a receipt may be printed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four processing steps. Do not credit descriptions of input or output devices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Apart from withdrawing cash, state three services that are available at many ATMs.
parts.answer: Checking the account balance; printing a mini statement; changing the PIN.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: check balance; mini statement; change PIN; transfer funds between accounts; pay bills; mobile phone top-up; deposit cash or cheques (some ATMs); order cheque book/statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by electronic funds transfer (EFT).
parts.answer: Moving money from one bank account to another electronically, without cash or cheques changing hands.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of the use of EFT.
parts.answer: A company paying its employees' salaries; a customer paying an electricity bill online.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: salary payments; bill payments; paying for goods with a debit card; transfers between friends/family; government payments/pensions; paying suppliers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages to an employer of paying staff salaries by EFT instead of in cash.
parts.answer: No need to collect and store large amounts of cash, so less risk of theft; it is quicker, as all payments can be made in one batch.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: less risk of theft/robbery; faster/less staff time; automatic records of payments; fewer counting errors; no need to visit bank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A customer phones her bank's automated telephone banking service. Give two security checks the system could use before she can make a payment.
parts.answer: Entering her account number and a telephone PIN using the keypad; answering security questions or certain characters of a password.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: account/card number; PIN entered on keypad; selected digits/characters of a passcode; security questions (e.g. date of birth); voice recognition; one-time code sent to her mobile.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage of telephone banking over visiting a branch.
parts.answer: It can be used from home at any time, without travelling.
parts.working: B1: no travel; available 24 hours; no queues; usable without internet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many shops in Pakistan now accept contactless card payments. Describe how a contactless payment is made.
parts.answer: The customer holds the card/phone close to the reader (within a few centimetres); data is transmitted wirelessly using RFID/NFC; payment is authorised (usually without a PIN for small amounts) and the amount is deducted from the account.
parts.working: 1 mark: card held near reader. 1 mark: RFID/NFC wireless transfer and payment authorised.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage to the customer of contactless payments.
parts.answer: Advantage: faster at the checkout; no need to enter a PIN; no need to carry cash. Disadvantage: a stolen card can be used for small payments without a PIN; easy to spend more than intended; risk of the card being read by a hidden reader (skimming).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Mr Raza pays a supplier Rs 75 000 by cheque. Describe how the cheque is cleared.
parts.answer: The supplier deposits the cheque at their bank. The cheque is scanned and the bank code, account number and cheque number printed in magnetic ink are read (MICR). The image and data are sent electronically to a clearing centre, which passes them to Mr Raza's bank.
