His bank checks the signature, that the cheque is valid and dated correctly, and that there are enough funds. If everything is correct the money is taken from his account and paid into the supplier's account; if not, the cheque is returned unpaid (bounces).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five of: cheque deposited at payee's bank; scanned / MICR reads bank code, account number and cheque number; data/image sent to clearing centre; passed to payer's (drawer's) bank; checks signature/date/validity; checks funds; payer's account debited; payee's account credited; cheque bounced if insufficient funds; takes a day or more.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the processing that takes place when a customer uses internet banking to pay a mobile phone bill of Rs 2 450.
parts.answer: The customer logs in with a user ID and password and a one-time code. They select bill payment, choose the phone company and enter the bill reference and amount. The bank checks the account has at least Rs 2 450 available. If so, the account is debited, the phone company's account is credited, the balance is updated and a confirmation/receipt is shown and sent by email or SMS.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: logs in with authentication (password/OTP/biometric); selects payee/biller and enters reference/amount; bank checks sufficient funds; customer confirms; customer's account debited; company account credited; balance updated; confirmation/transaction ID issued.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When a customer adds a new payee in a banking app, the bank sends a one-time passcode to the customer's registered mobile number. Explain why the bank does this.
parts.answer: Adding a payee lets money be sent to a new account, which is what a criminal would do after stealing login details. The code proves that the person adding the payee also has the customer's phone, so a criminal with only the password cannot do it. This is two-factor authentication.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: new payee is high-risk / used by fraudsters; code sent to registered phone that only customer has; stolen password alone is not enough / two-factor authentication; code valid only once/short time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A customer pays Rs 18 000 for a jacket using a credit card. Describe the checks carried out by the card company's computer before the payment is authorised.
parts.answer: It checks that the card number is valid and the card has not expired; that the card has not been reported lost or stolen; that the PIN or security code is correct; and that the payment will not take the customer over the credit limit. It may also check for unusual spending patterns (fraud detection). If all checks pass, an authorisation code is sent back to the shop's terminal.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: card valid/genuine; expiry date; not reported lost/stolen; PIN/security code correct; credit limit/available funds; unusual activity/fraud pattern; authorisation code returned to terminal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bank is encouraging its customers to use internet banking instead of visiting branches. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages to customers of internet banking.
parts.answer: Advantages: can bank at any time from anywhere; no travel costs or queuing; easy to check balances and statements; transfers and bill payments made instantly; useful for disabled or elderly people who find travel difficult; alerts for transactions. Disadvantages: needs internet access and a device; risk of phishing/pharming/hacking and fraud; less personal service/cannot discuss problems face to face; easy to make a mistake with account numbers; some customers (elderly) lack skills/confidence; branch closures affect those who cannot use internet banking; social isolation. Conclusion.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side only. 1 mark per expanded point; 1 mark for reasoned conclusion. Answers must be about customers, not the bank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: As more customers use internet banking, a bank is closing many of its branches. Evaluate the effects of this on the bank and on its staff.
parts.answer: Bank: saves money on rent, wages, cash handling and security, and can serve customers anywhere at any time; but it must spend money developing and securing its website and apps, becomes a target for cyber attacks and may have to repay fraud losses, and may lose customers who want personal service. Staff: some lose their jobs or must travel to branches further away; others are retrained to work in call centres, IT support or online services and gain new skills; there is stress and uncertainty about jobs. Overall the bank gains financially, but much of the cost falls on its branch staff, so retraining and redeployment are important.
parts.working: Max 6; effects on both the bank and staff, plus a judgement. Bank: lower costs (premises, wages, security); 24/7 service/wider reach; development and security costs; hacking/fraud and reputation risk; loss of customers wanting face-to-face service; need for IT staff. Staff: redundancy; redeployment/longer travel; retraining/new skills; deskilling; stress/uncertainty. 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare telephone banking with internet banking.
parts.answer: Both let customers manage their accounts from home at any time without visiting a branch, both need security checks such as PINs or passcodes, and both let customers pay bills and transfer money. Telephone banking only needs a phone, so it can be used by people with no internet, and a human operator can be asked for help, but menus can be slow and information is only spoken, so it is hard to see a full statement. Internet banking shows statements and transactions on screen, is quicker for several payments and lets customers download records, but needs an internet connection and device and is a target for phishing and hacking.
parts.working: Max 6; must include a similarity. Similarities: no travel/24-7; security checks; bill payment/transfers; check balance. Differences: phone only vs internet + device; spoken menus/human operator vs visual screens; seeing/downloading statements; speed; phishing/hacking risk vs phone fraud/overheard; costs of calls; accessibility for visually impaired (phone) vs hearing impaired (internet). Lists without linking max 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages to a bank of providing ATMs.
parts.answer: Advantages: customers can get cash 24 hours a day without the bank employing extra staff; fewer customers queue in branches, so fewer cashiers are needed; ATMs can be placed in shopping centres and petrol stations, reaching more customers; transactions are recorded automatically. Disadvantages: ATMs are expensive to buy, install and maintain; they must be refilled with cash securely; they can be targeted by skimming devices or physical attack, and the bank may have to repay customers; breakdowns cause complaints. Overall ATMs save the bank money in the long run because they reduce staff costs.
parts.working: Max 6, both sides needed. Advantages: 24/7 service; fewer staff/lower wage costs; less queueing in branches; more locations; automatic records; can sell services (e.g. top-up). Disadvantages: purchase/installation/maintenance cost; cash refilling/security transport; skimming/fraud/vandalism; breakdowns/out of cash; network costs. Conclusion for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why money paid by cheque takes longer to reach the payee's account than money sent by EFT.
parts.answer: A cheque is a paper document that must be physically deposited at a bank and then scanned and sent through a clearing centre to the payer's bank, which checks the signature and funds; this is done in batches, often only once or twice a day. EFT is entirely electronic: the payment instruction is checked and processed immediately, so the money can arrive within seconds.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: cheque must be physically deposited/scanned; passes through clearing centre/batch processing; payer's bank must check signature/funds before paying; EFT processed electronically in (near) real time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why some businesses still accept cheques.
parts.answer: Some customers do not use online banking, and a cheque gives a written record for large payments.
parts.working: B1: customers without online banking; paper record/signature; post-dated cheques for future payments; large payments over transfer limits.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Give one suitable use for each of these recognition systems.
(i) Radio frequency identification (RFID)
(ii) Near field communication (NFC)
(iii) Face recognition
(iv) Fingerprint recognition
parts.answer: (i) Tracking luggage at an airport (ii) Paying at a shop terminal with a smartphone (iii) Checking passengers at airport e-gates (iv) Staff clocking in at work
parts.working: 1 mark each. (i) tracking stock/luggage/animals/vehicles, library books, toll tags, contactless cards; (ii) contactless/phone payments, sharing data between phones, access cards; (iii) e-gates/border control, unlocking phones/laptops, identifying people in crowds; (iv) phone/laptop login, clocking in, door access, border control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three biometric methods that can be used to identify a person.
parts.answer: Fingerprint; face recognition; iris recognition.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: fingerprint; face; iris; retina; voice; hand geometry/palm vein; signature dynamics.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school uses optical mark recognition to mark multiple-choice tests. Give two advantages of using OMR rather than teachers marking the answer sheets.
parts.answer: Much faster; no human marking errors.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: faster; more accurate/no fatigue errors; teachers free for other work; results stored automatically/can be analysed; large numbers processed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of OMR.
parts.answer: Sheets with stray marks, light pencil or two boxes filled may be read wrongly or rejected.
parts.working: B1: misread forms (stray/faint marks, folds); special forms/equipment cost; only suitable for tick/shade answers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A lawyer's office in Multan scans old typed documents and uses OCR software. State why OCR is used.
parts.answer: To convert the scanned image of the text into editable, searchable text.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one problem that may occur when OCR is used on these documents.
parts.answer: Faded or smudged characters may be recognised wrongly, so the text must be proofread.
parts.working: B1: misread characters (faded, handwriting, unusual fonts); layout/tables lost; needs proofreading.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Each table in a restaurant in Islamabad has a QR code. Describe how a customer uses the QR code to see the menu.
parts.answer: The customer opens the camera or a QR app on a smartphone and points it at the code. The app decodes the QR code, which contains a web address (URL). The phone opens that website, which shows the menu.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: phone camera/app scans code; code decoded/contains URL; browser opens menu web page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between optical mark recognition (OMR) and optical character recognition (OCR), giving a suitable use for each.
parts.answer: OMR detects marks (shaded boxes/lines) in set positions on a pre-printed form, e.g. multiple-choice exam answer sheets, lottery tickets, school registers. OCR reads printed or handwritten characters from a scanned image and converts them into text that can be edited/stored, e.g. reading passports at airports, digitising printed documents, number plate recognition.
parts.working: 1 mark: OMR description. 1 mark: OMR use. 1 mark: OCR description. 1 mark: OCR use.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An airport uses RFID tags on checked-in bags. Describe how RFID is used to track a bag from check-in to the aircraft.
parts.answer: At check-in an RFID tag containing a unique ID is attached to the bag and linked to the passenger's flight in the database. As the bag travels on conveyors, RFID readers send radio waves that power the tag; the tag transmits its ID. Each reader records the bag's location and time and the system directs the bag to the correct loading area, and an alert is raised if a bag goes the wrong way.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: tag with unique ID attached; ID linked to passenger/flight in database; readers at points along the route; radio waves / tag transmits ID (no line of sight needed); location/time recorded; bag routed automatically; alert if misrouted / can be traced if lost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare fingerprint recognition with iris recognition as a way of checking employees entering a research laboratory.
parts.answer: Both are biometric methods that compare a scan with stored data and cannot be forgotten or easily shared. Fingerprint scanners are cheaper and quick, but readings can fail if fingers are dirty, wet or cut, and the scanner is touched by everyone. Iris recognition is more accurate and contactless, but the equipment is more expensive and some people find having their eye scanned uncomfortable.
parts.working: Max 4; must include a similarity. Similarities: both biometric/unique; data compared with stored template; cannot be lost/forgotten. Differences: cost; accuracy/false rejection; contact vs contactless (hygiene); effect of dirt/injury vs glasses/lighting; user acceptance; speed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some airports have automatic e-gates for passengers with biometric passports. Describe how face recognition is used at an e-gate.
parts.answer: The passenger places the passport on a reader, which reads the photograph and data stored on the passport's chip. A camera in the gate takes an image of the passenger's face. Software measures features such as the distance between the eyes and the shape of the nose and compares them with the chip photograph. If they match, and the passenger is not on a watch list, the gate opens; if not, an officer is alerted.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: passport chip read (RFID/NFC) or page scanned; stored photo retrieved; camera captures live face; features measured / converted to data; compared with stored image; checks against databases/watch lists; gate opens if match; officer called if no match.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car park uses automatic number plate recognition (ANPR). Give three reasons why the system may fail to read a number plate correctly.
parts.answer: The plate is dirty or damaged; the plate uses a non-standard font or decoration; poor lighting or heavy rain.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: dirty/muddy/damaged plate; non-standard font/spacing/decoration; poor light/glare/weather; camera angle/car moving fast; plate obscured (towbar, bike rack); similar characters confused (O/0, B/8); camera fault.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the car park should do when the system cannot read a plate.
parts.answer: Let an attendant check the image and enter the number manually (or issue a paper ticket).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shopping mall car park in Karachi uses automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) to record when cars enter and leave. Describe how ANPR is used when a car arrives at the entrance barrier.
parts.answer: A sensor (e.g. pressure/infrared) detects the car arriving; a camera captures an image of the front of the car; software locates the number plate in the image (and adjusts brightness/contrast); OCR is used to identify the individual characters; the registration number is stored in a database with the date and time of entry; the barrier is raised (actuator) and an LED display may show a welcome message; when the car leaves, the plate is read again and the time difference used to calculate the charge.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five valid steps in sequence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A secondary school is considering using fingerprint scanners for daily attendance instead of paper registers. Discuss the benefits and drawbacks.
parts.answer: Benefits: attendance is recorded instantly and accurately and stored on the school system; students cannot sign in for absent friends; teachers save lesson time; parents can be sent automatic alerts; reports are easy to produce. Drawbacks: scanners are expensive to buy and maintain; queues may form at the start of the day; dirty or injured fingers may not be read; storing children's biometric data raises privacy concerns and needs parental consent and strong security; if the system fails, a backup is needed. Conclusion: useful in a large school if data is protected and parents agree.
parts.working: Max 6; both sides and conclusion. Benefits: accurate/instant; prevents proxy sign-in; saves teacher time; automatic alerts/reports; data linked to other systems. Drawbacks: cost; queues; misreads; privacy/data protection/consent; security breach of biometric data cannot be 'reset'; system failure; some students/parents object.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An examinations office must mark 9 600 multiple-choice answer sheets. An OMR scanner processes 1 200 sheets per hour. Calculate how many hours the scanner needs.
parts.answer: 8 hours

parts.label: b
parts.text: A teacher can mark 25 sheets per hour by hand. Calculate the total teacher-hours needed, and the number of hours each teacher would work if the marking were shared equally between 12 teachers.
parts.answer: 384 teacher-hours; 32 hours each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain two reasons, other than speed, why the office might still check a sample of sheets by hand.
parts.answer: Some marks may be faint or crossed out and read wrongly by the scanner; checking a sample confirms the answer key and the scanner settings are correct.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: misreads of faint/extra marks; wrong answer key loaded; scanner calibration fault; damaged sheets rejected; quality assurance/fairness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some cities use cameras with face recognition in public places. Explain the privacy concerns this raises.
parts.answer: People are identified and tracked without their knowledge or consent; records of where people go are stored and could be misused or shared; innocent people may be wrongly matched and stopped.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: tracking without consent; data stored/profiles built; misuse by authorities/companies; data could be hacked; wrong matches/bias; chilling effect on free movement or protests.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a theft of stored biometric data is more serious than a theft of passwords.
parts.answer: A password can be changed after it is stolen, but a person cannot change their face or fingerprints, so the stolen data could be misused for the rest of their life.
parts.working: B1: biometrics cannot be changed/reset; B1: risk lasts permanently / used to impersonate on other systems.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bank is planning to let customers log in to its telephone banking service using voice recognition instead of a PIN. Evaluate this plan.
parts.answer: Voice recognition is convenient: customers just speak and do not need to remember a PIN, and it is harder to steal a voice than to watch someone enter a PIN. It suits customers with poor eyesight. However, a cold, background noise or a poor line can stop a genuine customer being recognised; a recording or AI-generated copy of the voice might be used to fool the system; customers must enrol their voice first, and some may worry about storage of their voice print. Conclusion: it is a useful extra factor, but should be combined with another check (such as a one-time code) for high-value transactions.
parts.working: Max 6; both sides and a conclusion. Benefits: no PIN to remember/forget; quicker; unique to user; helpful for visually impaired; cannot be 'shoulder-surfed'. Drawbacks: illness/noise/poor line causes false rejection; recordings/deepfakes; enrolment needed; privacy of stored voice print; cost of system. Conclusion e.g. use with second factor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: City planners in Lahore use a computer model to test the effect of new traffic lights at a busy junction before installing them. Give three advantages of using a computer model.
parts.answer: Any three: cheaper than building/testing the real junction; safer — no risk of accidents to real drivers; many different 'what if' scenarios/timings can be tried quickly; time can be speeded up so years of traffic can be simulated quickly; no disruption to real traffic; easy to change the variables and compare results.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why the results of the model might not match what happens in reality.
parts.answer: The model is only as good as the data and rules used — real drivers' behaviour, accidents, weather or events may not be included/may be unpredictable.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a computer model.
parts.answer: A computer representation of a real system or situation, using data and rules/formulas, which can be used to predict what will happen.
parts.working: B1: mathematical/computer representation of a real-life system used to test or predict.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of applications that use computer models.
parts.answer: Weather forecasting; designing a bridge.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: weather forecasting; personal finance/budgets; bridge or building design; flood water management; traffic management; flight/driving simulators; climate change; population or disease spread; business planning.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Ayesha uses a spreadsheet model of her monthly budget.
Income: Rs 85 000
Rent: Rs 30 000
Food: Rs 22 500
Transport: Rs 9 800
Bills: Rs 7 450
Savings = Income − (Rent + Food + Transport + Bills)
Calculate her monthly savings.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Her landlord increases the rent by 10%. Use the model to calculate her new monthly savings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'what if' question when using a computer model.
parts.answer: Changing one or more input values to see the effect on the results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one 'what if' question that a city could ask using a traffic management model.
parts.answer: What if the green light on the main road lasted 20 seconds longer?
parts.working: B1: any sensible change of input, e.g. adding a lane, closing a road, changing light timings, adding a flyover, increasing traffic by 20%.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A weather forecasting model uses data collected from weather stations, balloons and satellites. Name three types of data that are input to the model.
parts.answer: Air temperature; air pressure; wind speed and direction.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: temperature; air pressure; humidity; wind speed; wind direction; rainfall; cloud cover (satellite images); sea temperature; sunlight.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Architects in Islamabad use a computer model when designing a new 20-storey office building. State two things they could test using the model.
parts.answer: How the building would behave in an earthquake; how quickly people could leave in a fire.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: earthquake resistance; wind loads/strong winds; weight/load the structure can bear; fire evacuation routes/times; heating/cooling and energy use; lift traffic; sunlight and shadows; cost of materials.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a computer weather model produces a forecast for the next three days.
parts.answer: Data such as temperature, pressure, humidity and wind are collected automatically from sensors, weather stations, balloons and satellites. The data is input into the model, which uses mathematical rules about how the atmosphere behaves. A very powerful computer (supercomputer) runs the calculations for many points over the area, step by step into the future, and compares patterns with past weather. The outputs are turned into forecasts, maps and warnings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: data collected from sensors/stations/satellites/balloons; data input regularly/automatically; formulas/rules of atmospheric physics; run on supercomputer; calculated for grid points / time steps; compared with historical data/patterns; output maps/charts/forecasts/warnings; run many times with slightly different data to give probabilities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A savings model in a spreadsheet shows that Rs 200 000 is invested at 8% interest per year, with the interest added to the balance at the end of each year. Calculate the balance after 3 years. Give your answer to the nearest rupee.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a spreadsheet is suitable for creating this kind of model.
parts.answer: Formulas recalculate automatically when an input such as the interest rate is changed, so many 'what if' scenarios can be tried quickly, and the results can be shown in charts.
parts.working: B1: automatic recalculation when inputs change / what-if; B1: formulas can be replicated for many years / charts/graphs / goal seek.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A traffic management model is used to decide the best timings for the lights at a busy roundabout in Lahore. Describe the data and rules that are put into the model and how the results are used.
parts.answer: Data: the number of vehicles arriving on each road at different times of day (counted by sensors or cameras), vehicle speeds, number of lanes and pedestrian crossings. Rules: how long each light stays green, how vehicles move and queue. The model is run with different timings; the queue lengths and waiting times are output and compared, and the timing that gives the shortest overall waiting time is chosen for the real lights.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: traffic counts/flow data by time of day; road layout/lanes/speeds; pedestrian data; rules for light sequences/timings; vehicle behaviour rules; model run with different timings; outputs queue length/waiting time/journey time; best option chosen / tested before installing.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Airlines train pilots on flight simulators, which are computer models of real aircraft. Explain why flight simulators are used for training.
parts.answer: Dangerous situations such as engine failure or bad weather can be practised safely without risk to life or aircraft. Training is cheaper because no fuel is used and real aircraft are not taken out of service. Scenarios can be repeated many times and at any time of day, and the instructor can pause and replay to review mistakes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: practise dangerous situations safely; no risk to life/aircraft; cheaper (fuel, wear, aircraft time); situations can be repeated; any weather/airport/time can be created; can pause/replay/record performance; available whenever needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The government uses a computer model to predict flooding along the River Indus during the monsoon. Describe how the model could be used to help plan for floods.
parts.answer: Data such as rainfall, river levels, ground height, dam releases and past floods are entered; 'what if' questions are asked, e.g. what if rainfall is 30% above average; the model predicts which areas will flood and when; planners can use the predictions to decide where to build embankments, when to warn and evacuate people and where to place relief supplies.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three valid points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the predictions of a flood model may be inaccurate.
parts.answer: Any two: the model is a simplification of reality; input data may be incomplete or inaccurate (e.g. faulty sensors, rainfall forecasts); unexpected events such as embankment failure may not be included; the rules/formulas may be based on past events that do not represent the future (e.g. climate change).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A small business in Sialkot sells footballs. Its spreadsheet model uses these values:
Selling price per ball: Rs 450
Cost to make one ball: Rs 280
Fixed costs per month: Rs 68 000
Break-even number of balls = Fixed costs ÷ (Selling price − Cost per ball)
Calculate the break-even number of balls per month.
parts.answer: 400 balls

parts.label: b
parts.text: The owner asks 'What if the selling price increases by 10%?' Calculate the new break-even number of balls, rounded up to a whole ball.
parts.answer: 317 balls
parts.working: M1: new price 495, margin 495 − 280 = 215; A1: 68 000 ÷ 215 = 316.3 → 317 (round up because part of a ball cannot be sold).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the real number of balls needed to break even might differ from the model's answer.
parts.answer: The model assumes costs and price stay fixed; in reality a higher price may reduce sales, or costs may change.
parts.working: B1: assumptions in model; costs/prices change; demand changes; other costs not included.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Engineers are designing a new spillway for a dam on the River Swat. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using a computer model instead of building a physical scale model to test the design.
parts.answer: Advantages: a computer model is usually cheaper and quicker to change, so many designs and 'what if' flood levels can be tested; extreme floods can be simulated that would be impossible to create; results can be recorded and shown as graphs and animations; there is no risk. Disadvantages: the model is only as accurate as its data and rules, so unknown factors (debris, erosion, unusual rock) may be missed; complex water flow needs expensive software, powerful computers and skilled staff; engineers may trust results too much. Conclusion: use the computer model to narrow down designs, then check the final design with real tests if possible.
parts.working: Max 6; both sides and a conclusion. Advantages: cheaper; faster to modify/test many designs; extreme events simulated; repeatable; safe; detailed outputs/graphs. Disadvantages: simplifications/assumptions; inaccurate data → inaccurate results; costly software/hardware/expertise; cannot include every real-world factor; over-reliance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a weather forecast for tomorrow is usually more accurate than a forecast for ten days ahead.
parts.answer: Small errors or gaps in the starting data grow as the model calculates further into the future, and the atmosphere can change in unpredictable ways, so long-range predictions become less certain.
parts.working: B1: errors in initial data/assumptions grow over time; B1: weather is chaotic/unpredictable changes over longer periods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why weather models are run on supercomputers.
parts.answer: The model must do billions of calculations for many points in the atmosphere and many time steps, and the forecast must be ready quickly enough to be useful.
parts.working: B1: huge number of calculations/data; B1: results needed quickly / in time to issue forecast / run many versions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A family in Karachi wants to use a spreadsheet model to decide whether they can afford to buy a car in monthly instalments over 3 years. Describe how they should set up and use the model.
parts.answer: They enter inputs in separate labelled cells: monthly income, monthly expenses (food, rent, school fees, bills), the car price, deposit, interest rate and number of months. Formulas calculate the monthly instalment and the money left each month (income − expenses − instalment), copied across 36 months with absolute references to the input cells. A chart shows the balance over time. They then change inputs, e.g. a larger deposit, a cheaper car, or a rise in fuel prices, to see whether the money left stays positive, and choose the option that is affordable with some savings left for emergencies.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six of: inputs in labelled cells; expenses listed; car price/deposit/interest/term; formula for instalment; formula for balance each month; replicated for 36 months; absolute references to input cells; running costs (fuel, insurance, maintenance) included; chart/graph; what-if changes to inputs; decision based on balance staying positive / safety margin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Apart from car satellite navigation, give three uses of the Global Positioning System (GPS).
parts.answer: Navigation for ships and aircraft; tracking delivery vans; fitness watches recording running routes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: ships/aircraft navigation; vehicle/fleet tracking; phone maps/ride-hailing; fitness trackers; farming (guided tractors); surveying/mapping; tracking animals or people; geotagging photos; emergency location; timing for networks/banking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A taxi driver in Lahore uses a satnav. Give two advantages and one disadvantage to the driver.
parts.answer: Advantages: does not need to know the route or use a paper map; can be warned about traffic jams and re-routed. Disadvantage: may lose signal in tunnels or between tall buildings.
parts.working: 1 mark each, 2 advantages + 1 disadvantage. Advantages: no map/route knowledge needed; spoken directions so eyes stay on road; traffic updates/re-routing; estimated arrival time; finds addresses/fuel stations; recalculates after a wrong turn. Disadvantages: signal loss; out-of-date maps; may route on unsuitable/closed roads; distraction; over-reliance; cost of updates.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two uses of communication satellites.
parts.answer: Broadcasting television channels; phone and internet connections in remote areas.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: satellite TV/radio broadcasts; phone calls (satellite phones/long-distance); internet access in remote areas; live news reports from anywhere; ship/aircraft communications; emergency communications after disasters.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the minimum number of GPS satellites from which a receiver normally needs signals to work out its position including its height (altitude).
parts.answer: Four

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items of data that each GPS satellite transmits.
parts.answer: Its position in orbit; the exact time the signal was sent.
parts.working: 1 mark each: satellite position/orbit data; precise time from its atomic clock (accept satellite ID).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a satellite navigation (satnav) system in a delivery van works out the van's position and guides the driver.
parts.answer: The satnav receives signals from (at least three/four) GPS satellites; each signal includes the time it was sent; the satnav calculates its distance from each satellite from the time taken for the signal to arrive; the position is found by comparing the distances (trilateration); the position is shown on a stored map; the computer calculates a route to the destination and gives spoken/visual directions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four valid points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a geographic information system (GIS).
parts.answer: A computer system that captures, stores, analyses and displays data linked to geographical locations (maps) in layers.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three uses of a GIS.
parts.answer: Any three: emergency services planning routes/locating incidents; planning new roads, schools or hospitals; mapping flood risk or disease outbreaks; environmental agencies monitoring forests/wildlife; utility companies mapping pipes and cables; police mapping crime hotspots; telecom companies planning mast locations.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A television reporter in Gwadar sends live pictures to a studio in Islamabad through a geostationary satellite 35 786 km above the Earth. Radio signals travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Assuming the signal goes straight up and straight down, calculate the time for the signal to reach the studio. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how this delay affects a live two-way interview between the presenter and the reporter.
parts.answer: Each question and answer is delayed by about a quarter of a second each way, so there are awkward pauses and the two people may talk over each other.
parts.working: B1: noticeable delay/lag (round trip about half a second); B1: pauses / talking over each other / unnatural conversation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A provincial government uses a geographic information system (GIS) to choose a site for a new hospital. Describe how the GIS is used.
parts.answer: Different layers of data are placed on a digital map: population density, existing hospitals, roads, flood-risk areas and land available. Planners query the layers, e.g. 'areas with high population, more than 10 km from a hospital, near a main road, not in a flood zone'. The GIS highlights areas that meet all the conditions and can calculate travel times, so the best site can be chosen.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: data stored in layers on a map; examples of layers (population, roads, existing hospitals, flood zones, land use); layers overlaid/combined; queries/criteria used; matching areas highlighted; distances/travel times calculated; results shown as maps for decision makers; zoom in/out for detail.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three problems that can occur when a driver relies on a satnav.
parts.answer: The map may be out of date, so new roads or one-way changes are missing; the signal can be lost in tunnels or between tall buildings, so directions stop; it may send a large vehicle down a narrow or unsuitable road because it does not know the vehicle size.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three explained: out-of-date maps; signal loss (tunnels, tall buildings, dense trees); unsuitable routes for vehicle; road closures/roadworks not shown; incorrect address entered; driver distracted; over-reliance — driver does not notice signs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After severe monsoon floods in Sindh, relief agencies use images from Earth-observation satellites together with a GIS. Describe how this helps the relief work.
parts.answer: Satellite images taken before and after the floods are compared to show which villages and roads are under water. These images are added as a layer in the GIS with population and road data, so agencies can see how many people are affected and which roads are still usable. This helps them plan where to send boats, food and medical teams and where to set up camps on dry ground, and the maps are updated as the water moves.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: images cover large/inaccessible areas quickly; before/after comparison; flooded areas/roads identified; combined with population/road layers in GIS; estimate number of people affected; plan routes/where to send aid; choose safe camp sites; repeated images track changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare using a GIS on a computer with using a printed paper map for planning new bus routes in a city.
parts.answer: Both show the roads and places in the city and can be used to measure distances. A GIS can show many layers, such as population and existing routes, which can be switched on or off and combined, and it can be updated quickly and zoomed in or out; a paper map shows only fixed information, can become out of date and has a fixed scale, but it needs no computer, software or training and is cheap.
parts.working: Max 4; at least one similarity. Similarities: both show roads/locations; distances measured. Differences: layers/combining data vs fixed; queries/analysis; easy updating vs reprinting; zoom vs fixed scale; cost/equipment/skills; no power needed for paper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A logistics company fits GPS trackers to all its lorries. Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of this for the company and its drivers.
parts.answer: Company benefits: knows where every lorry is, so it can give customers accurate delivery times, plan routes and reduce fuel costs; stolen lorries can be traced; speeding or unauthorised stops can be detected. Driver benefits: help can be sent quickly after a breakdown or accident; routes are planned for them. Drawbacks: the equipment and monitoring software cost money; drivers may feel they are not trusted and their privacy is invaded, which can lower morale; data must be stored securely; signal can be lost in remote areas. Conclusion: benefits for efficiency and safety are high, provided drivers are told how the data is used.
parts.working: Max 6; benefits and drawbacks, both company and drivers mentioned, plus conclusion. Benefits: real-time location; delivery times/customer updates; route/fuel efficiency; theft recovery; monitoring driving behaviour; driver safety/help. Drawbacks: cost; privacy/feeling watched/morale; data security; signal loss; data used unfairly against drivers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Villages in a remote part of Balochistan have no fixed broadband and weak mobile signal. Evaluate the use of satellite internet for the schools and health centres in these villages.
parts.answer: Satellite internet can reach anywhere with a clear view of the sky, so it can be set up quickly without laying cables, giving schools access to online learning and health centres access to remote doctors and records. However, the dishes and monthly fees are expensive, there may be delays (latency) which affect video calls, the service can be disrupted by heavy rain or storms, and it needs a reliable power supply and someone to maintain the equipment. Overall it is the most practical option for remote areas until cables or towers arrive, if costs can be funded.
parts.working: Max 6; both sides and conclusion. Benefits: coverage anywhere; quick installation/no cables; online education resources; telemedicine; communication in emergencies. Drawbacks: equipment and subscription cost; latency (especially geostationary); weather disruption; power needed; maintenance/skills; shared bandwidth may be slow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A GPS satellite is 20 200 km above a receiver. Radio signals travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the time taken for its signal to reach the receiver, in seconds, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The receiver works out its distance from each satellite from the time the signal takes to arrive. Calculate the error in distance caused by a timing error of one microsecond (0.000 001 s).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use your answer to (b) to explain why GPS satellites carry very accurate atomic clocks.
parts.answer: Distance is calculated from time, so even a tiny timing error gives a large position error (300 m per microsecond); very accurate clocks are needed for positions accurate to a few metres.
parts.working: B1: position depends on precise timing; B1: tiny time errors → large distance errors (link to 300 m).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student uses a fitness watch with GPS that records every run and automatically shares the route maps on a public social media profile. Explain the risks of this and how the student could reduce them.
parts.answer: Risks: the route maps show where the student starts and finishes, which is often their home, so strangers could find where they live; regular times and routes show when they are out and the house may be empty; they could be followed or stalked. Reducing risks: make the profile private or share only with friends; hide the start and end of routes (privacy zones); turn off automatic sharing or location for some activities; do not run the same route at the same time every day.
parts.working: Max 5; max 3 for risks. Risks: home location revealed; routine/times revealed (empty home, burglary); stalking/following; data collected by companies. Reductions: private profile/friends only; privacy zones hiding start/end; turn off auto-share/GPS; vary routes/times; check app permissions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Patients in an intensive care unit are monitored by computers with sensors. Name two sensors that could be used.
parts.answer: Any two: temperature sensor; pressure sensor (blood pressure); pulse/heart-rate sensor; oxygen (oximeter) sensor; respiration/breathing sensor.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two advantages of using computers rather than nurses to monitor these patients.
parts.answer: Any two: readings taken continuously, 24/7, without breaks; more accurate readings/no human error; alarms sound immediately if readings go outside safe limits; readings stored and displayed as graphs automatically; nurses are freed to carry out other tasks; several patients monitored at once.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hospital stores an electronic record for each patient. State three items of data stored in a patient record.
parts.answer: Patient's name; date of birth; known allergies.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: unique patient ID; name; address; date of birth; gender; contact number; blood group; allergies; medical history; current medicines; test results; doctor/consultant; appointments; next of kin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two ways in which a pharmacy's computer system helps to prevent mistakes when medicines are given to patients.
parts.answer: It warns if a new medicine reacts dangerously with another medicine the patient is taking; it warns if the patient is allergic to the medicine.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: checks drug interactions; checks allergies from patient record; checks dosage within safe limits; prints clear labels with dose instructions; barcode check of correct medicine; avoids misreading handwritten prescriptions.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Other than making prosthetic limbs, state two uses of 3D printing in medicine.
parts.answer: Making artificial blood vessels; printing customised medicines.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: tissue engineering; artificial blood vessels; customised medicines/tablets; models of organs for planning surgery; dental implants/crowns; hearing aid shells; bone implants; surgical tools/splints.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A clinic in Multan is replacing paper patient files with electronic records. Give two advantages of electronic records.
parts.answer: Records can be found quickly by searching; they can be shared instantly with other doctors who need them.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: faster to search/retrieve; accessible from several places at once; easy to update; legible (no handwriting problems); less storage space; can be backed up; data can be analysed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of electronic records.
parts.answer: They could be hacked and private medical information stolen.
parts.working: B1: hacking/unauthorised access; system failure/power cut prevents access; cost of equipment and training; data loss if no backup; viruses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the type of file that a 3D printer needs to make an object, and describe how the object is built up.
parts.answer: A 3D design (CAD) file of the object; the printer builds the object by adding thin layers of material one on top of another.
parts.working: B1: CAD/3D model file (accept STL); B1: object built layer by layer (additive manufacturing).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A patient brings a prescription to a hospital pharmacy. Describe how the pharmacy system is used when the medicine is dispensed.
parts.answer: The pharmacist enters or scans the prescription and patient ID. The system finds the patient's record and checks the medicine against allergies and other medicines. The medicine's barcode is scanned to confirm it is the right one, a label with the patient's name, dose and instructions is printed, the patient's record is updated with the medicine given, and the stock level is reduced; if it falls below the reorder level, more is ordered.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: patient record retrieved; prescription entered/scanned; allergy/interaction checks; barcode of medicine scanned/verified; label printed with dosage instructions; patient record updated; stock reduced; automatic reorder when below reorder level.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why patient records must be kept secure.
parts.answer: They contain highly personal medical information; if seen by others it could cause embarrassment or discrimination, or be used for fraud or blackmail.
parts.working: B1: sensitive/confidential personal data; B1: consequence (discrimination, embarrassment, identity theft, blackmail, legal duty under data protection).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two methods the hospital can use to keep the records secure.
parts.answer: Each member of staff has their own user ID and strong password, with access only to the records they need; data is encrypted so it cannot be read if stolen.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two described: user IDs/passwords/biometrics; access levels/rights; encryption; firewall; anti-malware; audit logs of who viewed records; automatic log-off; physical security of servers; backups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how 3D printing can be used to produce customised medicines for individual patients.
parts.answer: A doctor decides the exact dose (and release rate) for the patient; the dose is entered into the design software; the 3D printer prints the tablet in layers with exactly that amount of medicine, so tablets can be made in a size, shape or combination that suits that patient, e.g. several medicines in one tablet.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: dose tailored to patient (weight/age/condition); design created in software; printed layer by layer; precise amount of drug; can combine several medicines in one tablet; control release rate/shape/size easier to swallow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A heart monitor records a patient's heart rate every 2 seconds for 12 hours. Calculate the number of readings taken.
parts.answer: 21 600 readings

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The monitor sounds an alarm if a reading is below 50 or above 120 beats per minute. These readings are taken:
72, 48, 95, 121, 120, 50, 133
State how many of these readings cause the alarm to sound, and list them.
parts.answer: 3 readings: 48, 121 and 133
parts.working: B1: 48, 121, 133 identified; B1: 120 and 50 do NOT trigger (not above 120 / not below 50).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which 3D printers are used in medicine.
parts.answer: Any two: making prosthetic limbs (artificial hands/legs) designed to fit an individual; making implants such as bone/joint or dental implants; making models of a patient's organs so surgeons can plan operations; making personalised medical tools; tissue engineering/printing artificial tissue (research).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two described uses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two benefits to patients of prosthetic limbs made by 3D printing.
parts.answer: Any two: custom-made from scans to fit the individual exactly, so more comfortable; much cheaper than traditional prosthetics, so more affordable; quick to produce, so children can easily get replacements as they grow; can be made in local clinics/remote areas.
parts.working: 1 mark each for an explained benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The government plans a national database so that any hospital in the country can see a patient's full medical record. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this plan.
parts.answer: Advantages: a doctor treating a patient in an emergency in another city can see allergies, medicines and history immediately, giving safer and faster treatment; tests do not need to be repeated, saving money; records are not lost when patients move; anonymised data helps plan health services. Disadvantages: very expensive to set up and maintain; a single database is an attractive target for hackers and a breach would expose millions of records; more staff can access data, increasing the risk of misuse; errors in a record spread everywhere; hospitals need compatible systems and staff training; patients may lose trust. Conclusion: it would improve care if strong security, access controls and patient consent are in place.
parts.working: Max 6; both sides and conclusion. Advantages: available anywhere/emergencies; safer treatment; avoids duplicate tests; continuity when moving; national planning/research. Disadvantages: cost; hacking/large-scale breach; misuse by staff; data errors spread; compatibility/training; privacy/consent concerns; system downtime.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how 3D printing is used in tissue engineering to make an artificial blood vessel, and explain one benefit to patients.
parts.answer: The patient is scanned (e.g. CT or MRI) to find the exact size and shape needed. A 3D model is designed in CAD software. The printer uses a 'bio-ink' containing living cells (often the patient's own cells) and a supporting gel, building the vessel up in thin layers. The printed tube is then kept in conditions where the cells grow and join together before it is implanted. Benefit: because it is made from the patient's own cells, the body is less likely to reject it, and it is an exact fit.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: scan of patient; CAD design; bio-ink/living cells (patient's own); layer by layer printing; scaffold/gel support; cells grow/mature before implanting. Plus 1 for a benefit: less rejection / exact fit / no waiting for a donor / fewer drugs to suppress immune system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hospital gives every in-patient a wristband with a barcode, and each medicine has a barcode. Before giving a medicine, the nurse scans both. Evaluate this system.
parts.answer: The system checks that the right medicine and dose is given to the right patient at the right time, using the patient's electronic record; it warns of allergies; it records automatically who gave what and when, reducing paperwork and errors from misreading names. However, it costs money for scanners, printers and software; scanning takes extra time in emergencies; barcodes can be damaged or wristbands removed; if the system fails, a manual backup is needed; nurses may rely on it too much. Overall it greatly improves patient safety, so the benefits outweigh the costs.
parts.working: Max 6; both sides and conclusion. Benefits: right patient/right medicine/right dose/time; allergy warnings; automatic records/audit trail; less paperwork; fewer identification errors. Drawbacks: equipment cost/training; extra time; damaged barcodes/wristband issues; system failure; over-reliance; still possible to scan wrong items if procedures not followed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hospital launches an app that lets patients view their own medical records, test results and appointments. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages to patients.
parts.answer: Advantages: patients can see results and appointment times quickly without phoning or visiting; they can check that their records (e.g. allergies) are correct; they can understand and manage their own health better; they can share results with another doctor easily. Disadvantages: some patients may receive worrying results without a doctor to explain them; the app needs a smartphone, internet and IT skills; if the phone is lost or the account is hacked, private information could be seen by others; some records may contain medical terms that are hard to understand. Conclusion: useful for most patients, but serious results should be explained by a doctor before being released to the app.
parts.working: Max 6; both sides and conclusion. Advantages: convenience/24-7; faster access to results; check accuracy; manage own health; share with other providers; fewer calls/visits. Disadvantages: results without explanation/anxiety; digital divide; security of phone/account; jargon; privacy if others use phone.

topics.name: Networks and the effects of using them

practice.stem: Ayesha uses the password ayesha2009 for her school email account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this is a weak password.
parts.answer: It is easy to guess because it uses her own name and probably her year of birth, and it has no capital letters or symbols.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: contains personal information (her name) | number looks like a birth year/date, easily found | no upper-case letters | no special characters/symbols | all lower case so fewer combinations to try | could be cracked quickly by software trying names/dates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two features of a strong password.
parts.answer: At least 8 characters long; a mix of upper case, lower case, digits and symbols (and no personal information or dictionary words).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: at least 8 (or more) characters | mixes upper and lower case letters | includes numbers | includes special characters such as # or ! | not a dictionary word | no personal details such as names or dates.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two other actions Ayesha should take to keep her password secure.
parts.answer: Change it regularly; never tell it to anyone or write it down (and use a different password for each account).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: change it regularly | do not share it | do not write it down / store it where others can see | use a different password for each account | log out on shared computers | do not let browser remember it on a shared device | watch for shoulder surfing when typing it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bank's mobile app asks a customer for a password and then sends a six-digit code by text message to the customer's phone. State the name of this method of authentication.
parts.answer: Two-factor authentication (2FA).
parts.working: B1 two-factor authentication / two-step verification / multi-factor authentication.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this method is more secure than using a password alone.
parts.answer: Two different factors are needed: something the user knows (password) and something they have (the phone). A hacker who has stolen the password still cannot log in without the phone, and the code changes every time and expires quickly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: needs two separate pieces of evidence | something you know plus something you have | stolen/guessed password alone is not enough | code is sent only to the registered phone | code is one-time / changes every login | code expires after a short time | user is alerted if a code arrives that they did not request.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Authentication methods are often grouped into three types of factor: something you know, something you have and something you are. Give one example of each type.
parts.answer: Know: a password or PIN. Have: a smart card, mobile phone or physical token. Are: a fingerprint, face or iris scan.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct example in the right group. Accept memorable word / pattern (know), bank card / key fob (have), voice / retina (are).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by two-factor authentication.
parts.answer: The user must prove their identity using two different types of factor (e.g. a password and a code sent to their phone).
parts.working: 1 mark. Must refer to two different types, not two passwords.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student is choosing a password for a new school learning account. The four options are:
P1  Lahore123
P2  qwerty
P3  11/03/2009
P4  Tr4in!Moon#Kite58
State which password is strongest and give two reasons.
parts.answer: P4. It is long (17 characters) and mixes upper case, lower case, digits and symbols; it is not a dictionary word, name or date.
parts.working: 1 mark for P4; 1 mark each for any two reasons: length; mix of character types; not a real word/place/date; hard to guess.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why P3 is a weak password even though it contains digits and symbols.
parts.answer: It looks like a date (for example a date of birth), which other people may know or guess.
parts.working: 1 mark: personal information / date that can be found or guessed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When Bilal types his password into a login screen, each character is shown as a dot. Explain why.
parts.answer: So that anyone looking at the screen (shoulder surfing) cannot read the password.
parts.working: 1 mark: hides the characters; 1 mark: from people nearby / shoulder surfers / people watching the screen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two other precautions Bilal should take when typing his password in a public place such as a library.
parts.answer: Cover the keyboard with his hand/body; check no one is watching; log out after use; do not let the browser save the password on a shared computer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two sensible precautions.

practice.stem: A hospital in Karachi wants staff to use biometric methods instead of passwords to unlock the computers that hold patient records.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two biometric methods the hospital could use.
parts.answer: Fingerprint recognition; face (facial) recognition.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: fingerprint | facial recognition | retina scan | iris scan | voice recognition | hand/palm vein recognition.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two advantages of biometric methods over passwords for the hospital staff.
parts.answer: Staff cannot forget or lose their fingerprint/face, so no resets are needed; biometrics are unique and very hard to copy or share, so only authorised staff can open records.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two expanded points: cannot be forgotten | cannot be lost or left behind | unique to each person so harder to fake | cannot be shared with or lent to a colleague | faster to log in during emergencies | no need to remember many passwords | stops shoulder surfing of a typed password.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe two disadvantages of biometric methods in a hospital.
parts.answer: Gloves, masks or injuries (cuts, dirty hands) can stop the fingerprint or face being recognised; the scanners are expensive to buy and set up, and the biometric data is personal data that must be protected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: surgical gloves/masks may block recognition | cuts, burns or dirt on fingers cause rejection | false rejections delay staff | expensive hardware | data is very personal – privacy concerns | if the stored biometric data is stolen it cannot be changed like a password | takes time to enrol every member of staff.

practice.stem: A company gives each employee a small physical token. When pressed, it shows a number that changes every 30 seconds. Employees type this number after their password to log in from home.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the physical token and the company's system make sure the number is accepted only once.
parts.answer: The token and the server share a secret and both run the same algorithm using the current time, so they generate the same number; the server checks the typed number matches the one it calculates for that time period, and once used (or after 30 seconds) it is no longer valid.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: token generates a one-time password (OTP) | token and server use the same algorithm/secret key | the number is linked to the time / changes every 30 s | server generates the same number and compares | if they match access is granted | the number expires and cannot be reused.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare a physical token with an electronic token (an authenticator app on a smartphone).
parts.answer: Both generate one-time codes used as a second factor and both must be in the user's possession. A physical token is a separate device that can be lost and costs money to issue, whereas the electronic token is software on a phone the user already owns, so it costs less, but it depends on the phone being charged and secure.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity: both create one-time passcodes / both are 'something you have' / both used for two-factor authentication. Up to 2 marks for differences: physical is extra hardware vs app on existing phone | physical costs the company to buy/replace vs app is free/cheap | physical has no network or battery dependence on phone vs app needs a working phone | phone can be infected with malware whereas token is a closed device.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An online banking website asks a customer for the 2nd, 5th and 7th characters of a memorable word, chosen from drop-down menus, instead of the whole word typed on the keyboard. Explain why drop-down menus are used.
parts.answer: Keylogging spyware records key presses; choosing characters from drop-down menus with the mouse means no keys are pressed, so the spyware cannot capture the word.
parts.working: 1 mark: protects against keyloggers/spyware; 1 mark: because no keystrokes are recorded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the website asks for only some of the characters, and different ones each time.
parts.answer: If someone sees or records one login they learn only a few characters, not the whole word, and the next login asks for different characters, so they cannot simply repeat what they saw.
parts.working: 1 mark: whole word never revealed in one session; 1 mark: changing positions means a captured answer cannot be reused.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 4-digit PIN uses only the digits 0–9. Calculate how many different 4-digit PINs are possible.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A bank changes to 6-digit PINs. Calculate how many different 6-digit PINs are possible and how many times more combinations this gives than a 4-digit PIN.
parts.answer: 1,000,000 PINs; 100 times more.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Even with many combinations, the bank also blocks a card after three wrong PIN attempts. Explain why.
parts.answer: Without a limit, a thief could keep trying PINs until one worked (a brute-force attack); after three attempts the chance of guessing is tiny.
parts.working: 1 mark: stops repeated guessing / brute force; 1 mark: only 3 of the many combinations can be tried.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a password manager is.
parts.answer: Software (or an app) that stores a user's passwords in an encrypted vault protected by one master password, and can generate and fill in strong passwords.
parts.working: 1 mark: stores passwords securely/encrypted; 1 mark: one master password / generates or auto-fills passwords.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using a password manager.
parts.answer: Advantage: the user can have a different strong password for every account without remembering them. Disadvantage: if the master password is forgotten or stolen, access to all accounts is lost or exposed.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept: single point of failure; depends on the provider's security.

practice.stem: A school is choosing a way for students to log on to the library computers. The options are: (1) user ID and password, (2) a smart card with a PIN, (3) zero login using face recognition.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by zero login.
parts.answer: The system authenticates the user without them typing anything, by using biometrics and behaviour (for example face, location or how they use the device) to recognise them automatically.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: no username or password is entered | user is recognised automatically by biometrics / behavioural patterns / known device or location.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the use of smart cards with a PIN for the students rather than user IDs and passwords.
parts.answer: Smart cards are quick and need two factors, but cards can be lost, forgotten or swapped and cost money; passwords cost nothing but are often weak or shared. Conclusion: smart cards with PINs are more secure if the school can afford the readers and replacement cards.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for benefits/drawbacks, max 4 on one side; 1–2 marks for a reasoned conclusion. Benefits: two factors (card + PIN) so a stolen card alone is useless | chip data is hard to copy | short PIN easier to remember than complex password | quicker log on | card can also be used for library loans/ID. Drawbacks: cards lost/forgotten so students cannot log on | cost of cards and readers | students may share card and PIN | PIN can be seen by shoulder surfing | replacement takes time. Passwords: no extra cost but often weak/written down/shared. Conclusion must weigh security against cost/convenience.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A user receives a message that says their online account has been locked after three wrong password attempts. Explain why systems lock an account after a small number of failed attempts.
parts.answer: To stop a hacker using software to try thousands of possible passwords (a brute-force attack); locking after a few attempts makes guessing impractical and alerts the real owner.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: prevents repeated guessing / brute-force attacks by programs | limits the number of tries so the chance of guessing is tiny / alerts the owner and administrator.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Magnetic stripe cards and smart cards (chip cards) are both used to authenticate users. Describe two reasons why smart cards are more secure.
parts.answer: The chip data is encrypted and much harder to copy (clone) than a magnetic stripe; a smart card normally needs a PIN as well, and the chip can create a different code for each transaction.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: chip data is encrypted | magnetic stripe data is easily read and cloned (skimming) | chip used with a PIN = two factors | chip can generate a unique code each use | magnetic stripe can be damaged by magnets / easier to tamper with.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why a user should not use the same password for every online account.
parts.answer: If one website is hacked and passwords are leaked, criminals can use that password to get into all the user's other accounts; one stolen password then exposes everything (email, bank, social media).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: a data breach at one site exposes all accounts | criminals try leaked passwords on other sites | the email account could be used to reset other passwords | damage from one phishing attack is multiplied.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A telephone banking service in Karachi identifies customers by voice recognition. Give two advantages of voice recognition for this service.
parts.answer: The customer does not have to remember a password or PIN; the voice is unique and cannot be forgotten; it works over the phone with no extra hardware; quick to use.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two situations in which voice recognition might wrongly reject a genuine customer.
parts.answer: If the customer has a cold or sore throat their voice changes; loud background noise or a poor phone line distorts the voice.
parts.working: 1 mark each: illness/voice change; background noise / poor line; accept age-related voice change.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one way a criminal might try to trick the system, and why the bank may still ask an extra security question.
parts.answer: A criminal could play a recording (or computer-generated copy) of the customer's voice. An extra question adds a second factor so a recording alone is not enough.
parts.working: 1 mark: recording / voice imitation; 1 mark: extra factor so one stolen factor is not sufficient.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A smartphone can be unlocked with face recognition or a fingerprint, but after it is restarted it always asks for the PIN first. Suggest why.
parts.answer: The PIN proves the owner is present and is needed to unlock the stored (encrypted) data and biometric settings; it stops someone simply holding the phone up to a sleeping or unwilling owner straight after a restart.
parts.working: 1 mark: PIN is the main/fallback secret that the owner alone knows; 1 mark: extra protection after restart, e.g. biometrics can be forced or fooled, or the PIN unlocks the encrypted storage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare face recognition and fingerprint scanning as methods of unlocking a phone.
parts.answer: Face: no contact needed, works with wet or dirty fingers, but may fail in poor light or with masks/sunglasses and some systems can be fooled by a photo or a twin. Fingerprint: works in the dark and is usually accurate, but fails with cuts, wet or dirty fingers, and the scanner must be touched.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to four valid comparative points; to get full marks both methods must be covered with at least one advantage and one drawback.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A university in Islamabad is setting rules for the passwords students use on its online examination portal. Describe three rules it should include and explain why each is needed.
parts.answer: Minimum length of at least 8–12 characters – makes guessing harder. Must mix upper and lower case, digits and symbols – increases the number of possible passwords. Must not contain the student's name or ID – these are easy to guess. Account locked after several wrong attempts – stops brute-force attacks. Must not reuse previous passwords – an old leaked password cannot be used.
parts.working: For each of three rules: 1 mark for the rule, 1 mark for a matching reason. Accept two-factor authentication required with a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by cloud storage.
parts.answer: Files are saved on remote servers owned by a provider and accessed over the internet through an account; the data is usually copied on several servers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: data stored on remote/off-site servers | owned/managed by a third-party provider | accessed via the internet using an account/login | data may be duplicated across many servers in different places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the three types of cloud storage.
parts.answer: Public cloud, private cloud, hybrid cloud.
parts.working: 1 mark each: public | private | hybrid.

practice.stem: Bilal is a university student in Lahore. He saves all his assignments to a cloud storage service instead of his laptop's hard disk.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three advantages to Bilal of using cloud storage.
parts.answer: He can open his files from any device with internet access, e.g. a university computer; his files are backed up on the provider's servers so they are safe if his laptop is lost or damaged; he can easily share files with classmates.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: access from anywhere / any device with internet | no need to carry a storage device | automatic backup by provider | files safe if laptop is lost/stolen/broken | easy sharing and collaborating on the same file | extra storage can be bought as needed | files synchronise across devices.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two disadvantages to Bilal of using cloud storage.
parts.answer: He cannot reach his files without an internet connection; his data is held by a third party, so it could be hacked or lost if the provider has problems.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: needs an internet connection | slow upload/download on a poor connection | security risk – provider could be hacked | he loses control of his data | provider could go out of business / service outage | ongoing subscription cost for more space | uses mobile data allowance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A photographer in Murree has 38 GB of photos to store in the cloud. A provider offers: Free plan 15 GB; Standard plan 100 GB for Rs 450 per month; Premium plan 2 TB for Rs 1,800 per month. State the cheapest plan that will hold all the photos.
parts.answer: Standard plan (100 GB).
parts.working: 38 GB > 15 GB so the free plan is too small; 38 GB ≤ 100 GB (B1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the cost of this plan for one year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one reason why the photographer should still keep a copy of the photos on an external hard disk.
parts.answer: If the internet is unavailable, the account is hacked, or the provider closes/loses data, she still has her photos.
parts.working: 1 mark for any valid reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three things a user needs in order to open a file saved in cloud storage.
parts.answer: An internet connection; a device such as a computer or phone with a browser or the provider's app; the user name and password for the account.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why a user might not be able to open the file even when they have all three.
parts.answer: The provider's servers are down/under maintenance; the file has been deleted or the owner has stopped sharing it; the account has been locked or the subscription has ended.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sana needs to send a 300 MB video of a school play to 25 parents. Give two reasons why sharing a cloud storage link is better than sending the video as an email attachment.
parts.answer: Email attachments are usually limited in size (often 20–25 MB) so 300 MB would be rejected; a link is one small message; parents' inboxes are not filled; she can update or remove the file later.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one risk of sharing the video with the setting 'anyone with the link can view'.
parts.answer: The link could be forwarded to people outside the school, so strangers could see the children in the video.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A small architecture firm in Islamabad has eight employees. It is deciding whether to use a public cloud service or to keep a server in its own office.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between a public cloud and a private cloud.
parts.answer: A public cloud is run by a third-party provider and its servers are shared by many customers over the internet; a private cloud is used by one organisation only, often behind its own firewall and controlled by that organisation.
parts.working: 1 mark for public: third-party provider / storage shared by many customers / accessed over the internet. 1 mark for private: dedicated to one organisation / controlled by the organisation / behind its firewall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages to the firm of using a public cloud service rather than a server in its office.
parts.answer: Public cloud: no server to buy or maintain, provider handles backups and security updates, staff can work from site visits and home, storage can grow easily; but monthly fees continue, a fast reliable internet connection is essential, large drawing files are slow to upload, the firm depends on the provider and client data is held by a third party. Conclusion based on cost and connectivity.
parts.working: Max 4 marks for one side; 6th mark for a reasoned conclusion. Advantages: no hardware purchase | no IT staff needed for maintenance | backups done by provider in several locations | access from anywhere (site visits) | easy to increase storage | software/security updated by provider. Disadvantages: needs reliable internet | large CAD files slow to transfer | ongoing subscription | less control over data security | provider outage stops work | legal concerns about where client data is stored.

parts.label: a
