parts.text: Three students are writing a group report. They each edit the same document saved in cloud storage at the same time. Describe two benefits of working this way compared with emailing copies of the file to each other.
parts.answer: Everyone works on one up-to-date copy, so there is no confusion about which version is newest and no need to merge changes; edits appear immediately and the version history lets them see who changed what and restore earlier versions.
parts.working: Two benefits, each 1 mark for identification + 1 mark for expansion: single shared copy – no conflicting versions to merge | real-time editing – see each other's changes instantly | version history – can undo/restore and see who edited | no attachment size limits | comments can be added for discussion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two security precautions the students should take when sharing the file.
parts.answer: Share only with named people (not 'anyone with the link'), giving view-only access where editing is not needed; use strong passwords with two-factor authentication on their cloud accounts.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: share with specific accounts only | set appropriate permissions (view/comment/edit) | do not post the share link publicly | strong passwords on accounts | two-factor authentication | log out on shared computers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A film student uploads a 2.4 GB video project to cloud storage. Her upload speed is 8 Mbps. Taking 1 GB = 1000 MB and 1 byte = 8 bits, calculate the time the upload takes in minutes.
parts.answer: 40 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Her download speed is 40 Mbps. Explain why downloading the same file would be quicker, and give one reason why the real upload may take longer than calculated.
parts.answer: Home broadband usually gives much faster download than upload speed, so the same data transfers in less time. Real time is longer because of network congestion, other devices sharing the connection, or the provider's server speed.
parts.working: 1 mark: download speed higher (≈ 8 minutes); 1 mark: any valid reason for slower real transfer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teacher keeps a spreadsheet of students' exam marks in cloud storage. She shares it with the other subject teachers. Describe two sharing settings she should choose and explain why.
parts.answer: Share only with named teachers' accounts, not 'anyone with the link' – so only authorised staff can see personal data. Give 'view only' (or comment) to teachers who do not enter marks – so marks cannot be changed by accident. Give edit access only to teachers who need to enter marks. Set an expiry date on access – removes access after the term.
parts.working: For each of two settings: 1 mark for the setting, 1 mark for the reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why version history is useful for this shared file.
parts.answer: If someone deletes or changes marks wrongly, an earlier version can be restored, and the teacher can see who made each change and when.
parts.working: 1 mark: restore earlier version; 1 mark: see who changed what / when.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A business in Faisalabad stores customer records with a cloud provider whose data centres are in another country. Explain two concerns this may raise.
parts.answer: The other country's data protection laws may be different/weaker, so customers' data may not be protected as Pakistani law requires; the business has no physical control over the servers, so it relies on the provider's security; authorities in the other country may be able to demand access to the data; if the provider goes out of business data may be hard to recover.
parts.working: For each of two concerns: 1 mark for the concern, 1 mark for the expansion.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State who is responsible for keeping the customers' data secure.
parts.answer: The business (the data controller) remains responsible, even though the provider stores it.
parts.working: 1 mark. Accept 'both, but the business is still legally responsible'.

practice.stem: A manufacturing company keeps its customer database on servers in its own building but stores its marketing videos and staff training files with a cloud provider. Both systems are linked so staff can reach either from the same software.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of cloud storage the company is using and justify your answer.
parts.answer: Hybrid cloud – it combines a private cloud (the customer database on its own servers) with a public cloud (videos and training files at a provider).
parts.working: B1 hybrid. B1 justification: mixture of private (in-house, sensitive data) and public (third party, less sensitive data) linked together.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the company may have chosen to keep the customer database on its own servers.
parts.answer: The customer data is personal and sensitive; keeping it in-house gives the company full control over security and access and helps it meet data protection laws.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: personal/sensitive data | full control of security | less risk from a third party being hacked | meets data protection rules about where data is held | fast access on the local network without depending on internet.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why public cloud storage is suitable for the videos and training files.
parts.answer: These files are large and not sensitive, so the provider can store them cheaply and staff in any branch or at home can stream them over the internet without the company buying extra storage.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: large files would need expensive in-house storage | not confidential, so lower risk | accessible by staff anywhere | provider scales storage as more videos are added | provider handles backups.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A freelance graphic designer in Dubai syncs her work folder between her laptop and a cloud service. Explain what happens when she edits a file on her laptop while it is offline and then reconnects.
parts.answer: The change is saved locally first; when the laptop reconnects the sync software detects the file has changed and uploads the new version to the cloud servers; other synced devices then download the updated version (if the file was also changed elsewhere, a conflict copy may be created).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: edit stored on the local copy | sync software monitors for changes | on reconnection the new version is uploaded | cloud copy is replaced/updated (old version kept in history) | other devices download the update | if edited in two places a conflicted copy is made.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cloud storage on its own should not be her only backup.
parts.answer: Syncing copies mistakes too: if she deletes or corrupts a file, or ransomware encrypts it, the damaged version is synced to the cloud. The provider could also suffer an outage or close her account, so she should keep a separate backup, for example on an external drive.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: deletions/corruption are synced across | ransomware-encrypted files overwrite good copies | provider outage or account lock-out means no access | provider could close / lose data | needs internet to recover | a second, independent backup (external drive/another service) is good practice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hira keeps her coursework in a folder that syncs automatically between her laptop and cloud storage. Her laptop is infected by ransomware, which encrypts all the files in the folder. Explain why the copies in the cloud may also become unusable.
parts.answer: Syncing copies every change to the cloud, so the encrypted versions replace the good copies in cloud storage too.
parts.working: 1 mark: sync sends changes automatically; 1 mark: the encrypted files overwrite the cloud copies.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two features or practices that would allow Hira to recover her work.
parts.answer: Version history / file restore on the cloud service – roll back to a version from before the attack. A separate backup that does not sync, e.g. an external drive disconnected after backing up – the ransomware cannot reach it. The cloud 'recycle bin' may hold earlier copies of deleted files for a period.
parts.working: For each of two: 1 mark for naming, 1 mark for explaining how it helps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A private hospital in Lahore plans to move its X-ray and scan images from servers in its own building to a public cloud service. Evaluate this plan.
parts.answer: Advantages: images can be viewed by doctors at other sites or at home; storage can grow as needed without buying servers; provider handles maintenance and backups in several locations; lower start-up cost. Disadvantages: sensitive medical data is held by a third party – privacy and legal risk; depends on a fast, reliable internet connection – large images may be slow to load; if the provider has an outage, images are unavailable during treatment; ongoing subscription cost; risk of hacking of a high-profile target. Conclusion: suitable only with encryption, strict access control and a reliable connection/backup link.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for advantages and up to 4 for disadvantages (max 5 if one-sided); 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion. Max 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school stops installing an office suite on its computers and instead uses online office software that runs in a web browser from the provider's cloud servers. Describe two advantages and two disadvantages for the school.
parts.answer: Advantages: no installation or updates on each computer – always the latest version; students can work on the same files at home and in school; files saved automatically to the cloud; can run on low-cost devices. Disadvantages: cannot work if the internet fails or is slow; ongoing subscription; student data stored by a third party; some advanced features may be missing compared with installed software.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of two advantages and two disadvantages.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Match each device to its description by writing the correct letter next to each number.
Devices: 1 Router, 2 Switch, 3 Network interface card (NIC)
Descriptions:
P Lets a single computer connect to a network and has a unique MAC address
Q Connects a LAN to another network such as the internet and directs packets using IP addresses
R Connects devices within a LAN and sends data only to the device it is addressed to
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct match.

practice.stem: A family home in Peshawar has a laptop, two smartphones, a smart TV and a printer. All of them use the internet through one box supplied by the internet provider.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the name of the device that allows all the devices to share the single internet connection.
parts.answer: Router.
parts.working: B1 router (accept wireless router).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two functions of this device.
parts.answer: It forwards data packets between the home network and the internet using IP addresses; it gives each device on the home network a local IP address (and often provides Wi-Fi and a firewall).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: connects the LAN to the internet/WAN | routes/forwards packets to the correct destination using IP addresses | assigns local IP addresses to devices | stores a routing table | can act as a wireless access point | may include a firewall.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the network device described in each statement.
(i) Converts digital data from a computer into analogue signals to send along a telephone line, and back again.
(ii) Connects a LAN to the internet and forwards data packets to other networks using IP addresses.
(iii) Sends a data packet only to the device on the LAN whose MAC address matches the destination.
(iv) Sends every data packet it receives to all devices connected to it.
parts.answer: (i) Modem (ii) Router (iii) Switch (iv) Hub
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two differences between an IP address and a MAC address.
parts.answer: A MAC address is fixed to the network interface card by the manufacturer, but an IP address is given by the network and can change. A MAC address identifies a device on the local network, while an IP address identifies where a device is on the internet/between networks. MAC is written in hexadecimal pairs; IPv4 is four numbers 0–255.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid differences.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the letters NIC stand for.
parts.answer: Network interface card.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the purpose of a NIC.
parts.answer: It allows a device to connect to a network; it contains the device's unique MAC address and prepares data to be sent and received over the network.
parts.working: 1 mark: connects device to network; 1 mark: holds MAC address / sends and receives data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A laptop has two NICs. Suggest why.
parts.answer: One is for a wired (Ethernet) connection and the other is a wireless NIC for Wi-Fi.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a hub and a switch.
parts.answer: Both connect devices in a LAN. A hub sends every data packet it receives to all connected devices, whereas a switch reads the MAC address of the destination and sends the packet only to that device, so a switch reduces unnecessary traffic and is more secure.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity: both connect devices on a LAN. 1 mark: hub broadcasts packets to all devices. 1 mark: switch uses MAC addresses / a lookup table to send only to the intended device. (Max 3; accept 'switch is more secure / less traffic' as expansion.)

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by a MAC address.
parts.answer: A unique identifier given to a network interface card by the manufacturer, normally written as 12 hexadecimal digits (48 bits).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: unique number identifying a device/NIC | set by the manufacturer | made up of 48 bits / 12 hexadecimal digits / 6 pairs | part identifies manufacturer, part identifies device.

practice.stem: A school computer room has 30 desktop computers connected by cables. The network technician says the room needs a switch, and each computer needs a NIC.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why each computer needs a NIC.
parts.answer: The NIC is the hardware that physically connects the computer to the network (cable or wireless) and gives it a unique MAC address so data can be sent to it.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: provides the connection/interface to the network | has a unique MAC address so the device can be identified.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The school wants students' laptops to join the same network without cables. Name the extra device needed and describe what it does.
parts.answer: A wireless access point (WAP); it connects to the wired network (for example to the switch) and sends and receives data to and from devices by radio waves (Wi-Fi), so wireless devices become part of the LAN.
parts.working: B1 wireless access point. Then 1 mark each for any two of: connects to the wired LAN/switch | transmits/receives data using radio waves/Wi-Fi | allows wireless devices to join the LAN | can require a password/encryption key.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a router decides where to send a data packet that arrives from the internet.
parts.answer: It reads the destination IP address in the packet; it looks up this address in its routing table; it forwards the packet to the correct device on its own network (or to the next router on the route if the packet is for another network).
parts.working: 1 mark each for: reads destination IP address; uses routing table; forwards to correct device / next router.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small accounts office in Faisalabad has six computers connected to a hub. Staff say the network becomes very slow when large files are copied between computers. Explain why using a hub causes this problem.
parts.answer: A hub sends every packet to all connected computers, not just the one it is meant for. This creates a lot of unnecessary traffic, so there are more collisions and less capacity for other data.
parts.working: 1 mark: hub broadcasts to all devices; 1 mark: unnecessary traffic; 1 mark: collisions / bandwidth used up, so slower.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend a replacement device and give one further benefit of it apart from speed.
parts.answer: A switch. It is more secure because data goes only to the intended computer, so other computers cannot read it.
parts.working: 1 mark: switch; 1 mark: more secure / data not sent to all.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the purpose of a wireless access point (WAP).
parts.answer: It allows wireless devices (with wireless NICs) to connect to a wired network, by sending and receiving data using radio waves.
parts.working: 1 mark: connects wireless devices to wired network/LAN; 1 mark: using radio waves / Wi-Fi.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A three-storey school building has one WAP on the ground floor. Students on the top floor get a weak signal. Explain why and suggest a solution.
parts.answer: Wi-Fi has a limited range and the signal is weakened by floors and walls; add a WAP on each floor (or a repeater/mesh unit) connected to the network.
parts.working: 1 mark: limited range / walls and floors absorb signal; 1 mark: more WAPs / extenders.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many homes have one box from the internet provider that contains a modem, a router, a switch and a wireless access point. State the job of each of these four parts inside the box.
parts.answer: Modem – converts between the digital data of the home devices and the signal used on the telephone/cable line. Router – connects the home network to the internet and sends packets to the right device using IP addresses. Switch – connects the wired devices (via the Ethernet ports) and sends data to the right one. Wireless access point – lets phones and laptops connect by Wi-Fi.
parts.working: 1 mark for each part correctly described.

practice.stem: A company has two office buildings in different cities. Each building has its own LAN of about 50 computers connected through switches.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a document sent from a computer in the first office reaches a computer in the second office. Refer to switches and routers in your answer.
parts.answer: The document is split into packets. The switch in the first office reads the MAC address and forwards the packets to the router. The router reads the destination IP address and sends the packets out over the internet/WAN, where other routers pass them on. The router at the second office receives them and passes them to its switch, which uses the MAC address to deliver them only to the destination computer, where they are reassembled.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: data split into packets | switch forwards packets within the LAN using MAC addresses | router connects the LAN to the WAN/internet | router uses IP address to route the packets | packets may travel different routes via other routers | receiving router passes packets to its LAN | switch sends to correct computer | packets reassembled in order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The company replaced its old hubs with switches. Give two benefits of doing this.
parts.answer: Less network traffic, because data goes only to the intended computer so the network is faster; better security, because other computers do not receive data meant for someone else.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: less unnecessary traffic | fewer collisions / faster network | more secure as data not broadcast to all | better performance as more devices are added.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A laptop's MAC address is shown as 3C-52-82-A1-07-F4. State how many bits are in a MAC address, showing how you worked it out from this example.
parts.answer: 48 bits
parts.working: 6 groups of 2 hexadecimal digits; each hex digit is 4 bits, so each group is 8 bits; 6 × 8 = 48 (M1 A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify which part of this MAC address identifies the manufacturer, and what the rest identifies.
parts.answer: 3C-52-82 (the first three pairs / first 24 bits) identifies the manufacturer; A1-07-F4 is the serial number of that device.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a MAC address is sometimes called a physical address.
parts.answer: It is fixed into the network hardware (NIC) when it is made, rather than given by the network.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a home, a laptop is connected by Wi-Fi to a router that contains a switch and a wireless access point. A printer is plugged into the router with a cable. The family sends a document from the laptop to the printer, and then opens a news website. Describe how the data travels in each case, naming the devices involved.
parts.answer: Printing: laptop's wireless NIC → wireless access point in the router → switch sends it out of the port with the printer's MAC address → printer; the data never leaves the home network. Web page: laptop → WAP → router, which sees the destination IP address is outside the LAN and sends the request through the modem to the ISP/internet; the reply returns to the router, which sends it to the laptop's address.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: printer data stays on the LAN; switch uses MAC address to reach printer; router forwards web request outside using IP address; reply routed back to the laptop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the print job does not need to go to the internet.
parts.answer: The printer is on the same local network, so the switch can deliver the data directly without the router sending it outside.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ali's laptop has one IP address when it is connected at home and a different one when he uses it in a café, but its MAC address is the same in both places. Explain why.
parts.answer: The MAC address is fixed into the laptop's NIC by the manufacturer, so it does not change. An IP address is given to the laptop by the router of whichever network it joins, so the home router and the café router each give it an address from their own network. The IP address shows where the device is connected, so it changes when the laptop moves.
parts.working: 1 mark: MAC fixed in hardware; 1 mark: IP given by the network/router it joins; 1 mark: each network uses its own range of addresses; 1 mark: IP depends on location / network, so it changes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three items of hardware a person needs to take part in a video conference from home, other than a computer.
parts.answer: Webcam, microphone, speakers (or headphones).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: webcam/video camera | microphone | speakers | headphones/headset | large monitor/screen | router/internet connection device. Do not accept 'computer' or 'laptop'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one item of software needed for video conferencing.
parts.answer: Video conferencing software (with a codec to compress the video).
parts.working: B1 video conferencing software/app | codec / compression software | webcam/microphone drivers | echo cancellation software.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of electronic conferencing described.
(i) Participants talk to each other using only telephones.
(ii) Participants can see and hear each other using webcams, microphones and screens, in real time.
(iii) Participants join through the internet and can share their screens, send chat messages and use an online whiteboard.
parts.answer: (i) Audio conferencing (ii) Video conferencing (iii) Web conferencing
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a company organises an audio conference using a PIN.
parts.answer: The organiser contacts the phone company and is given a phone number and PINs; the organiser sends the number and participant PIN to everyone; at the meeting time each person dials the number and enters the PIN to join (the organiser uses a separate PIN to start the conference).
parts.working: 1 mark each for: organiser obtains number and PIN(s); number and PIN shared with participants; participants dial in and key in the PIN.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teacher in Hyderabad runs online lessons using web conferencing software. Give three features of the software that help her run the lesson.
parts.answer: Screen sharing to show slides; text chat for questions; 'raise hand' button; host can mute participants; breakout rooms for group work; polls/quizzes; recording the lesson; shared whiteboard.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why a company might still choose a face-to-face meeting rather than a video conference.
parts.answer: Body language and trust are easier to judge in person; important contracts may need signing in person; poor internet connections could disrupt a vital meeting; visitors may need to inspect products or premises.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A charity has volunteers in Pakistan, Kenya and the UK. The manager wants to hold monthly meetings by video conference instead of flying volunteers to one place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three advantages to the charity of using video conferencing.
parts.answer: It saves the cost of flights and hotels; no time is lost travelling, so meetings can be arranged quickly; volunteers can see each other's faces and share documents on screen during the meeting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: no travel costs | no travel time | meetings can be arranged at short notice | people do not have to leave family/home | less carbon emission | can see facial expressions/body language | documents/screens can be shared | meetings can be recorded.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three disadvantages of video conferencing for this charity.
parts.answer: Different time zones make it hard to find a time that suits everyone; a slow or unreliable internet connection causes lag or dropped calls; some volunteers may need to buy equipment or need training, and it is harder to build personal relationships.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: time zone differences | poor/unreliable connection causes lag, freezing or dropped calls | cost of equipment / data | volunteers need training to use the software | less personal than meeting face-to-face | security risk of uninvited people joining | power cuts in some areas.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by audio conferencing.
parts.answer: A meeting held between people in different places using only sound, through telephones, mobile phones or computers (VoIP); a host usually sets it up with a number and PIN for others to join.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: meeting using sound/voice only | people in different locations | uses telephones/mobile phones or internet calling (VoIP) | organiser gives participants a phone number/PIN to join.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two features of web conferencing that are not available in audio conferencing.
parts.answer: Participants can share their screen or slides so everyone sees the same document; they can use text chat, polls or a shared whiteboard during the meeting.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: screen sharing / presentations | video of participants | instant messaging/chat | shared whiteboard | polls/voting | file transfer | breakout rooms.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In January, a company in Karachi (UTC+5) holds a video conference starting at 14:00 Karachi time with staff in London (UTC+0) and New York (UTC−5). Calculate the start time in London and in New York.
parts.answer: London 09:00; New York 04:00

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why time zones are a disadvantage of international video conferencing.
parts.answer: It is hard to find a time that is within working hours for everyone; some people must join very early or late, when they are tired and less effective.
parts.working: 1 mark: hard to find suitable time; 1 mark: some attend outside normal hours / tiredness.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student in Gilgit attends online video classes from home using mobile data. Each one-hour class uses about 1.2 GB. She attends 3 classes per week for 4 weeks and her monthly data allowance is 20 GB. Calculate how much of her allowance is left at the end of the 4 weeks if she uses data only for the classes.
parts.answer: 5.6 GB

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two problems she may experience during the classes if her connection has low bandwidth.
parts.answer: The picture freezes, becomes blurred or pixelated; the sound is delayed, breaks up or is out of sync with the video; she may be disconnected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Video conferencing software uses codecs. Describe the purpose of a codec.
parts.answer: It compresses (encodes) the video and audio before sending so less data travels over the network, then decompresses (decodes) it at the receiving end.
parts.working: 1 mark: compress/encode for sending; 1 mark: decompress/decode on receiving.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the purpose of echo-cancellation software.
parts.answer: It stops the sound from a participant's speakers being picked up by their own microphone and sent back, which would cause echoes; it removes this repeated sound in real time.
parts.working: 1 mark: removes echo/feedback; 1 mark: speaker sound picked up by microphone is filtered out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An NGO records its monthly web conference with field workers in Sindh. Give two advantages of recording the conference.
parts.answer: Workers who could not attend can watch it later; it provides a record of decisions made; it can be used for training new staff.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the NGO should tell participants before it starts recording.
parts.answer: Participants have a right to know their image and voice are being stored; in many countries consent is needed under data protection law, and people may choose what they say or switch off their camera.
parts.working: 1 mark: privacy / personal data; 1 mark: consent/legal requirement or chance to opt out.

practice.stem: A secondary school in Quetta wants to hold parent–teacher meetings by web conferencing instead of in the school hall.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using web conferencing for parent–teacher meetings.
parts.answer: Advantages: parents do not need to travel or take time off work, meetings can be scheduled flexibly and parents in other cities can join, teachers can share the student's work on screen. Disadvantages: some families have no device or reliable internet, power cuts and poor connections cause problems, it is harder to discuss sensitive issues, some parents lack the skills, and privacy must be protected. Conclusion: offer web meetings as an option alongside in-person meetings.
parts.working: Max 4 marks for one side; 1–2 marks for a reasoned conclusion. Advantages: no travel time/cost | flexible times | working parents/those far away can attend | screen-share student work | shorter queues / timed slots | can be recorded with consent. Disadvantages: not all parents have devices/internet | poor connection/load-shedding | less personal, harder to read body language | parents may need help to use software | security/privacy of meeting links | staff need training.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A government health programme plans to let patients in remote villages in Balochistan consult doctors in Quetta by video conference from a local health centre. Evaluate this plan.
parts.answer: Advantages: patients do not travel long distances – saves time and money; faster access to specialists; doctors can see more patients; reduces crowding at city hospitals. Disadvantages: doctor cannot physically examine the patient; needs reliable internet and power, which may be poor in remote areas; cost of equipment and trained staff at each centre; patients may be uncomfortable with technology or privacy; image/sound quality may affect diagnosis. Conclusion: useful for follow-ups and first advice, with referrals for physical examinations.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for advantages and up to 4 for disadvantages (max 5 if one-sided); 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion. Max 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two security risks of holding company meetings by web conference.
parts.answer: Uninvited people join the meeting if they get the link (and listen or disrupt it); data could be intercepted if not encrypted; a participant could record the meeting secretly; confidential files shared on screen could be seen by others in the room.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three settings or actions the host can use to reduce these risks.
parts.answer: Use a meeting password/passcode; use a waiting room so the host admits each person; lock the meeting once everyone has joined; only allow signed-in company accounts; turn off screen sharing for participants; use end-to-end encryption; send links only to invited people.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A company in Islamabad sends 4 managers to Dubai for a meeting four times a year. Each manager's flight costs Rs 120,000 and hotel Rs 30,000 per trip. A video conferencing system would cost Rs 900,000 to install plus Rs 15,000 per month. Calculate the annual travel cost and the first-year cost of the video conferencing system.
parts.answer: Travel Rs 2,400,000 per year; video conferencing Rs 1,080,000 in the first year.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the saving in the first year.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two factors other than cost that the company should consider before stopping the trips.
parts.answer: Managers lose face-to-face contact and relationship-building; reliability of the connection; time saved and less tiredness from travel; staff training needed; confidentiality of discussions.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Tick (✓) the correct network type for each description.
(i) Covers a small area such as one building and uses cables. LAN / WLAN / WAN
(ii) Covers a large geographical area, such as a country, and may use public communication links. LAN / WLAN / WAN
(iii) Covers a small area and uses radio waves to connect devices. LAN / WLAN / WAN
parts.answer: (i) LAN; (ii) WAN; (iii) WLAN.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct tick.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each is an example of a LAN, a WLAN or a WAN.
(i) The internet.
(ii) Phones and laptops connected by Wi-Fi to a router in a family home.
(iii) Thirty desktop computers connected by cables in one computer room.
(iv) A supermarket chain linking the computers in its stores in Lahore, Karachi and Peshawar.
parts.answer: (i) WAN (ii) WLAN (iii) LAN (iv) WAN
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three advantages to a school of connecting its computers in a network rather than using them as stand-alone computers.
parts.answer: Share printers and other hardware; share files and software; share one internet connection; central backup of work; students can log on at any computer and reach their files; software updated centrally; staff can monitor use.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which network type, LAN or WAN, usually covers the larger area.
parts.answer: WAN.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which network type is usually owned and managed by one organisation in one place.
parts.answer: LAN.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which network type usually uses telecommunication links rented from other companies, such as telephone lines, fibre cables or satellites.
parts.answer: WAN.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Siddiqui family in Multan connect their phones, a tablet and a smart TV to their broadband router by Wi-Fi. Name the type of network this forms.
parts.answer: WLAN (wireless local area network).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two things the family can share over this network.
parts.answer: The internet connection; a printer; files/photos; streaming from a phone to the smart TV.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A coffee shop in Karachi offers free internet to customers through a WLAN.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages to customers of using a WLAN rather than a cabled LAN.
parts.answer: They can connect their own phones and laptops without any cables, and they can move around the shop and stay connected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: no cables needed | can move around while connected | easy to connect personal devices | many devices can join at once.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two disadvantages of a WLAN compared with a cabled LAN.
parts.answer: Data transfer is usually slower and less reliable because of interference from walls and other devices; it is less secure because signals can be intercepted by people nearby.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: slower data transfer rate | signal weakened by walls/distance | interference from other devices | less secure – signals can be intercepted | limited range | more devices sharing the connection reduces speed.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe one way the coffee shop can stop people outside the shop using its WLAN.
parts.answer: Protect the network with WPA2/WPA3 encryption and a password that is given only to paying customers (and changed regularly).
parts.working: 1 mark for the method + 1 mark for expansion: password/encryption (WPA2/WPA3) + only given to customers / changed regularly | reduce transmitter power so signal does not reach outside | captive login page with a code on the receipt.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bank has 400 branches across Pakistan. Each branch has its own LAN. Explain why the bank also needs a WAN.
parts.answer: The branches are spread over a large area, so a WAN is needed to link all the branch LANs to each other and to head office, so customer account data can be shared and updated everywhere.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: branches far apart / large geographical area | WAN connects the separate LANs so data (customer accounts) can be shared/accessed centrally.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Compare a LAN with a WAN.
parts.answer: Both connect computers so they can share data and resources. A LAN covers a small area such as one building, whereas a WAN covers a large area such as a country. A LAN normally uses the organisation's own cables and equipment, but a WAN uses leased lines, telephone networks or satellites owned by other companies. LANs usually have faster data transfer than WANs.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity (both share data/resources / both can use routers/switches). Up to 3 marks for linked differences: small area vs large area | own cables/equipment vs public/leased links | faster vs slower | cheaper vs more expensive to run | fewer vs very many connected devices. Comparisons must state both sides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how devices communicate in a WLAN.
parts.answer: Each device has a wireless NIC; data is sent as radio waves (Wi-Fi) between the device and a wireless access point; the access point is connected to the wired network/router; devices must be within range of the access point.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small travel agency in Rawalpindi is connecting its eight computers into a network. Describe three disadvantages of networking the computers.
parts.answer: Viruses and malware can spread quickly from one computer to all others; if the server or switch fails, no one can work with shared files; cost of cabling, devices and setting up; may need a network manager/technician; greater risk of hacking/unauthorised access to shared data.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three described disadvantages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why data transfer across a WAN is usually slower or more expensive than across a LAN.
parts.answer: Data must travel long distances through many routers and links; WAN links are rented from telecom companies; the connection is shared with many other users; satellite links add delay.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two types of communication link a WAN may use.
parts.answer: Telephone lines, fibre-optic cables, satellite links, microwave/radio links, mobile (4G/5G) networks.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A warehouse near Port Qasim uses a WLAN so staff can scan stock with handheld devices. The signal is very weak between rows of tall metal shelves. Explain why.
parts.answer: Wi-Fi uses radio waves; metal shelves (and stock) block or reflect the signal, so less signal reaches devices behind them; the distance from the access point also weakens it.
parts.working: 1 mark: radio waves blocked/reflected by metal; 1 mark: weaker signal further away / behind obstacles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways the warehouse could improve coverage.
parts.answer: Install more wireless access points between the rows / on the ceiling; use Wi-Fi extenders or a mesh system; place the access points higher; use cables for fixed computers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A hospital is replacing its cabled LAN on the wards with a WLAN so doctors can use tablet computers at patients' bedsides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the decision to use a WLAN on the wards.
parts.answer: Benefits: doctors can update patient records at the bedside immediately, no trailing cables, tablets can be moved between wards, cheaper to add new devices. Drawbacks: signals may be intercepted so strong encryption is needed for confidential data, interference from medical equipment or thick walls may cause dead spots, slower than cable for large scans, tablets need charging and can be lost or stolen. Conclusion: suitable if access points are planned carefully and data is encrypted.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side; 1–2 marks for a reasoned conclusion. Benefits: bedside access/updating records | fewer errors from copying notes later | no cables to trip over | flexible/mobile | easy to add devices. Drawbacks: security of patient data – interception | need encryption/strong authentication | interference/dead spots | slower for large image files | coverage needs many access points | device loss/theft | battery life.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a WLAN is less secure than a cabled LAN, and describe two ways of making a WLAN more secure.
parts.answer: Wireless signals spread beyond the building, so anyone in range can try to pick them up, whereas a cable needs physical access. Security measures: use strong encryption (WPA2/WPA3) with a strong network key; only allow known devices (MAC address filtering); use a firewall; change the router's default admin password; turn off WPS.
parts.working: 1 mark: signals travel outside building/can be intercepted; 1 mark: cable needs physical connection; 1 mark each for two security methods (max 2).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why hiding the network name (SSID) on its own does not make a WLAN secure.
parts.answer: The network still transmits signals, so special software can still detect it; an attacker who finds it can try to break in if there is no strong encryption/password.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A university has campuses in Peshawar, Abbottabad, Mardan and Swat. It needs (1) computer laboratories in each campus, (2) students to use their own laptops in the libraries and (3) all campuses to share one student records system. Recommend the type of network for each need and justify your choices.
parts.answer: (1) LAN with cables – fixed computers in one room; cables give faster, reliable and more secure connections. (2) WLAN – students move around with their own laptops; no cables needed; many devices can join; secure with WPA encryption and student log-ins. (3) WAN – the campuses are in different cities, so the LANs must be linked using telecom links / internet (e.g. leased lines or VPN) to reach one central database.
parts.working: For each of the three needs: 1 mark for the correct network type and 1 mark for a justification linked to the scenario.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 750 MB file is copied across a cabled LAN running at 100 Mbps and across a WLAN with an effective speed of 40 Mbps. Taking 1 MB = 8 megabits, calculate the time in seconds for each, and the difference.
parts.answer: LAN 60 s; WLAN 150 s; difference 90 s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The WLAN is advertised as 300 Mbps. Give two reasons why its effective speed is much lower.
parts.answer: The bandwidth is shared between all connected devices; distance from the access point and walls weaken the signal; interference from other wireless networks or devices; extra data for encryption and error correction.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two similarities between Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
parts.answer: Both are wireless technologies that send data using radio waves; both can be secured using encryption/passwords.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: both wireless | both use radio waves (both can use the 2.4 GHz band) | both use encryption/security keys | both connect devices without cables | both have limited range.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two differences between Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
parts.answer: Wi-Fi has a greater range (up to about 100 m) than Bluetooth (about 10–30 m); Wi-Fi has a faster data transfer rate, so it suits larger files and internet access, while Bluetooth suits a small number of nearby devices.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two differences, both sides stated: Wi-Fi longer range vs Bluetooth shorter | Wi-Fi faster vs Bluetooth slower | Wi-Fi connects many devices to a network/internet vs Bluetooth pairs a few devices directly (WPAN) | Bluetooth uses less power.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether Wi-Fi or Bluetooth matches each description.
(i) Has the shorter range, usually up to about 10 metres.
(ii) Usually has the faster data transfer rate.
(iii) Normally used to connect devices to the internet through a router.
parts.answer: (i) Bluetooth (ii) Wi-Fi (iii) Wi-Fi
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three examples of devices that are commonly connected to a smartphone using Bluetooth.
parts.answer: Wireless earbuds/headphones; a smartwatch or fitness band; a car's hands-free system; a wireless speaker; a wireless keyboard or mouse.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps a user takes to connect a new laptop to a home Wi-Fi network.
parts.answer: Turn on the laptop's Wi-Fi; select the network name (SSID) from the list of available networks; enter the network password/key; the router checks the key and the laptop is connected (and given an IP address).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three steps in a sensible order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a Wi-Fi hotspot.
parts.answer: A place (or device) that provides wireless internet access for nearby users, e.g. in a café, airport or from a phone.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one risk of using a free public hotspot and one precaution.
parts.answer: Risk: data sent may be intercepted by others on the network / the hotspot may be fake. Precaution: avoid logging into banking or entering personal data; use only https websites; use a VPN.
parts.working: 1 mark for risk, 1 mark for precaution.

practice.stem: Zainab wants to send a photo from her smartphone to her friend's phone, which is next to her, using Bluetooth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps involved in connecting the two phones using Bluetooth.
parts.answer: Turn Bluetooth on in both phones; set the friend's phone to be discoverable; Zainab's phone searches for nearby devices and selects her friend's phone; a pairing code/PIN is shown and confirmed on both phones; the phones are paired and the photo can be sent.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: switch Bluetooth on on both devices | make receiving device discoverable/visible | sending device searches/scans for devices | select the device from the list | pairing code/PIN is displayed/entered | code confirmed on both devices (matching) | devices paired and connection made | file sent and accepted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Bluetooth uses spread-spectrum frequency hopping.
parts.answer: Bluetooth changes randomly between many channels (79) many times a second, which reduces interference from other devices using the same frequencies and makes the transmission harder to intercept.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: channel/frequency is changed rapidly/randomly among many channels | reduces interference from other devices / makes eavesdropping more difficult.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a home Wi-Fi network should use encryption with a strong password (for example WPA2 or WPA3).
parts.answer: Without it, anyone in range can join and use the internet connection, and can intercept and read the data being sent; encryption scrambles the data so it cannot be understood.
parts.working: 1 mark: stops unauthorised users joining; 1 mark: intercepted data cannot be read.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two problems that could happen if the network is left open.
parts.answer: Neighbours use the connection, making it slower or using up the data allowance; criminals could carry out illegal activity traced back to the owner's connection; hackers could access shared files or devices on the network.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bluetooth creates a wireless personal area network (WPAN). Describe what is meant by a WPAN.
parts.answer: A small network that connects devices around one person over a short distance (a few metres), such as a phone, earbuds and a watch.
parts.working: 1 mark: personal / devices of one user; 1 mark: very short range.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why Bluetooth is suitable for this kind of network.
parts.answer: It uses little power, so batteries in small devices last longer; it connects devices directly without a router; a short range is all that is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Usman sends a 45 MB video from his phone to his friend's phone. Using Bluetooth the transfer rate is 2 Mbps; using a Wi-Fi direct link it is 50 Mbps. Taking 1 MB = 8 megabits, calculate the transfer time for each. Give the Bluetooth time in minutes.
parts.answer: Bluetooth 3 minutes (180 s); Wi-Fi 7.2 seconds.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why Bluetooth is still often used for small files such as contacts.
parts.answer: It is quick to set up between nearby phones, uses little battery and needs no router or internet; for small files the slower speed does not matter.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a wireless computer mouse uses Bluetooth rather than Wi-Fi.
parts.answer: A mouse sends very small amounts of data, so the high speed of Wi-Fi is not needed; Bluetooth uses much less power, so the mouse battery lasts longer; it connects directly to the computer without a router; it only needs to work over a short distance.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each situation, state whether Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is more suitable and give a reason.
(i) Connecting wireless earbuds to a phone.
(ii) Giving 25 laptops in a classroom access to the internet.
(iii) Streaming high-definition video from a home network storage device to a smart TV in another room.
parts.answer: (i) Bluetooth – short range, low power, one device paired directly to the phone. (ii) Wi-Fi – many devices can connect to the network/internet through an access point. (iii) Wi-Fi – needs a high data transfer rate and greater range through walls.
parts.working: 1 mark per situation; choice and matching reason required.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one security risk of leaving Bluetooth switched on and discoverable in a public place, and one precaution.
parts.answer: A hacker nearby could try to pair with the phone or send unwanted files/malware; precaution: switch Bluetooth off or set the device to non-discoverable, and never accept pairing requests from unknown devices.
parts.working: 1 mark for risk: unauthorised pairing / data stolen / malware sent / unsolicited messages. 1 mark for precaution: turn off or non-discoverable when not in use | reject unknown pairing requests | keep software updated.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a block of flats in Karachi, many families have Wi-Fi routers using the 2.4 GHz band. Explain why the Wi-Fi in each flat may be slow in the evening.
parts.answer: Many networks share the same few channels in the 2.4 GHz band, so they interfere with each other; in the evening more devices are in use, causing more congestion.
parts.working: 1 mark: interference / overlapping channels from neighbouring networks; 1 mark: more devices/traffic in the evening.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A router can also use the 5 GHz band. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using 5 GHz.
parts.answer: Advantage: more channels, less interference and higher data rates. Disadvantage: shorter range and weaker through walls.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A family in Islamabad buys a smart door lock. It can be controlled by Bluetooth or by Wi-Fi through an app. The parents want to unlock the door for a delivery while they are at work. Explain which connection is needed and why.
parts.answer: Wi-Fi, because the lock must be connected through the home router to the internet so the app can reach it from far away; Bluetooth only works within about 10 m of the lock.
parts.working: 1 mark: Wi-Fi; 1 mark: remote access needs internet, Bluetooth range is too short.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss one security advantage of Bluetooth-only control and one security risk of Wi-Fi control for this lock.
parts.answer: Bluetooth only: an attacker must be physically close to the door, so remote hackers cannot reach it. Wi-Fi: the lock is reachable over the internet, so weak passwords or software flaws could let a hacker unlock it remotely.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student shares her phone's mobile data with her laptop. She can use a Wi-Fi hotspot or Bluetooth tethering. Compare the two methods.
parts.answer: Wi-Fi hotspot: faster, can connect several devices and works across a room, but uses more battery and must be protected with a strong password or others may join. Bluetooth tethering: slower and usually one device, shorter range, but uses less battery and requires pairing, so it is harder for others to join.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to four valid comparisons (speed, battery use, number of devices, range, security).

parts.label: a
parts.text: At an airport, a criminal sets up a laptop that broadcasts a free Wi-Fi network called 'Airport_Free_WiFi', with the same name as the real airport network. Explain how this 'evil twin' hotspot can be used to steal data.
parts.answer: Travellers connect to it thinking it is the real network; all their traffic passes through the criminal's laptop; the criminal can capture unencrypted data such as passwords, or redirect users to fake login pages to collect their details.
parts.working: 1 mark each: users join fake network; traffic passes through criminal's device; data captured / fake pages shown.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two precautions a traveller can take.
parts.answer: Check the official network name with airport staff; use a VPN; only use websites with https; avoid online banking on public Wi-Fi; use mobile data instead; turn off automatic connection to open networks.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by the internet.
parts.answer: A worldwide network of interconnected computer networks; it is public and anyone with a connection can access it.
parts.working: 1 mark: worldwide / global; 1 mark: network of networks / interconnected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two services provided over the internet.
parts.answer: The World Wide Web; email; video calling/conferencing; file transfer; online gaming; cloud storage; instant messaging.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each would be found on the internet, an intranet or an extranet.
(i) A company's staff handbook that only employees can read.
(ii) A public news website.
(iii) Pages where shops that buy from a wholesale supplier log in to check their orders.
(iv) A hospital's internal staff duty rota.
parts.answer: (i) Intranet (ii) Internet (iii) Extranet (iv) Intranet
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why a company uses an intranet.
parts.answer: Information is available only to employees, so it is more private/secure; staff can find company policies, forms and news in one place; information is relevant to the company; documents can be updated centrally so everyone sees the latest version.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an extranet.
parts.answer: Part of an organisation's private network (intranet) that selected people from outside the organisation, such as customers or suppliers, can access using a log-in.
parts.working: 1 mark: private/based on intranet; 1 mark: access for authorised outsiders.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of how a school might use an extranet.
parts.answer: Parents log in to see their own child's reports, attendance or fees.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by an intranet.
parts.answer: A private network used inside one organisation, which uses internet technologies such as web pages, and can only be accessed by the organisation's staff (with a login).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: private network | belongs to one organisation | uses the same protocols/technology as the internet (web pages, browsers) | only accessible by authorised members/employees | usually behind a firewall.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three differences between the internet and an intranet.
parts.answer: The internet is public and can be used by anyone, an intranet only by members of the organisation; internet information is not controlled and may be unreliable, intranet content is checked and relevant to the organisation; the internet is a worldwide network of networks, an intranet is usually within one organisation's buildings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three linked differences: public vs private | open to anyone vs needs login/authorised | worldwide vs organisation-only | information not moderated vs controlled/policed | huge amount of general information vs company-specific information | intranet more secure/behind firewall.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one example of information a school might put on its intranet.
parts.answer: Homework timetables and class notes for students.
parts.working: B1 any suitable internal item: timetables, homework, staff notices, policies, internal forms, exam schedules.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why information on a company intranet is usually more reliable than information found on the internet.
parts.answer: Intranet content is written and checked by the company and is controlled by its administrators; anyone can publish on the internet without checks.
parts.working: 1 mark: controlled/checked by organisation; 1 mark: internet content is unregulated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why information on an intranet may still be wrong.
parts.answer: Pages may be out of date if no one updates them, or an employee may have made a mistake.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three ways a company makes sure that only its employees can use its intranet.
parts.answer: Staff must log in with a user ID and password (or other authentication); a firewall blocks access from outside the company network; the intranet can be reached only from computers on the company LAN (or through a VPN); access rights are given only to staff accounts.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school's intranet gives teachers and students different access rights. Explain why, giving one example of something teachers can do that students cannot.
parts.answer: Some information is confidential (e.g. other students' marks or personal details) or must not be changed by students. Different access levels protect it. Example: teachers can edit the homework pages / enter marks / view all students' reports, while students can only view.
parts.working: 1 mark: protect confidential data; 1 mark: stop unauthorised changes; 1 mark: suitable example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the internet is not owned by any single person or organisation, and give one consequence of this.
parts.answer: It is made of millions of networks owned by many different companies, governments and individuals, joined together; no one body controls it all. Consequence: there is no single authority to check or remove content, so false or harmful material can be published (laws differ between countries).
parts.working: 1 mark: made of many separately owned networks; 1 mark: no central control; 1 mark: a valid consequence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Staff at a bank say pages on their intranet load faster than pages on the internet. Give two reasons why.
parts.answer: The intranet server is on the bank's own local network, so data travels a short distance; there are fewer users than on the internet; data does not pass through the ISP and many routers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A car manufacturer allows its parts suppliers to log in to part of its private network to check stock levels and place delivery schedules.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the type of network the suppliers are using and explain your answer.
parts.answer: An extranet – it is part of the company's intranet that has been opened to authorised people outside the organisation (the suppliers) through a secure login.
parts.working: B1 extranet. B1 explanation: private network extended to selected outside users / suppliers given restricted access via login.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss the benefits and drawbacks to the manufacturer of giving suppliers this access.
parts.answer: Benefits: suppliers see stock levels in real time so parts arrive just in time, fewer phone calls and emails, fewer ordering errors, faster reordering. Drawbacks: security risk if a supplier's login is stolen, cost of setting up secure access and firewalls, must limit what each supplier can see, competitors' information must be protected, dependence on the system working. Conclusion: beneficial if access is controlled and monitored.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side; 1–2 marks for conclusion. Benefits: real-time stock information | automatic/just-in-time deliveries | lower admin cost/time | fewer errors | stronger supplier relationship | available 24/7. Drawbacks: unauthorised access/hacking via supplier accounts | set-up and maintenance cost | need strict permissions | confidential data could leak to rival suppliers | downtime stops ordering.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare an intranet with an extranet.
parts.answer: Both are private networks using internet technology (web pages, browsers) and need log-ins. An intranet is for the organisation's own staff only; an extranet also gives limited access to selected outside users such as suppliers or customers. An extranet is reached over the internet, so it needs extra security such as strong authentication and encryption; outsiders see only the parts they need.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity; up to 3 marks for differences (who uses it, how it is reached, level of security/access).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A university in Karachi wants its former students (alumni) to be able to download their transcripts and see job adverts posted by the university. It is deciding between putting this on its public website or on an extranet. Recommend one option and justify your recommendation.
parts.answer: Extranet. Transcripts contain personal data, so each alumnus should log in and see only his or her own records; a public website would let anyone see the pages. The extranet lets the university control who has access and remove access when needed, while still reaching alumni anywhere over the internet. Job adverts could be on either, but keeping them on the extranet gives a benefit to alumni.
parts.working: 1 mark: extranet; up to 3 marks for justification: personal data/privacy; log-in controls access; reachable from outside the university; general information could be public.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Staff at an engineering company now work from home two days a week. They need to use the company intranet, which is hosted on servers in the office. Explain how a virtual private network (VPN) lets them do this securely.
parts.answer: The VPN creates an encrypted connection (tunnel) across the internet between the home computer and the company network; the employee must log in to the VPN; once connected the computer acts as if it were on the office LAN, so the intranet can be used while outsiders cannot read the data.
parts.working: 1 mark: encrypted connection over the internet; 1 mark: authentication to the VPN; 1 mark: appears as part of company LAN / intranet accessible.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one risk that remains when staff use the intranet from home.
parts.answer: The home computer could have malware that spreads to the company network, or family members could see confidential information on screen.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hospital in Rawalpindi plans to create an extranet so that local family doctors can log in to see their own patients' appointment dates and test results. Evaluate this plan.
parts.answer: Advantages: doctors get results quickly without phone calls or posted letters; fewer errors from copying; available at any time; reduces hospital staff workload; better care because information is up to date. Disadvantages: medical data is very sensitive – risk of hacking or data leaks; needs strong authentication and encryption; doctors must be given access only to their own patients; cost of setting up and maintaining; doctors need training and a reliable internet connection. Conclusion with justification.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for advantages and up to 4 for disadvantages (max 5 if one-sided); 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion. Max 6.

topics.name: Types and components of computer systems

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three functions of an operating system.
parts.answer: Any three: manages memory; manages the processor/multitasking; manages input and output devices (peripherals) using drivers; manages files and folders (file management); provides a user interface; handles security/user accounts and passwords; handles interrupts and errors; loads/runs application software.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of user interface described in each statement.
(i) The user types commands such as copy report.txt backup at a prompt.
(ii) The user clicks icons and chooses options from menus using a pointer.
(iii) The user says 'call home' to a phone, which carries out the action.
(iv) The user waves a hand in front of a smart TV's camera to change the channel.
parts.answer: (i) command line interface (CLI) (ii) graphical user interface (GUI) (iii) dialogue-based interface (iv) gesture-based interface
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A graphical user interface is often called a WIMP interface. State what each letter of WIMP stands for.
parts.answer: Windows, Icons, Menus, Pointer (or pointing device)
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why a GUI is suitable for a young child using a computer for the first time.
parts.answer: The child does not need to learn/type commands — they can click/tap pictures (icons) that are easy to recognise.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by multitasking.
parts.answer: Several programs appear to run at the same time because the operating system shares the processor between them, switching quickly from one to another.
parts.working: 1 mark: more than one program is active or running at once. 1 mark: the OS shares or switches processor time between the programs. Do not accept 'the computer does many things' alone.

practice.stem: A railway ticket kiosk in Lahore shows passengers a list of options on the screen, such as 'Buy ticket', 'Check timetable' and 'Cancel'. Choosing an option opens a new list of options. Passengers choose by touching the option on the screen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of user interface described.
parts.answer: Menu-driven interface
parts.working: 1 mark. The screen shows lists of options that lead to further lists; there are no windows or commands to type.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage of this interface for a passenger who has never used a computer.
parts.answer: Any one: the options are shown on screen so no commands need to be remembered; each choice leads to a clear next step; very little typing is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark for one valid advantage linked to the passenger.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a command line interface.
parts.answer: The user types instructions/commands using a keyboard at a prompt; commands must be in an exact format/syntax and the computer responds with text output.
parts.working: 1 mark: typed commands. 1 mark: exact syntax/text-only display.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of a command line interface compared with a graphical user interface.
parts.answer: Advantages: the user can access/configure everything directly, giving more control; uses less memory and processing power; commands can be combined/run as scripts to automate tasks; faster for expert users. Disadvantages: many commands must be learnt/remembered; commands must be typed exactly so errors are easy to make; difficult for beginners; no pictures/icons so less intuitive.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two advantages and two disadvantages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car has a dialogue-based interface for controlling the radio, phone and satnav. Describe how a dialogue-based interface works.
parts.answer: The user speaks commands into a microphone; voice recognition software compares the words with stored commands and carries out the action, often replying with speech.
parts.working: 1 mark: spoken commands via microphone. 1 mark: recognised/compared with stored commands and action carried out.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using this interface while driving.
parts.answer: Advantage: the driver keeps hands on the wheel and eyes on the road, so it is safer. Disadvantage: background noise or accents may not be recognised; limited set of commands; the driver may still be distracted.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe one advantage and one disadvantage of a gesture-based interface on a smart television.
parts.answer: Advantage: no remote control is needed so it cannot be lost; natural/intuitive movements so easy for young children; hygienic as nothing is touched. Disadvantage: unintended movements may be read as commands; the user must learn/remember the gestures; may not work well in poor light or if the user is out of the camera's view; can be tiring to use.
parts.working: 1 mark for each advantage/disadvantage, 1 mark each for its expansion (2 + 2).

practice.stem: A school network uses a server. Before a pupil can open the shared folders, the server checks the pupil's user name and password.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the operating system function that checks user names and passwords and controls which folders each user can open.
parts.answer: User management (user accounts and access rights / security)
parts.working: 1 mark. Accept 'security' if the answer refers to login and access rights.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one other function that the operating system on the server performs.
parts.answer: Any one, e.g. file management: it stores, names and organises files on the server's storage; memory management: it allocates RAM to the programs that are running; peripheral management: it handles printing requests from the network.
parts.working: 1 mark for naming a valid function. 1 mark for a description that relates to the server.

practice.stem: A driver in Sindh uses a satellite navigation (satnav) system that responds to spoken commands such as 'Navigate to Hyderabad' while both hands stay on the steering wheel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a voice-controlled user interface works.
parts.answer: The user speaks a command into a microphone; the software converts the speech into text and recognises the command; the system carries out the command and responds, for example with speech or a message on the screen.
parts.working: 1 mark: the user speaks a command that is picked up by a microphone. 1 mark: software recognises and interprets the speech, then carries out the command.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two drawbacks of this interface for a driver on a busy road.
parts.answer: Any two: background noise (traffic or radio) can cause commands to be misheard; the driver may be distracted by speaking and listening rather than watching the road; commands must be said in the exact form the system expects; a strong accent may be misunderstood.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid drawback with a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare a dialogue-based interface with a gesture-based interface.
parts.answer: Similarities: both are natural/intuitive ways to give commands without a keyboard or mouse; both allow hands-free or touch-free control (e.g. of a smart TV or car system); both rely on software to recognise the input and compare it with stored commands; both can misinterpret input and have a limited set of commands that must be learnt. Differences: a dialogue-based interface uses spoken commands picked up by a microphone, whereas a gesture-based interface uses body/hand movements detected by a camera or motion sensors; a dialogue-based interface is affected by background noise and accents, whereas a gesture-based interface is affected by poor lighting or the user being out of the camera's view; a dialogue-based interface lets the user keep hands on another task (e.g. driving), whereas gestures need the hands/body to move; gestures can be used in noisy places or where speaking is unsuitable, whereas speech cannot.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid comparative point, up to 5; at least one similarity and one difference needed for full marks. Points must link the two interfaces, not be two separate lists.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A technician manages 300 computers on a school network. She can use either a command line interface or a graphical user interface. Discuss which type of interface would be better for her work.
parts.answer: CLI: can write scripts to carry out the same task (e.g. installing updates, creating user accounts) on all 300 computers automatically; direct access to system settings; uses fewer resources so works on remote/low-powered machines; faster for an expert; but she must remember exact commands and a typing error could damage many machines. GUI: easier to learn and see the effects; fewer errors through choosing from menus; visual tools can show the network clearly; but repetitive tasks on 300 machines are slow, needs more memory, some settings may not be available. Conclusion: CLI is likely better for an experienced technician doing repetitive network tasks, perhaps with GUI tools for occasional jobs.
parts.working: Max 4 if only one interface discussed. 1 mark per expanded point applied to the scenario; 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Smartphones use a post-WIMP interface. Explain how the interface of a smartphone differs from the WIMP interface of a desktop computer.
parts.answer: A smartphone uses a touch screen, so fingers replace the mouse pointer; actions are made with gestures such as tap, swipe, pinch to zoom and rotate, which WIMP does not use; there are usually no overlapping windows — apps fill the whole screen; icons are larger so they can be pressed with a finger; menus are often hidden or replaced by on-screen buttons.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four valid explained differences.

practice.stem: An Islamabad bank is choosing a user interface for 150 cashiers. Each cashier uses the same five transactions all day: deposit, withdrawal, balance enquiry, transfer and print statement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a command line interface, a graphical user interface (GUI) or a menu-driven interface is the most suitable for the cashiers.
parts.answer: Sample points. Command line: fast for expert users, but cashiers would have to memorise commands and typing errors are easy to make. GUI: icons and windows are easy to learn, but each transaction may need several clicks and screens and it uses more processing power. Menu-driven: each of the five transactions is one option, quick to learn, and only valid options are shown, so fewer errors; less flexible if new transactions are added. Conclusion: a menu-driven interface (or a simple GUI with large buttons for the five transactions) is most suitable because the work is repetitive, the choices are limited and staff must learn quickly.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: 2 marks for clear points on each interface type linked to this work (command line, GUI and menu-driven, given with reasons), and 2 marks for a balanced conclusion that is justified. Points that describe an interface without linking to cashiers or the five transactions score at most half marks.

practice.stem: A shared laser printer in an office is used by twelve computers on a network. Several people send print jobs at almost the same time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the role of the operating system in managing these print jobs.
parts.answer: The operating system (with the print spooler) stores each job in a print queue; jobs are printed in order, first in first out; the next job is sent when the printer is ready; status and error messages are shown; users can pause or delete their own waiting jobs; the printer is handled as a peripheral through its driver.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: jobs stored in a queue; queue order is kept; next job sent when printer is free; status or error messages; a job can be paused or deleted; the printer is controlled through the operating system and its driver.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages of a desktop computer compared with a laptop for a family's home use.
