parts.answer: Any two: usually cheaper for the same specification; easier to upgrade/repair parts; full-size keyboard and larger monitor are more comfortable; less likely to be stolen or dropped; better cooling so less overheating; often more powerful.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three uses of a smartphone other than making phone calls.
parts.answer: Any three: sending text/instant messages; accessing the internet/browsing; sending emails; taking photos/videos; using satnav/maps; online banking/payments; social media; playing games/music; video calling; using apps such as a calculator or calendar.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of computer described in each statement.
(i) A large, powerful computer with a separate monitor, keyboard and mouse that stays in one place.
(ii) A thin, portable device with only a touch screen, larger than a phone, usually without a physical keyboard.
(iii) A device that combines the features of a smartphone and a tablet, with a screen larger than a typical phone.
parts.answer: (i) desktop computer (ii) tablet (iii) phablet
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A bank uses a very large computer that processes millions of transactions every day. Many branch terminals connect to it at the same time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name this type of computer.
parts.answer: Mainframe computer
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why the bank uses this type of computer rather than a network of desktop computers.
parts.answer: Any one: it can handle very large numbers of users and transactions at the same time; it is very reliable and rarely stops; it processes very large volumes of data quickly and securely.
parts.working: 2 marks for a valid reason explained in terms of the bank's use. 1 mark for a reason without explanation, such as 'it is faster'.

practice.stem: A smartwatch is a type of computer that a user wears on the wrist.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two features that a smartwatch usually has which a laptop does not.
parts.answer: Any two: a small screen worn on the wrist; sensors such as a heart-rate sensor or step counter; it is worn all day and needs no bag; it can be controlled by touch on the small screen.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a valid feature that a laptop does not normally have.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one function that a smartwatch and a smartphone both have.
parts.answer: Any one: showing notifications or messages; telling the time or setting alarms; running apps; tracking fitness.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid shared function.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare a phablet with a smartphone.
parts.answer: Similarities: both can make calls and send messages; both have touch screens, internet access, cameras and run apps; both are portable and use mobile networks. Differences: a phablet has a larger screen than a smartphone (between a phone and a tablet); a phablet is easier for reading and watching video; a smartphone is smaller and lighter so fits in a pocket more easily; a phablet usually has a bigger battery but uses more power; a phablet is harder to use with one hand.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid comparative point up to 4; at least one similarity and one difference for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Census workers in rural Sindh use tablet computers to record household information. Give two advantages and two disadvantages of using tablets for this work.
parts.answer: Advantages: light and portable, easy to carry between houses; long battery life; touch screen with on-screen forms that can validate data; data can be sent to the central database immediately via mobile network; built-in camera/GPS records location. Disadvantages: touch screen typing slower than a keyboard; small screen; can be stolen or damaged; battery may run out with no charging point; poor mobile signal in remote areas prevents sending data.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two advantages and two disadvantages applied to the scenario.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two features of a laptop computer that make it suitable for a salesperson who travels between cities.
parts.answer: Any two: lightweight and portable with a built-in keyboard, screen and touchpad (all in one unit); runs on a rechargeable battery so it can be used on trains/in hotels without mains power; built-in Wi-fi to connect to networks; built-in webcam for video conferencing.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two disadvantages of laptops for the salesperson.
parts.answer: Any two: easily stolen or lost when travelling; battery needs recharging/runs out; can be damaged if dropped; can overheat; small keyboard/screen can cause strain over long periods.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A school in a rural area of Balochistan is choosing a portable computer for each pupil. The school has a small budget, and the pupils carry the computers between home and school.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which a netbook differs from a laptop.
parts.answer: Any two: a netbook has a smaller screen and keyboard; a netbook has a less powerful processor, less RAM and smaller storage; a netbook is cheaper and lighter.
parts.working: 2 marks for each difference: 1 mark for the difference and 1 mark for a description or comparison. Do not accept 'netbooks are smaller' without a comparison to the laptop.

practice.stem: A games console is connected to a television in a home. The console is designed to run games and media apps only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a 'dedicated' computer.
parts.answer: A computer designed to do one specific job or a small set of jobs, rather than many general-purpose tasks.
parts.working: 1 mark: designed for one specific purpose. 1 mark: a contrast with a general-purpose computer such as a laptop or desktop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one other example of a dedicated computer and state its purpose.
parts.answer: Any valid example with its purpose, e.g. a satnav for navigation; an ATM for withdrawing cash; a digital camera for taking photographs; the controller in a washing machine for running wash programmes.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid example. 1 mark for the job it does. Do not accept a laptop, desktop or tablet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A secondary school in Islamabad plans to replace the desktop computers in its computer room with laptops that students can also take to other classrooms. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this plan.
parts.answer: Advantages: laptops can be used in any classroom, so ICT can be used in other subjects; take up less space; use less electricity; can work during power cuts using batteries; can connect wirelessly to the network; students can work in groups anywhere. Disadvantages: more expensive for the same performance; easier to steal or drop/damage; batteries wear out and need charging/charging trolleys; smaller screens and keyboards may cause poor posture; harder to upgrade/repair; Wi-fi may be slower than wired connections; can overheat. Conclusion.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side only. 1 mark per expanded point; 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A university student is deciding whether to buy a tablet or a laptop for writing assignments and attending online lectures. Compare a tablet with a laptop for this student.
parts.answer: Similarities: both portable with batteries; both can connect to Wi-fi to attend online lectures; both have screens, cameras and microphones for video calls. Differences: a laptop has a physical keyboard and touchpad so typing long assignments is quicker, whereas a tablet relies on an on-screen keyboard; a tablet is lighter and smaller so easier to carry; a laptop usually has more storage and processing power and runs full versions of software; a tablet usually has longer battery life; a laptop has more ports (USB) for connecting devices.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid comparative point up to 5; at least one similarity and one difference; points must relate the two devices.

practice.stem: A hospital keeps all patient records on a central server. Forty computers in the wards and offices access the records through the hospital network.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name this type of computer and explain one benefit of storing the records centrally.
parts.answer: Server. Benefit: all staff see the same up-to-date copy of each record; there is only one copy, so no conflicting versions; backups and security can be managed from one place.
parts.working: 1 mark for 'server'. 2 marks for a benefit that is explained (1 mark for the benefit, 1 for the explanation).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two risks of storing all the records on one central server, and one way to reduce each risk.
parts.answer: Any two risks with a reduction: if the server fails, records may be lost or unavailable, so use regular backups and a second server; hackers could reach every record, so use passwords, encryption and a firewall; the network could fail and staff cannot reach the records, so use a backup connection.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid risk and 1 mark per matching way to reduce it (4 marks maximum).

practice.stem: A delivery company gives each driver a rugged tablet with a built-in barcode scanner and GPS. The company is considering using smartphones instead.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of rugged tablets rather than smartphones for this work.
parts.answer: Advantages of tablets: a larger screen to read delivery details and maps; a rugged case survives drops and rain; built-in scanner and a battery that lasts a full shift; company devices can be managed centrally. Disadvantages: more expensive to buy and repair; heavier and bulkier to carry; they do not fit in a pocket; drivers may already own a smartphone, which is cheaper. A balanced conclusion weighs these points, e.g. a rugged tablet suits a full day of scanning, but cost may favour smartphones for a small company.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: 2 marks for clear advantages linked to deliveries, 2 marks for clear disadvantages linked to deliveries, and 2 marks for a balanced, justified conclusion. Points without a reason or link to deliveries score at most half marks.

practice.stem: A student in Karachi must buy one computer for a year of study. She will write long essays, edit scanned photos for a project and join video lessons. She carries the computer between home and her college every day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Recommend one type of computer for her. Give two reasons linked to her needs.
parts.answer: Laptop (accept another type only with a valid reason). Reasons: it is light enough to carry each day; it has a full keyboard for long essays; it has enough processing power, RAM and storage for photo editing and video lessons; its battery can last a day at college.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid recommendation. 2 marks for two reasons, each linked to her needs (1 mark each).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one drawback of this type of computer for her and suggest how to reduce it.
parts.answer: Any valid drawback with a reduction, e.g. laptops cost more than tablets, so buy a good-value or refurbished model; the battery wears down, so keep a charger; the screen is small, so connect a monitor at home.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid drawback and 1 mark for a suggestion that reduces it. A drawback without a suggestion scores 1 mark at most.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of internal memory that holds the operating system, programs and data currently in use.
parts.answer: RAM (random access memory)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student's computer becomes slow when several programs are open at the same time. Explain why adding more RAM could make the computer run faster.
parts.answer: More programs and data can be held in RAM at the same time, so less data has to be moved between RAM and backing storage (e.g. the hard disk), which is much slower to access.
parts.working: 1 mark: more programs/data can be stored in RAM at once. 1 mark: less swapping to/from slower backing storage.

practice.stem: A student is revising the parts of the central processing unit (CPU) of a computer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the part of the CPU that carries out arithmetic and logic operations.
parts.answer: Arithmetic logic unit (ALU)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the purpose of the control unit.
parts.answer: It controls and co-ordinates the operation of the CPU: it fetches instructions from memory, decodes them and sends control signals to the other parts of the computer.
parts.working: 1 mark for controls or co-ordinates the operations. 1 mark for a valid detail (fetches and decodes instructions, or sends control signals).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name one other part of the CPU that temporarily holds data or instructions.
parts.answer: Registers (accept: cache memory).
parts.working: 1 mark. Accept 'registers' or 'cache' as a small store on or very close to the CPU.

practice.stem: The motherboard of a desktop computer holds several components.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two components that are normally fixed to the motherboard.
parts.answer: Any two of: the CPU socket or processor; RAM slots; the chipset; expansion slots; the BIOS/ROM chip.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a valid component. Accept 'CPU' and 'RAM' only if they are described as sockets or slots on the motherboard.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one function of the motherboard.
parts.answer: It connects the components so that they can communicate, for example carrying data and signals between the CPU, memory and other devices.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid function.

practice.stem: A processor has a small amount of cache memory.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by cache memory.
parts.answer: A small and very fast memory, inside or very close to the CPU, that holds frequently used data or instructions so that the CPU does not have to wait for the slower RAM.
parts.working: 1 mark: small and very fast memory. 1 mark: holds data or instructions the CPU needs often, avoiding waits for RAM.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why cache memory is faster than RAM.
parts.answer: Cache is on or close to the CPU, so data travels a shorter distance; it uses faster (more expensive) memory technology than RAM.
parts.working: 1 mark for being closer to the CPU or on the CPU. 1 mark for faster technology or shorter distance explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the purpose of each internal component.
(i) Central processing unit (CPU)
(ii) Network interface card (NIC)
(iii) Graphics card
(iv) Motherboard
parts.answer: (i) processes instructions/carries out calculations and controls the computer. (ii) allows the computer to connect to a network. (iii) processes image data and sends the output to the monitor/screen. (iv) the main circuit board that connects all components together and allows them to communicate.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A washing machine contains a microprocessor and a small amount of ROM. Explain why the washing programmes (cycles) are stored in ROM.
parts.answer: The programmes must not be lost when the machine is switched off, so non-volatile ROM is needed; the user should not be able to change/erase them accidentally, so read-only memory is suitable.
parts.working: 1 mark: non-volatile. 1 mark: cannot be altered.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The washing machine also has some RAM. Suggest what might be stored in the RAM.
parts.answer: e.g. the current settings chosen by the user (temperature, spin speed, delay time); the current stage of the cycle/time remaining; sensor readings such as water level or temperature.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Two computers are being compared for a school office.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the clock speed of a processor affects performance.
parts.answer: The clock speed is the number of clock cycles per second, measured in GHz (billions of cycles per second). A higher clock speed means more instructions can be processed each second, so the processor is faster.
parts.working: 1 mark: clock speed is cycles or steps per second. 1 mark: higher clock speed means more instructions per second, so faster.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A quad-core processor at 2.4 GHz is compared with a single-core processor at 3.0 GHz. Explain why the quad-core processor may still be faster for some tasks.
parts.answer: Four cores can process instructions at the same time, so tasks that can be split between cores (for example video editing) finish sooner; the single core handles only one stream of instructions at a time.
parts.working: 1 mark: several cores work at the same time. 1 mark: a task can be shared across the cores. 1 mark: the single core handles one stream at a time, so it is slower for suitable tasks.

practice.stem: A computer has 4 GB of RAM.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the amount of RAM in MB. Use 1 GB = 1024 MB.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why having more RAM usually makes a computer run several programs more smoothly.
parts.answer: RAM holds the programs and data in use, so the computer needs fewer slow reads from the hard disk or SSD; less switching to storage means programs respond faster.
parts.working: 1 mark: more programs and data kept in fast memory. 1 mark: fewer slow accesses to storage.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the contents of RAM are lost when the computer is switched off.
parts.answer: RAM is volatile memory, so it needs power to keep its contents.
parts.working: 1 mark for 'volatile' or 'needs power to keep data'.

practice.stem: A CPU runs a program one instruction at a time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the three stages of the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
parts.answer: Fetch: the next instruction is fetched from memory at the address held in the program counter and placed in the instruction register. Decode: the control unit works out what the instruction means. Execute: the instruction is carried out, for example by the ALU, and the result is stored.
parts.working: 1 mark for each stage described correctly: fetch from memory (address in PC or into the instruction register); decode by the control unit; execute by the CPU or ALU with the result stored.

practice.stem: A laptop has 8 GB of RAM. It is running several large programs at once, and the RAM is almost full.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by virtual memory.
parts.answer: Part of the hard disk or SSD is used as if it were extra RAM, so that programs can keep running when the RAM is full.
parts.working: 1 mark: secondary storage is used as extra memory. 1 mark: this lets programs keep running when RAM is full.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one disadvantage of relying heavily on virtual memory.
parts.answer: Any one: the computer becomes slower because storage is much slower than RAM; the computer may appear to freeze while data is moved; repeated writing can wear out an SSD.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare RAM and ROM.
parts.answer: Similarities: both are internal memory/directly accessed by the CPU; both are solid-state chips on the motherboard; both store data/instructions. Differences: RAM is volatile while ROM is non-volatile; RAM is read/write while ROM is read-only; RAM holds the OS, programs and data currently in use while ROM holds the boot program/BIOS; RAM is usually much larger in capacity.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid comparative point; at least one similarity and one difference for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the instructions used to start up a computer are stored in ROM rather than RAM.
parts.answer: ROM is non-volatile so the instructions are still there when the computer is switched on (RAM is empty at start-up); ROM is read-only so the instructions cannot be accidentally erased or changed.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A journalist is typing a news report in a word processor when there is a power cut. She had last saved the report 20 minutes earlier. Explain what happens to her work and why.
parts.answer: While she types, the word processor and the open document are held in RAM; RAM is volatile, so its contents are lost when the power is cut; the work typed in the last 20 minutes is lost and only the version saved to backing storage (which is non-volatile) remains.
parts.working: 1 mark: document being edited is in RAM. 1 mark: RAM is volatile/contents lost. 1 mark: only saved copy on backing storage kept/last 20 minutes lost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one way she could reduce the amount of work lost in future.
parts.answer: e.g. save more often / turn on the autosave (autorecover) option; use an uninterruptible power supply (UPS); use cloud software that saves continuously; use a laptop with a charged battery.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A CPU runs at 3.2 GHz, which means 3.2 × 10⁹ clock cycles per second. Each instruction takes 4 clock cycles to complete. Assume the CPU is never idle in the first two parts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of instructions the CPU completes in one second.
parts.answer: 8 × 10⁸ instructions per second (800 000 000).
parts.working: M1: 3.2 × 10⁹ cycles ÷ 4 cycles per instruction. A1: 8 × 10⁸ instructions per second.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how many instructions the CPU completes in 2 minutes. Give your answer in standard form.
parts.answer: 9.6 × 10¹⁰ instructions

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why this answer is only a theoretical maximum and not the real number of instructions completed.
parts.answer: The processor sometimes waits for data from RAM or input/output, or instructions may take more cycles, so fewer instructions are completed.
parts.working: 1 mark for a reason the CPU is not always busy (waiting for memory or devices). 1 mark for stating that the real number is lower.

practice.stem: A processor makes 1 000 000 requests for data during a program. 920 000 of these requests are found in the cache; the rest must be fetched from RAM.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of requests found in the cache.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of requests that had to be fetched from RAM.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a higher cache hit rate makes the program run faster.
parts.answer: Cache is much faster than RAM, so most data arrives quickly; fewer slow accesses to RAM means the CPU spends less time waiting; so the program finishes sooner.
parts.working: 1 mark: cache is faster than RAM. 1 mark: fewer slow RAM accesses. 1 mark: less waiting, so the program finishes sooner.

practice.stem: A tablet has 4 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage. A laptop has 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage. Both devices contain ROM.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why both devices need ROM even though the laptop has more RAM.
parts.answer: ROM holds the start-up (boot) instructions and firmware that the device needs when it is switched on; ROM is non-volatile, so these instructions remain when the power is off; RAM is volatile and cannot store the start-up instructions, and it is cleared at power-off; a larger RAM does not replace the need for ROM because RAM only holds programs and data that are in use.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: ROM stores start-up or boot instructions; ROM is non-volatile so it keeps its contents without power; RAM is volatile so cannot hold start-up instructions; RAM holds programs in use; more RAM does not replace the start-up role of ROM.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR).
parts.answer: VR creates a completely computer-generated 3D environment that replaces the real world, usually seen through a headset. AR overlays computer-generated images/information onto the user's view of the real world, e.g. through a phone camera or glasses.
parts.working: 1 mark: VR = fully artificial environment replacing reality. 1 mark: AR = digital content added to the real world.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of a use of AR.
parts.answer: e.g. seeing how furniture would look in a room through a phone app; games such as catching virtual creatures in real places; showing directions on a car windscreen (head-up display); showing labels on museum exhibits; virtual try-on of glasses/clothes.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A household has a fridge, lights and a thermostat, each with a sensor and an internet connection. A family member can switch the lights off and check the fridge temperature from a phone while away from home.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name this emerging technology.
parts.answer: Internet of Things (IoT)
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one benefit of this technology for the family.
parts.answer: Any one: they can check and control devices from anywhere; electricity is saved by switching off lights remotely; they receive an alert if the fridge becomes too warm.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid benefit.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one risk of this technology for the family.
parts.answer: Any one: the devices could be hacked; the controls stop working if the internet fails; the sensor data reveals when the family is at home.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid risk.

practice.stem: A courier company in Gilgit plans to use drones to deliver small parcels to mountain villages where roads are blocked in winter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages of using drones for this delivery.
parts.answer: Any two: they can reach villages cut off by roads or snow; they are faster than travelling over mountain roads; no driver is needed; deliveries can be made quickly in an emergency.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a valid advantage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of using drones for this delivery.
parts.answer: Any one: limited battery life and payload (weight), so only small parcels can be carried; strong winds, snow or fog can stop flights; flying rules and privacy concerns may restrict use.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.

practice.stem: A smartphone has a voice assistant that answers spoken questions such as 'What is the weather in Quetta today?'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the letters AI stand for.
parts.answer: Artificial Intelligence
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the voice assistant uses AI to answer the question.
parts.answer: Speech recognition converts the spoken words into text; AI (natural language processing) works out what the question means; the assistant looks up the answer, such as the weather data, and replies with speech or text.
parts.working: 1 mark: speech is converted into text or commands. 1 mark: the meaning is interpreted and the answer is found from data.

practice.stem: A bank's computer system checks card transactions. It has been trained on millions of past transactions, some of which were fraud, and it flags new transactions that look similar to past fraud.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of AI that learns from past data in this way.
parts.answer: Machine learning
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why this system may flag a genuine transaction as fraudulent.
parts.answer: The system relies on patterns in past data; a genuine but unusual purchase, such as a large payment in a new city, can match a fraud pattern, so it is flagged as a false alarm.
parts.working: 1 mark: the system uses patterns from past data. 1 mark: an unusual genuine transaction can match the pattern (false positive).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An airline trains its pilots using virtual reality. Give three advantages of using VR for this training.
parts.answer: Any three: dangerous situations (engine failure, bad weather) can be practised safely; no risk to aircraft or passengers; cheaper than using real aircraft/no fuel used; scenarios can be repeated as many times as needed; the trainee's performance can be recorded and reviewed; training can take place at any time regardless of weather.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of VR training.
parts.answer: e.g. headsets can cause motion sickness/headaches/eye strain; equipment is expensive; it may not feel exactly like the real situation.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is used in many everyday applications. Describe two examples of AI being used in everyday life.
parts.answer: Any two, described: chatbots on websites answer customers' questions by understanding their messages; voice assistants recognise speech and answer questions/carry out commands; streaming and shopping websites recommend films or products based on what the user has watched/bought before; self-driving or driver-assist cars use sensors and AI to recognise road signs, lanes and obstacles; email spam filters learn to recognise spam; facial recognition to unlock phones.
parts.working: For each example: 1 mark for naming a valid use, 1 mark for describing how AI is involved.

practice.stem: A farm in rural Punjab needs a replacement plastic part for a water pump. The manufacturer no longer sells the part. A local workshop has a 3D printer that can make the part from a digital design.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two benefits to the farm of making the part with a 3D printer.
parts.answer: Any two with a description: the part can be made locally, so there is no delivery wait; a part no longer sold can still be made from a design; it is cheaper than buying a new pump; the design can be changed to improve the part; only the plastic needed is used.
parts.working: 2 marks for each benefit: 1 mark for the benefit and 1 mark for an explanation linked to the farm.

practice.stem: An electricity company fits smart meters that send a reading to a central computer every 15 minutes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of readings one meter sends in one day.
parts.answer: 96 readings

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the number of readings one meter sends in one week (7 days).
parts.answer: 672 readings

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one benefit of smart meters to the electricity company and one benefit to a customer.
parts.answer: Company: readings are sent automatically so staff do not need to visit to read the meter; faults and high demand can be spotted quickly. Customer: the bill is based on actual use, so estimated bills are avoided; the customer can see how much electricity is used.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid benefit to the company and 1 mark for a valid benefit to the customer.

practice.stem: A museum in Karachi uses two new technologies. In gallery A, visitors look at a tablet that shows a 3D model of an extinct animal on top of the real floor. In gallery B, visitors wear a headset that shows a completely computer-generated room.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify which gallery uses augmented reality and which uses virtual reality.
parts.answer: Gallery A uses augmented reality. Gallery B uses virtual reality.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct identification.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one drawback of augmented reality for the museum.
parts.answer: Any one: visitors need a suitable tablet or phone; the overlay is hard to see in bright light; the software and 3D models cost money to develop; the overlay may distract from the real exhibits.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid drawback.

practice.stem: A warehouse in Lahore uses robots to carry shelves of goods to packing staff. Each robot follows a route using sensors and is controlled by a central computer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways in which the robots are controlled.
parts.answer: Any two: a central computer sends instructions to the robots over a wireless network; sensors detect obstacles and positions so the robots can avoid collisions; each robot's microprocessor follows a programmed route; markers or GPS-type positioning on the floor tell the robot where it is.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a valid method of control, with a description of how it works.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one risk to workers of this system and one way of reducing it.
parts.answer: Risk: a robot may collide with a worker. Reduction: use sensors that stop the robot when a person is near, mark out or fence off the robot routes, or use warning lights.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid risk and 1 mark for a matching way to reduce it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A furniture shop in Karachi is planning an augmented reality app that lets customers see how its sofas and tables would look in their own homes. Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of this app for the shop.
parts.answer: Benefits: customers can see the size, colour and fit of furniture in their own room before buying, so fewer returns; more confidence leads to more online sales; customers who cannot visit the shop can still choose; modern image attracts younger customers; fewer display models needed in the showroom. Drawbacks: expensive to develop and maintain the app and 3D models of every product; customers need a suitable smartphone; the app may show sizes or colours inaccurately, causing complaints; customers cannot feel the comfort or material; the app must be updated when stock changes. Conclusion.
parts.working: Max 4 for one side only. 1 mark per expanded point applied to the shop; 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion.

practice.stem: A hospital in Karachi plans to use AI software to examine chest X-ray images and flag possible signs of disease for a doctor to check.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the benefits and risks of using AI to examine chest X-ray images before a doctor checks them.
parts.answer: Benefits: results can come faster so patients are seen sooner; the AI checks every image consistently and does not tire; it can help where there are few specialists; it may spot patterns that are hard for humans to see. Risks: the AI can make mistakes (false alarms or missed signs) that delay treatment; its accuracy depends on the training data, which may not represent all patients; doctors may rely on it too much; patient data must be kept private and secure. Conclusion: the AI should support the doctor, who must make the final decision.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: 2 marks for clear benefits with reasons, 2 marks for clear risks with reasons, and 2 marks for a balanced conclusion that keeps a human in the final decision.

practice.stem: A greenhouse sensor records the temperature every 10 minutes, from the reading at 00:00 to the reading at 23:50 on the same day. Each reading is stored as 16 bytes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of readings recorded in one day.
parts.answer: 144 readings

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total size in bytes of one day's readings.
parts.answer: 2304 bytes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Convert the total to kilobytes (1 KB = 1024 bytes). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

practice.stem: A car company is developing a car that can drive itself on motorways in Pakistan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the car needs several different sensors and AI, rather than only a camera.
parts.answer: A camera alone is affected by darkness, glare, dust and rain; radar or LIDAR measures the distance and speed of other vehicles even in poor visibility; ultrasonic sensors detect objects very close to the car; GPS gives the car's position; AI combines and interprets the data to recognise lanes, signs and vehicles and to decide what to do; several sensors give a backup if one fails.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks, 1 mark each for: a limitation of cameras; a named sensor (radar, LIDAR, ultrasonic or GPS) with its use; AI interprets the combined sensor data to make decisions; the sensors give backup or redundancy if one fails; a clear link to safe driving on motorways.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between hardware and software.
parts.answer: Hardware is the physical parts of a computer system that can be touched, e.g. keyboard, processor. Software is the programs/instructions that tell the computer what to do, e.g. an operating system, a word processor.
parts.working: 1 mark: hardware = physical components. 1 mark: software = programs/instructions.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Classify each of these as internal hardware or external hardware: motherboard, printer, RAM, monitor.
parts.answer: Internal: motherboard, RAM. External: printer, monitor.
parts.working: 2 marks all four; 1 mark for two or three.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each item is system software or application software:
(i) spreadsheet
(ii) compiler
(iii) photo editing software
(iv) device driver
(v) operating system
(vi) video editing software
parts.answer: System: compiler, device driver, operating system. Application: spreadsheet, photo editing software, video editing software.
parts.working: 3 marks all six correct; 2 marks four or five; 1 mark two or three.

practice.stem: A student says: 'My school's computer is slow, so the software must be faulty.'

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two hardware components that could limit the speed of the computer.
parts.answer: Any two: too little RAM; a slow or old processor; a slow hard disk instead of an SSD; a weak graphics card for graphics work.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a valid hardware component that limits speed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of software that can remove unused files to free up storage and speed up the computer.
parts.answer: Utility software (for example a disk clean-up utility)
parts.working: 1 mark. Accept 'disk clean-up utility' or 'utility program'.

practice.stem: A student connects a new printer to a computer. The printer does not work until the device driver is installed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of a device driver.
parts.answer: A device driver is system software that allows the operating system and application programs to communicate with and control a particular hardware device, such as a printer.
parts.working: 1 mark: software that lets the OS communicate with the device. 1 mark: it controls the device or translates instructions for it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of software that a computer needs to start up and manage the hardware and applications.
parts.answer: Operating system (system software)
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A computer user wants to protect the computer and keep its files organised.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two utility programs that help protect the computer or keep its files organised, and give one function of each.
parts.answer: Any two with a function: anti-virus software scans for and removes malware; a backup utility copies files so they can be restored after loss; a disk defragmenter reorganises the files on a hard disk; a file compression utility reduces file sizes.
parts.working: 2 marks for each: 1 mark for naming a valid utility and 1 mark for its correct function.

practice.stem: A tablet has an operating system, a note-taking app and a game installed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State whether the operating system is system software or application software.
parts.answer: System software
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the type of software used for the note-taking app and for the game, and give one reason why they are the same type.
parts.answer: Application software for both. Reason: each is a program that helps the user carry out a task (writing notes or playing), rather than managing the hardware.
parts.working: 1 mark for application software. 1 mark for a valid reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Describe the purpose of each type of system software.
(i) Device driver
(ii) Compiler
(iii) Utility software
parts.answer: (i) allows the operating system to communicate with/control a hardware device such as a printer. (ii) translates a whole program written in a high-level language into machine code so it can be run. (iii) carries out specific tasks to maintain/look after the computer, e.g. anti-virus, backup, defragmentation, compression.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of utility software.
parts.answer: Any two: anti-virus; anti-spyware; backup; disk defragmenter; file compression; disk formatter; file management/security (encryption) software.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A programmer writes a program in a high-level language.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between a compiler and an interpreter.
parts.answer: A compiler translates the whole program into machine code before it is run and produces a separate executable file; an interpreter translates and runs the program one line or statement at a time; a compiler reports errors after translating the whole program; an interpreter stops at the first line with an error.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: compiler translates the whole program before running; produces an executable or machine-code file; interpreter translates and runs one line at a time; compiler reports errors together; interpreter stops at the first error.

practice.stem: A small business in Karachi uses anti-virus software on all of its computers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why the business should use anti-virus software.
parts.answer: Any two: to detect and remove malware and viruses; to protect customer and financial data; to stop malware from stopping the computers from working.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a valid reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the anti-virus software must be updated regularly.
parts.answer: New viruses and malware appear all the time, so the software needs the latest updates to recognise and stop them.
parts.working: 1 mark: new threats appear, so updates are needed to detect them.

practice.stem: The hard disk of a laptop is almost full and the laptop has become slow. The user does not want to delete any personal files.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two steps the user can take with utility software to free space or improve performance.
parts.answer: Any two with a description: use a disk clean-up utility to delete temporary files and empty the recycle bin; use a disk defragmenter to reorganise fragmented files on the hard disk so they are read faster; use a file compression utility to shrink rarely used files; use an uninstall utility to remove programs that are not needed.
parts.working: 2 marks for each step: 1 mark for naming the utility or action and 1 mark for describing how it helps.

practice.stem: A home computer runs an operating system, a web browser, a printer driver and a music player.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State which of these items are system software and which are application software.
parts.answer: System software: the operating system and the printer driver. Application software: the web browser and the music player.
parts.working: 1 mark for both system items named correctly. 1 mark for both application items named correctly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the printer driver is system software and not application software.
parts.answer: The driver controls and communicates with a hardware device and works with the operating system; it does not carry out a task for the user in the way that an application does.
parts.working: 1 mark: it controls or communicates with hardware. 1 mark: it works with the OS and is not used directly to do a user task.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare system software with application software.
parts.answer: Similarities: both are programs/instructions stored on the computer; both are needed for the user to do useful work. Differences: system software controls and manages the computer hardware and provides a platform for other software, whereas application software lets the user carry out specific tasks (e.g. writing letters); application software cannot run without system software (an operating system) but system software can run without applications; system software usually runs in the background, whereas the user interacts directly with application software; examples: operating system/compiler vs word processor/spreadsheet.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid comparative point; at least one similarity and one difference for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a new computer needs an operating system before the user can run a word processor.
parts.answer: The word processor relies on the operating system to manage memory, the processor, files and devices (e.g. keyboard, printer) and to provide the user interface; without the operating system the word processor cannot load or communicate with the hardware.
parts.working: 1 mark: OS manages hardware/resources for the application. 1 mark: application cannot be loaded/run or use devices without it.

practice.stem: A secondary school in Hyderabad must choose application software for its computer lab. Option 1 is free application software. Option 2 is paid software with a licence fee of Rs 40 000 per year for 200 computers. The school has a small budget.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each option for the school.
parts.answer: Free software: no or low licence fee, so it saves money; but support, training and updates may be limited, and it may have fewer features. Paid software: a licence fee is needed, but support, training, regular updates and more features are usually included; the licence may restrict how many computers can use it. Conclusion: the school should choose based on its budget and whether its staff can support the software, e.g. free software if money is very tight and staff can manage it.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: 2 marks for clear advantages and disadvantages of the free option linked to the school, 2 marks for the same for the paid option, and 2 marks for a justified conclusion based on the budget and support.

practice.stem: A school's computer lab has ten computers that are seven years old. A new version of a photo-editing application can be installed on them, but it will not run properly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the new software will not run on these computers, referring to the operating system and the hardware.
parts.answer: The application has minimum system requirements; the old computers may not have enough RAM or a fast enough processor; the operating system on them may be too old for the software's requirements; the graphics hardware or drivers may not support the features the software needs, so it cannot run correctly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: minimum requirements not met; not enough RAM or processor speed; the OS version is too old or not supported; the graphics hardware or drivers do not support the software.

practice.stem: A company uses a database application, a spreadsheet application and a utility that backs up its files every night.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the company should use a utility that backs up its data automatically, and why the backups should be kept in a different location from the computers.
parts.answer: Automatic backup means backups are not forgotten, so little work is lost if a fault happens; a separate location protects the backups from fire, flood, theft or malware on the main computers; a backup kept in another building is still usable if the main site is destroyed; regular test restores check the backups actually work.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks, 1 mark each for: automatic backup is reliable and regular; backup is up to date so little data is lost; separate location protects against fire, flood or theft; backups are not infected by malware on the main computers; backups must be checked or restorable.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text: A systems analyst is designing an on-screen data capture form for new members of a sports club in Abbottabad. Give three features of a well-designed on-screen form.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g. a clear title so users know the purpose; clear instructions/labels for each field; drop-down lists or radio buttons for fixed choices; tick boxes for yes/no answers; boxes of a suitable size for the data; fields in a logical order; navigation buttons (next/back/submit); no unnecessary fields/uncluttered layout; consistent font and colours; help/error messages.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three distinct features.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a primary key in a database table.
parts.answer: A field that uniquely identifies each record in the table.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A car hire company in Sharjah stores these fields about each car: Make, Model, Colour, RegistrationNumber, Seats. State which field should be the primary key.
parts.answer: RegistrationNumber.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text:
An on-screen booking form for a youth hostel in Naran is being designed. For each field, name the most suitable form control.
(i) RoomType: one of Single, Double or Dormitory
(ii) GuestName
(iii) BreakfastIncluded: yes or no
(iv) HomeCity: one of 35 cities in a fixed list
parts.answer: (i) Radio buttons (option buttons) (ii) Text box (iii) Check box (iv) Drop-down list (combo box)
parts.working: 1 mark each. (i) Only three options, one must be chosen, so radio buttons (a drop-down also accepted). (iv) A long fixed list fits a drop-down list better than 35 radio buttons.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text: A blood donation camp in Multan uses a paper form that donors fill in by hand. The data is later typed into a computer. Give two features of the paper form that would help the data to be typed in accurately.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. one box for each character; tick boxes for yes/no or multiple-choice answers; clear instructions such as 'write in CAPITAL letters'; date shown as DD/MM/YYYY boxes; fields in the same order as the input screen.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two features, each linked to accuracy. Do not accept 'nice colours' or 'easy to read' without a reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the order of the fields on the paper form should match the order of the fields on the data entry screen.
parts.answer: The typist can work down the form and the screen together without searching, so it is faster and fields are less likely to be missed or typed into the wrong box.
parts.working: 1 mark: typist moves through both in the same sequence / no need to search. 1 mark: fewer transcription errors or fields skipped / faster entry.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cricket club stores whether each member has paid this year's fee. The analyst chooses a Boolean (Yes/No) field rather than a text field. Give two reasons for this choice.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. only two values are possible so invalid entries such as 'Yse' or 'paid' cannot be stored; uses less storage; searching for unpaid members is simpler and more reliable; can be shown as a check box on the form.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures
practice.stem:
A school library in Quetta is setting up a database table called BOOKS. Sample data for one record is shown.
BookID: QL-0457
Title: Hills of the North
DatePurchased: 14/03/2025
Price: 1850.00 (Pakistani rupees)
OnLoan: Yes
Copies: 3

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the most suitable data type for each of the six fields.
parts.answer:
BookID: Text (alphanumeric)
Title: Text
DatePurchased: Date/Time
Price: Currency (accept Number with 2 decimal places)
OnLoan: Boolean (Yes/No)
Copies: Number – Integer
parts.working: All six correct: 3 marks; four or five: 2 marks; two or three: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which field should be the primary key and give a reason.
parts.answer: BookID, because it is unique for each record/no two books have the same ID (Title could be repeated).
parts.working: 1 mark for BookID, 1 mark for reason.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a file of customer details, the analyst stores telephone numbers such as 03001234567 in a text field, not a numeric field. Explain why.
parts.answer: A numeric field would remove the leading zero; telephone numbers may contain + or spaces/dashes; no calculations are carried out on them.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The analyst stores each customer's date of birth rather than their age. Explain why.
parts.answer: Age changes every year so the stored value would become wrong/need updating; age can always be calculated from the date of birth and today's date.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text: When designing a file of student records, an analyst decides to code some data, for example storing the city as LHR for Lahore and KHI for Karachi. Give two advantages of coding data.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. less storage space is needed; faster to type so data entry is quicker; fewer spelling errors/consistent entries; easier to validate against a list of codes; faster to search/sort.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of coding data.
parts.answer: Users must know or look up the meaning of codes; codes may be confusing/similar; information may be lost if the coding is too general; codes run out or need changing.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A mobile phone repair shop in Rawalpindi stores details of each repair job. Sample data: JobNo R00412; IMEI 356938035643809 (always 15 digits); DateReceived 14/09/2026; RepairCost 3500.00; Collected No.
For each field, state a suitable data type and, where relevant, a field length.
parts.answer: JobNo: text/alphanumeric, length 6. IMEI: text, length 15. DateReceived: date/time (format DD/MM/YYYY). RepairCost: currency (or real/decimal, 2 decimal places). Collected: Boolean (Yes/No).
parts.working: 1 mark per field. IMEI must be text: it is an identifier, is never used in calculations and could be too long for some integer types; text length 15 also lets a length check be used.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A courier company stores the destination city for each of its 40 000 parcel records. City names are on average 9 characters long. The analyst replaces each name with a 3-character code, for example LHE for Lahore. Each character uses 1 byte.
Calculate how many bytes are saved. Then give the saving in kilobytes, correct to 1 decimal place (1 KB = 1024 bytes).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a validation check that should be used on the city code field and explain how it works.
parts.answer: Lookup check: the code entered is compared with the stored list of valid city codes (e.g. LHE, KHI, ISB) and is accepted only if it is in the list.
parts.working: 1 mark: lookup check. 1 mark: compared with a stored list of valid codes / rejected if not in the list. Accept length check (exactly 3 characters) for 1 mark only if explained.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A sports academy in Islamabad designs a file of member records. Each record has these fields and sizes:
MemberID 6 bytes; FullName 30 bytes; Phone 11 bytes; JoinDate 8 bytes; Balance 4 bytes; Active 1 byte.
Calculate the size of one record in bytes.
parts.answer: 60 bytes

parts.label: b
parts.text: There will be 2500 members. The analyst adds 10% to allow for extra data stored by the software. Calculate the estimated file size in kilobytes, correct to 1 decimal place (1 KB = 1024 bytes).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the analyst needs to estimate the file size during design.
parts.answer: So that backing storage of a large enough capacity (with room for growth) can be chosen/bought for the new system.
parts.working: 1 mark for linking file size to choosing storage capacity.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text: A clinic in Hyderabad needs an on-screen form to register new patients. The data needed is: full name, gender, date of birth, blood group (one of 8 types), telephone number and whether the patient has any allergies. Describe how the form should be designed to make data entry quick and accurate. Refer to the fields listed.
parts.answer: Title such as 'New patient registration' and short instructions; full name in a text box large enough for long names, perhaps split into first name/family name; gender chosen with radio buttons; date of birth entered with a date picker or set format dd/mm/yyyy; blood group from a drop-down list of the 8 types so it cannot be mistyped; telephone number in a text box with a set format/input mask; allergies as a yes/no tick box with a text box for details only if yes; fields in a logical order; validation on fields with clear error messages; submit/clear/next buttons; consistent layout, no clutter.
parts.working: 1 mark per feature linked to a field or explained, max 6. Generic features without reference to the scenario max 3.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures
practice.stem:
An online bookshop in Lahore sends you a file ORDERS.csv to import into a new database table. These are the first two rows:
OrderNo,CustomerCode,OrderDate,Total,Delivered,Items
ORD7711,C1043,03/11/2026,2499.5,Y,3
ORD7712,C0098,04/11/2026,780,N,1

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each field, state the data type and any format you would set so that the data is stored and displayed correctly. Total must be shown in rupees with 2 decimal places and OrderDate as day/month/year.
parts.answer: OrderNo – Text (primary key); CustomerCode – Text (leading zero in C0098 kept); OrderDate – Date, format dd/mm/yyyy; Total – Currency (or Number, decimal) with 2 decimal places, shown with the Rs symbol; Delivered – Boolean (Yes/No); Items – Number, integer.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct pair, max 5 (six fields, any five correct).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the design of the output formats, such as the delivery report, must be tested before the system is used.
parts.answer: To check the report shows all the required data, correctly laid out and formatted, so that users can read and use it.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A student designed this on-screen form for a computer course in Peshawar:
• the title is 'Form 1'
• Gender is a free-text box
• Date of birth is one text box with no format shown
• Course is a text box, although there are only four courses
• there are no instructions and no buttons except a small 'OK' in the top left corner
Identify four weaknesses of this form and describe how each should be improved.
parts.answer: e.g. Title not meaningful → use 'Course Registration Form'. Gender free text → radio buttons or drop-down. Date with no format → show DD/MM/YYYY or use separate day/month/year boxes or a date picker. Course typed → drop-down list of the four courses. No instructions → add short instructions/help text. Only OK button, badly placed → add Submit, Clear/Reset and Next buttons at the bottom right.
parts.working: For each of four weaknesses: 1 mark for identifying it, 1 mark for a matching improvement (max 8). Improvements must fit the weakness identified.

practice.subtopic: Design: data capture forms and file structures

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A city council in Islamabad starts an electric bicycle hire scheme. Each hire records who hired the bicycle, which bicycle, when it was taken, how long it was used and whether the charge has been paid.
Design a file structure for the HIRE file. Give five suitable field names, with a data type and an example item of data for each, and state which field is the primary key.
parts.answer: e.g. HireID – text – H000921 (primary key); CustomerID – text – C3045; BikeID – text – EB-118; StartDateTime – date/time – 21/10/2026 08:45; Minutes – integer – 37; Paid – Boolean – Yes.
parts.working: 1 mark for each of five sensible fields with a correct data type and matching example (max 5). 1 mark for a unique primary key (HireID, not CustomerID or BikeID, which repeat across hires). Field names must not contain spaces if the student says so; accept any consistent naming.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Describe what is meant by each type of test data.
(i) Normal data
(ii) Abnormal data
(iii) Extreme data
parts.answer:
(i) Data within the acceptable range/of the correct type that should be accepted.
(ii) Data outside the range or of the wrong type that should be rejected.
(iii) Data on the boundaries of the acceptable range (the largest and smallest acceptable values) that should be accepted.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a test plan.
parts.answer: A document listing each test to be carried out, the test data to be used and the expected outcome (with space for the actual outcome).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items that are recorded for each test in a test plan.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. test number; what is being tested; test data; type of test data; expected outcome; actual outcome; remedial action.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A ride-hailing app lets a customer book a car for 1 to 7 passengers inclusive. Give the two items of extreme data for the NumberOfPassengers field.
parts.answer: 1 and 7
parts.working: 1 mark each. Extreme data is on the boundaries of the range and should be accepted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why extreme data is used when testing the system.
parts.answer: To check that values exactly on the boundary are accepted, which shows the validation rule uses the correct operators (for example ≥ not >).
parts.working: 1 mark: tests the boundaries/limits are accepted. 1 mark: detects errors in the rule such as > instead of ≥.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A test plan has columns for the test data, the expected outcome and the actual outcome. Explain the difference between the expected outcome and the actual outcome.
parts.answer: The expected outcome is written before testing and states what should happen; the actual outcome is what really happens when the test is carried out.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what must happen if the actual outcome is different from the expected outcome.
parts.answer: The system (or validation rule) must be corrected and the test carried out again.
parts.working: 1 mark: fix the error and re-test.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Email field on a school's online admission form must not be left blank. State the name of the validation check used.
parts.answer: Presence check
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the abnormal test data you would use to test this check and state the expected outcome.
parts.answer: Leave the field empty (blank) and try to submit; expected outcome: the form is rejected with an error message asking for an email address.
parts.working: 1 mark: blank/empty entry. 1 mark: rejected with an error message.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A secondary school in Sialkot accepts students aged 11 to 18 inclusive. The Age field is validated. Give one example of normal data, two examples of extreme data and one example of abnormal data for this field, with the expected result for each.
parts.answer: Normal: any whole number 12–17 (e.g. 14) – accepted. Extreme: 11 – accepted and 18 – accepted. Abnormal: e.g. 9, 19, -3 or 'twelve' – rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark normal, 1 mark each extreme (both 11 and 18), 1 mark abnormal; expected results must be correct.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a new computer system must be tested before it is implemented.
parts.answer: To find and remove errors/bugs before real data is used; to make sure the system meets the requirements set in analysis; to check it works with real volumes of data; to avoid data loss or wrong results that would cost the company money.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the file structure of the new system must be tested.
parts.answer: To check that each field has the correct data type and size so that data can be stored without being cut short/rejected; to check the validation rules accept/reject the right data; to check links between tables/searching and sorting work.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A banking app requires a password of 8 to 20 characters inclusive. Using passwords of your own, give one item of normal data, two items of extreme data and one item of abnormal data. State the length of each password.
parts.answer: Normal: karachi2027 (11 characters). Extreme: Lhr@2027 (8 characters) and MountainsOfHunza2027 (20 characters). Abnormal: abc12 (5 characters) or a 21-character password.
parts.working: 1 mark normal (length 9–19). 1 mark each extreme (exactly 8 and exactly 20). 1 mark abnormal (fewer than 8 or more than 20). Lengths must be correct for the password given.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A new payroll system for 250 staff is tested using last month's live data, which was already processed by the old system. Explain how this test shows whether the new system calculates pay correctly.
parts.answer: The correct results (each payslip and the total paid) are already known from the old system, so the new system's outputs can be compared with them; if they match, the new calculations are correct.
parts.working: 1 mark: results already known from the old system. 1 mark: compare the new outputs with these known results.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the new system must still be tested with abnormal and extreme data as well as live data.
parts.answer: Live data is mostly normal data that has already been checked, so it may contain no invalid or boundary values; without abnormal and extreme data the validation rules and error messages would not be tested.
parts.working: 1 mark: live data contains few or no invalid/boundary values. 1 mark: so validation rules/error handling would not be tested.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A new library system is made of separate modules: member records, book loans and fines. Explain why each module is tested on its own before the whole system is tested.
parts.answer: Errors are easier to find because only a small part is being tested; each module can be fixed before it affects others; then the whole system is tested to check the modules work together and data passes correctly between them.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three points.

practice.stem: A field called ExamMark must contain a whole number from 0 to 100 inclusive. A tester uses these test values: 0, 57, 100, 101, −1, fifty.

parts.label: a
parts.text: For each test value, state the type of test data and whether it should be accepted or rejected.
parts.answer:
0 – extreme, accepted
57 – normal, accepted
100 – extreme, accepted
101 – abnormal, rejected
−1 – abnormal, rejected
fifty – abnormal, rejected
parts.working: All six correct: 3 marks; four or five: 2 marks; two or three: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: After testing with test data, the system is tested with live data. Explain what live data is and why it is used.
parts.answer: Real data from the organisation that has known results (e.g. data used with the old system); used to check the new system produces the same results as the old system/works with real data and real volumes.
parts.working: 1 mark for meaning, 1 mark for reason.

practice.stem: A hotel booking system in Murree only accepts a booking date from today up to and including 90 days after today. Today's date is 25/10/2026.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the two extreme test values for the booking date.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Days after today: 6 (rest of October) + 30 (November) + 31 (December) + 23 (January) = 90.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one example of abnormal data for this field and explain why it should be rejected.
parts.answer: E.g. 24/10/2026 – a date in the past; or 24/01/2027 – more than 90 days ahead; or 31/11/2026 – not a real date.
parts.working: 1 mark for value, 1 mark for reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school's exam timetable system only accepts exam dates from 01/06/2027 to 30/06/2027 inclusive, entered as DD/MM/YYYY. Give two different items of abnormal data for the date field, and explain why each should be rejected.
parts.answer: e.g. 31/05/2027 – a real date but outside the range (one day before the first allowed date). 15/13/2027 – not a valid date because there is no month 13. Also accept text such as 'June' (wrong data type/format).
parts.working: For each of two different kinds: 1 mark for the data, 1 mark for the reason. The two examples must fail for different reasons.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A recruitment system should accept ages from 18 to 65 inclusive. During testing, the extreme value 18 was rejected, but 65 was accepted. The rule used was:
>18 AND <=65
Explain why 18 was rejected.
parts.answer: The rule uses > (greater than) for the lower limit, so 18 itself fails the test because 18 is not greater than 18.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies the > operator. 1 mark: 18 is not greater than 18 so it is outside the rule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the corrected rule.
parts.working: 1 mark. Accept 'Between 18 And 65'.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why using only normal data would not have found this error.
parts.answer: Normal values such as 30 lie well inside the range and pass both versions of the rule; only a boundary value shows the difference.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A new online ticket system for a cricket stadium in Lahore passed every test in its test plan. On the first day of sales it failed. Explain three reasons why a system that passes all its planned tests may still fail when it is used for real.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g. far more users/data at once than was tested (volume or load not tested); users enter data the testers did not think of; it runs on different hardware, browsers or networks; the test plan missed some routes through the system; real data contained errors not in the test data.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three distinct reasons.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three methods a systems analyst can use to research the current system.
parts.answer: Any three of: observation; interviews; questionnaires; examining documents.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two things a systems analyst can learn by examining the documents used in the current system.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. what data is input/collected; what outputs are produced; the format/layout of current forms and reports; how much data is handled/volumes of data; the processing that takes place.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of examining documents.
parts.answer: It can be time-consuming; documents may be out of date/incomplete; difficult to understand without knowing the business; does not show users' opinions.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: During the analysis stage a systems analyst studies the current system. State four things the analyst identifies.
parts.answer: Any four: the inputs; the outputs; the processing; the problems with the current system; the user requirements; the information requirements; the hardware needed; the software needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small bakery in Faisalabad has three members of staff. An analyst decides to interview them about the current ordering system. Give two advantages of interviews in this situation.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. the analyst can ask follow-up questions; questions can be changed to suit each person; the analyst can see body language; with only three staff it does not take long; staff tend to give fuller answers.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Answers should fit a small number of staff.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of interviews.
parts.answer: e.g. staff may not answer honestly because they are not anonymous / it takes the staff away from work / it is time-consuming to arrange.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a systems analyst must research the current system before designing a new one.
parts.answer: To find out exactly what the current system does and what its problems are, so the new system keeps the needed functions and solves those problems / meets the users' requirements.
parts.working: 1 mark: understand inputs, processing and outputs of the current system. 1 mark: so the new system meets requirements and fixes the problems.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An analyst is studying how a busy hospital pharmacy in Lahore records medicines given to patients. Give two advantages of using observation to research the current system.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. the analyst sees what actually happens rather than what staff say happens; reliable first-hand information; sees the whole process, including problems staff may not mention; relatively cheap/does not take staff away from work.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two disadvantages of using observation in this pharmacy.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. staff may work differently/better when they know they are watched; time-consuming for the analyst; the analyst may be in the way in a busy area; patient confidentiality – analyst may see private information; may not see rare problems during the visit.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A textile company has 800 employees working in offices in Karachi, Lahore and Faisalabad. Compare using questionnaires and interviews to find out what the employees think of the current system.
parts.answer: Both collect the views of users. Questionnaires can reach all 800 employees in different cities quickly and cheaply, whereas interviews take much longer and need travel; questionnaires can be anonymous so answers may be more honest, while in interviews staff may say what they think the analyst wants; interviews let the analyst ask follow-up questions and explain, but questionnaires have fixed questions; questionnaires may not all be returned; questionnaire answers are easier to analyse.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A university in Lahore wants the views of its 5000 students on a new online timetable system. The analyst uses an online questionnaire. Explain two reasons why the information collected might be unreliable.
parts.answer: e.g. Many students may not reply, so the answers may not represent all students. Students may give the answer they think the university wants rather than the truth. Questions may be misunderstood and the analyst cannot explain them. Closed questions may not let students give their real view.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for the point and 1 mark for the explanation of why it makes the data unreliable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After the analysis stage an analyst produces a system specification for a pharmacy chain's new stock system. State two hardware items and two software items that could be listed in the specification.
parts.answer: Hardware, e.g. bar code readers, a server with enough storage, receipt printers, touch screens. Software, e.g. a database management system, an operating system, stock control software, backup software.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two hardware and two software items. Brand names are not accepted.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State the most suitable method of researching the current system in each situation. Choose from: observation, interviews, questionnaires, examining documents.
(i) Factory workers work on three different shifts and there are 300 of them.
(ii) Only the owner of a small shop uses the system.
(iii) The analyst wants to see how cashiers deal with long queues at busy times.
(iv) The analyst wants to know what data is printed on the current invoices.
parts.answer: (i) Questionnaires (ii) Interviews (iii) Observation (iv) Examining documents
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An analyst writes a questionnaire for the 120 staff of a hotel in Murree. Give two features of a well-designed questionnaire.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. mostly closed questions with tick boxes; short and quick to complete; clear simple wording; questions in a logical order; space for comments at the end.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the questionnaire should be anonymous.
parts.answer: Staff can give honest answers, including criticism of managers or the system, without fear of being identified, so the information is more reliable.
parts.working: 1 mark: staff cannot be identified. 1 mark: so answers are more honest/reliable.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A courier company in Karachi records parcel deliveries on paper. A systems analyst has been asked to produce a new computerised system. Describe the tasks the analyst carries out in the analysis stage.
parts.answer: Research the current system using observation/interviews/questionnaires/examining documents; record the inputs (e.g. parcel details, addresses), processing (e.g. allocating parcels to drivers) and outputs (e.g. delivery lists, receipts) of the current system; identify problems with the current system (e.g. lost parcels, slow tracking); identify user requirements (what staff need the new system to do); identify information requirements; identify the hardware and software needed for the new system; produce a requirements specification/cost-benefit.
parts.working: 1 mark per task, max 6. Max 4 if no reference to the courier scenario.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When an analyst observes workers, the workers may change the way they behave. Explain why this is a problem for the analyst.
parts.answer: The analyst does not see the normal way the work is done, so the information about the current system (speed, errors, shortcuts) may be wrong, and the new system may be designed on a false picture.
parts.working: 1 mark: behaviour is not normal (work better/slower than usual). 1 mark: so the analysis gives an inaccurate picture.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways the analyst could reduce this problem.
parts.answer: e.g. observe over several days so workers get used to the analyst; observe at different times; combine observation with documents or questionnaires to cross-check; observe without interrupting/standing apart.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school canteen in Peshawar uses paper tokens. The analyst wants to understand how the cashiers take orders and money at break time. Recommend two research methods and justify each choice.
parts.answer: e.g. Observation: the analyst sees the real process at break time, including queues and problems the cashiers may not mention; it gives first-hand, reliable information.
