Interviews with the cashiers and the canteen manager: few people are involved, so detailed answers and follow-up questions are possible, and the analyst can find out about problems that cannot be seen, e.g. end-of-day counting. (Examining documents, e.g. token records and daily takings sheets, is also acceptable.)
parts.working: For each method: 1 mark for naming a suitable method, up to 2 marks for justification linked to the canteen (busy break time, few cashiers, paper tokens). Max 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A textile company has 640 staff. An analyst sends them all a questionnaire and 35% are returned. Calculate how many questionnaires are returned.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The manager suggests interviewing every member of staff who returned a questionnaire instead. Each interview takes 30 minutes. Calculate the total interview time in hours.
parts.answer: 112 hours

parts.label: c
parts.text: Using your answers, explain why interviewing a small sample of staff, together with the questionnaire, is a better plan.
parts.answer: 112 hours of interviews is far too long and costly and takes staff away from work; a few interviews with a sample give detail and follow-up while the questionnaire gives the views of many staff quickly.
parts.working: 1 mark: refers to the large time/cost (112 hours). 1 mark: sample interviews give depth while questionnaires give breadth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the four methods of implementing a new system.
parts.answer: Direct changeover; parallel running; pilot running; phased implementation.
parts.working: All four: 2 marks; two or three: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe direct changeover.
parts.answer: The old system is stopped and the new system is started at the same time/immediately replaces it.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe phased implementation.
parts.answer: The new system is introduced one part (module) at a time; when one part is working correctly the next part is introduced, until the whole old system has been replaced.
parts.working: 1 mark: one part/module at a time. 1 mark: next part only when the previous part works / old system replaced gradually.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the implementation method described in each statement.
(i) The old system stops on Friday and the new system starts on Monday.
(ii) The new system is used in one branch only; the other branches keep the old system until it has been proved.
(iii) The old and new systems both run at the same time for a month.
(iv) The payroll part is changed first, then the stock part, then the sales part.
parts.answer: (i) Direct changeover (ii) Pilot running (iii) Parallel running (iv) Phased implementation
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shop is about to start using a new computerised stock system. State three tasks that must be done before the new system can be used.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g. install the hardware/network; install the software; transfer (convert) the existing data files to the new system; train the staff; test the system; produce user documentation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bank introduces a new payroll system using parallel running. Describe parallel running.
parts.answer: The old and new systems are both used together for a period, processing the same data, until the new system is shown to work.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two advantages and one disadvantage of parallel running for the bank.
parts.answer: Advantages (any two): if the new system fails, the old one is still running so no data/pay is lost; results of the two systems can be compared to check the new system is correct; staff can be trained gradually. Disadvantage (any one): expensive because data is entered twice/extra staff or overtime needed; extra workload for staff; takes longer to fully implement.
parts.working: 1 mark each, max 2 advantages and 1 disadvantage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A supermarket chain with 60 stores across Pakistan is introducing a new stock control system using pilot running. Describe pilot running in this context.
parts.answer: The new system is introduced in one store (or a few stores) first; when it works there it is introduced in the other stores.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of pilot running for the supermarket chain.
parts.answer: Advantage: if the system fails only one store is affected; staff in the pilot store can help train others; problems can be fixed before full roll-out; cheaper than parallel running across all stores. Disadvantage: takes longer to implement across all 60 stores; if the system fails, the pilot store is affected/loses data; the pilot store may not be typical of all stores.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A clothes shop in Hyderabad replaces its old website with a completely new one. The owner uses direct changeover. Give two reasons why direct changeover is suitable here.
parts.answer: e.g. it would be confusing for customers to have two websites at once; the new website is available to everyone immediately; it is the cheapest/quickest method; the old website can be kept as a backup to restore if there is a serious fault.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two reasons linked to a website.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one risk of using direct changeover.
parts.answer: If the new website has errors or fails, there is no working system to fall back on, so customers cannot place orders and sales are lost.
parts.working: 1 mark: failure leaves no working system. 1 mark: consequence, e.g. lost orders/income.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A transport company introduces a new accounts system using phased implementation. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of this method.
parts.answer: Advantage: if a phase fails only that part is affected / staff can be trained one part at a time / errors are easier to trace. Disadvantage: it takes a long time before the whole system is in use / data must pass between old and new parts during changeover.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A company uses parallel running for 20 working days. During this time 12 staff each work 2 extra hours per day, paid at Rs 600 per hour. Calculate the total extra cost of staff time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why parallel running increases the staff's workload.
parts.answer: Every item of data has to be entered and processed in both the old and the new system, so the same work is done twice, and outputs must be compared.
parts.working: 1 mark: work/data entered twice. 1 mark: results of the two systems must be compared.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A supermarket chain is choosing between pilot running and phased implementation. Compare these two methods.
parts.answer: Both introduce the new system gradually, so the risk is smaller than direct changeover and staff can learn it step by step. In pilot running the whole new system is tried in one branch or department first, whereas in phased implementation one part of the system is introduced at a time across the whole organisation. A failure in a pilot affects only one branch, while a failure in a phase affects only one part but in every branch.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity, up to 3 marks for linked differences. A pros list for each method with no comparison gets max 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Recommend the most suitable implementation method for each situation and explain your choice.
(i) A hospital's new patient records system, where no data must be lost.
(ii) A restaurant chain with 40 branches that all do the same work.
(iii) A factory's new system made of separate stock, payroll and sales modules.
parts.answer:
(i) Parallel running – the old system continues so if the new system fails records are not lost; results can be compared.
(ii) Pilot running – try it in one branch first; any problems affect only one branch before roll-out to the others.
(iii) Phased implementation – introduce one module at a time so each part can be tested and staff trained gradually; a failure affects only one part.
parts.working: For each: 1 mark for method, 1 mark for explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small school in Murree is replacing its paper attendance registers with a computerised system. The head teacher wants to use direct changeover during the summer holidays. Evaluate this choice.
parts.answer: For: cheapest method – no duplication of work; the new system is used straight away so benefits are immediate; during the holidays no attendance is being taken, so there is time to set up and test before term; staff only have to learn one system. Against: if the new system fails at the start of term there is no backup, so attendance data could be lost (important for safety/fire registers); all staff need training before day one; any errors affect the whole school at once. Mitigations: test thoroughly; keep paper registers ready in case. Conclusion, e.g. suitable for a small school with a simple system, given the holiday timing.
parts.working: 5–6: both sides developed with conclusion linked to the scenario; 3–4: both sides with some development; 1–2: simple points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An airline replaces the check-in system at a busy international airport. Explain why direct changeover would not be suitable.
parts.answer: If the new system failed, no passengers could be checked in, causing delayed or cancelled flights, safety and security problems and large financial losses; the system is too critical to have no fallback.
parts.working: 1 mark: no backup system if it fails. 1 mark: serious consequence linked to the airline.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Recommend a more suitable method and justify your choice.
parts.answer: Parallel running (or pilot running at one airport/terminal first): the old system is still available if the new one fails, and outputs can be compared to check the new system is correct.
parts.working: 1 mark: suitable method. 1 mark: justification linked to safety/fallback.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A land records office has 18 000 paper records to type into a new system. Six clerks each type 45 records per hour and work 7 hours per day. Calculate the number of whole working days needed to type all the records.
parts.answer: 10 days
parts.working: M1: 6 × 45 × 7 = 1890 records per day. A1: 18 000 ÷ 1890 = 9.52, so 10 working days.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the typed data can be verified.
parts.answer: Double entry: the data is typed in twice (by two clerks) and the computer compares the two versions, reporting differences; or a visual check: the typed record is compared on screen against the paper record.
parts.working: 1 mark: named method. 1 mark: how it works.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An electricity company is introducing a new billing system that sends monthly bills to 2 million customers. Evaluate the use of direct changeover and parallel running for this system, and recommend one method.
parts.answer: Direct: cheapest and quickest, staff use only one system and the benefits start at once; but if the new system fails or has errors there is no fallback, so wrong bills or no bills could be sent to millions of customers, causing complaints and lost income. Parallel: the old system is still there if the new one fails, and each month's bills can be compared with those from the old system to prove the new one is correct; staff can train while still using the old system; but it is expensive, doubles the workload and needs extra staff time to enter data twice and compare outputs. Recommendation: parallel running (or pilot running in one region), because errors in millions of bills would cost far more than running two systems for a short time.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points on direct, up to 2 marks for points on parallel, 1 mark for comparison/context, 1 mark for a justified recommendation. Max 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the most suitable validation check for each field.
(i) StudentID must have exactly 6 characters.
(ii) Gender must be M, F or X.
(iii) Mark must be from 0 to 100.
(iv) Email address must contain one @ symbol followed by a dot.
parts.answer:
(i) Length check
(ii) Lookup check (list/table lookup)
(iii) Range check
(iv) Format check
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a validation check.
parts.answer: An automatic check made by the computer that data entered is reasonable/sensible and follows set rules before it is accepted.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why data that passes all validation checks can still be wrong.
parts.answer: Validation only checks that data is reasonable/within the rules, not that it is the true value; e.g. an age of 35 typed instead of 53 is within range and is accepted.
parts.working: 1 mark: checks sensible not correct. 1 mark: example or explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A university admission form has these fields: ApplicantName, MatricMarks (a whole number), PhoneNumber (11 digits). Describe a type check and a length check, using a field from this form for each.
parts.answer: Type check: checks the data is the right data type, e.g. MatricMarks must be a whole number, so 'nine hundred' is rejected. Length check: checks the number of characters, e.g. PhoneNumber must have exactly 11 characters.
parts.working: For each check: 1 mark description, 1 mark suitable field and example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a lookup check.
parts.answer: The data entered is compared with a list of allowed values stored by the system; it is accepted only if it matches one of them.
parts.working: 1 mark: compares with a stored list. 1 mark: accepted only if found.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give a field in a national database of schools that could use a lookup check.
parts.answer: e.g. Province (Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan…) / District / SchoolType.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a presence check and give one field in an online shop's delivery form that should have one.
parts.answer: Checks that data has been entered, i.e. the field is not left blank; e.g. DeliveryAddress.
parts.working: 1 mark description, 1 mark field.

practice.stem: A hardware shop in Gujranwala uses a database table called SALES. The field Quantity must be a whole number from 1 to 50.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the validation rule you would enter for the Quantity field.
parts.answer: >=1 And <=50 (accept Between 1 And 50)
parts.working: 1 mark for correct operators and both limits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the data type and field size you would set so that only whole numbers are accepted.
parts.answer: Number – Integer (accept Long Integer/Byte).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write suitable validation text that would be shown if the rule is broken.
parts.answer: E.g. 'Quantity must be a whole number from 1 to 50.'
parts.working: 1 mark for a message that tells the user what to enter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A car park system stores vehicle registrations in the form ABC-123: three capital letters, a hyphen, then three digits. Describe how a format check would validate this field.
parts.answer: It checks that the data matches the pattern: three letters, then '-', then three digits (in the right positions).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one registration that would pass the format check and one that would fail.
parts.answer: Pass e.g. LEB-472; fail e.g. LEB472 / 12-ABC / LE-4721.
parts.working: 1 mark for both correct.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a registration that passes the format check could still be wrong.
parts.answer: Validation only checks that data is sensible/matches the rules, not that it is correct; e.g. LEB-427 typed instead of LEB-472 would pass.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hotel's database table BOOKINGS has a field Nights. A guest can stay from 1 to 28 nights inclusive. Write the validation rule for this field.
parts.working: 1 mark each correct boundary with the correct operator. Accept 'Between 1 And 28'.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The rule was entered by mistake as >1 AND <28. State the two valid numbers of nights that would be wrongly rejected.
parts.answer: 1 and 28
parts.working: 1 mark for both. The boundary values fail because > and < exclude them.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A receptionist types 15 instead of 5. Explain why the range check does not detect this error.
parts.answer: 15 is still within the range 1 to 28 so it is accepted.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A college library card number has four digits followed by a check digit. The check digit is calculated like this:
• multiply the four digits by 5, 4, 3 and 2 in turn
• add the results
• find the remainder when the total is divided by 11
• the check digit is 11 minus the remainder (if this is 11 use 0; if it is 10 use X).
Calculate the check digit for the digits 7305. Show your working.
parts.answer: 9 (full card number 73059)

parts.label: b
parts.text: A clerk types 7350 followed by the check digit 9. Show that the error is detected.
parts.answer: For 7350: 35 + 12 + 15 + 0 = 62; 62 ÷ 11 remainder 7; check digit should be 4, not 9, so the number is rejected.
parts.working: M1: correct weighted sum 62. A1: calculated check digit 4 ≠ 9, so error detected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a consistency check.
parts.answer: A check that compares the data in one field with the data in another field to make sure they agree / do not contradict each other.
parts.working: 1 mark: compares two (or more) fields. 1 mark: data must be consistent/logical.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A library system stores DateBorrowed and DateReturned. Give a consistency check for these two fields and an example of data it would reject.
parts.answer: DateReturned must be on or after DateBorrowed; e.g. DateBorrowed 12/10/2026 and DateReturned 05/10/2026 would be rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark: rule. 1 mark: example that breaks it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A mobile top-up website asks for: PhoneNumber (11 digits, starting 03), Network (one of five companies), Amount (Rs 100 to Rs 5000) and EmailForReceipt (must be filled in). Name the most suitable validation check for each field.
parts.answer: PhoneNumber: format check (or length check). Network: lookup check. Amount: range check. EmailForReceipt: presence check.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept length check for PhoneNumber. Do not accept the same check name for Network and Amount.

practice.stem:
A bookshop checks book numbers using a check digit. The first 12 digits of a book number are 978627880415. The check digit is calculated like this:
• multiply the 1st, 3rd, 5th … 11th digits by 1 and the 2nd, 4th, 6th … 12th digits by 3
• add the results
• find the remainder when the total is divided by 10
• if the remainder is 0 the check digit is 0, otherwise the check digit is 10 minus the remainder.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the check digit for this book number. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A shop assistant types the number as 978627880451 followed by the check digit 1. Explain how the computer detects the error.
parts.answer: The computer recalculates the check digit from the 12 digits typed: total becomes 131, remainder 1, check digit 9; 9 does not match the typed check digit 1, so the number is rejected (transposition error found).
parts.working: 1 mark for recalculating and comparing, 1 mark for correct values 131/9.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A warehouse uses a 6-digit product number followed by a check digit. The digits are multiplied by weights 1, 3, 1, 3, 1, 3 in turn and added. The check digit is the number that must be added to this total to reach the next multiple of 10 (0 if the total is already a multiple of 10).
Calculate the check digit for 482916.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A worker swaps the second and third digits and types 428916. Show that the check digit detects this.
parts.answer: 4 + 6 + 8 + 27 + 1 + 18 = 64, so the check digit would be 6, not 4; the number is rejected.
parts.working: M1: sum 64. A1: 6 ≠ 4, error detected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Another worker swaps the last two digits and types 482961. Show that this error is not detected, and explain why.
parts.answer: 4 + 24 + 2 + 27 + 6 + 3 = 66, check digit 4, the same as before, so it is accepted. The swapped digits 1 and 6 differ by 5; 3×1 + 1×6 = 9 and 1×1 + 3×6 = 19 differ by 10, so the last digit of the total is unchanged.
parts.working: M1: sum 66 giving check digit 4. A1: explanation that the change in total is a multiple of 10 (digits differ by 5).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A national identity card number is stored in the form 35202-1234567-1: five digits, a hyphen, seven digits, a hyphen and one digit. Describe how a format check (input mask) could be set up for this field.
parts.answer: Set the input mask so that positions 1–5, 7–13 and 15 must be digits and positions 6 and 14 are fixed hyphens, e.g. 00000-0000000-0; any entry not matching this pattern is rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark: digits required in the correct positions. 1 mark: fixed hyphens in positions 6 and 14 / total of 15 characters.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A developer suggests using only a length check of exactly 15 characters instead. Give one entry that the length check would accept but the format check would reject, and explain why the format check is better.
parts.answer: e.g. 35202-12345X7-1 (or 352021-234567-1): it has 15 characters, so the length check accepts it, but it has a letter (or a hyphen in the wrong place). The format check tests the type of character in each position, not just the number of characters.
parts.working: 1 mark: a 15-character entry with the wrong pattern. 1 mark: format check tests each character position, length check only counts characters.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cricket scoring system stores the number of runs a batter scores in one innings. The analyst first suggests a range check of 0 to 400. Explain one problem with the upper boundary of 400.
parts.answer: There is no fixed maximum score in an innings; a genuine score above 400, though rare, would be rejected, so correct data could not be entered.
parts.working: 1 mark: no real maximum for runs. 1 mark: a genuine high score would be wrongly rejected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two checks that should be used on the Runs field and justify each.
parts.answer: Type check: runs must be a whole number, so text or decimals are rejected. A check with only a lower boundary (Runs >= 0): runs cannot be negative, but no upper boundary is set, so genuine record scores are accepted. (Presence check also accepted: every completed innings must have a score.)
parts.working: For each check: 1 mark name/rule, 1 mark justification linked to runs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three items that are found in user documentation.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g. how to load/run the software; how to save and print; how to add, edit and delete records; how to search/sort; hardware and software requirements; error messages and what to do (troubleshooting); FAQs; glossary; tutorials; screenshots; index/contents.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two items that are found in technical documentation but not in user documentation.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. program listing/code; flowcharts/algorithms; file structures; validation rules; programming language used; system design/data flow diagrams; test plans and results; known bugs.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State who uses user documentation and who uses technical documentation.
parts.answer: User documentation: the people who use the system (end users). Technical documentation: programmers/analysts/technicians who maintain, repair or upgrade the system.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The technical documentation for a school's new attendance app lists the hardware requirements and the software requirements. Give one example of each and explain why these requirements are included.
parts.answer: Hardware, e.g. a tablet with at least 4 GB RAM and a camera (for scanning ID cards). Software, e.g. Android 12 or later / a database management system. They are included so the technician installs the app only on equipment it will run on, and knows what to buy or upgrade.
parts.working: 1 mark hardware example. 1 mark software example. 1 mark reason (system will run correctly / correct equipment chosen). Brand names alone are not accepted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: User documentation for a school fees system includes a list of error messages and what they mean. Explain why.
parts.answer: If an error message appears, the user can look it up to understand what went wrong and what to do to fix it, without needing to call a technician.
parts.working: 1 mark: understand the error. 1 mark: can solve the problem themselves.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a glossary in user documentation and why it is included.
parts.answer: An alphabetical list of technical terms used in the guide with their meanings; included so that users who are not experts can understand the words used.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why technical documentation is produced for a new system and state who uses it.
parts.answer: Used by systems analysts/programmers/technicians; so that the system can be maintained, updated or repaired later; so that errors can be found and fixed by someone who did not write the system; so that the system can be upgraded/extended.
parts.working: 1 mark for who uses it, 2 marks for reasons.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A parking app has been developed for a city in Punjab. For each item, state whether it belongs in user documentation, technical documentation or both.
(i) program listing
(ii) how to log in
(iii) hardware and software requirements
(iv) list of variables
(v) troubleshooting guide
(vi) validation routines
parts.answer: (i) technical (ii) user (iii) both (iv) technical (v) user (vi) technical
parts.working: 1 mark for every two correct answers (max 3).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the limitations of a system are included in its documentation.
parts.answer: So users know what the system cannot do (e.g. maximum number of records or users) and do not try to use it for things it was not designed for; and so programmers know what may need improving later.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Technical documentation for a new exam results system includes sample runs with the test data used and the results produced. Explain why.
parts.answer: It shows the system was tested and works correctly; a programmer making changes later can re-run the same tests and compare results to check nothing has been broken.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A software company provides its user guide as online help built into the program instead of as a printed manual. Give two advantages for users of online help.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. available whenever the program is open, so it cannot be lost; can search for a topic quickly; can include hyperlinks, videos or animations; can be updated when the software is updated; help for the current screen can be shown.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of online help.
parts.answer: e.g. cannot be used if the program will not start / it takes up part of the screen while working / harder to read on screen for long periods.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: User documentation often includes examples of input screens and sample outputs (such as screenshots of a completed form and a printed report). Explain why.
parts.answer: Users can compare what they see with the examples, so they know how data should be entered and what correct output looks like, making it easier to learn the system and spot mistakes.
parts.working: 1 mark: shows how to enter data / what to expect. 1 mark: helps users learn or check results.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare user documentation and technical documentation.
parts.answer: Both describe the system and both include hardware/software requirements. User documentation is written for people who use the system, whereas technical documentation is for people who maintain/develop it; user documentation explains how to carry out tasks (save, print, search) in plain language, while technical documentation includes program code, file structures and validation rules; user documentation has tutorials/FAQs/troubleshooting, technical documentation has algorithms/flowcharts/test results.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 4; at least one similarity for full marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why user documentation often includes a troubleshooting section.
parts.answer: Users can solve common problems/error messages themselves without needing a technician; this saves time and support costs and the user can continue working.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A company in Karachi hires a new programmer to update a stock system written five years ago by someone who has since left. Explain how the technical documentation will help the programmer. Refer to three items in the documentation.
parts.answer: e.g. Program listing and comments show how the code works so the programmer can find where to make changes. File structures show the fields, data types and sizes so new fields can be added without damaging data. Test plan and results let the programmer re-test after changes to make sure the system still works. (Also accept list of variables, flowcharts/algorithms, validation routines, known bugs.)
parts.working: For each of three items: 1 mark for naming the item, 1 mark for explaining how it helps the update.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A troubleshooting section is being written for a school fees system used by office staff. Write three entries, each giving a problem the user might meet and the action to take.
parts.answer: e.g. 'Receipt does not print' – check the printer is switched on, has paper and is selected, then click Reprint. 'Error: student ID not found' – check the ID was typed correctly; search by name instead. 'Cannot log in' – check Caps Lock is off; after three failed attempts ask the administrator to reset the password.
parts.working: 1 mark for each entry that gives a realistic problem with a sensible, specific action. Vague actions such as 'ask for help' alone are not enough.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A wholesale company is deciding whether to give its shopkeeper customers a printed user manual or a set of short video tutorials for its new ordering app. Many of the shopkeepers have little experience of computers. Evaluate the two options and give a recommendation.
parts.answer: Videos: show exactly what to tap and in which order, easier for beginners and for people less confident reading; can be watched again; but need internet/data, cannot easily find one small detail, may be hard to watch while using the app on the same phone. Printed manual: can be read beside the phone while using the app, no internet needed, easy to flick to a page; but can be lost, costs money to print and post, may be hard to follow without pictures and becomes out of date when the app changes. Recommendation, e.g. short videos plus a simple printed quick-start card, because users have little experience.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for points about videos, up to 2 marks for points about the manual, 1 mark for relating to the users' inexperience, 1 mark for a justified recommendation. Max 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by phishing.
parts.answer: The criminal sends a legitimate-looking email (or message) that contains a link to a fake website, to trick the user into entering personal details such as passwords or bank details.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: email/message that appears to come from a genuine organisation | contains a link/attachment | link leads to a fake website | user tricked into giving personal/financial data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways a user can protect themselves from phishing.
parts.answer: Do not click links in unexpected emails – type the organisation's web address yourself; check the sender's address and look for spelling mistakes or urgent threats; use a spam filter.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: do not click links/open attachments from unknown senders | type the URL directly / use bookmarks | check the sender's email address carefully | look for poor spelling/grammar, generic greetings, urgency | use anti-spam/phishing filters | check for https/padlock before entering details | contact the organisation directly to confirm.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete each sentence using the correct term from this list: smishing, vishing, pharming, shoulder surfing.
(i) A fake text message that tries to get a person to call a number or visit a website is called ……
(ii) Watching a person type their PIN at a cash machine is called ……
(iii) A phone call in which a criminal pretends to be from the bank is called ……
(iv) Malicious code that redirects a user from a genuine website to a fake one is called ……
parts.answer: (i) smishing; (ii) shoulder surfing; (iii) vishing; (iv) pharming.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct term.

practice.stem: Usman's computer has started running slowly, files are disappearing and strange messages appear on screen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a computer virus.
parts.answer: A program that copies (replicates) itself and is designed to cause harm, such as deleting or corrupting files or making the computer malfunction.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: program/software that replicates itself | causes damage – deletes/corrupts data or makes the computer crash/run slowly. Accept: attaches itself to other files.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how anti-virus software helps protect Usman's computer.
parts.answer: It scans files and compares them with a database of known virus signatures; it also looks for suspicious behaviour (heuristics); infected files are quarantined or deleted, and the database must be updated regularly.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: scans files/memory/downloads | compares against a database of known virus signatures | heuristic checking for suspicious behaviour | quarantines or deletes infected files | warns the user | runs in the background / scans automatically | needs regular updates to recognise new viruses.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two signs that an email may be a phishing email.
parts.answer: It starts with a general greeting such as 'Dear customer', and it urges you to act quickly or your account will be closed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: generic greeting | spelling/grammar mistakes | urgent or threatening tone | sender address does not match the organisation | asks for personal details/passwords | link address differs from the displayed text | unexpected attachment | offer too good to be true.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why a bank will never ask a customer to send their PIN by email.
parts.answer: The bank already holds what it needs to verify the customer; a PIN must stay secret, and email is not secure, so any request for a PIN must be a scam.
parts.working: B1: PIN must be known only to the customer | email is not secure/can be intercepted | banks have other ways of verifying – any such request is fraud.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a brute force attack.
parts.answer: An automated program tries many possible passwords or combinations one after another until the correct one is found.
parts.working: 1 mark: systematic/automated trial of many combinations. 1 mark: continues until the correct password is found.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one way to make a system resistant to brute force attacks.
parts.answer: Lock the account after a set number of failed attempts, or use two-factor authentication, or a long password.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid prevention.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between phishing and pharming.
parts.answer: Both try to get personal data using a fake website. In phishing the user must open an email and click a link to reach the fake site. In pharming, malicious code installed on the computer (or a corrupted DNS server) redirects the user to the fake site even when they type the correct web address, so the user does not need to click anything.
parts.working: 1 mark for similarity: both aim to obtain personal data via fake websites. 1 mark: phishing relies on the user clicking a link in an email/message. 1 mark: pharming uses malicious code/altered DNS so a correctly typed URL is redirected without user action.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two methods that can be used to prevent pharming.
parts.answer: Use anti-malware software that can detect and remove pharming code; check that the website uses https and look at its certificate/address before entering details.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: up-to-date anti-malware/anti-spyware software | check URL is correct in the address bar | look for https/padlock and check digital certificate | use a trusted DNS service | be suspicious if a familiar site looks different.

practice.stem: A shop owner in Faisalabad finds that customers' card details have been stolen after they used the card reader at the shop counter.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe card cloning and explain how it could have happened at the shop.
parts.answer: Card cloning is copying the data from a card's magnetic stripe to make a fake card. A criminal could have attached a skimmer (a small reading device) to the card reader so that each card's stripe data was read when swiped, and a hidden camera or overlay keypad recorded the PIN.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: copying data from the card's magnetic stripe | to create a duplicate card | a skimmer fitted to/inside the reader | captures data when card is swiped | PIN recorded by hidden camera/fake keypad/shoulder surfing.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is meant by key-logging software and how it could be used to commit card fraud.
parts.answer: Spyware that records every key pressed on a keyboard and sends the log to a criminal; it could capture card numbers, PINs and passwords typed into online shopping or banking sites, which are then used to make purchases.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: a type of spyware | records keystrokes | sends the recorded data to a third party | captures card numbers/PINs/passwords typed by user | criminal uses the stolen details for purchases/withdrawals. Prevention not required.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a firewall protects a computer network.
parts.answer: A firewall sits between the network and the internet and examines all incoming and outgoing traffic. It checks each packet against rules set by the user or administrator and blocks traffic that does not meet them, such as from undesirable websites or unknown IP addresses. It can log attempted attacks and warn the user, and helps stop hackers gaining access.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: between the computer/network and the external network | monitors incoming and outgoing traffic | checks against a set of rules/criteria | blocks traffic that fails the rules | can block specified IP addresses/websites | keeps a log of traffic | warns the user of attempted access | helps prevent hacking/unauthorised access. Can be hardware or software.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two things a firewall cannot prevent.
parts.answer: It cannot stop a user deliberately sharing their password or data (or an employee misusing access); it cannot stop a virus brought in on a USB stick or one that is already on the computer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: users bypassing it e.g. with their own modem | viruses on removable media | individuals within the network misusing access | social engineering / phishing where user gives away details | attacks via encrypted traffic it cannot inspect.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each type of malware, describe what it does.
(i) Trojan horse
(ii) Ransomware
(iii) Adware
parts.answer: (i) Malicious code disguised as useful or legitimate software, which installs harmful programs (such as spyware) once run. (ii) Encrypts the user's files and demands payment before the decryption key is given. (iii) Displays unwanted advertisements on screen, often by redirecting the browser to advertising sites.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A worm does not need to attach itself to a file. Explain why worms can spread faster across a network than viruses.
parts.answer: A worm is a stand-alone program that replicates itself and spreads through networks automatically by exploiting security holes, without needing a user to open or run an infected file.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: stand-alone / does not need a host program | spreads by itself through the network / does not need user action.

practice.stem: A user posts to an online forum, but finds that the forum is full of offensive posts and links to dangerous downloads.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between a moderated forum and an unmoderated forum.
parts.answer: In a moderated forum an administrator checks posts and removes those that break the rules before or after they appear; in an unmoderated forum posts are not checked, so anything can be posted.
parts.working: 1 mark each: moderated – posts checked/filtered by an administrator, rule-breaking posts removed, users can be banned | unmoderated – no checks, posts appear without control.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two problems caused by spam and one way to reduce spam.
parts.answer: Spam fills inboxes and wastes users' time and storage; it may contain phishing links or malware. To reduce it, use a spam filter (or never reply to spam / do not publish your email address).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two problems: clogs inbox / wastes time deleting | uses storage/bandwidth | may contain phishing links / malware | replying confirms address is active. 1 mark for one reduction: spam filter | do not reply or click 'unsubscribe' on unknown mail | keep email address private | block senders | untick marketing opt-in boxes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a keylogger records what a user types.
parts.answer: It runs in the background and records each key that is pressed, then stores or sends the list of keystrokes to the attacker.
parts.working: 1 mark: runs unseen and records each keystroke. 1 mark: the record is stored or sent to the attacker.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one way to protect against keyloggers when a password is entered.
parts.answer: Use a password manager with autofill, or click an on-screen keyboard, instead of typing the password.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid method (on-screen keyboard, password manager, anti-spyware).

practice.stem: A company's network administrator reports that someone outside the company gained unauthorised access to the server and changed customer records.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by hacking and give one effect it could have on the company.
parts.answer: Hacking is gaining unauthorised access to a computer system. It can lead to data being deleted, changed or stolen, to identity theft of customers, and to loss of reputation and possible fines for the company.
parts.working: 1 mark for definition (unauthorised access to a computer system). 1 mark for one effect: data deleted/corrupted/changed | data stolen / identity theft | malicious software planted | loss of customer trust/reputation | legal action/fines.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Evaluate the use of user IDs with passwords, firewalls and two-factor authentication as methods for preventing hacking at this company.
parts.answer: User IDs and passwords are cheap and give each user their own access level, but weak, reused or stolen passwords are easily exploited. Firewalls block traffic from unknown sources and log attempts but cannot stop an attacker using stolen valid credentials. Two-factor authentication means a stolen password alone is not enough, though it adds cost and inconvenience. Conclusion: a combination of all three, with strong password policies, gives much better protection than any single method.
parts.working: Max 4 marks for comments on methods, at least one benefit and one drawback required; 1–2 marks for reasoned conclusion. Passwords: cheap, levels of access | weak/reused/shared/phished. Firewall: blocks unauthorised incoming traffic, logs attempts | does not stop insiders or stolen credentials, needs correct configuration. 2FA: stolen password insufficient | extra device/cost, staff inconvenience, phone lost. Conclusion: layered security / combination best.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A message arrives on Hamza's phone: 'Your parcel could not be delivered. Pay the Rs 150 redelivery fee within 2 hours at this link.' Hamza has not ordered anything. Explain why this message is likely to be smishing and what Hamza should do.
parts.answer: It is unexpected (he ordered nothing), it creates urgency with a 2-hour deadline, and it asks for payment through a link, which would take him to a fake site to steal his card details. He should not click the link or reply, delete or report the message, and if unsure contact the courier using its official number or website.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for reasons: unsolicited/he has no parcel | urgency/deadline pressure | link to unknown site | asks for card/payment details | small fee to make it seem harmless. Up to 2 marks for actions: do not click link | do not reply | delete/block/report as spam | check with company via official channels | install security software on phone.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why criminals ask for a small payment such as Rs 150 rather than a large amount.
parts.answer: A small amount seems believable and not worth worrying about, so more people pay without checking; the real aim is to capture the full card details, which are then used for much larger fraudulent payments.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: small amount lowers suspicion / seems genuine | the goal is the card details / personal data, which are misused for larger amounts.

practice.stem: An online games company stores the account details of two million players, including email addresses, dates of birth and saved payment cards.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three different security threats to this data.
parts.answer: Hackers breaking into the servers to steal the database; staff being tricked by phishing emails into revealing administrator passwords; ransomware encrypting the database and demanding payment.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three different threats applied to the company: hacking | phishing/social engineering of staff | malware/spyware | ransomware | pharming of players to fake login pages | key-loggers on players' computers | insider misuse | card fraud with stolen saved cards.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three measures the company should take to protect the data, explaining how each one helps.
parts.answer: Encrypt the stored data so that if it is stolen it cannot be read without the key; use firewalls and keep server software patched to block unauthorised access; require two-factor authentication for staff logins so stolen passwords are not enough.
parts.working: 1 mark per measure with how it helps, any three: encryption – data unreadable if stolen | firewall – blocks unauthorised traffic | 2FA/strong passwords for staff | access rights – staff see only what they need | anti-malware – detects malicious software | staff training on phishing | regular backups – recover after ransomware | do not store full card numbers / use payment provider.

practice.stem: A company's online shop is taken offline by a DDoS attack that lasts for two hours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack stops a website from being available to its customers.
parts.answer: Many computers, often infected and controlled remotely, send so much traffic to the server that it cannot respond to genuine customers.
parts.working: 1 mark: a very large amount of traffic from many computers (botnet). 1 mark: the server is overloaded and cannot serve real users.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one method that a company can use to reduce the effect of a DDoS attack.
parts.answer: Use a traffic filter or firewall that blocks traffic from suspicious sources; use a content delivery network or cloud service that spreads the load.
parts.working: 1 mark: a valid method (filtering, rate limiting, load balancing, cloud DDoS protection). 1 mark: explained as a way the traffic is blocked or spread out.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State three examples of personal data.
parts.answer: Name, home address, date of birth.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: name | address | date of birth | phone number | email address | ID card/passport number | bank details | photograph | medical history | school name. Sensitive personal data such as religion or ethnicity also accepted.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a student should not post their home address and school name on a social media profile.
parts.answer: Strangers could use the information to find where the student lives or studies, putting them at risk of being stalked or harmed, and it could be used for identity theft.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: can be located by strangers/predators | risk of physical harm/stalking/grooming | identity theft | information stays online and is hard to remove.

practice.stem: Sana, aged 14, has just joined an online gaming community.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three precautions Sana should take to stay safe while playing online games.
parts.answer: Use a nickname that does not reveal her real name; never give out personal details such as her address or school; do not agree to meet anyone she has met through the game (and report or block players who are abusive).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: use a username that is not her real name | do not reveal personal information | do not share photos | turn off location settings | do not meet online friends in person | use privacy settings | block and report abusive players | only use voice/video chat with known friends | be wary of links/downloads offered in-game | tell a trusted adult about anything upsetting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two risks of online gaming, other than strangers finding personal information.
parts.answer: Cyberbullying by other players; downloading malware disguised as game add-ons or cheats.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: cyberbullying | grooming by predators | malware/viruses in downloads/cheats | phishing for game accounts | in-game purchases/financial loss | addiction | violence in games.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why it is safer to use a website that the user knows is trustworthy when buying items online.
parts.answer: A trusted website is more likely to protect payment details with encryption and to deliver the goods; unknown sites may be fake and steal card details or take money without sending anything.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: trusted sites secure/encrypt payment data | unknown/fake sites may steal personal or card data | risk of not receiving goods / fraud.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a user should not let the browser save their card details when shopping on a shared computer.
parts.answer: Anyone who uses the computer later could make purchases with the saved card, or malware/other users could read the stored details, so the card could be used fraudulently.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: other users of the shared computer can see/use the saved details | could make purchases without permission | stored details may be stolen by spyware/hackers | user may forget to log out, leaving the account open.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a digital footprint.
parts.answer: The trail of data a person leaves online through their posts, searches, photos and activity, which can be found and may stay online for a long time.
parts.working: 1 mark: the record of a person's online activity. 1 mark: it can be seen by others and is hard to remove.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why a student should not post a photograph that shows the name of their school and their uniform.
parts.answer: Any two: it tells strangers where the student can be found; it can be used to target or bully the student; it reveals personal information about the student's routine.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid reason, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe four ways to stay safe when using email.
parts.answer: Only open emails and attachments from known senders; never reply to or forward emails asking for personal details; check the sender's address and do not click on links in suspicious emails; use a spam filter and report phishing emails.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: open emails only from known sources | do not open unknown attachments | do not click links in suspicious emails | never give personal details by email | use spam/junk filters | do not reply to spam | check sender address | use strong password on email account | be wary of emails asking for urgent action | do not forward chain emails.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a user should use bcc rather than cc when sending one email to 50 parents.
parts.answer: With bcc, recipients cannot see each other's email addresses, so the parents' personal data is protected and their addresses cannot be harvested for spam or misused.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: bcc hides recipients' addresses from each other | protects personal data/privacy / prevents addresses being collected for spam / avoids 'reply all' to everyone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Data protection legislation sets out principles that organisations must follow. Describe three of these principles.
parts.answer: Data must be processed fairly and lawfully; it must be collected for a specified purpose and not used in other ways; it must be accurate and kept up to date.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: processed fairly and lawfully | used only for the purpose it was collected for | adequate, relevant and not excessive | accurate and up to date | not kept longer than necessary | processed in line with the data subject's rights | kept secure | not transferred to countries without adequate protection.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why data protection legislation is needed.
parts.answer: It protects people's personal data from being misused, sold, lost or stolen, and gives people rights to see and correct the data held about them.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: protects individuals from misuse of their data | prevents data being shared/sold without consent | makes organisations keep data secure | gives individuals rights to view/correct data | reduces identity theft risk.

practice.stem: A private clinic in Lahore keeps patients' names, addresses, phone numbers and medical histories on its computer system.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the clinic must take extra care with medical histories compared with phone numbers.
parts.answer: Medical history is sensitive personal data; if it is leaked it could lead to discrimination, embarrassment or harm to the patient, so the law requires stronger protection.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: medical history is sensitive personal data | misuse could cause discrimination/embarrassment/harm (e.g. by employers or insurers) | stricter legal requirements.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three ways the clinic can keep the patient data secure.
parts.answer: Encrypt the data so it cannot be read if stolen; give each staff member a user ID and strong password with access only to the records they need; keep the server in a locked room and make regular backups.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: encryption | user IDs and strong passwords | access levels / permissions | firewall | anti-malware | physical security of the server room | regular backups stored securely | audit logs of who accessed records | staff training | two-factor authentication.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three ways a person can stay safe when using social networking sites.
parts.answer: Set the profile to private so only friends can see posts; accept friend requests only from people they know in real life; never post personal details such as their address, phone number or holiday plans.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: privacy settings / private profile | only accept friends known in real life | do not post personal information | do not post location/check-ins or holiday plans | think before posting photos | do not meet online friends alone | block and report bullying or abuse | use a strong password | be wary of links in messages.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why posting a photo of yourself in school uniform outside your house is a risk.
parts.answer: The uniform identifies the school and the house shows where you live, so a stranger could work out where to find you; once posted, the photo can be copied and shared beyond your control.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: identifies school and home location | allows strangers to find/track you | photo can be copied/shared and is permanent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how geotagging a photograph can put a person at risk.
parts.answer: The photo stores GPS coordinates; anyone who sees the photo can find where it was taken, which may show a home address or a regular place such as a school.
parts.working: 1 mark: the location (GPS) is stored in the photo's data. 1 mark: this reveals where the person is or lives.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways a victim of cyberbullying can respond to protect themselves.
parts.answer: Any two: keep screenshots of the messages as evidence; block the bully; report the account to the website or app; tell a trusted adult.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid response, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teenager receives friendly messages from someone who claims to be the same age and asks to keep their chats secret. Explain why this could be dangerous and what the teenager should do.
parts.answer: The person may not be who they claim – this could be grooming by an adult who builds trust and asks for secrecy to stop parents finding out, possibly leading to requests for photos or a meeting. The teenager should not share personal information or photos, should not agree to meet, should keep evidence, block and report the account, and tell a trusted adult.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for dangers: identity cannot be verified / could be an adult pretending | secrecy is a warning sign of grooming | may lead to requests for photos/personal details/meeting. Up to 2 marks for actions: tell a trusted adult | do not share personal data/images | do not meet | block and report | save the messages as evidence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why it is hard to remove information once it has been posted online.
parts.answer: Others may have taken screenshots or shared it before it is deleted; copies may be stored on servers, caches or archives that the person cannot control.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: screenshots/copies made by others | shared/reposted on other sites | stored in backups/caches/archives | search engines index it.

practice.stem: A school wants to put photographs of students taking part in sports day on its public website, with each student's full name under the photo.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the eSafety and data protection issues the school should consider before doing this.
parts.answer: Photos with full names are personal data, so the school needs consent from parents (and students) and must use the images only for the stated purpose. Naming students alongside their school lets strangers identify and locate children, creating a risk of grooming. Images on a public site can be copied and misused. Some students may have safeguarding reasons not to be shown. Benefits: celebrating achievement and promoting the school. Conclusion: publish only with written consent, use first names or no names, avoid close-ups, or use a password-protected area.
parts.working: Up to 5 marks for issues/benefits, 1 mark for reasoned conclusion. Points: personal data requires consent | purpose limitation | identifying children + school location = safeguarding risk | images copied/edited/misused | permanent once online | some students must not be identifiable (custody/safeguarding) | right to withdraw consent | benefit – celebrates students, promotes school. Conclusion: consent, no surnames, private area, review regularly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what a cookie is.
parts.answer: A small file that a website stores on the user's computer or phone to remember information about the user or their visits.
parts.working: 1 mark: a small file stored by the website on the user's device.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a user might refuse non-essential cookies when a website asks for permission.
parts.answer: Non-essential cookies may track the user's browsing across sites and build a profile of their interests, which is personal data the user may not want shared.
parts.working: 1 mark: tracking or profiling. 1 mark: the user's personal data is collected and shared without them needing it.

practice.stem: A parent is considering installing parental control software on the phone of their 14-year-old child.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of parental controls for a 14-year-old's privacy and safety.
parts.answer: Benefits: the parent can block harmful websites, limit screen time, and see who the teenager is contacting, which protects against grooming and inappropriate content. Drawbacks: the teenager's privacy is reduced; monitoring can damage trust; controls can be bypassed and do not teach the teenager to make safe decisions.
parts.working: Mark bands: 5–6 marks for a balanced discussion with at least two benefits and two drawbacks, each linked to privacy and safety. 3–4 marks for a list of points with some reasoning. 1–2 marks for a few general statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways a user can tell that a website is using SSL.
parts.answer: The web address starts with https:// instead of http://; a padlock symbol appears in the browser's address bar.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: https at start of URL | padlock icon | can click padlock to view the digital certificate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is meant by encryption.
parts.answer: Scrambling data using an encryption key/algorithm so that it is unreadable if intercepted; only someone with the correct key can decrypt it back to its original form.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: data is scrambled/converted into a form that cannot be understood (cipher text) | a key is needed to decrypt / unauthorised people cannot read it. Encryption does not stop data being intercepted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by encryption.
parts.answer: Scrambling data using a key so that it cannot be read without the matching key.
parts.working: 1 mark: data is scrambled/converted with a key so only authorised users can read it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference between plaintext and ciphertext.
parts.answer: Plaintext is data in a readable form; ciphertext is the scrambled form produced by encryption.
parts.working: 1 mark: plaintext is readable. 1 mark: ciphertext is the encrypted (unreadable) form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a private key in asymmetric (public-key) encryption, and who keeps it secret.
parts.answer: A key that only the owner (for example the web server) holds and keeps secret; it decrypts data that was encrypted with the matching public key.
parts.working: 1 mark: the key is known only to the owner and kept secret. 1 mark: it decrypts data encrypted with the matching public key (it is not shared like the public key).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the abbreviation HTTPS stands for.
parts.answer: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure.
parts.working: 1 mark: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what HTTPS tells the user when a website uses it.
parts.answer: That the connection between the browser and the website is encrypted.
parts.working: 1 mark: the data sent between browser and website is encrypted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps that take place when a browser connects to a web server that uses SSL.
parts.answer: The browser asks the web server to identify itself; the server sends a copy of its SSL (digital) certificate; the browser checks that the certificate is valid and issued by a trusted authority; if it trusts it, the browser tells the server, and the server acknowledges; an encrypted session then starts and data sent between them is encrypted.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: browser requests server to identify itself | server sends its SSL certificate | browser checks certificate is authentic/trusted/in date | browser sends a message to the server confirming trust | server sends back a digitally signed acknowledgement | encrypted session begins | data exchanged is encrypted with session key.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two items contained in a digital certificate.
parts.answer: The name of the organisation it belongs to, and the expiry date of the certificate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: organisation/owner name | serial number | expiry date | public key | name of the certificate authority (issuer) | digital signature of the issuer.

practice.stem: A student in Rawalpindi has a laptop with an encrypted hard disk. He also emails coursework to his teacher.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why encrypting the hard disk is useful if the laptop is stolen.
parts.answer: The thief cannot read any files on the disk without the decryption key/password, so personal data remains protected even though the laptop is gone.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: data is scrambled/unreadable | cannot be decrypted without the key/password, so data stays private.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why encryption does not stop an email being intercepted, and why it is still useful.
parts.answer: Encryption does not prevent a hacker copying the data as it travels across the network, but the copied data is meaningless to them without the key.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: data can still be intercepted/copied | but cannot be understood without the decryption key.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State two other situations where encryption is used.
parts.answer: Online banking transactions; storing data on a USB memory stick.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: online banking/shopping (https) | encrypting email | encrypting backups/USB drives | cloud storage | Wi-Fi (WPA2/WPA3) | messaging apps (end-to-end).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption.
parts.answer: Symmetric encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt; asymmetric encryption uses a pair of keys, a public key for encrypting and a private key for decrypting.
parts.working: 1 mark: symmetric uses one shared key. 1 mark: asymmetric uses a public and private key pair.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage of asymmetric encryption over symmetric encryption for sending data over the internet.
parts.answer: The public key can be shared openly without revealing the private key, so the two parties do not have to share a secret key in advance.
parts.working: 1 mark: no secret key needs to be sent or shared beforehand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A browser warns that the certificate for a page asking for a password was issued for a different website name from the one in the address bar. Explain why the user should not enter the password.
parts.answer: The certificate does not confirm that the page belongs to the site the user typed, so the page could be a fake site set up to steal the password; the browser cannot confirm the identity of the website.
parts.working: 1 mark: the certificate does not match the website's name, so its identity cannot be confirmed. 1 mark: the page may be a fake site that collects the password.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one thing the user should do after seeing this warning.
parts.answer: Stop and do not enter any password, personal details or card details; close the page or go to the site by typing its genuine address.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid action, such as leaving the page or not entering details.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a home Wi-Fi network should use WPA2 or WPA3 encryption rather than no encryption.
parts.answer: Without encryption, anyone within range of the signal can capture and read the data sent over the network, including passwords; WPA2 or WPA3 encrypts the data so it cannot be read.
parts.working: 1 mark: unencrypted data can be intercepted by anyone within range. 1 mark: WPA2/WPA3 encrypts the data so it cannot be read.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between encryption and hashing when a website stores passwords.
parts.answer: Encryption is reversible with the correct key so the original password can be recovered; hashing is one-way, so the original password cannot be recovered from the stored hash.
parts.working: 1 mark: encryption can be reversed with a key. 1 mark: hashing is one-way; the website compares hashes instead of recovering the password.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the purpose of a certificate authority (CA) in the use of digital certificates.
parts.answer: A CA is a trusted organisation that checks the identity of the website owner before issuing a digital certificate and digitally signs it. Browsers trust certificates signed by known CAs, so users can be confident that the website really belongs to the organisation named and is not a fake.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: trusted third party | verifies identity of organisation before issuing | issues and digitally signs certificate | browsers hold list of trusted CAs to check signature | gives users confidence site is authentic | can revoke certificates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A user sees a browser warning: 'Your connection is not private – the certificate has expired.' Explain what this means and what the user should do.
parts.answer: The website's certificate is no longer valid, so the browser cannot confirm that the website is genuine or that the connection is safe; it may be a fake site or poorly maintained. The user should not enter any personal or payment details and should leave the site (or contact the organisation by another method).
parts.working: 1 mark: certificate out of date/not valid. 1 mark: identity of site/secure connection cannot be guaranteed – possibly fake/pharming. 1 mark: do not enter personal details / leave site / check URL / contact organisation another way.

practice.stem: An online bookshop in Lahore wants customers to trust its website when they pay by card.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how SSL and digital certificates together protect customers when they buy from the bookshop.
parts.answer: The digital certificate, issued by a certificate authority, proves that the website really belongs to the bookshop, so customers know they are not on a fake site. SSL then creates an encrypted link between the browser and the web server, so card numbers and personal details are scrambled while they travel and cannot be read if intercepted. The padlock and https show customers the protection is in use.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: certificate authenticates the website/proves identity | issued/verified by a trusted certificate authority | protects against fake sites | SSL encrypts data between browser and server | card details unreadable if intercepted | https/padlock visible to reassure customers | data integrity – changes in transit detected.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the bookshop still needs other security measures even though it uses SSL.
parts.answer: SSL only protects data while it is being transmitted; once the card data is stored on the bookshop's server it must be protected with firewalls, encryption and access controls, and SSL cannot stop a customer giving details to a phishing site.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: SSL protects data in transit only | stored data on server needs encryption/firewall/access control | does not prevent hacking of the server | does not stop phishing/malware on customer's computer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 40-bit encryption key is compared with a 128-bit key. Calculate how many times more possible keys the 128-bit key gives. Give your answer as a power of 2.
parts.answer: 2⁸⁸ times more keys
parts.working: M1: 2¹²⁸ ÷ 2⁴⁰ = 2^(128−40). A1: 2⁸⁸ times more possible keys.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a longer key makes a brute force attack harder.
parts.answer: A brute force attack must try each possible key, and a longer key has far more possibilities, so it takes far longer.
parts.working: 1 mark: more possible keys, so trying them all takes much longer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by end-to-end encryption in a messaging app.
parts.answer: The message is encrypted on the sender's device and only decrypted on the recipient's device, so the company running the service cannot read the messages.
parts.working: 1 mark: encrypted on the sender's device. 1 mark: decrypted only on the recipient's device. 1 mark: the service provider cannot read the content.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why a law enforcement agency may not be able to read such messages.
parts.answer: Only the sender and recipient hold the keys needed to decrypt the messages.
parts.working: 1 mark: keys held only by the sender and recipient.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fake shopping website copies the padlock symbol from a real site. Describe how a customer can check the website's digital certificate before entering card details.
parts.answer: Click the padlock and view the certificate; check that the name on the certificate matches the website address and that the certificate is valid and issued by a trusted certificate authority.
parts.working: 1 mark: view the certificate through the padlock. 1 mark: check the domain name matches the website address. 1 mark: check the expiry date and the issuing authority.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a padlock symbol alone is not enough to show that a website is genuine.
parts.answer: The padlock only shows the connection is encrypted; a fake site can have a valid certificate for a different domain or use one issued to a fraudster.
parts.working: 1 mark: the padlock only confirms encryption. 1 mark: the site can still be fake and have its own certificate.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each physical safety risk in a computer room, give one way to prevent it.
(i) Electrocution
(ii) Fire from overloaded sockets
(iii) Tripping over trailing cables
parts.answer: (i) Do not bring drinks near computers / check cables for damage. (ii) Do not plug too many devices into one socket. (iii) Use cable ducts or tie cables together and keep them under desks.
parts.working: 1 mark each, any suitable prevention: (i) no drinks/liquids near equipment, check insulation, use RCCB, don't open casings while on | (ii) avoid overloading sockets, ventilate equipment, have CO₂ extinguishers, check wiring | (iii) cable ducts, cable ties, cables under floor/along walls, use wireless.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what a trailing cable hazard is.
parts.answer: A loose cable across a floor that people can trip over.
parts.working: 1 mark: a loose cable on the floor that can cause someone to trip.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one way to prevent trailing cable hazards in a computer room.
parts.answer: Tidy the cables with cable ties or trunking, or route them along the walls under the desks.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid prevention.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name one type of fire extinguisher suitable for an electrical fire.
parts.answer: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) extinguisher (or dry powder).
parts.working: 1 mark: CO₂ or dry powder.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why a water extinguisher must not be used on electrical equipment.
parts.answer: Water conducts electricity, which could electrocute the user.
parts.working: 1 mark: water conducts electricity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two precautions to take when lifting a heavy printer or server.
parts.answer: Any two: keep the back straight and bend the knees; get help or use a trolley; switch off and unplug the equipment first.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid precaution, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two features of a computer room that help people escape safely in a fire.
parts.answer: Any two: clearly marked exit signs; fire doors that open easily and are not locked; no furniture or boxes blocking the exit route.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid feature, up to 2.

practice.stem: A small office in Multan has computers on narrow desks, several extension leads plugged into each other and a kettle placed beside a printer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three safety hazards in this office and explain why each is dangerous.
parts.answer: Computers on narrow desks may fall and injure someone; extension leads plugged into each other overload the sockets and can overheat and cause a fire; the kettle could spill water onto the printer, causing electrocution.
parts.working: 1 mark per hazard with reason, any three: heavy equipment on narrow/unstable desk – may fall and injure | daisy-chained extension leads – overload, overheating, fire | kettle/liquids next to equipment – spill, electrocution/short circuit | trailing leads – tripping.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why water extinguishers should not be used on electrical fires, and state a suitable type.
parts.answer: Water conducts electricity, so the user could be electrocuted; a carbon dioxide (CO₂) extinguisher should be used instead.
parts.working: 1 mark: water conducts electricity / risk of electrocution. 1 mark: CO₂ (accept dry powder) extinguisher.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a health risk and a safety risk when using computers. Give one example of each.
parts.answer: A health risk is something that causes illness over time from using computers, such as repetitive strain injury (RSI) from long periods of typing. A safety risk is an immediate danger that could cause an accident or injury, such as electrocution from damaged cables.
parts.working: 1 mark: health risk – harm to the body built up over time from use. 1 mark: example (RSI, back pain, eye strain, headaches). 1 mark: safety risk – accident/immediate danger from the equipment. 1 mark: example (electrocution, fire, tripping, heavy equipment falling).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an overloaded socket with several adaptors can cause a fire.
parts.answer: Too many appliances draw more current than the cable or socket is rated for, so the wires overheat; the heat can melt the insulation and ignite nearby material.
