parts.working: 1 mark: total current exceeds the rating. 1 mark: the wires overheat. 1 mark: the insulation melts or nearby material catches fire.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe why drinks should be kept away from computer equipment.
parts.answer: A spill can short-circuit the electronics, which can cause electric shock or damage the equipment.
parts.working: 1 mark: spill causes a short circuit. 1 mark: danger of electric shock or damage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what should be done if a drink is spilled on a keyboard that is still plugged in.
parts.answer: Switch off and unplug the keyboard and computer before cleaning up, and do not touch the equipment with wet hands.
parts.working: 1 mark: isolate the power before cleaning.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a server room needs air conditioning.
parts.answer: Servers give off a lot of heat; air conditioning keeps the room cool so the equipment does not overheat and fail.
parts.working: 1 mark: servers produce heat. 1 mark: cooling prevents overheating and failure.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two features of a fire-resistant safe used to store backup disks.
parts.answer: Any two: it is made of thick metal that resists heat; it is insulated; it is sealed against smoke; it is rated to keep the contents below a set temperature for a time.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid feature, up to 2.

practice.stem: A school is setting up a new computer room with 32 computers, a projector and two laser printers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe four measures the school should take to reduce physical safety risks in the new room, giving a reason for each.
parts.answer: Use cable ducts or floor channels so cables are not trailing and students cannot trip; provide enough sockets so extension leads are not overloaded, which reduces fire risk; ban food and drink so spills cannot cause electrocution; place the printers and projector on strong, wide tables or fixed mounts so they cannot fall and injure anyone.
parts.working: 1 mark per measure with reason, any four: cable management – tripping | sufficient sockets/no daisy-chaining – overheating/fire | no drinks – electrocution/short circuit | sturdy desks / heavy items at the back – falling equipment | ventilation/air conditioning – overheating | CO₂ extinguishers – electrical fires | regular PAT testing of equipment – faulty wiring | RCCB/circuit breakers – electrocution | clear walkways/fire exits.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why laser printers should be placed away from students' desks.
parts.answer: Laser printers become hot (the fuser) and give off ozone and fine toner particles, which can irritate breathing, so they should be in a well-ventilated area away from where students sit; it also reduces noise.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: hot fuser – burn risk | ozone/toner particle emissions – breathing problems | needs ventilation | heavy – needs a stable base | noise/distraction.

practice.stem: A teacher plugs a 1800 W heater, a 350 W computer, a 120 W monitor and a 600 W printer into one extension lead. The lead is rated at 13 A and is connected to a 230 V supply.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total power of the four appliances.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the current drawn when the total power is supplied at 230 V. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether the extension lead is safe for these four appliances and suggest one change.
parts.answer: It is within the 13 A rating, but only just; a heater or other appliance should be moved to a separate socket to leave a margin.
parts.working: 1 mark: the current (12.48 A) is less than 13 A so it is within the rating. 1 mark: a valid change, such as moving the heater to its own socket or leaving a safety margin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a risk assessment identifies physical hazards in a computer room and ranks them in order of importance.
parts.answer: Walk through the room and list each hazard (for example cables, water, overheating, heavy equipment); for each one, decide how likely it is to happen and how serious the harm would be; then rank the hazards by the risk score and decide what controls are needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: lists the physical hazards in the room (e.g. cables, water, overheating, heavy equipment); estimates how likely each hazard is to happen; estimates how serious the harm would be; combines likelihood and severity into a risk level or score; ranks the hazards by this score and decides which controls are needed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the physical safety measures a bakery in Multan should take for a new office with 12 workstations, one fire exit and a server cabinet.
parts.answer: Measures: keep the exit and walkways clear and mark them; check cables and sockets so there are no overloaded sockets or trailing cables; keep food and drinks away from the equipment; provide CO₂ or dry-powder extinguishers suitable for electrical fires and train staff; secure the server cabinet, keep it cool and fix it so it cannot topple; test the fire alarm and carry out fire drills; provide an RCD and earthing.
parts.working: Mark bands: 5–6 marks for at least four measures each with a reason linked to the room. 3–4 marks for three or four measures with limited reasons. 1–2 marks for vague measures without reasons.

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A public library in Lahore is replacing the bar code labels in its books with RFID tags. State two advantages to the library of using RFID tags rather than bar codes.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. several books can be read at the same time; no line of sight is needed so books need not be turned to face the reader; tags can be read through covers/bags; tags are harder to damage than printed labels; data on the tag can be changed/updated.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two distinct advantages. Do not accept 'faster' alone without a reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one disadvantage to the library of using RFID tags.
parts.answer: Any one, e.g. tags cost more than bar code labels; tags can be read by unauthorised readers nearby; signals can be blocked/jammed by metal or interference; tags on adjacent books may be read by mistake.
parts.working: 1 mark for one valid disadvantage.

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write down the direct data entry device that is most suitable for each task.
(i) Reading the account and cheque numbers printed in special ink at the bottom of a bank cheque.
(ii) Reading pencil marks on 2000 multiple-choice answer sheets in a school.
(iii) Reading the strip on the back of an old-style hotel room key card.
(iv) Reading the price label on a packet of biscuits at a supermarket checkout.
parts.answer:
(i) Magnetic ink character reader (MICR)
(ii) Optical mark reader (OMR)
(iii) Magnetic stripe reader
(iv) Bar code reader/scanner
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct device. Brand names not accepted.

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps that take place when a cashier scans the bar code on a tin of beans at a supermarket checkout.
parts.answer: The reader shines (red/laser) light on the bar code; the light is reflected from the white spaces, not the black bars; the reflections are converted into a number (product code); the code is looked up in the stock database/file; the price and description are sent back to the till and shown/printed on the receipt; the stock level for the item is reduced by 1.
parts.working: 1 mark per step, max 4.

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)
practice.stem: A hotel in Murree gives each guest a plastic key card with a magnetic stripe. The guest swipes the card through a reader on the room door.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the data on the key card is read when it is swiped.
parts.answer: The stripe passes the read head of a magnetic stripe reader; the head detects the pattern of magnetised areas and converts it to digital data (the room code), which the door's microprocessor checks.
parts.working: 1 mark: stripe swiped past read head / magnetic stripe reader detects magnetised data. 1 mark: data converted to digital and compared with the code stored for the door.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two disadvantages of magnetic stripe key cards compared with key cards that contain a chip.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. the stripe is easily damaged by magnets/phones/scratches; the data can be copied (cloned) easily; stripe wears out with repeated swiping; must be swiped in the correct direction.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid disadvantages.

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two differences between a QR code and a one-dimensional bar code.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. a QR code is two-dimensional (squares in a grid) while a bar code is a row of lines; a QR code holds much more data (e.g. a whole web address); a QR code can be read from any angle; a QR code can be read by a smartphone camera without a dedicated scanner; a QR code still reads if partly damaged.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid difference (must compare both).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A fruit stall in Quetta displays a QR code so that customers can pay with a mobile banking app. Describe how a customer pays using the QR code.
parts.answer: The customer opens the banking app and uses the phone camera to scan the QR code; the app reads the stall's account details from the code; the customer types the amount and confirms with a PIN/fingerprint; the money is transferred and both see a confirmation.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: scan with phone camera/app; account details decoded from code; amount entered and authorised (PIN/biometric); payment transferred and confirmation shown.

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A warehouse in Karachi stores boxes of spare parts. It is deciding whether to label the boxes with bar codes or with RFID tags. Compare the use of bar code readers and RFID readers for identifying the boxes.
parts.answer: Similarities and differences written as linked comparisons, e.g. both read data without typing so reduce errors; both identify the box and look up its record in the stock file. RFID reads by radio waves while a bar code reader uses light reflected from the code; RFID needs no line of sight but a bar code must face the reader; RFID can read many boxes at once whereas bar codes are scanned one at a time; RFID tags can be read from further away; RFID tag data can be rewritten but a printed bar code cannot be changed; RFID tags cost more than printed labels; bar codes are easily damaged/dirtied, RFID tags are more robust.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point, max 6. At least one similarity needed for full marks. Points must compare the two (e.g. 'RFID…whereas bar code…'); a list of separate features in two columns max 4.

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A museum in Istanbul places a QR code next to each exhibit. Describe how a visitor uses the QR code to see more information about an exhibit.
parts.answer: Visitor opens the camera/QR app on their smartphone; points the camera at the QR code; the app decodes the pattern (into a URL/text); the phone opens the web page/shows the information or plays a video/audio guide.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three steps in a sensible order.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two advantages to the museum of using QR codes rather than printed information boards.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. information can be updated online without reprinting; can link to video/audio/multiple languages; QR code takes very little wall space; cheap to produce; can store more data than a bar code.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of QR codes for visitors.
parts.answer: Any one, e.g. visitor needs a smartphone with a camera; needs internet access/mobile data to open the page; a QR code can be replaced by a fake one linking to a malicious site.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A national survey in Pakistan uses printed forms. Part of each form has answer boxes that people shade in with a pencil. Another part asks people to write their address in capital letters. Explain why an optical mark reader (OMR) is used for the shaded boxes.
parts.answer: OMR detects the position of the marks in set positions; very fast so thousands of forms are processed quickly; more accurate than a person typing the answers.
parts.working: 1 mark for how it works/what it detects, 1 mark for a linked benefit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the addresses are read using a scanner with optical character recognition (OCR) software and not an OMR.
parts.answer: OMR can only detect whether a box is shaded, not read letters; OCR converts the scanned image of the handwriting/characters into editable text that can be stored in the database.
parts.working: 1 mark for why OMR is unsuitable, 1 mark for what OCR does.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one disadvantage of using OCR to read the addresses.
parts.answer: Handwriting may be unclear so characters are misread/errors need checking; poor-quality forms are rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A customer in a restaurant in Dubai pays by inserting a chip and PIN card into a hand-held card reader. Describe the steps involved in making this payment.
parts.answer: The waiter enters the amount; the card is inserted into the reader; the customer types the PIN on the keypad; the PIN is checked against the one stored on the chip; if correct, the card details are sent to the bank (securely/encrypted); the bank checks the account has enough funds; the payment is authorised and the money is transferred; the reader displays 'approved' and a receipt is printed; if the PIN is wrong the transaction is rejected (after limited attempts card locked).
parts.working: 1 mark per valid step in order, max 5.

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)
practice.stem: Cars using a motorway have an RFID tag stuck on the inside of the windscreen. When a car passes through the toll plaza, the barrier lifts without the car stopping and the toll is taken from the driver's prepaid account.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the RFID system identifies the car and charges the toll.
parts.answer: A reader at the toll plaza sends out radio waves; the tag's antenna picks them up and the tag sends back its unique ID; the computer looks up the ID in the database of accounts, deducts the toll from that account and opens the barrier.
parts.working: 1 mark each: reader sends radio waves / tag responds; unique tag ID transmitted; ID matched to account in database and toll deducted (and barrier raised).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage of this system for drivers and one advantage for the motorway company.
parts.answer: Drivers: no need to stop/queue or carry cash, so journeys are faster. Company: fewer toll staff needed / fewer cash-handling errors / traffic flows faster with less congestion.
parts.working: 1 mark for a driver advantage; 1 mark for a company advantage.

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)
practice.stem: Many smartphones can make contactless payments using near field communication (NFC).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a customer pays for groceries using NFC on a smartphone.
parts.answer: The cashier enters the total on the card reader; the customer unlocks the payment app with fingerprint/face/PIN; the phone is held close to (within a few cm of) the reader; the payment details are sent by NFC radio and the payment is authorised.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: amount entered on reader; customer authenticates on phone; phone held very close to reader; data passed by short-range radio/NFC and payment approved.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why paying with a smartphone can be more secure than tapping a contactless bank card.
parts.answer: The phone must be unlocked with a fingerprint/face/PIN before paying, so a thief who steals it cannot easily use it; the phone sends a one-time code (token) instead of the real card number, so intercepted data is useless.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two explained points (biometric/PIN check before every payment; real card number not transmitted / token used).

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A café in Islamabad accepts contactless card payments for amounts up to a set limit. Describe how a contactless payment is made.
parts.answer: Total is entered on the card reader/till; customer holds the card (or phone) close to the reader; data is sent by radio waves (RFID/NFC) from the chip; the transaction is encrypted; the card details are checked with the bank and the payment is authorised; reader shows that the payment is accepted (beep/green light) and a receipt can be given. No PIN is needed below the limit.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 4.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two security concerns about contactless payments.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. a stolen card can be used without knowing the PIN (up to the limit); a criminal with a hidden reader close by could read card data (skimming/eavesdropping); a customer might pay twice by mistake if the card is near the reader again.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two explained concerns.

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: A dairy farm near Sahiwal puts a passive RFID tag in each cow's ear. Describe how the reader obtains the data from a passive RFID tag.
parts.answer: The reader sends out radio waves; the tag's antenna picks up the radio signal, which provides the energy to power the tag (no battery); the tag sends back its stored data (unique ID) as radio waves; the reader receives the data and passes it to the computer (where the cow's record is looked up).
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain three reasons why RFID tags are more suitable than bar code labels for identifying the cows.
parts.answer: Cows move, and RFID needs no line of sight so the cow does not need to be held still; many cows can be read at once as they pass through a gate; a tag works when covered in mud/dirt whereas a bar code would become unreadable; tags are tough/waterproof; data on the tag (e.g. vaccination date) can be updated.
parts.working: 1 mark for each explained reason, max 3.

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)

parts.label: a
parts.text: An international airport is planning to attach RFID tags to all checked-in luggage instead of using printed bar code labels. Evaluate this plan.
parts.answer: Benefits: bags read automatically as they pass on conveyors without line of sight, so fewer lost/misrouted bags; many bags read at once speeds up sorting; tags readable at longer range and when label is creased/torn; passengers could track bags; data can be updated along the route. Drawbacks: tags cost more per bag than paper labels; all airports on the route need RFID readers or bags still need bar codes; radio signals can be blocked by metal/liquids in bags; tags may be read by unauthorised readers (privacy); setup costs of new readers and staff training. Conclusion with a justified judgement.
parts.working: Level marking: 5–6 marks: benefits and drawbacks both well developed with a reasoned conclusion; 3–4 marks: both sides with some development; 1–2 marks: one side or list-like points. Up to 1 mark per developed point, max 6.

practice.subtopic: Direct data entry devices (bar codes, RFID, QR)
practice.stem: A hospital in Karachi plans to give each patient a wristband with a bar code. Nurses will scan the wristband and the bar code on each medicine packet before giving a dose.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of bar codes on patient wristbands and medicine packets in this hospital.
parts.answer: Benefits: correct patient is identified, reducing the risk of giving the wrong medicine; the system can check that the medicine and dose match the prescription and warn the nurse; doses are recorded automatically with the time, so records are accurate and complete; faster than writing notes. Drawbacks: cost of scanners, printers and software; bar codes can be damaged/wet/smudged and fail to scan, so manual entry may be needed; nurses need training; if the system fails, a backup paper method is needed; a scan must be in line of sight, which may disturb a sleeping patient. Conclusion: likely worthwhile because patient safety improves.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for benefits/drawbacks explained in context (max 4 if only one side); 1 mark for balance of both sides; 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write down the most suitable input device for each task.
(i) A journalist recording a spoken interview to be stored on a laptop.
(ii) A passenger selecting a destination on a ticket machine at a railway station.
(iii) A pilot in training controlling a flight simulator.
(iv) A student copying a printed photograph into a school magazine file.
parts.answer:
(i) Microphone
(ii) Touch screen
(iii) Joystick
(iv) Scanner
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept keypad for (ii); do not accept mouse.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teacher in Peshawar wants to put copies of her printed worksheets on the school website. Name the input device she should use.
parts.answer: Scanner (flatbed scanner).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: She uses optical character recognition (OCR) software with this device. Give two advantages of using OCR software instead of retyping the worksheets.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. faster than retyping; text can then be edited in a word processor; fewer typing errors; text can be searched; text can be converted to other formats/read aloud.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how a television remote control sends instructions to the television.
parts.answer: By infrared signals (accept Bluetooth/radio for some models).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two uses of a driving wheel as an input device.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. driving games; driving simulators for learner drivers; training lorry/bus drivers; remote control of model cars/drones.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write down the most suitable input device for each task.
(i) Moving the pointer on a laptop when there is no space for a mouse.
(ii) Showing a student's face to her teacher during an online lesson.
(iii) Selecting items directly on a screen by pointing at it with a pen-shaped device connected to the computer.
(iv) Typing the text of a long letter.
parts.answer: (i) Touchpad (ii) Webcam (iii) Light pen (iv) Keyboard
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct device.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a light pen is.
parts.answer: A pen-shaped pointing device connected to the computer that is used to select items or draw directly on the screen; it detects light from the screen to work out its position.
parts.working: 1 mark: pen-shaped device used directly on the screen. 1 mark: used to select/draw; detects light/position on screen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one use of a light pen and one disadvantage of using it.
parts.answer: Use: e.g. selecting options or drawing on screen in CAD / point-of-sale or design work. Disadvantage: e.g. holding the arm up to the screen is tiring; it may not work with all types of monitor; it blocks part of the screen; it needs a cable.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid use; 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fast-food restaurant in Lahore installs touch screens so that customers can place their own orders. Explain two advantages of using touch screens for this purpose.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. easy to use by selecting pictures/icons so little training needed; no separate keyboard/mouse that can be stolen or damaged; options limited to the menu, so fewer input errors; can be cleaned/wiped easily; faster for customers so queues are shorter.
parts.working: 1 mark each for an advantage with a reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages of using touch screens for this purpose.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. screens get dirty/greasy and need regular cleaning (hygiene); limited options compared with a keyboard for special requests; screens can be scratched or cracked; people with poor eyesight/disabilities may find them hard to use; arm fatigue if used for a long time.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A doctor in a clinic is choosing between a keyboard and a microphone with speech recognition software to enter patient notes. Compare these two input methods for this task.
parts.answer: Both enter text into the patient record. A microphone is faster/hands-free so the doctor can examine the patient while speaking, whereas typing needs both hands; speech recognition may misrecognise medical words/accents and needs training, while typing is more accurate for unusual words; background noise in a busy clinic affects the microphone but not a keyboard; speaking aloud may let others hear confidential details, whereas typing is private; a keyboard is cheap and familiar.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid comparison point, max 4. Points must compare the two methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A power station control room uses trackerballs instead of mice. Describe what a trackerball is.
parts.answer: A pointing device with a ball on top that the user rolls with the fingers/thumb/palm; the device itself stays still, and buttons are used to click/select.
parts.working: 1 mark for the rolled ball, 1 mark for staying stationary/buttons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why trackerballs are suitable for the control room.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. needs less desk space because the device does not move; can be fixed into the control desk so it cannot be knocked off/stolen; easier for people with limited hand/wrist movement; more accurate control of the pointer for fine positioning.
parts.working: 1 mark each for an explained reason.

practice.stem: A burger shop in Hyderabad uses a till with a concept keyboard. Each key has a picture of a menu item, such as a burger, a drink or chips.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why a concept keyboard is suitable for this till.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. staff press one key for a whole item, so orders are entered very quickly; pictures/words on keys mean little training is needed and fewer errors are made; keys are often sealed under a flat membrane so spilled drinks and grease do not damage it and it is easy to clean.
parts.working: For each of two reasons: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for the explanation linked to the shop.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one drawback of using a concept keyboard.
parts.answer: When the menu changes, the key overlay/pictures must be changed; it cannot be used for typing general text.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid drawback.

practice.stem: A taxi company in Islamabad fits each car with a microphone and voice-recognition software so that drivers can speak commands such as 'Accept next booking'.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why voice input is safer than a touch screen for the drivers.
parts.answer: The driver can keep both hands on the steering wheel and eyes on the road because nothing needs to be looked at or pressed.
parts.working: 1 mark: hands stay on the wheel. 1 mark: eyes stay on the road / no distraction looking at a screen.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two problems the drivers might have with the voice-recognition system.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. road/engine/passenger noise causes commands to be misheard; strong accents or mixing Urdu and English words may not be recognised; the driver may have to repeat commands, which is frustrating; the software may need training to each voice.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid problems.

practice.stem: A university in Lahore is buying laptops with a built-in webcam for online tutorials.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages of a built-in webcam compared with a separate webcam.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. nothing extra to carry or connect; no extra cost; always in the correct position at the top of the screen; no cable or USB port needed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two disadvantages of built-in webcams.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. image quality is often lower; the camera cannot be moved/angled separately from the screen; malware could switch it on to spy on the user; cannot be replaced easily if it breaks.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A fashion designer in Faisalabad currently draws designs with a mouse. Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of using a graphics tablet instead of a mouse.
parts.answer: Benefits: pen/stylus is held like a pencil so drawing is more natural and accurate; pressure sensitivity gives thicker/thinner lines; fine detail is easier; less strain on the wrist than gripping a mouse for long periods; hand-drawn designs can be traced. Drawbacks: more expensive than a mouse; takes time to learn because the hand moves on the tablet while looking at the screen; takes up more desk space; stylus can be lost; not as good for general tasks such as clicking menus. Conclusion, e.g. worthwhile for a designer who draws all day.
parts.working: Up to 1 mark per developed point, max 4 for one side only; 6 marks needs both sides and a conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why ATMs use a numeric keypad rather than a full keyboard.
parts.answer: Only numbers are needed (PIN, amount), so a small keypad is enough; it is smaller, tougher and easier to make weatherproof/vandal-proof; fewer keys means faster and fewer errors.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two explained points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two problems customers may have when using the numeric keypad at an ATM.
parts.answer: People nearby can watch the PIN being typed (shoulder surfing); keys are small, so people with large fingers or poor eyesight can press the wrong key; keypads can be fitted with fake overlays to record PINs; hard to use in bright sunlight.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest one feature of the keypad that helps a customer who is blind or partially sighted.
parts.answer: A raised dot on the 5 key / braille on keys; or a headphone socket for spoken instructions; large high-contrast keys.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A photographer's digital camera takes photos that are 6000 pixels wide and 4000 pixels high. Each pixel uses 3 bytes. Use 1 MB = 1 048 576 bytes and 1 GB = 1024 MB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the size of one uncompressed photo in MB. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The camera saves each photo as a .jpg with an average size of 8 MB. Calculate how many photos fit on a 64 GB memory card.
parts.answer: 8192 photos

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a high number of pixels is useful when the photo will be printed as a large poster.
parts.answer: More pixels means more detail; the image can be enlarged to poster size without the pixels becoming visible (pixelation/blurring).
parts.working: 1 mark: more detail/higher resolution. 1 mark: can be printed large without pixelation.

practice.stem: Zubair has a condition that makes it very difficult for him to control the fine movements of his hands. He wants to write essays and use the internet on his computer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the suitability of a microphone with speech-recognition software, a trackerball and a large-key keyboard as input devices for Zubair.
parts.answer: Microphone with speech recognition: he can dictate essays and commands without using his hands, much faster than typing; but software must be trained to his voice, errors need correcting, background noise causes mistakes. Trackerball: the ball is moved with the thumb/palm while the device stays still, so less precise movement is needed than a mouse and it cannot be knocked off the desk; but still needs some hand control and clicking. Large-key keyboard: bigger keys are easier to hit, fewer typing errors; but typing remains slow and tiring. Conclusion: speech recognition for text with a trackerball for pointing is likely the best combination.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks per device for points about suitability (advantages and limitations) in context; maximum 5 if no conclusion; 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of sensor that is most suitable for each use.
(i) Checking whether the soil in a greenhouse is too dry.
(ii) Turning street lights on automatically at dusk.
(iii) Detecting a person entering a room in a burglar alarm system.
(iv) Checking how acidic the water is in a river near a factory.
parts.answer:
(i) Moisture sensor
(ii) Light sensor
(iii) Infrared (motion) sensor (accept pressure sensor under a mat, acoustic/sound sensor)
(iv) pH sensor
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an actuator.
parts.answer: A device that converts a signal from a computer/microprocessor into physical action/movement (or other output such as heat).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of actuators used in a home.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. motor (in a fan, washing machine, automatic gate); pump; heater (element); solenoid/valve (in a water tap or door lock); buzzer.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write down the most suitable sensor for each use.
(i) Checking the acidity of the water in a fish farm.
(ii) Detecting a leak of cooking gas in a kitchen.
(iii) Detecting the sound of breaking glass in a shop at night.
(iv) Checking how damp the air is in a museum store room.
parts.answer: (i) pH sensor (ii) Gas sensor (iii) Acoustic (sound) sensor (iv) Humidity sensor
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct sensor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a computer monitoring system and a computer control system.
parts.answer: In a monitoring system the computer reads sensor data and displays/records it or warns a person, but does not change the conditions; in a control system the computer uses the sensor data to make decisions and sends signals to actuators to change the conditions.
parts.working: 1 mark: monitoring only records/displays/alerts. 1 mark: control uses actuators/outputs to change conditions.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
State whether each system is monitoring or control.
(i) A weather station that records rainfall every hour.
(ii) An oven that switches its heater on and off to stay at 180 °C.
parts.answer: (i) Monitoring (ii) Control
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A computer controls the temperature in a greenhouse. A temperature sensor sends readings to the computer. Explain why an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) is needed.
parts.answer: The sensor produces analogue data (continuously varying voltage); the computer can only process digital (binary) data, so the readings must be converted.
parts.working: 1 mark for sensor output analogue, 1 mark for computer needs digital.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The computer opens a window using a motor. Explain why a digital-to-analogue converter (DAC) may be needed and name the type of device that the motor is.
parts.answer: The computer's digital signal must be converted to an analogue signal/voltage to drive the motor; the motor is an actuator.
parts.working: 1 mark for DAC reason, 1 mark for actuator.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shopping centre car park has an automatic barrier that rises when a car drives up to it. Name a suitable sensor to detect the car.
parts.answer: Pressure sensor (in the road) / proximity sensor / magnetic field sensor / infrared sensor.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the role of an actuator in this system.
parts.answer: The microprocessor sends a signal to the actuator; the actuator (motor) converts the signal into movement to raise and lower the barrier.
parts.working: 1 mark for receiving signal from the processor, 1 mark for producing movement.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the sensor does not control the barrier by itself.
parts.answer: A sensor only measures/detects and sends data; a microprocessor must compare the data with stored values and decide what to do.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A house in Lahore has a microprocessor-controlled burglar alarm with infrared sensors in each room and pressure sensors under the doormats. The owner sets the alarm with a code on a keypad.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the alarm system detects an intruder and responds.
parts.answer: The sensors send data continuously to the microprocessor (through an ADC for analogue readings); the microprocessor compares the readings with stored/preset values; if the infrared sensor detects movement/heat or the pressure is above the preset value, it sends a signal to the actuators to sound the siren/flash a light (and may send a message to the owner); if not, it keeps checking in a continuous loop.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: sensors send readings to microprocessor; ADC converts analogue readings; compared with stored values; alarm/siren activated (signal sent) when value outside range; owner alerted; process repeats continuously while set.

practice.stem: A shopping mall in Karachi has automatic sliding doors at its entrance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name a suitable sensor to detect a person approaching the doors.
parts.answer: Infrared (motion) sensor / proximity sensor.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the microprocessor uses the sensor to open and close the doors.
parts.answer: The microprocessor receives readings from the sensor and compares them with a stored value; if a person is detected it sends a signal to the actuator (motor) to open the doors; the doors stay open while someone is detected and close after a set time with no one detected.
parts.working: 1 mark each: reading compared with stored value; signal sent to motor/actuator to open; doors closed after set time when no person detected / loop repeats.

practice.stem: A data logger monitors a river in Sindh using three sensors: temperature, pH and oxygen level. Each sensor takes one reading every 10 minutes and each reading uses 2 bytes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of bytes needed to store all the readings for 7 days.
parts.answer: 6048 bytes
parts.working: M1: readings per sensor per day = 24 × 6 = 144; × 7 days × 3 sensors = 3024 readings. A1: × 2 bytes = 6048 bytes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The logger has 64 KB of memory (1 KB = 1024 bytes). Calculate the greatest number of whole days of readings it can store.
parts.answer: 75 days

practice.stem: In a chemical factory, a computer monitors the pressure inside a large storage tank.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages of using a computer and pressure sensor rather than a worker reading a dial.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. readings are taken continuously, day and night, so a sudden rise is not missed; the computer reacts faster than a person, so an alarm sounds immediately; workers are not exposed to a dangerous area; readings are more accurate/consistent and are stored automatically for later analysis.
parts.working: For each of two: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for the explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what the computer does when the pressure rises above the safe limit.
parts.answer: It compares each reading with the preset maximum; if it is higher, it sounds an alarm/warns the operator (and in a control system opens a release valve using an actuator).
parts.working: 1 mark: compares with preset value. 1 mark: alarm/warning output (or valve opened).

practice.stem: A scientist leaves a temperature sensor connected to a data logger beside a glacier in Gilgit-Baltistan. The logger takes one reading every 30 seconds for 6 hours. Each reading is stored using 2 bytes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of readings taken.
parts.answer: 720 readings

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the storage space needed for the readings, in bytes.
parts.answer: 1440 bytes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why a data logger is used instead of a person taking the readings.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. readings are taken at exact equal intervals; works in dangerous/very cold conditions; can run day and night without breaks; readings are more accurate (no human error); readings are stored automatically ready for analysis.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A farm in Faisalabad uses a computerised irrigation system. Moisture sensors are placed in the soil and a pump supplies water. Describe how the system uses the sensors, conversion and actuator to keep the soil at the right moisture level.
parts.answer: Moisture sensor continuously measures the soil moisture; readings are analogue and sent to an ADC which converts them to digital; the microprocessor compares the reading with a pre-set value stored in memory; if the reading is below the pre-set value the processor sends a signal (through a DAC) to the actuator to switch on the pump/open a valve; if the reading is at or above the pre-set value the pump is switched off/valve closed; the process repeats continuously in a loop.
parts.working: 1 mark per correct point in a logical order, max 6. Do not credit 'the sensor turns on the pump'.

practice.stem: A poultry farm near Rawalpindi uses a microprocessor to keep the temperature in a chicken shed between 26 °C and 30 °C. The shed has an electric heater and an extractor fan.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the microprocessor uses sensor data to keep the temperature within the range.
parts.answer: A temperature sensor measures the temperature continuously and sends analogue data; an ADC converts it to digital; the microprocessor compares the reading with the stored values 26 °C and 30 °C; if below 26 °C it sends a signal to switch the heater on (and fan off); if above 30 °C it switches the heater off and the fan on (via actuators/relays, with a DAC if the device needs an analogue signal); if within range no change is made; the process repeats in a continuous loop.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any six: sensor reads temperature; ADC converts analogue to digital; compared with preset values; below 26 °C → heater on; above 30 °C → heater off / fan on; signals sent to actuators (DAC if needed); in range → no action; continuous loop.

practice.stem: Traffic lights at a busy junction in Peshawar are controlled by a microprocessor. Pressure sensors under the road count the cars waiting at each approach.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the microprocessor uses the sensor data to decide how long each light stays green.
parts.answer: The sensors send data on cars passing/waiting to the microprocessor; it counts the cars/calculates the queue length for each road; it compares these values with stored values/the other roads; it keeps the green light on longer for the road with the longest queue (up to a maximum time) and sends signals to change the lights.
parts.working: 1 mark each: data sent continuously; queue length/count calculated; compared with stored values / other approaches; timing changed and signal sent to the lights.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a sensor-controlled system is better than lights that change at fixed times.
parts.answer: It responds to the actual traffic, so cars do not wait at a red light when the other road is empty; queues are shorter and traffic flows better at different times of day.
parts.working: 1 mark: adapts to real traffic. 1 mark: less waiting/congestion/pollution.

practice.stem: A hospital uses incubators for babies born early. The air temperature and humidity inside each incubator are controlled by a microprocessor.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a digital-to-analogue converter (DAC) may be needed between the microprocessor and the heater.
parts.answer: The microprocessor outputs digital signals, but the heater may need a varying analogue voltage to change its power, so the DAC converts the digital signal into an analogue one.
parts.working: 1 mark: microprocessor output is digital. 1 mark: device needs analogue signal, so conversion is needed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why a microprocessor-controlled incubator is better than a nurse adjusting the heater by hand.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. it checks conditions continuously, day and night; it responds immediately to small changes; it is more accurate; nurses are free to do other care; readings are recorded automatically.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest what the system should do if a sensor stops sending readings.
parts.answer: Sound an alarm/alert staff immediately, and switch to a safe default setting (or a backup sensor) until the fault is fixed.
parts.working: 1 mark: alarm/alert nurses. 1 mark: safe default / backup sensor.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write down the most suitable output device for each task.
(i) Printing 600 report cards in a school office in one afternoon.
(ii) Printing one high-quality colour photograph at home.
(iii) Making a plastic model of a replacement part for a bicycle.
(iv) Playing train announcements to passengers on a platform.
parts.answer:
(i) Laser printer
(ii) Inkjet printer
(iii) 3D printer
(iv) Speakers
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teacher in Multan uses a multimedia projector in her classroom. Give two advantages of using a projector instead of a large monitor.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. produces a very large image so the whole class can see; cheaper than a monitor of the same size; portable/can be moved between rooms; can project onto an interactive whiteboard.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two disadvantages of using a projector.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. image is less clear in a bright room; bulb/lamp is expensive and may fail; fan can be noisy; people walking in front cast shadows; needs setting up/focusing.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write down the most suitable output device for each task.
(i) Printing multi-part invoices with carbon copies in a dusty workshop.
(ii) Playing a recorded announcement in a railway station.
(iii) Showing a presentation to 200 people in a hall.
(iv) Opening a valve in a water-treatment plant under computer control.
parts.answer: (i) Dot matrix printer (ii) Speakers (iii) Multimedia projector (iv) Actuator (e.g. motor/solenoid)
parts.working: 1 mark for each.

practice.stem: A car-parts warehouse in Gujranwala still uses dot matrix printers.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why the warehouse uses dot matrix printers.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. they are impact printers so can print on multi-part/carbon stationery; they work in dusty, damp or dirty conditions; continuous (fan-fold) paper can be used for long reports; running costs are very low.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two drawbacks of dot matrix printers.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. they are very noisy; print quality is poor; they are slow; colour printing is limited/expensive.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two uses of speakers connected to a computer.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. playing music/videos; listening to a video call; hearing voice output from a screen reader for blind users; alarms/warning sounds; language-learning recordings.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sound file is stored in digital form. Describe how it is turned into sound by the speaker.
parts.answer: A digital-to-analogue converter changes the digital data into an analogue electrical signal, which is amplified; the signal makes the speaker cone vibrate, producing sound waves.
parts.working: 1 mark: DAC converts digital to analogue (amplified). 1 mark: signal makes the cone/diaphragm vibrate to produce sound.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small accounting office in Islamabad prints about 3000 pages of black-and-white letters and invoices each week. Compare laser printers and inkjet printers for this office.
parts.answer: Both are non-impact printers that print text and graphics from the computer on plain paper. Laser printers are faster than inkjet printers, which suits large volumes; laser toner cartridges print many more pages than ink cartridges so cost per page is lower; laser output does not smudge, whereas inkjet ink can smudge while wet; inkjet printers are cheaper to buy; laser printers are larger and produce ozone/toner particles; inkjet printers are better for high-quality photographs; laser paper trays hold more paper. Conclusion: laser more suitable for this office.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 6. At least one similarity needed for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a 3D printer produces a solid object.
parts.answer: A design is created with CAD software/file; the software slices the design into thin layers; the printer builds the object one layer at a time (additive manufacturing) from material such as plastic/resin/powder; each layer is melted/bonded or hardened onto the layer below.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two uses of 3D printers in medicine.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. prosthetic limbs; artificial joints/implants; dental crowns/braces; models of organs for surgeons to practise on; tissue engineering; medical tools/splints.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each device is an input device, an output device, or both.
(i) Touch screen
(ii) Actuator
(iii) Light sensor
(iv) 3D printer
(v) Microphone
(vi) Multimedia projector
parts.answer:
(i) Both
(ii) Output
(iii) Input
(iv) Output
(v) Input
(vi) Output
parts.working: All six correct: 3 marks; four or five correct: 2 marks; two or three correct: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a touch screen can be described as both an input device and an output device.
parts.answer: It displays information/images to the user (output) and detects where the user touches the screen to make selections (input).
parts.working: 1 mark for both roles.

practice.stem: An office in Islamabad is replacing old LCD monitors that use fluorescent tubes behind the screen with LED-backlit monitors.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages of the LED-backlit monitors.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. LEDs reach full brightness immediately, so no warm-up time; they use less power, reducing electricity bills; they last longer, so fewer replacements; the monitors are thinner and lighter, saving desk space; they give brighter images with better contrast/colour.
parts.working: For each of two: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for the explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a thermal-bubble inkjet printer prints a page.
parts.answer: The data is sent to the printer (stored in a buffer); paper is fed in and the print head moves across the page; tiny resistors in the nozzles heat the ink, forming a bubble that pushes a droplet of ink onto the paper; as the bubble collapses, more ink is drawn in from the cartridge; the paper moves up a line at a time until the page is complete.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of the steps.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage of an inkjet printer over a laser printer for a family printing a few photos each month.
parts.answer: Cheaper to buy / produces high-quality colour photos / smaller.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem:
A school compares two printers for its office.
Inkjet: an ink cartridge costs Rs 4500 and prints 300 pages.
Laser: a toner cartridge costs Rs 18 000 and prints 2400 pages.
The office prints 1200 pages a month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost per page for each printer in rupees.
parts.answer: Inkjet Rs 15 per page; laser Rs 7.50 per page.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much the school saves each month on cartridges by using the laser printer.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The laser printer costs Rs 45 000 more to buy. Calculate how many months it takes for the savings to cover this extra cost.
parts.answer: 5 months

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps a laser printer goes through to print a page.
parts.answer: The page data is sent to the printer and stored in its memory/buffer; the drum is given a (positive) electrostatic charge; a laser beam scans the drum, removing the charge where the image will be (or vice versa), forming an electrostatic image; the drum is coated with charged toner, which sticks only to the charged/image areas; the paper is given an opposite charge and the toner is transferred to it as it passes the drum; the fuser heats and presses the toner so it melts onto the paper; the drum is discharged/cleaned for the next page.
parts.working: 1 mark per step, max 5.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a laser printer is suitable for printing a large number of copies of the same page.
parts.answer: The whole page image is formed on the drum at once so pages are printed very quickly/the toner lasts for many pages.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A tractor-repair workshop in Sahiwal often waits weeks for a small plastic bracket that costs Rs 650 to buy. It is thinking of printing the brackets on a 3D printer. The printer deposits 15 cm³ of material per hour. Each bracket has a volume of 22.5 cm³ and the material costs Rs 12 per cm³.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how long it takes to print 8 brackets, in hours.
parts.answer: 12 hours

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the material cost of one printed bracket and the total saving for 8 brackets compared with buying them.
parts.answer: Rs 270 each; saving Rs 3040

parts.label: c
parts.text: Evaluate whether the workshop should buy the 3D printer.
parts.answer: For: parts are made on site in hours instead of weeks, so tractors are repaired faster; each part is cheaper; parts can be customised. Against: printer cost and training; printing is slow for large numbers; plastic may be weaker than the factory part; designs (CAD files) are needed. Conclusion: worthwhile if brackets are needed often.
parts.working: 1 mark for an advantage, 1 mark for a disadvantage, 1 mark for a justified conclusion.

practice.stem: A lecture theatre in Faisalabad must choose between an LCD projector and a DLP (digital light processing) projector.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare LCD and DLP projectors.
parts.answer: Both project a large image from a computer and use a bright lamp. Most LCD projectors pass the light through three LCD panels (red, green, blue), whereas a DLP projector reflects light from a chip with millions of tiny mirrors and a colour wheel. LCD projectors often give brighter, more saturated colours, whereas DLP projectors often give higher contrast and deeper blacks. DLP projectors are usually smaller and lighter and give smoother video, whereas LCD images can show a visible grid of pixels ('screen door'). Some viewers see a 'rainbow' effect with DLP, and LCD panels can be affected by dust and can fade with age.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point that refers to both types (max 6). Max 4 if points are not linked comparisons.

practice.stem: A monitor has a resolution of 1920 × 1080 pixels and uses 3 bytes for the colour of each pixel. Use 1 MB = 1 048 576 bytes and 1 GB = 1024 MB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the memory needed to store one full screen image, in MB, correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A 10-second uncompressed video clip is shown at 30 frames per second. Calculate its size in GB, correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why videos are compressed before being streamed to a monitor over the internet.
parts.answer: Uncompressed video is far too large; compression reduces the amount of data, so it can be sent quickly over the available bandwidth without buffering and uses less data/storage.
parts.working: 1 mark: uncompressed files very large. 1 mark: compressed data streams faster / less bandwidth / no buffering.
