practice.stem: Bilal works in a call centre in Lahore, typing customer details for eight hours a day.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two health problems Bilal could develop from this work.
parts.answer: Any two: repetitive strain injury (RSI) in the wrists/fingers; back and/or neck problems; eyestrain; headaches.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept 'pain' without location.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For one of the problems named, describe one way of reducing the risk.
parts.answer: e.g. RSI – use a wrist rest / ergonomic keyboard and take regular breaks; back pain – use an adjustable chair with back support and sit upright; eyestrain – take regular breaks and use an anti-glare screen.
parts.working: B1 prevention matched to the named problem.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by repetitive strain injury (RSI).
parts.answer: Damage/pain to the muscles, tendons or nerves of the fingers, hands, wrists or arms caused by repeating the same movements many times.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two causes of RSI when using a computer.
parts.answer: Any two: continuous typing on a keyboard; repeated clicking/using a mouse; poor wrist position; not taking breaks; repeated texting on a phone.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each of the following health problems, give one cause when using a computer.
Problem 1: eyestrain
Problem 2: neck pain
Problem 3: headache
parts.answer: Eyestrain – staring at a screen for a long time / screen glare or flicker / poor lighting. Neck pain – screen at the wrong height so the head is tilted for long periods. Headache – glare or flickering screen / poor lighting / looking at screen too long without breaks.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why taking regular breaks from a computer helps to prevent health problems. Refer to two different problems.
parts.answer: Breaks rest the hands and wrists from repeated movements, reducing RSI; they also let the eyes rest from focusing on the screen, reducing eyestrain (and moving/stretching reduces back pain).
parts.working: 1 mark each for two problems linked to reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two items of equipment that reduce the risk of RSI.
parts.answer: Any two: wrist rest; ergonomic keyboard; ergonomic/vertical mouse; voice-recognition software; adjustable desk/chair (so arms are at the correct height).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two health problems that can result from sitting for long periods at a computer.
parts.answer: Any two: obesity; poor blood circulation (blood clots in the legs); back and neck pain; weakened muscles.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid health problem, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how screen glare and screen brightness can cause headaches.
parts.answer: The eyes have to work harder to focus on the screen when light reflects off it or the screen is too bright, which strains the eye muscles and causes headaches.
parts.working: 1 mark: glare or brightness makes the eyes strain. 1 mark: the strain causes headaches.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one way to reduce glare from a screen.
parts.answer: Position the screen away from windows or lights, or use an anti-glare screen filter.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid method.

practice.stem: A school in Karachi has opened a new computer room for students.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe four features of the room or its furniture that would help to reduce health problems.
parts.answer: Any four: adjustable chairs with back support; desks at the correct height; monitors that can be tilted/raised so the top of the screen is at eye level; anti-glare screens or blinds to reduce glare; good lighting; footrests; wrist rests / ergonomic keyboards and mice; enough space to move.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

practice.stem: A graphic designer uses a computer for long periods each day. An eye specialist advises the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet (about 6 metres) away for 20 seconds.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many of these short breaks the designer should take in a 7.5-hour working day.
parts.working: M1 7.5 × 60 ÷ 20 = 22.5. A1 22 complete 20-minute periods.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how the rule helps prevent eyestrain.
parts.answer: Looking into the distance lets the eye muscles relax after focusing on a close screen for a long time.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why sitting with poor posture at a computer can cause back problems.
parts.answer: Slouching or leaning forward for long periods puts strain on the muscles and spine of the back; without support the spine is not kept in its natural position, leading to pain.
parts.working: B1 poor posture / no back support for long periods. B1 strain on spine/back muscles.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways of preventing back problems.
parts.answer: Any two: use an adjustable chair with lumbar support; sit upright with feet flat on the floor or on a footrest; take regular breaks to stand and stretch; have the screen at eye level so you do not lean forward.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Sana's monitor faces a large window and the afternoon sun shines on the screen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how this could affect Sana's health.
parts.answer: Glare/reflections on the screen make it hard to see, so she strains her eyes and may squint, causing eyestrain and headaches.
parts.working: B1 glare/reflection. B1 eyestrain or headache.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest two ways of solving the problem.
parts.answer: Any two: move/turn the monitor so it is not facing the window (at right angles to it); fit blinds/curtains; use an anti-glare screen filter; adjust the screen brightness.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A teenager in Islamabad plays online games on a laptop on his bed for several hours each night.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify three health problems that could result and give a cause of each in this scenario.
parts.answer: Back/neck pain – sitting hunched on the bed with no back support and the screen too low; RSI – repeated use of keys/mouse/controller; eyestrain/headaches – looking at the screen for hours, often in a dark room.
parts.working: 1 mark per problem with scenario-based cause.

practice.stem: An office manager measures one employee's set-up: the top of the screen is 15 cm above her eye level and the screen is 30 cm from her face.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems with this set-up and how each should be changed.
parts.answer: Screen too high makes her tilt her head back, causing neck pain – lower it so the top of the screen is at or slightly below eye level. Screen too close (30 cm) makes the eyes work harder, causing eyestrain – move it back to about arm's length (roughly 50–70 cm).
parts.working: For each problem: 1 mark for the effect, 1 mark for the correction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how using a phone screen in bed late at night can affect a person's sleep.
parts.answer: The light from the screen can stop the body producing the hormone that makes people sleepy, and the activity keeps the brain alert, so it takes longer to fall asleep.
parts.working: 1 mark: screen light reduces the hormone that brings sleep. 1 mark: brain stays alert or stimulated so sleep is delayed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a lack of physical activity linked to long hours at a computer can lead to health problems. Give two health problems.
parts.answer: Staying seated for long periods burns fewer calories, which can lead to weight gain and obesity; poor circulation can result, and the risk of heart disease and diabetes increases.
parts.working: 1 mark: less physical activity means fewer calories burned. 1 mark: this leads to weight gain or obesity. 1 mark: any other linked health problem (poor circulation, heart disease, diabetes).

practice.stem: A data-entry company in Faisalabad has received complaints from employees about wrist pain, back pain and headaches.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the actions the company could take to reduce these health problems, including any drawbacks.
parts.answer: Actions: buy ergonomic keyboards, mice and wrist rests (reduces RSI); provide adjustable chairs and monitor stands (reduces back/neck pain); fit anti-glare screens and blinds, improve lighting (reduces headaches); schedule regular breaks and vary tasks; give training on correct posture; offer eye tests. Drawbacks: cost of new equipment; breaks reduce working time/output; staff may not follow advice; some solutions take time to show results. Conclusion: health measures reduce sick leave so are worthwhile.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point; max 5 without drawbacks or conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare the causes and prevention of RSI and eyestrain.
parts.answer: Both are caused by using a computer for long periods without breaks, and both are reduced by taking regular breaks. RSI is caused by repeated hand/finger movements on keyboard and mouse, whereas eyestrain is caused by staring at a screen, glare or flicker. RSI is prevented with wrist rests and ergonomic keyboards/mice, whereas eyestrain is prevented with anti-glare screens, correct lighting and regular eye tests.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity; up to 3 for linked differences (causes/prevention). Must compare, not list separately.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says, 'A laptop is better for your health than a desktop computer.' Evaluate this statement.
parts.answer: Points against: laptop screen is attached to the keyboard so the screen is usually below eye level, causing neck strain; small keyboard and touchpad can increase RSI; often used on laps or sofas with poor posture. Points for: the user can move it to a better-lit place; can be used standing; easier to take breaks and move. A laptop can be made healthier with an external keyboard, mouse and stand. Conclusion: neither is automatically healthier; it depends on how it is set up and used.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point on either side; max 4 if one-sided; 6th mark for a reasoned conclusion.

practice.stem: A hospital is introducing tablet computers so that nurses record patient observations at the bedside instead of on paper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two health risks to the nurses from using tablets in this way, and suggest a precaution for each.
parts.answer: Any two: neck strain from looking down at the tablet for long periods – hold it at eye level / use a stand on the trolley; RSI from repeated tapping/typing on a small screen – use voice input or a stylus and take breaks; eyestrain from small text – increase font size and screen brightness to suit lighting.
parts.working: For each risk: 1 mark risk with cause, 1 mark precaution.

practice.stem: A software company is considering software that records how long each developer works at a computer without a break.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether a company should monitor employees' computer use to protect their health and wellbeing. Refer to benefits and privacy.
parts.answer: Benefits: the company can spot long periods without breaks, encourage breaks and reduce RSI, eyestrain and stress; it can show a duty of care. Drawbacks: monitoring can invade privacy and damage trust; staff may feel pressured and more stressed by being watched; monitoring software may record personal data that must be protected under data protection law. A balanced answer reaches a reasoned conclusion, for example monitoring that is open, limited to health needs and agreed with staff.
parts.working: Mark bands: 5–6 marks for a balanced discussion of at least two benefits and two drawbacks, including privacy, with a reasoned conclusion. 3–4 marks for clear points with limited reasoning. 1–2 marks for one-sided or vague statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name three microprocessor-controlled devices commonly found in the home.
parts.answer: Any three: washing machine; microwave oven; smart fridge; central heating/air-conditioning controller; burglar alarm; smart TV; dishwasher; robotic vacuum cleaner; bread maker; smart lighting.
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept brand names.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a microprocessor-controlled washing machine increases the leisure time of the user.
parts.answer: The user selects a programme and the microprocessor controls filling, heating, washing, rinsing and spinning automatically, so the user does not need to stay with it and can do other things.
parts.working: B1 automatic control of the cycle. B1 user free to do other activities.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two microprocessor-controlled devices found in a car, other than the engine management system.
parts.answer: Any two: anti-lock braking system; airbags; parking sensors; cruise control; satellite navigation; climate control; lane-departure warning; automatic windscreen wipers.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two microprocessor-controlled devices used in a hospital ward.
parts.answer: Any two: patient monitor; infusion pump; ventilator; adjustable hospital bed.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid device, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the role of a light sensor in an automatic streetlight.
parts.answer: The light sensor detects the level of daylight and sends the reading to the microprocessor, which switches the light on when it gets dark.
parts.working: 1 mark: sensor measures the level of light. 1 mark: microprocessor switches the light on or off based on the reading.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a smart meter.
parts.answer: An electricity meter that records the amount of electricity used digitally and sends the readings to the supplier, often shown on a display in real time.
parts.working: 1 mark: records electricity use digitally. 1 mark: sends readings automatically or displays usage in real time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two positive effects of microprocessor-controlled household devices on people's lifestyles.
parts.answer: Any two: they save time because people do not have to carry out manual tasks (e.g. washing), giving more leisure time; devices can be set to run while people are out; they can be controlled remotely (e.g. switching on air-conditioning before arriving home); energy savings when devices switch off automatically; improved home security.
parts.working: 1 mark each, described.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two negative effects.
parts.answer: Any two: people may become lazy and less physically active; people lose household skills; smart devices connected to the internet can be hacked, risking data and security; dependence on technology when devices fail; cost to buy and repair; people may socialise less.
parts.working: 1 mark each, described.

practice.stem: Many new cars sold in Pakistan have microprocessor-controlled features such as parking sensors, anti-lock brakes and cruise control.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two advantages to drivers of microprocessor-controlled features in cars.
parts.answer: Any two: safer driving because sensors react faster than humans (e.g. anti-lock brakes stop skidding); parking sensors warn of obstacles, reducing accidents; cruise control keeps a steady speed, reducing fatigue and saving fuel; satnav reduces getting lost; better fuel efficiency.
parts.working: 1 mark each, explained.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two disadvantages.
parts.answer: Any two: drivers may rely on the systems and become less alert or lose driving skills; systems can fail or give false readings; more expensive to buy and repair; connected systems could be hacked; drivers may be overconfident.
parts.working: 1 mark each, explained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how microprocessor-controlled devices can affect a person's physical fitness and social interaction.
parts.answer: Fitness: devices do manual work (e.g. robotic vacuum, remote controls) so people are less active, which can lead to an unhealthy lifestyle; but saved time may be used for exercise, and fitness trackers can encourage activity. Social: people may spend more time on smart TVs/gaming devices and less time with others; but devices such as smartphones/video calls help people keep in touch with distant family.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for fitness, up to 2 for social interaction; balanced points credited.

practice.stem: A microprocessor-controlled air-conditioner in a flat in Multan keeps the room at 24 °C.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how the microprocessor keeps the room at the required temperature.
parts.answer: A temperature sensor sends readings (converted by an ADC) to the microprocessor; the microprocessor compares each reading with the preset 24 °C; if it is higher it switches the cooling on (via an actuator/DAC), if lower it switches it off; this repeats continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three: sensor reading; ADC; compares with preset; switches cooler on/off via actuator; continuous loop.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways that a microprocessor in a vending machine makes sure the customer gets the correct product and the right change.
parts.answer: The keypad or selection sends the product code to the microprocessor, which checks the stock and sends a signal to a motor (actuator) to release only the chosen item; coins are detected by sensors, the microprocessor works out the change and the change is returned, or the money is refunded if the product is out of stock.
parts.working: 1 mark: selection is received and stock checked by the microprocessor. 1 mark: a signal to an actuator releases only the chosen item. 1 mark: coins are detected and the change is calculated and returned, or a refund is given.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one positive and one negative effect that a microprocessor in a smart watch can have on a user's health habits.
parts.answer: Positive: it counts steps and monitors heart rate, which encourages exercise. Negative: constant alerts and notifications can cause stress or make the user check the watch and sit still for longer.
parts.working: 1 mark: positive effect explained. 1 mark: negative effect explained. 1 mark: link to health habits (activity, stress or sleep).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two steps a microprocessor takes to decide which floor a lift should serve next.
parts.answer: The microprocessor reads the buttons pressed by passengers and the current floor from the sensors; it then chooses the next requested floor according to the direction of travel.
parts.working: 1 mark: reads the calls (buttons) and the position of the lift. 1 mark: chooses the next floor in the direction of travel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how automatic lighting in an office can reduce energy use.
parts.answer: Sensors switch the lights off when no one is in the room or when there is enough daylight, so the lights are on only when they are needed.
parts.working: 1 mark: the lights are switched off when unused (occupancy sensor). 1 mark: or dimmed/off when there is enough daylight.

practice.stem: A family in Islamabad installs smart devices (lights, door lock, cameras, thermostat) that can be controlled from a smartphone app over the internet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the effects of these devices on the family's security and privacy.
parts.answer: Positive: can check cameras and lock the door remotely; alerts sent to phone if someone enters; lights can be switched on while away so the house looks occupied; logs show who came and went. Negative: devices can be hacked so criminals could unlock doors or watch camera feeds; personal data (when the family is home) collected by companies may be shared or leaked; weak default passwords; loss of internet or power may stop devices working. Measures: strong passwords, updates, two-factor authentication. Conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point; max 4 if one-sided; 6th mark for reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some smart fridges can monitor the food inside and order more automatically. Evaluate the use of such a fridge for a busy family.
parts.answer: Benefits: saves time shopping; food is less likely to run out; can warn of expiry dates, reducing waste; can suggest meals. Drawbacks: expensive to buy and repair; may order items not wanted or at higher prices; needs internet and stored payment details, so security risk; privacy – data about eating habits collected; family loses the habit of planning meals. Conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point; max 4 if one-sided; 6th mark for conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the energy use of a home may go down when microprocessor-controlled devices are used, but the overall cost to the household may still rise.
parts.answer: Devices switch off automatically or run at efficient times (e.g. lights turning off in empty rooms, heating only when needed), reducing energy use; however the devices are expensive to buy, may need replacing or repairing by specialists, and many draw standby power or need internet subscriptions, so overall costs may increase.
parts.working: B1 automatic/efficient control saves energy. B1 high purchase/repair cost. B1 standby power or subscription/replacement cost.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the effects of automatic lift control systems on people with disabilities.
parts.answer: Benefits: voice announcements and tactile buttons help people with sight loss; the lift can be called and held open for a longer time; the lift can be used without help. Drawbacks: if the system fails, people may be trapped or unable to use the lift without assistance; the controls may be unreachable or not clearly labelled; the system depends on power and maintenance.
parts.working: Mark bands: 5–6 marks for at least two benefits and two drawbacks linked to people with disabilities, with reasoning. 3–4 marks for points with limited reasoning. 1–2 marks for vague comments.

practice.stem: A smart meter reads 1245.6 kWh at the start of a month and 1389.2 kWh at the end. The electricity costs Rs 45 for each kWh.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of the electricity used in the month. Show your working.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why the smart meter reading gives a more accurate bill than an estimated reading.
parts.answer: The meter records the actual units used, so the bill is based on real consumption rather than an estimate.
parts.working: 1 mark: the reading is of actual use, not an estimate.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate whether a school in Lahore should replace its garden timer with a microprocessor-controlled sprinkler system that uses soil moisture sensors. Refer to water use and cost.
parts.answer: Benefits: the sensors water only when the soil is dry, so less water is wasted and the water bill falls; the microprocessor can stop the sprinklers when the soil is already wet. Drawbacks: the sensors and controller cost more to buy and install; a faulty sensor can give wrong readings, so plants may be underwatered or flooded; the system needs maintenance and someone to set it up. Conclusion: likely worthwhile if water is expensive or scarce, but a timer may be enough for a small garden.
parts.working: Mark bands: 5–6 marks for a balanced evaluation that refers to water use and cost to the school, with a reasoned judgement. 3–4 marks for both sides with limited reasoning. 1–2 marks for an unsupported opinion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two types of job that have been lost because of the introduction of IT.
parts.answer: Any two: manufacturing/production-line workers (replaced by robots); typing pool / secretarial staff; bank clerks/cashiers; car-park attendants; shop checkout staff; printing and typesetting workers; telephone operators.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two types of job that have been created by IT.
parts.answer: Any two: programmers/software developers; network managers/technicians; website designers; maintenance engineers for robots/computers; IT trainers; data analysts; cybersecurity specialists.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two ways that the growth of IT has changed the working hours or work patterns of many employees.
parts.answer: Any two: shift or flexible working; some staff work outside normal hours to serve customers in other time zones; work can be done from home or remotely; online systems let work continue around the clock.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid way, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by teleworking.
parts.answer: Working from home or from a remote location and communicating with the employer using a computer and the internet.
parts.working: 1 mark: working from home or away from the office. 1 mark: using computers and the internet to communicate and do the work.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two advantages to an employer of allowing staff to telework.
parts.answer: Any two: lower costs for office space; access to a wider pool of workers; possible higher productivity; less sick leave.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid advantage, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by outsourcing.
parts.answer: Paying an external company to do work that was previously done by the organisation's own staff.
parts.working: 1 mark: work is contracted to an outside company.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two tasks in a car factory that are now often carried out by robots.
parts.answer: Any two: welding; painting or spraying; moving heavy parts; assembling components.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid task, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the working patterns of part-time working, flexible hours (flexi-time) and job sharing.
parts.answer: Part-time – working fewer hours per week than a full-time employee; flexible hours – working the full number of hours but choosing start and finish times (often around a core time); job sharing – two people share the hours and duties of one full-time job.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A car factory near Karachi replaces many of its paint-shop workers with robots.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two effects of this on the workers who remain at the factory.
parts.answer: Any two, explained: they need retraining to operate/maintain robots, gaining new skills; work becomes less dangerous as robots do the hazardous painting (fumes); jobs may become more boring/supervisory; fear of further job losses; some may move to new higher-skilled, better-paid roles; may work different shift patterns as robots run continuously.
parts.working: For each effect: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two ways that self-checkout machines change the role of a supermarket cashier.
parts.answer: Cashiers spend less time scanning items and more time supervising the machines and helping customers; fewer cashiers are needed so jobs may be lost; cashiers may be asked to deal with problems such as unexpected items or payment failures.
parts.working: 1 mark: the cashier supervises machines rather than scanning. 1 mark: fewer cashiers are needed. 1 mark: the cashier takes on different tasks (help, problems, age checks).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two effects of automation on the skills that factory workers need.
parts.answer: Workers need computer and maintenance skills to operate and repair the machines; manual skills are needed less, so workers may need retraining.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid effect, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one effect of online shopping on small shops on a high street.
parts.answer: Customers buy from online shops and do not visit the high street, so takings fall; some shops close and the staff lose their jobs; shops have to make their own websites or compete on price.
parts.working: 1 mark: fewer customers visit the shops. 1 mark: sales fall, shops close or staff lose jobs. 1 mark: a response, such as an online shop or a niche service.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two effects of teleworking on a worker's family life or travel.
parts.answer: Any two: less time spent commuting so more time is available for family; flexible hours allow the worker to look after children; fewer travel costs; the boundary between home and work can blur.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid effect, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of online recruitment for a job applicant.
parts.answer: Advantage: the applicant can apply for jobs in many places quickly without travelling, and can apply for jobs advertised far away. Disadvantage: applicants without internet access or computer skills are at a disadvantage; the volume of applications makes it harder to be noticed.
parts.working: 1 mark: a valid advantage. 1 mark: a valid disadvantage. 1 mark: developed with an explanation.

practice.stem: A bank in Pakistan is closing several branches because more customers now use online and mobile banking.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the effects of this change on the bank's employees.
parts.answer: Negative: loss of jobs for cashiers and counter staff; staff may have to move/travel to other branches; need to learn new skills; job insecurity and stress. Positive: new jobs in call centres, IT support, cybersecurity and app development; chance of retraining to better-paid roles; possible flexible/home working for some staff; less handling of cash so safer. Conclusion weighing effects.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point; max 4 if one-sided; 6th mark for reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how IT has made compressed hours and working from home possible for many office workers, and give one drawback for the employer.
parts.answer: Compressed hours: the full weekly hours are worked in fewer days, possible because systems are available all day and work is tracked electronically. Working from home: laptops, internet access, cloud storage, VPNs, email and video-conferencing allow staff to access files and communicate as if in the office. Drawback for employer (any one): harder to supervise staff / monitor productivity; data security risks on home networks; cost of equipment; team communication may suffer.
parts.working: B1 compressed hours described. B1 IT link. B1 home working technologies. B1 drawback.

practice.stem: Before a factory bought an automated line, 60 machine operators each worked an 8-hour day. After the automation, 12 operators work an 8-hour day and produce the same output.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the percentage reduction in operators. Show your working.
parts.working: M1: reduction = 60 − 12 = 48 operators. A1: 48 ÷ 60 × 100 = 80%.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other effect the change may have on the remaining workers.
parts.answer: They may need training to operate or maintain the new machines, or they may be expected to supervise more machines.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid effect such as training, more responsibility or stress.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the effects of a new computerised stock system on the warehouse staff of a retail company.
parts.answer: Effects include: fewer staff needed to count and check stock, so some jobs are lost; remaining staff need computer skills and training; the work may become more monitored and faster-paced; staff may be more productive and the work less physically demanding; some staff may be moved to new roles such as stock controllers or data entry.
parts.working: Mark bands: 5–6 marks for a discussion of at least two effects on different groups of staff with reasons, reaching a judgement. 3–4 marks for clear effects with limited reasons. 1–2 marks for vague comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the argument that the growth of IT always increases unemployment.
parts.answer: Against: IT creates new jobs (web developers, support technicians, data analysts) and makes some businesses more competitive, so overall employment can grow; the effect depends on the skills of the workforce and on retraining. For: automation and self-service replace routine jobs; workers who lack digital skills may be left unemployed; the jobs created may be in different places or need different qualifications. A reasoned evaluation reaches a supported judgement.
parts.working: Mark bands: 5–6 marks for a balanced evaluation with reasons on both sides and a supported judgement. 3–4 marks for points on both sides with limited evaluation. 1–2 marks for a one-sided opinion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the impact of teleworking on employers, employees and the environment.
parts.answer: Employers: lower office costs, access to a wider pool of staff, but harder to supervise and to build team loyalty. Employees: no commuting, more flexible hours, but may feel isolated, have a blurred work-life balance and need a suitable home workspace. Environment: less commuting reduces fuel use and emissions, but home energy use may increase.
parts.working: Mark bands: 5–6 marks for points on all three groups, with reasons and a link between them. 3–4 marks for two groups discussed with reasons. 1–2 marks for vague points about one group.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss how the digital divide affects employment opportunities for people in rural areas of Pakistan.
parts.answer: Rural people may have poor internet connections or no access to a computer, so they cannot apply for jobs online or take online training; employers may not advertise locally; jobs requiring digital skills go to people in cities; the gap widens as more services move online. Solutions include mobile internet, local training centres and offering applications by phone or in person.
parts.working: Mark bands: 5–6 marks for a discussion of at least two effects on employment with a link to rural areas and a suggested solution. 3–4 marks for clear effects with limited reasoning. 1–2 marks for vague generalisations.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web.
parts.answer: The internet is the worldwide network of interconnected computer networks (the hardware and connections); the World Wide Web is a collection of web pages/websites that are accessed using the internet.
parts.working: B1 internet = global network of networks / infrastructure. B1 WWW = web pages/sites (resources) accessed via the internet using HTTP/browser.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
practice.stem:
A passenger types this address into a web browser:
https://www.railbook.com.pk/timetables/karachi-lahore.html

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the protocol.
parts.answer: https
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Identify the domain name.
parts.answer: www.railbook.com.pk (accept railbook.com.pk)
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Identify the folder (path) name.
parts.answer: timetables
parts.working: B1

parts.label: d
parts.text: Identify the file name.
parts.answer: karachi-lahore.html
parts.working: B1 must include .html

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three features of a web browser that help a user to find pages again or move between pages.
parts.answer: Any three: bookmarks/favourites; history; back and forward buttons; tabs; address bar; home page button; hyperlinks; search within the address bar.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a web browser and a search engine.
parts.answer: A web browser is software installed on the device used to display web pages from a URL; a search engine is a website/service used inside the browser to find web pages that match keywords.
parts.working: B1 browser = software that displays/retrieves web pages. B1 search engine = finds pages from keywords.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an Internet Service Provider (ISP).
parts.answer: A company that provides users with access to the internet (usually for a monthly fee).
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two services, other than internet access, that an ISP may provide.
parts.answer: Any two: email accounts; web hosting; security/filtering such as parental controls or firewalls; online storage; technical support; IP address allocation.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a URL.
parts.answer: Uniform Resource Locator: the text address of a web page or file on the internet.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the difference between http and https at the start of a URL.
parts.answer: Both are protocols for transferring web pages; https is the secure version – data sent between the browser and the web server is encrypted (using SSL/TLS), while with http it is not.
parts.working: 1 mark: https is secure; 1 mark: data is encrypted.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State what each ending in a web address usually suggests about the organisation that owns the website.
(i) .gov.pk
(ii) .edu
(iii) .org
(iv) .com
parts.answer: (i) A government organisation in Pakistan (ii) An educational institution (iii) A non-profit organisation/charity (iv) A commercial business
parts.working: 1 mark each. (i) must mention both government and Pakistan for the mark.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a cookie.
parts.answer: A small text file stored on the user's computer by a website, holding information about the user's visit or preferences.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two ways a shopping website uses cookies.
parts.answer: To remember items in the shopping basket; to keep the user logged in; to remember preferences such as language or currency; to show items related to what the user has looked at.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the letters HTTP stand for.
parts.answer: Hypertext Transfer Protocol.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the job of HTTP.
parts.answer: It is the set of rules used to send web pages (and other files) between a web server and a browser.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State what HTML is used for.
parts.answer: HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) describes the content and structure of a web page so a browser can display it.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A customer uses this address: https://shop.kitabghar.pk/books/science/physics-guide.php
Identify:
(i) the protocol
(ii) the domain name
(iii) the path (folders)
(iv) the file name
parts.answer: (i) https (ii) shop.kitabghar.pk (iii) /books/science/ (iv) physics-guide.php
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the .pk at the end of the domain name tells the customer.
parts.answer: It is a country code: the website is registered in Pakistan.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
practice.stem:
A student finds information at:
http://climate.uni-example.ac.uk/research/glaciers/hunza.htm

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what the 'ac.uk' part tells the student about the website.
parts.answer: ac shows it belongs to an academic/educational institution (e.g. a university); uk is the country code for the United Kingdom.
parts.working: B1 academic/educational organisation. B1 country code – UK.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The website does not use https. Explain why this matters if the site had a login form.
parts.answer: Without https the data is sent unencrypted, so a username and password could be intercepted and read by someone else on the network.
parts.working: B1 http not encrypted / no SSL/TLS. B1 login details could be intercepted/read.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe two ways a user can tell that a website uses a secure connection.
parts.answer: The URL begins with https (rather than http); a padlock symbol appears in the address bar (clicking it shows a valid digital certificate).
parts.working: 1 mark each: https; padlock icon; valid certificate details.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a hyperlink.
parts.answer: Text or an image on a web page that, when clicked, takes the user to another web page, another part of the same page, or opens a file/email.
parts.working: B1 clickable text/image. B1 moves to another page/location/file.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
practice.stem: A student in Hyderabad wants information about mangrove forests in the Indus Delta but not about mangroves in other countries. A search for the single word mangroves returned millions of results.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three ways the student could refine the search to get more useful results.
parts.answer: Any three: add more specific keywords such as 'Indus Delta' and 'Pakistan'; put an exact phrase in quotation marks, e.g. "Indus Delta mangroves"; use operators such as AND / + to require words and − (minus/NOT) to exclude words; use advanced search filters such as date, region, file type or domain (e.g. .edu.pk).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three described methods.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
practice.stem: Many students use the internet rather than school library books for their projects.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three ways a student could judge whether a website is reliable.
parts.answer: Any three: check who the author/organisation is and their expertise; check the date it was last updated; look at the domain type (e.g. .gov or .edu is more likely reliable); cross-check the facts with other sources; look for references/citations; check for poor spelling and grammar or heavy advertising; check whether it is biased/selling something.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three explained.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
practice.stem: An online forum helps parents in Karachi share advice about schools.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a moderated and an unmoderated forum.
parts.answer: In a moderated forum posts are checked by a moderator (before or after posting) and unsuitable posts are removed; in an unmoderated forum posts appear without any checking.
parts.working: B1 moderated – checked/administrator removes inappropriate posts. B1 unmoderated – no checking.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why the forum owners choose to make it moderated.
parts.answer: To remove offensive, abusive, false or spam posts and keep users (and children's information) safe.
parts.working: B1

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
practice.stem: A web page for a science fair contains a link to the website https://www.examplemuseum.org/space.html

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the HTML to show the text 'Space gallery' as a hyperlink to this page so that it opens in a new browser window or tab.
parts.answer: Space gallery
parts.working: B1 with correct URL. B1 target="_blank". B1 text Space gallery and closing .

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why an absolute URL is used here rather than a relative one.
parts.answer: The page is on a different website, so the full address (protocol and domain) is needed; a relative path only works for files on the same site.
parts.working: B1

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens after a user types a URL into a web browser and presses Enter, until the web page appears.
parts.answer: The browser sends the domain name to a DNS server; the DNS server looks up and returns the matching IP address of the web server; the browser sends a request (using HTTP/HTTPS) to that IP address; the web server sends back the page's HTML and other files; the browser interprets the HTML and displays the page.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four steps in a sensible order.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Nimra wants recipes for chicken karahi that do not use tomatoes. Explain the effect of each search below.
(i) chicken karahi recipe
(ii) "chicken karahi" recipe
(iii) "chicken karahi" recipe -tomato
parts.answer: (i) Finds pages containing these words anywhere, in any order – many irrelevant results. (ii) The quotation marks make the search engine look for the exact phrase 'chicken karahi', so results are more relevant. (iii) As (ii) but the minus sign leaves out pages containing the word 'tomato'.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct explanation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why search (iii) might still leave out a recipe that would suit her.
parts.answer: A suitable recipe page might mention the word tomato, e.g. 'no tomato needed', and so be excluded.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why information on a wiki may not be reliable.
parts.answer: Anyone (or any registered user) can add or edit content, and they may not be experts; mistakes or deliberate false information can be added and may not be noticed straight away.
parts.working: 1 mark: anyone can edit; 1 mark: errors or false information may remain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways a wiki can reduce this problem.
parts.answer: It keeps a history of edits so wrong changes can be undone; moderators/editors check changes; contributors must provide references; pages can be locked from editing.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a web server.
parts.answer: A computer that stores web pages/websites and sends them to browsers that request them over the internet.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A small business in Sialkot pays a company to host its website. Give two advantages of paying a hosting company rather than running its own web server.
parts.answer: The hosting company's servers are online 24 hours a day with fast connections; it handles security, maintenance and backups; the business does not need to buy a server or employ technical staff.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Ahmed downloads a 1.8 GB software update at a connection speed of 25 Mbps. Taking 1 GB = 1000 MB and 1 MB = 8 megabits, calculate the download time in minutes.
parts.answer: 9.6 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why the download may take longer than this.
parts.answer: Other devices are using the same connection; the web server is busy; network congestion; the actual speed is lower than advertised.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using the internet rather than printed books to find information for a geography project.
parts.answer: Advantages: information is often more up to date; huge amount available; quick to search with keywords; available at any time from home; multimedia such as videos and maps; usually free. Disadvantages: information may be unreliable or biased because anyone can publish; too many results to sort through; may find irrelevant pages; distractions; needs a device and internet connection; risk of plagiarism or copyright issues; books are often checked/edited before publishing.
parts.working: Max 4 for advantages only or disadvantages only. 1 mark per valid point; 6th mark for a reasoned conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a search engine finds and ranks the web pages it shows in its results.
parts.answer: Web crawlers (spiders/bots) automatically visit pages and follow links; the content and keywords of each page are stored in an index; when a user enters a search the engine looks up matching pages in its index rather than the live web; results are ranked by an algorithm using factors such as relevance of keywords, number and quality of links to the page, how recent it is and location/popularity.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four: crawler/spider; follows links; index built; search looks up index; ranking algorithm; ranking factors.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the differences between a blog and a wiki.
parts.answer: A blog is usually written by one person (or a small group) and only they can edit it; entries appear in reverse date order; readers can usually only comment. A wiki can be edited by many users, who can add, change and delete content; it is organised by topic pages, not date; it keeps a history of edits.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three linked differences (authorship, who can edit, organisation by date vs topic, comments vs editing, edit history).

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss whether the internet should be policed.
parts.answer: For policing: helps stop illegal material and criminal activity (e.g. fraud, terrorism); protects children from unsuitable content; reduces false information and cyberbullying; protects copyright. Against: material is already illegal under existing laws; difficult and expensive to enforce worldwide because no single body owns the internet; limits freedom of speech/information; may be used by governments for censorship; people can bypass controls. A reasoned conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point; max 4 if only one side; 6th mark only with a conclusion.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
practice.stem:
A school website stores its pages in this folder structure on the web server:
/index.html
/events/sports.html
/events/images/trophy.jpg

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the relative URL that sports.html should use to link back to index.html.
parts.answer: ../index.html
parts.working: B1 ../index.html

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the relative path that sports.html should use for the image trophy.jpg.
parts.answer: images/trophy.jpg
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain one advantage of using relative rather than absolute URLs for links within the same website.
parts.answer: The links still work if the whole website is moved to a different domain or server (or tested locally), because they do not contain the domain name.
parts.working: B1

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sara wants to book train tickets. She types the railway company's name into a search engine and clicks the first result, which is marked 'Sponsored'. Explain the risks of doing this, and why typing the known official URL is safer.
parts.answer: A sponsored result is a paid advert, not necessarily the official site; criminals can pay for adverts or create look-alike sites to steal card details or sell fake tickets; she may also pay extra fees to an agent site. Typing the official URL (or using a saved bookmark) takes her directly to the genuine site, and she can check it uses https and the correct domain name.
parts.working: 1 mark: sponsored = paid advert; 1 mark: fake/copycat sites steal data or money; 1 mark: third-party agent / extra fees; 1 mark: typed URL/bookmark goes to genuine site.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: Two students in different cities search for the same words at the same time but get different results in a different order. Explain why.
parts.answer: Search engines personalise results using the user's location (e.g. showing local businesses), previous search history and cookies, language settings and whether the user is signed in to an account; results are also updated constantly as the index changes.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three valid reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the first result in a search is not necessarily the most accurate one.
parts.answer: Results are ranked by relevance and popularity (e.g. keywords, links, visits) or by payment for adverts, not by checking that the information is true.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: A message claiming that a city's water supply is poisoned is being shared widely on social media. Explain why false information like this spreads quickly on the internet.
parts.answer: Anyone can post without checks; it can be shared to many people instantly with one click; alarming stories are shared more and promoted by algorithms; people share before checking.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe three things a reader should do to check the story before sharing it.
parts.answer: Check whether reliable sources such as official government or water-board websites or established news organisations report it; look at who first posted it and whether they are trustworthy; check the date; look for evidence such as named sources; use a fact-checking website.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.subtopic: Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'Search engines check every web page before showing it, so the information in the top results must be correct.' Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: Search engines use automatic programs (crawlers) to index pages; they rank pages using factors such as keywords, links and popularity; no one checks whether the content is true; some results are paid adverts; pages can be designed to rank highly (SEO) even if inaccurate.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three valid points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between cc and bcc when sending an email.
parts.answer: Recipients in cc (carbon copy) receive a copy and their addresses are visible to all other recipients; recipients in bcc (blind carbon copy) receive a copy but their addresses are hidden from the other recipients.
parts.working: B1 cc – copy sent, address visible. B1 bcc – copy sent, address hidden.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by spam.
parts.answer: Unsolicited (unwanted) emails sent to many people at once, often advertising.
parts.working: B1 unsolicited/junk bulk email.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three ways of reducing the amount of spam received.
parts.answer: Any three: use a spam filter; do not reply to spam or click 'unsubscribe' on suspicious messages; do not publish your email address on websites/forums; untick boxes that allow companies to share your address; use a separate address for online sign-ups; block the sender.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between 'reply', 'reply all' and 'forward'.
parts.answer: Reply sends a response only to the sender; reply all sends the response to the sender and everyone else who received the original (in To and cc); forward sends the original message (with attachments) to a new recipient chosen by the user.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Hamza's email address is hamza.r@unimail.edu.pk

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the user name (local part) and the domain name in this address.
parts.answer: User name: hamza.r; domain name: unimail.edu.pk
parts.working: B1 each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the symbol that separates them and what it means.
parts.answer: @ – 'at', separating the user from the mail server/domain.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why an email should have a clear, meaningful subject line.
parts.answer: The receiver can see what the email is about before opening it; it helps the receiver sort, prioritise and search for emails later; emails with an empty or vague subject are more likely to be treated as spam.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three signs that an email attachment might be dangerous.
parts.answer: It is from someone the user does not know; it was not expected; it has an executable file type such as .exe or a double extension such as invoice.pdf.exe; the message urges the user to open it quickly; the anti-malware software gives a warning.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an email signature.
parts.answer: Text added automatically to the end of each email sent, usually giving the sender's details.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two items that should be included in a professional email signature for an employee.
parts.answer: Full name; job title; company name; phone number; company website or address.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by an email attachment.
parts.answer: A file, such as a document or photo, that is sent along with an email.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two examples of file types often sent as attachments.
parts.answer: PDF documents; word-processed documents (.docx); images (.jpg, .png); spreadsheets (.xlsx); compressed folders (.zip).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two things a spam filter may check when deciding whether an incoming email is spam.
parts.answer: Whether the sender's address or domain is on a blocklist; words and phrases commonly used in spam; suspicious links or attachments; whether many people have marked similar emails as spam; whether the sender's address is faked.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three reasons why spam is a problem for email users.
parts.answer: It wastes the user's time deleting it; it fills up the inbox/storage; important emails may be missed among it; it may contain phishing links or malware; it uses network bandwidth.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

practice.stem: A school in Quetta sends a weekly email newsletter to the parents of 600 students.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the school should put the parents' addresses in the bcc field.
parts.answer: So parents cannot see each other's email addresses, which protects their personal data/privacy and stops addresses being misused for spam or 'reply all'.
parts.working: B1 addresses hidden / privacy / data protection. B1 avoids misuse e.g. spam or reply-all chains.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how an email group (contact list) would help the school.
parts.answer: All 600 addresses are saved under one group name, so the newsletter is sent by typing just the group name; this saves time and avoids missing anyone or typing addresses wrongly.
parts.working: B1 one name for many addresses. B1 saves time / fewer errors / nobody missed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe four rules of netiquette that should be followed when writing emails.
parts.answer: Any four: do not use capital letters for whole sentences (seen as shouting); do not use abusive or offensive language; check spelling and grammar; use a clear subject line; keep messages short and relevant; respect privacy – do not forward others' messages without permission; do not send spam or chain emails; be careful with humour/sarcasm which can be misunderstood.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

practice.stem: Ayesha wants to email holiday photos to her cousin in Toronto. The photos are 4.2 MB, 3.8 MB, 6.5 MB, 7.9 MB and 5.1 MB. Her email service allows attachments of up to 25 MB in total per message.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total size of the photos and state whether they can all be sent in one email.
parts.answer: 27.5 MB; no – this is more than the 25 MB limit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways Ayesha could still send all the photos.
parts.answer: Any two: compress the files (zip or reduce image resolution/quality); split them over two emails; upload them to cloud storage and email a link instead.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three features of an email that suggest it is spam or a scam.
parts.answer: Any three: sent from an unknown or odd-looking address; generic greeting such as 'Dear customer'; spelling and grammar mistakes; urgent requests or threats; offers that seem too good to be true (prizes, lottery wins); asks for personal or bank details; suspicious links whose address does not match the company; unexpected attachments.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A web page for a charity book sale in Lahore must contain a hyperlink that opens the visitor's email software with the address sales@bookdrive.org and the subject Book donation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the HTML for this hyperlink, using the text Email us.
parts.answer: Email us
parts.working: B1 mailto: with correct address. B1 ?subject=Book donation (accept the space typed directly or as %20). B1 correct … with text Email us.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages and one disadvantage of sending an attachment rather than pasting the text into the body of an email.
parts.answer: Advantages (any two): keeps the original formatting/layout; recipient can save, edit and print the file; non-text files such as images or spreadsheets can be sent; large documents keep the email body short. Disadvantage (any one): attachments may carry viruses; size limits; recipient needs suitable software to open the file; may be blocked by filters.
parts.working: 1 mark each for two advantages and one disadvantage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many countries have laws about companies sending marketing emails. Describe three requirements such laws often include.
parts.answer: The company must have the person's consent (opt-in) before sending marketing emails; every email must include a clear way to unsubscribe, and requests must be acted on promptly; the sender's identity and contact address must be shown truthfully; the subject line must not be misleading; email addresses must not be sold without consent.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Faisal receives an email with these features:
• From: security@hbl-account-verify.co
• Greeting: 'Dear Valued Customer'
• Text: 'Your account will be closed in 24 hours unless you confirm your details.'
• A button labelled 'Verify now'; when he hovers over it, the address shown is http://198.51.100.23/login
• Several spelling mistakes
Identify four features that suggest this is a phishing email and explain why each is suspicious.
parts.answer: The sender's domain is not the bank's real domain; the greeting is general, not his name, so it was sent to many people; the 24-hour threat creates urgency to make him act without thinking; the link goes to an IP address over http, not the bank's secure website; spelling mistakes are unusual in genuine bank emails; banks do not ask customers to confirm details by email.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four features with an explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Kamran's email account has 15 GB of storage, of which 12.6 GB is used. He receives about 40 MB of email each day and deletes nothing. Taking 1 GB = 1000 MB, calculate how many days it will be until the storage is full.
parts.answer: 60 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways he could free up space.
parts.answer: Delete emails with large attachments after saving the attachments elsewhere; empty the trash/deleted items and spam folders; unsubscribe from newsletters; archive old emails to local storage.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Rabia receives a chain email that says: 'Forward this to 10 friends or you will have bad luck.' Explain why she should not forward it.
parts.answer: Chain emails often contain false information (hoaxes) and spread it; they waste people's time and fill inboxes; forwarding exposes all her friends' email addresses, which spammers can collect; they may contain harmful links.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to an email from the moment the sender clicks Send until the receiver reads it.
parts.answer: The email is sent from the sender's device to the sender's email server; the server uses the domain after the @ to find the receiver's email server and passes the email to it; the email is stored there in the receiver's mailbox until the receiver's email software or webmail downloads/displays it.
parts.working: 1 mark each: sent to sender's mail server; forwarded to receiver's mail server using the domain; stored until accessed by receiver.

practice.stem: A trading company in Faisalabad currently posts letters to its suppliers in China and Turkey.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of email instead of posted letters for this company.
parts.answer: Benefits: arrives almost instantly regardless of distance; cheaper (no postage); can attach documents and send to many suppliers at once; replies are faster; copies are stored and searchable. Drawbacks: needs devices and internet connection; risk of viruses/phishing in attachments; emails can be intercepted or sent to the wrong person; some formal documents may still need signed paper copies; may be filtered as spam and not read; information overload. Conclusion weighing these.
parts.working: 1 mark per point; max 4 if only one side; 6th mark for reasoned conclusion.

practice.stem: A software company in Islamabad gives employees a policy about how they must use company email.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three things that such an email policy is likely to include and why each is needed.
parts.answer: Any three, each with a reason: only use email for work purposes – to reduce wasted time and system load; no offensive or discriminatory language – the company could be sued and its reputation harmed; do not send confidential data unencrypted or to outsiders – data protection laws; do not open unknown attachments – to prevent malware; emails may be monitored/stored – legal requirement and security; follow copyright law when attaching material; use a standard signature/house style – professional image.
parts.working: For each of three points: 1 mark for the rule, 1 mark for the reason (max 6).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a spam filter may sometimes put a genuine email in the junk folder, and what the user should do about it.
parts.answer: The filter uses rules (e.g. certain words, many recipients, unknown sender, links or attachments) and may wrongly match a genuine email – a false positive; the user should regularly check the junk folder and mark genuine emails as 'not spam' / add the sender to a safe senders list so the filter learns.
parts.working: B1 filter uses keywords/rules/sender reputation. B1 genuine mail matches these rules (false positive). B1 check junk folder / mark not spam / safe sender list.

practice.stem: A hospital in Rawalpindi needs to send a patient's test results to a specialist at another hospital.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the precautions staff should take if these results are sent by email.
parts.answer: Any four: encrypt the email or the attachment / send through a secure email system; check the recipient's address carefully before sending (avoid autocomplete errors); password-protect the attachment and send the password by another method; include only the data that is needed; use a professional, clear subject line without personal details; follow data protection law and hospital policy; confirm receipt.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Spammers send millions of emails even though very few people respond. Explain why spam is still profitable for them.
parts.answer: Sending email costs almost nothing, so even a tiny percentage of replies or purchases (or stolen bank details) earns money from a huge number of messages.
parts.working: 1 mark: very low cost per email; 1 mark: small response rate × huge numbers still gives profit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways spammers obtain email addresses.
parts.answer: Software that collects addresses published on websites and forums; buying lists from data breaches; guessing common addresses at a domain (e.g. info@, ali@); from chain emails where addresses are visible.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why clicking 'unsubscribe' in an obvious spam email may increase the amount of spam received.
parts.answer: It confirms to the spammer that the email address is real and active, so it is worth more and gets more spam.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small marketing team in Lahore uses email for all internal communication. The manager is considering an instant messaging app for the team. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of instant messaging compared with email for the team.
parts.answer: Instant messaging advantages: messages arrive and are answered in real time; good for quick questions; group chats and presence status show who is available; less formal. Disadvantages: constant notifications interrupt work; important information gets lost in long chats; less suitable for formal records, long documents or external clients; may be harder to search and archive; staff may feel they must reply at all hours. Email advantages: better for formal, detailed messages with attachments; works with anyone outside the company; easy to file and keep as a record. Conclusion: use both — IM for quick internal coordination, email for formal and external communication.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for points about instant messaging and up to 4 for points about email/disadvantages (max 5 if one-sided); 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion. Max 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A sports equipment exporter in Sialkot wants to email its new 45 MB PDF catalogue to 300 overseas buyers. Discuss the problems it may meet and suggest better ways to send the catalogue.
parts.answer: Problems: many email services limit attachments to about 20–25 MB, so the email may be rejected; large emails fill buyers' inboxes; a bulk email with a large attachment may be blocked as spam; sending 300 copies uses a lot of bandwidth; putting all addresses in To/cc would reveal the buyer list to competitors. Better methods: upload the catalogue to the company website or cloud storage and email a link; compress or reduce the PDF image quality; use bcc or a mailing-list service with an unsubscribe link.
parts.working: Up to 3 marks for problems and up to 3 marks for suitable solutions; max 5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A clinic in Hyderabad sends an appointment reminder to 80 patients by putting all their email addresses in the 'To' box. Explain the problems this causes and what the clinic should have done.
parts.answer: Every patient can see the email addresses of all the others, which reveals personal data and that they are patients of the clinic – a breach of privacy/data protection; patients might 'reply all', sending messages to everyone; the visible list could be collected by spammers. The clinic should have used bcc, or better, sent individual emails through a mail-merge or appointment system.
parts.working: 1 mark each for up to three problems; 1 mark for the correct alternative (bcc / individual emails). Max 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A company tells its employees that their work email accounts may be monitored. Discuss whether employers should monitor employees' work emails.
parts.answer: For: the email system and data belong to the company; monitoring can detect leaks of confidential information, harassment or illegal activity; protects against malware and phishing; makes sure staff use time productively; may be needed to meet legal obligations. Against: invades employees' privacy, especially for personal messages; may reduce trust and morale; staff may feel stressed; monitoring must follow the law and the company should tell staff clearly; reading personal content may be disproportionate. Conclusion: acceptable if staff are told in a clear policy and monitoring is limited and proportionate.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for points for and up to 4 for points against (max 5 if one-sided); 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion. Max 6.

Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines
Internet, WWW, URLs and search engines

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Write down the most suitable storage medium for each use.
(i) Backing up all the data on a bank's servers every night and keeping the copies for ten years.
(ii) Selling a high-definition feature film in shops.
(iii) Carrying homework files between home and school.
(iv) Storing the operating system in a thin, light laptop.
parts.answer:
(i) Magnetic tape
(ii) Blu-ray disc
(iii) USB flash drive / pen drive (accept memory card)
(iv) Solid-state drive (SSD)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Do not accept brand names.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how data is stored on a magnetic hard disk drive.
parts.answer: The disk has platters coated in a magnetic material; the platters spin at high speed; a read/write head moves across the surface on an arm; the head magnetises tiny areas in one of two directions to represent 1s and 0s; data is stored in concentric tracks/sectors.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by direct access to data.
parts.answer: Data can be read straight from where it is stored without reading through all the data before it.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by serial access to data.
parts.answer: Data is read in the order it was stored, starting from the beginning, until the required item is found.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one example of a storage medium that uses each type of access.
parts.answer: Direct: hard disk/SSD/DVD/Blu-ray/flash drive. Serial: magnetic tape.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two advantages to students of using USB flash drives to store their school work.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. small/portable; robust (no moving parts); plugs into any computer with a USB port without extra software; large capacity for the size; fast to transfer files.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of using USB flash drives.
parts.answer: Easily lost or stolen (data may be seen by others); can transfer viruses between computers; can be damaged if removed while writing; limited number of write cycles.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name two devices that use memory cards for storage.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. digital camera; smartphone/tablet; drone; dashboard camera; handheld games console.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State whether a memory card is magnetic, optical or solid-state storage.
parts.answer: Solid-state.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each storage medium is magnetic, optical or solid-state.
(i) Blu-ray disc
(ii) Hard disk drive
(iii) Magnetic tape
(iv) SD card
(v) DVD-RW
(vi) USB pen drive
parts.answer:
(i) Optical
(ii) Magnetic
(iii) Magnetic
(iv) Solid-state
(v) Optical
(vi) Solid-state
parts.working: All six correct: 3 marks; four or five: 2 marks; two or three: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Give one suitable use for each of these storage media.
(i) magnetic tape
(ii) Blu-ray disc
(iii) solid-state drive (SSD)
parts.answer: (i) e.g. long-term archive/backup of a large organisation's data. (ii) e.g. distributing high-definition films or video games. (iii) e.g. the main storage in a laptop or tablet.
parts.working: 1 mark each for a realistic use.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of storage (magnetic, optical or solid-state) described by each statement.
(i) Data is stored as pits and lands read by a laser.
(ii) Data is stored by trapping electrons in flash memory cells.
(iii) Data is stored as magnetised and demagnetised areas on a coated surface.
parts.answer: (i) optical (ii) solid-state (iii) magnetic
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a solid-state drive uses less power than a magnetic hard disk drive, and why this is an advantage in a laptop.
parts.answer: It has no moving parts, so no motor is needed to spin platters or move a read-write head; lower power use means the laptop battery lasts longer (and less heat is produced).
parts.working: 1 mark: no motor/moving parts. 1 mark: longer battery life / less heat.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two disadvantages of storing files on optical discs compared with a USB flash drive.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. lower storage capacity; slower to read and write; many computers no longer have an optical drive; discs scratch easily; recordable discs (-R) cannot be rewritten.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bilal is a university student who carries his laptop to lectures every day. He is choosing between a laptop with a magnetic hard disk drive (HDD) and one with a solid-state drive (SSD) of the same capacity. Compare HDDs and SSDs for Bilal's laptop.
parts.answer: Both are non-volatile backing storage that store the OS and files with direct access. An SSD has no moving parts whereas an HDD has spinning platters and a moving head, so the SSD is less likely to be damaged if the laptop is dropped while carried; an SSD reads and writes data faster so the laptop starts up and loads files quicker; an SSD uses less power so the battery lasts longer; an SSD is lighter and thinner; an SSD is silent and runs cooler; an HDD is cheaper per gigabyte, so more storage for the same price; an HDD can be rewritten more times/has a longer lifespan for frequent writes.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 6. At least one similarity for full marks. Points must be linked to both devices.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how data is read from an optical disc such as a DVD.
parts.answer: The disc spins; a laser beam is shone onto the surface; the surface has pits and lands (in a spiral track); light reflects differently from pits and lands (or at the change between them); a sensor/light detector reads the reflections and converts them into 1s and 0s.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which colour of laser is used to read a DVD.
parts.answer: Red laser.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A large insurance company in Karachi backs up its database onto magnetic tape every night. Explain two reasons why magnetic tape is used for this.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. very large capacity so the whole database fits on one/few tapes; low cost per gigabyte; tapes are robust and can be stored off-site for many years; fast to write large amounts of data in one continuous stream.
parts.working: 1 mark each for an explained reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why magnetic tape is not suitable for looking up one customer's record while the customer waits on the telephone.
parts.answer: Tape uses serial access; the tape must be wound through from the start until the record is reached, so finding one record is very slow.
parts.working: 1 mark for serial access, 1 mark for consequence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a solid-state drive stores data.
