parts.answer: It uses flash memory chips (NAND) made of transistors; electrons are trapped in each cell (in the floating gate) to represent 1 or 0; data stays when power is off; there are no moving parts.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain two reasons why smartphones use solid-state storage.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. very small and light so fits in a thin phone; no moving parts so not damaged when dropped; low power use so longer battery life; fast access so apps open quickly.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a DVD-ROM, a DVD-R and a DVD-RW.
parts.answer: DVD-ROM: data is written when the disc is made and can only be read, not changed. DVD-R: can be written (recorded) once by the user, then only read. DVD-RW: can be written, erased and re-written many times.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest a suitable use for a DVD-RW.
parts.answer: Any suitable use where data changes, e.g. regular backups that are overwritten; recording TV programmes to watch and then record over; moving files between computers.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A photography club in Lahore wants to back up 60 GB of photos onto single-layer DVD-R discs. Each disc holds 4.7 GB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the smallest number of discs needed.
parts.answer: 13 discs
parts.working: 60 ÷ 4.7 = 12.77… (M1); round up to 13 discs because 12 discs only hold 56.4 GB (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a portable hard disk drive would be a better choice for this backup.
parts.answer: One portable HDD holds all 60 GB so there is no need to split files across 13 discs; it can be overwritten for each new backup whereas DVD-R can only be written once; it is quicker to copy to and to restore from.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two explained points.

practice.stem: A news reporter in Dhaka records video on a camera with a 32 GB memory card. One minute of video uses 120 MB. Use 1 GB = 1024 MB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the largest number of whole minutes of video that can be stored on the card.
parts.answer: 273 minutes

parts.label: b
parts.text: The reporter copies the video to her laptop at the end of each day. Give one reason why she should also keep a second copy on a different storage device.
parts.answer: If the laptop is lost/stolen/fails the video is not lost (backup).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The Khan family want to back up 400 GB of photos and videos. Compare using a portable hard disk drive and USB flash drives for this backup.
parts.answer: Both are portable and connect by USB, and both can be overwritten. A portable HDD holds 400 GB or more on one device whereas several flash drives might be needed; an HDD is cheaper per GB; a flash drive has no moving parts so is less easily damaged if dropped; flash drives are smaller and lighter; an HDD may be slower to access/needs more power.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A server in a factory writes sensor readings to its solid-state drive every second, all day and night. Explain why the limited number of write cycles of an SSD could be a problem for this server.
parts.answer: Each flash memory cell can only be written/erased a limited number of times; with constant writing the cells wear out sooner, so the drive could fail and data could be lost.
parts.working: 1 mark: limited write/erase cycles. 1 mark: constant writing shortens its life / risk of failure.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest one way the factory could reduce the risk of losing data.
parts.answer: e.g. back up the data regularly to another device/cloud; use a magnetic hard disk for the constant logging; replace drives on a schedule; use two mirrored drives.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shop in Gujranwala has 4 CCTV cameras. Each camera records 1.5 GB of video per hour, 24 hours a day, onto a 2 TB hard disk drive (1 TB = 1024 GB). Calculate the number of complete days of video the drive can hold.
parts.answer: 14 days

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why a magnetic hard disk drive is a suitable choice for this CCTV recorder.
parts.answer: e.g. large capacity at a low cost per gigabyte; can be overwritten many times; fast enough to record video continuously.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how data is written to a recordable DVD (DVD-R).
parts.answer: A laser in the drive heats points on a dye layer in the disc; the heated spots change and reflect less light, acting like pits, while unheated areas act like lands; the pattern represents the binary data, written in a spiral track from the centre outwards.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: laser heats/burns the dye layer; marked areas reflect light differently (act as pits/lands); written along a spiral track. Max 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A company compares two drives: an 8 TB hard disk drive costing Rs 52 000 and a 2 TB solid-state drive costing Rs 38 000. Using 1 TB = 1024 GB, calculate the cost per gigabyte of each drive, correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.answer: HDD Rs 6.35 per GB; SSD Rs 18.55 per GB

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why data centres still use many hard disk drives.
parts.answer: Data centres need enormous capacity; HDDs are much cheaper per gigabyte (about a third of the SSD cost here), and much of the stored data is not read often, so the slower access speed matters less.
parts.working: 1 mark: cost per GB/capacity linked to calculation. 1 mark: speed less important for rarely used data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A single-layer Blu-ray disc can hold about five times as much data as a single-layer DVD, even though both discs are the same size. Explain why.
parts.answer: Blu-ray uses a blue/blue-violet laser which has a shorter wavelength than the red laser used for DVDs; the shorter wavelength can be focused to a smaller spot so the pits can be smaller; the tracks can be closer together; so more pits fit on the same area of disc.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why films are often sold on Blu-ray rather than DVD.
parts.answer: Higher capacity allows high-definition (or 4K/3D) video/extra content on one disc; Blu-ray discs have a protective coating so are less easily scratched.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: Ayesha is a wildlife photographer in Chitral. Her camera uses a 64 GB memory card. Each photo is stored as a 48 MB file. Use 1 GB = 1024 MB.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the largest number of whole photos that can be stored on the memory card.
parts.answer: 1365 photos

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name the type of storage used by the memory card.
parts.answer: Solid-state (flash memory).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why this type of storage is suitable for use in a camera carried in the mountains.
parts.answer: No moving parts so it is not damaged by knocks/vibration; small and light; works in cold conditions; uses very little power so battery lasts longer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two explained points.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school in Rawalpindi plans to replace the hard disk drives in its file server with solid-state drives. Evaluate this plan.
parts.answer: Benefits: SSDs read/write faster so students' files open and save more quickly, especially when many users log on at once; no moving parts so less likely to fail/be damaged and quieter; lower power use and less heat so cheaper to run and cool; smaller. Drawbacks: SSDs cost more per gigabyte so the same budget buys less storage; files may need to be moved/server set up again, causing disruption; SSDs have a limited number of write cycles, which matters for a server that saves files all day; HDD capacity may be enough if current speed is acceptable. Conclusion with justification.
parts.working: 5–6: balanced, developed points with a conclusion; 3–4: both sides, some development; 1–2: simple points/one side only.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A team of geologists will spend three months in the Thar Desert collecting data on laptops. Temperatures are very high, there is fine dust, and the vehicles travel over rough tracks. Recommend the most suitable type of backing storage for the laptops and explain your choice by comparing it with the other two types of storage.
parts.answer: Recommend solid-state (SSD). No moving parts, so it is not damaged by vibration on rough tracks, whereas the heads of a magnetic disk could crash into the platters; dust can stop an optical drive working/scratch discs, but sealed flash memory is unaffected; SSDs cope better with heat and use less power, important when charging is limited; optical discs have low capacity and are slow to write.
parts.working: 1 mark for SSD with a reason, then 1 mark per comparison with magnetic or optical, max 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a solid-state drive can find and read a file faster than a magnetic hard disk drive.
parts.answer: An HDD must wait for the read/write head to move to the correct track and for the platter to spin to the correct sector; an SSD has no moving parts and reads electronically from any memory cell almost instantly.
parts.working: 1 mark for the HDD mechanical delay, 1 mark for the SSD electronic access.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Video games are still sold on optical discs. Explain two reasons why.
parts.answer: Any two explained, e.g. discs are very cheap to mass-produce by pressing; ROM discs cannot be changed or erased by accident/by a virus; easy to sell and package in shops; large enough capacity (Blu-ray) for a game; buyers without fast internet do not need to download a very large file; the disc can be resold/lent.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A film editor copies a 24 GB video file. The SSD in her laptop reads at 150 MB/s and her old external hard disk reads at 90 MB/s (1 GB = 1024 MB). Calculate how many seconds faster the file is read from the SSD. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 109.2 seconds faster

parts.label: b
parts.text: Her laptop SSD holds 512 GB. Explain why she still keeps finished projects on the external hard disk.
parts.answer: Hard disks give much more capacity for the cost, so many large video files can be archived cheaply; this keeps the smaller, more expensive SSD free for current work, and the external drive also acts as a backup copy.
parts.working: 1 mark: HDD lower cost per GB / larger capacity. 1 mark: frees SSD space for current projects / acts as a backup.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teacher in Gilgit moves between classrooms with no internet connection. She needs to carry presentations of about 3 GB each week and update them often. Compare using a USB flash drive and a DVD-RW disc for this.
parts.answer: Both are portable and can be rewritten. The flash drive holds far more data (many GB) whereas a single-layer DVD-RW holds only 4.7 GB; the flash drive is faster to read and write and is more robust because it cannot be scratched, while a DVD can be damaged; a DVD-RW needs an optical drive, which many classroom computers do not have, but a USB port is almost always available. The DVD-RW is cheaper, but the flash drive is the better choice.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity; up to 3 marks for linked differences (capacity, speed, robustness, drive availability, cost). Separate lists with no comparison max 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A hospital radiology department must keep patient scans for 25 years. The scans are rarely looked at after the first year. Evaluate the use of magnetic tape and hard disk drives for archiving these scans, and recommend one.
parts.answer: Tape: very large capacity at a very low cost per GB; long shelf life and suited to archive/backup; can be stored off-site; but serial access means finding one scan is slow, and it needs a tape drive. HDD: direct access, so any scan can be found quickly; but more expensive per GB for this volume, uses power if kept online and has moving parts that can fail, so drives would need replacing during 25 years. Recommendation: tape for the long-term archive (perhaps with recent scans kept on HDD), because old scans are rarely needed and cost and capacity matter most.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for tape points, up to 2 marks for HDD points, 1 mark for linking to the 'rarely looked at' context, 1 mark for justified recommendation. Max 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two differences between RAM and ROM.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. RAM is volatile (contents lost when power is off) but ROM is non-volatile; RAM can be written to and read from but ROM can only be read; RAM stores the programs/data currently in use, ROM stores the start-up instructions (BIOS/boot program); RAM is usually much larger than ROM in a computer.
parts.working: 1 mark for each difference that refers to both.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is normally stored in ROM in a personal computer.
parts.answer: The start-up/boot instructions (BIOS/firmware) needed when the computer is switched on.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is stored in RAM while a computer is being used.
parts.answer: The parts of the operating system, applications and data currently in use.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the contents of RAM would be lost during a power cut.
parts.answer: RAM is volatile: it needs a constant power supply to keep its contents.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement is true or false.
(i) ROM keeps its contents when the computer is switched off.
(ii) Data in RAM can be read but cannot be changed.
(iii) Backing storage is usually larger than RAM.
(iv) A solid-state drive is an example of internal memory.
parts.answer:
(i) True
(ii) False
(iii) True
(iv) False
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of storage described in each statement. Choose from RAM, ROM or backing storage.
(i) It holds the program the processor is running right now.
(ii) It holds the instructions used when the computer is first switched on.
(iii) It keeps the user's photos and documents when the computer is switched off.
parts.answer:
(i) RAM
(ii) ROM
(iii) Backing storage
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by volatile memory and name one type of volatile memory.
parts.answer: Memory that loses its contents when the power is switched off; RAM.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When a computer is switched on, the first instructions it runs are the start-up (BIOS) instructions. State where these are stored and explain why.
parts.answer: In ROM, because ROM is non-volatile, so the instructions are still there when the power is switched on, and they cannot be changed or deleted accidentally.
parts.working: 1 mark: ROM. 1 mark: non-volatile / cannot be altered.

parts.label: a
parts.text: From this list, identify the two items that are internal memory: solid-state drive, RAM, USB flash drive, ROM, memory card.
parts.answer: RAM and ROM
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two examples of backing storage devices found in or used with a smartphone.
parts.answer: e.g. the phone's built-in flash (solid-state) storage; a microSD memory card; (cloud storage also accepted).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a smartphone needs backing storage as well as RAM.
parts.answer: RAM is volatile and loses its contents when the phone is turned off; backing storage keeps photos, apps and settings permanently, ready for the next time the phone is used.
parts.working: 1 mark: RAM loses data when off. 1 mark: backing storage keeps files/apps permanently.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete each sentence using RAM, ROM or backing storage.
(i) Programs are copied from ……… into ……… before they are run.
(ii) ……… can be read from but not normally written to.
(iii) A user's saved essays are kept on ……….
parts.answer: (i) backing storage; RAM (ii) ROM (iii) backing storage
parts.working: 1 mark for each gap (4 gaps).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two characteristics of ROM.
parts.answer: Any two: non-volatile (keeps contents without power); read-only, contents cannot normally be changed; small capacity; holds the start-up/BIOS instructions; part of internal memory directly accessed by the processor.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why RAM is called random access memory.
parts.answer: Any location (address) in RAM can be read or written directly, in any order, and every location takes the same time to reach.
parts.working: 1 mark: any location accessed directly/in any order. 1 mark: same access time for each location.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare internal memory with backing storage.
parts.answer: Both store data and programs. Internal memory (RAM/ROM) is accessed directly by the processor, whereas backing storage must be loaded into RAM first; RAM is volatile while backing storage is non-volatile, so it keeps files when switched off; backing storage has much larger capacity; RAM is faster to access; backing storage is cheaper per GB; backing storage may be removable/external, internal memory is on the motherboard.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 4.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a computer needs both RAM and backing storage.
parts.answer: RAM holds the programs and data the processor is currently using; RAM is fast so the processor can work quickly; RAM is volatile so files would be lost when switched off; backing storage keeps files/programs permanently when the power is off; backing storage has a much larger capacity than RAM so it can store all programs and files; RAM is too expensive to provide that capacity.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 4. Must address both RAM and backing storage for full marks.

practice.stem: A laptop is advertised with 16 GB of RAM and a 512 GB solid-state drive.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate how many times larger the solid-state drive is than the RAM.
parts.answer: 32 times

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why computers have much less RAM than backing storage.
parts.answer: RAM costs much more per gigabyte than backing storage; RAM only needs to hold the programs and data currently in use, while backing storage holds every file and program.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Backing storage is described as non-volatile. State what this means.
parts.answer: It keeps its data when the power is switched off.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Usman is typing an essay when a power cut happens. He saved the file ten minutes earlier. Explain what he will find when the power returns and why.
parts.answer: The version saved ten minutes ago is still there because it was saved to non-volatile backing storage; the work typed since then is lost because it was only in volatile RAM.
parts.working: 1 mark for each half.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A laptop has 8 GB of RAM. These are in use: operating system 2.5 GB, web browser 1.8 GB, spreadsheet 0.6 GB, photo editor 2.9 GB. Calculate how much RAM is still free.
parts.answer: 0.2 GB

parts.label: b
parts.text: The user now opens a video editor that needs 1.5 GB. Calculate by how much the demand for RAM exceeds the RAM fitted.
parts.answer: 1.3 GB

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain what will happen to the performance of the laptop and why.
parts.answer: The laptop will slow down, because there is not enough RAM, so data has to be moved back and forth between RAM and the much slower backing storage.
parts.working: 1 mark: slows down. 1 mark: swapping data with slower backing storage.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A smart TV contains ROM, RAM and flash backing storage. State which of these holds each item.
(i) the instructions that start the TV when it is switched on
(ii) the part of a film that has just been downloaded and is about to be shown
(iii) streaming apps that the user has installed
parts.answer: (i) ROM (ii) RAM (iii) flash backing storage
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a program is copied from the solid-state drive into RAM before it is run.
parts.answer: The processor can only run instructions directly from internal memory; RAM is much faster to access than backing storage, so the program runs quickly.
parts.working: 1 mark: processor accesses RAM directly. 1 mark: RAM is faster than backing storage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Users cannot change the contents of ROM. Explain why this is an advantage.
parts.answer: The start-up instructions cannot be deleted or changed by mistake or by malware, so the computer can always start correctly.
parts.working: 1 mark: cannot be accidentally deleted/changed. 1 mark: so the computer will always boot / is protected.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A phone has 8 GB of RAM and 256 GB of flash storage. The operating system and apps use 18% of the flash storage. Each photo the user takes is 4.2 MB. Using 1 GB = 1024 MB, calculate the largest number of whole photos that fit in the remaining storage.
parts.answer: 51 180 photos

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the 8 GB of RAM is not used to store the photos.
parts.answer: RAM is volatile, so the photos would be lost when the phone is switched off (and RAM is needed for running apps).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A point-of-sale terminal in a supermarket saves the details of each sale to backing storage as soon as the sale is complete, rather than keeping them in RAM until the end of the day. Explain why.
parts.answer: If there is a power cut or the terminal crashes, the contents of RAM are lost; saving to non-volatile backing storage after every sale means no sales records are lost.
parts.working: 1 mark: RAM lost on power failure. 1 mark: backing storage is non-volatile so records are kept.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to ROM, RAM and backing storage when a computer is switched on and starts up.
parts.answer: The processor runs the start-up (BIOS) instructions stored in ROM; these check the hardware and find the operating system on backing storage; the operating system is then loaded (copied) from backing storage into RAM, where it runs.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: start-up instructions from ROM; operating system found on backing storage; copied into RAM to run.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Sana's computer becomes very slow when she has a web browser, a spreadsheet and a video editor open at once. A technician says that adding more RAM will help. Explain why.
parts.answer: All open programs and their data must be held in RAM; when RAM is full, the operating system moves some data to backing storage (virtual memory) and back again; backing storage is much slower than RAM, so the computer slows down; more RAM means more programs/data can be held in fast memory at once, so less swapping is needed.
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The program that controls a washing machine is stored in ROM. Explain why ROM is used for this program.
parts.answer: ROM is non-volatile so the program is still there when the machine is unplugged/switched on again; ROM cannot be changed so the program cannot be erased or altered by accident.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The washing machine also contains a small amount of RAM. Explain why RAM is needed.
parts.answer: To store data that changes during a wash, e.g. the user's chosen programme/temperature, the time remaining and current sensor readings; this data must be written and changed, which is not possible in ROM.
parts.working: 1 mark for an example of temporary data, 1 mark for needing to change it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hira edits videos for a YouTube channel about Pakistani cooking. She has enough money either to double the RAM in her computer or to double the capacity of its backing storage, but not both. Discuss which upgrade she should choose.
parts.answer: RAM upgrade: video editing software and high-resolution video frames need lots of RAM; more RAM lets her preview/edit without the computer swapping data to slower storage, so editing is smoother and faster; allows other programs to stay open. Backing storage upgrade: video files are very large, so a full drive stops her saving new projects; more space lets her keep raw footage and finished videos; but extra storage does not make editing faster. Other points: she could store old videos on an external drive/cloud instead; the choice depends on whether her problem is speed or space. Conclusion justified from the points made.
parts.working: 5–6: both options discussed in detail with a justified conclusion; 3–4: both options with some explanation; 1–2: simple statements.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student says: 'My new laptop has 1 TB of memory.' The laptop has 8 GB of RAM and a 1 TB solid-state drive. Explain why the student's statement is not correct and rewrite it using the correct terms.
parts.answer: The 1 TB is backing storage (the SSD), not memory; memory means internal memory such as RAM, of which there is 8 GB. Correct: 'My laptop has 8 GB of RAM (memory) and 1 TB of backing storage on a solid-state drive.'
parts.working: 1 mark: 1 TB is backing storage. 1 mark: memory refers to RAM/ROM, which is 8 GB. 1 mark: correct rewritten sentence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A shopkeeper in Sukkur needs a laptop to run a point-of-sale program, an accounts program and a web browser at the same time. Laptop A has 4 GB RAM and a 1 TB hard disk drive. Laptop B has 16 GB RAM and a 256 GB solid-state drive. Evaluate the two laptops for this use and recommend one.
parts.answer: A: much more storage, so space for years of records and backups; but 4 GB RAM is not enough for three programs at once, so it would be slow, and the HDD is slower to load programs and files. B: 16 GB RAM lets all three programs run smoothly; the SSD loads programs quickly, uses less power and is more robust; 256 GB is smaller but sales and accounts files are small, so it is enough (backups can go to an external drive or the cloud). Recommendation: Laptop B, because speed when serving customers matters more than very large storage.
parts.working: Up to 2 marks for A, up to 2 marks for B, 1 mark for linking to the shopkeeper's needs, 1 mark for justified recommendation. Max 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A computer's hard disk drive is replaced with a solid-state drive of the same capacity. Explain why the computer now starts up and opens programs faster, but still cannot run more programs at the same time without slowing down.
parts.answer: The operating system and programs are loaded from backing storage into RAM; the SSD has no moving parts, so it reads data much faster than the HDD and loading takes less time. The number of programs that can run together depends on the amount of RAM, which has not changed; when RAM is full, data is swapped to backing storage, which slows the computer.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: OS/programs copied from backing storage into RAM; SSD faster access (no moving parts/no seek delay); programs running at once limited by RAM capacity, which is unchanged; full RAM causes swapping and slows the computer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A weather data logger has 64 KB of RAM for storing readings. Each reading uses 2 bytes and a reading is taken every 5 seconds (1 KB = 1024 bytes). Calculate how many hours it takes to fill the RAM. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: 45.5 hours

parts.label: b
parts.text: The data logger copies its readings to a flash memory card every hour. Explain why.
parts.answer: RAM is volatile, so if the battery fails all readings in RAM would be lost; the memory card is non-volatile and has more capacity, so readings are kept safe and RAM space is freed.
parts.working: 1 mark: RAM volatile / data lost if power fails. 1 mark: card keeps data permanently / frees RAM.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A USB flash drive and RAM both store data electronically using semiconductor chips. Compare a USB flash drive with RAM.
parts.answer: Both are solid-state with no moving parts. RAM is volatile and loses data when the power is off, whereas the flash drive is non-volatile and keeps data. RAM is internal memory directly accessed by the processor and is much faster, whereas the flash drive is backing storage connected through a USB port. The flash drive is portable and usually has a larger capacity per unit cost, whereas RAM is fixed inside the computer.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity; up to 3 marks for linked differences (volatility, speed/direct access, portability, purpose/capacity).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by validation.
parts.answer: An automatic check by the computer that data entered is sensible/reasonable/follows set rules.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what is meant by verification.
parts.answer: A check that data has been copied/entered accurately from the source document (or transferred without change).
parts.working: 1 mark. Do not accept 'checks that data is correct'.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each method is a validation check or a verification method.
(i) Range check
(ii) Double data entry
(iii) Visual check against the original form
(iv) Presence check
parts.answer:
(i) Validation
(ii) Verification
(iii) Verification
(iv) Validation
parts.working: All four correct: 2 marks; two or three correct: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A hospital uses an admission form. Name a suitable validation check for each field.
(i) PatientName must not be left blank.
(ii) WardNumber must be from 1 to 25.
(iii) BloodGroup must be one of A+, A−, B+, B−, AB+, AB−, O+, O−.
(iv) DischargeDate must not be before AdmissionDate.
parts.answer:
(i) Presence check
(ii) Range check
(iii) Lookup check (list/table lookup)
(iv) Consistency check (cross-field check)
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name one verification method that could be used when the form is typed in.
parts.answer: Double data entry or visual check.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A college in Lahore stores students' results in a database table. The field Grade must contain only A, B, C, D, E or U.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a validation rule for the Grade field.
parts.answer: "A" Or "B" Or "C" Or "D" Or "E" Or "U" (accept In ("A","B","C","D","E","U"))
parts.working: 1 mark for all six values correctly combined.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the field size you would set for Grade.
parts.answer: 1 (one character).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An online shop in Lahore asks customers to type their email address twice when they register. Name the type of check this is.
parts.answer: Verification (double entry).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two validation checks the shop could carry out on the delivery details, stating the field each applies to.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. presence check on name/address; format check on email/phone number; length check on phone number (11 digits); lookup check on city; type check that postcode contains digits.
parts.working: 1 mark for each check correctly matched to a field.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why an online shop validates data on its checkout page. Give one example of a validation check it might use.
parts.answer: To stop unreasonable/impossible data being stored (e.g. so orders are not sent to incomplete addresses); e.g. presence check on the delivery address, or range check that quantity is at least 1.
parts.working: 1 mark for purpose, 1 mark for example.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A weather station in Jacobabad records air temperatures in °C. The database accepts only temperatures from −10 to 50 inclusive. Name this type of validation check.
parts.answer: Range check.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a validation rule for the field.
parts.working: 1 mark. Accept Between -10 And 50.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State which of these values would be rejected: 23, −12, 50, 51.5
parts.working: 1 mark each; deduct 1 for each accepted value listed as rejected (50 is accepted because the range is inclusive).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the validation check that would be used in each case.
(i) The Quantity field must contain a whole number.
(ii) A library membership code must be three capital letters followed by three digits, for example LIB418.
(iii) A mobile number must contain exactly 11 characters.
(iv) The last digit of a book's ISBN is calculated from the other digits and recalculated when the number is entered.
parts.answer: (i) Type check (ii) Format check (iii) Length check (iv) Check digit
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement describes validation or verification.
(i) The computer checks that data is reasonable and follows set rules.
(ii) Data is checked to make sure it matches the original source.
(iii) Data can be rejected even though it was copied correctly from the form.
(iv) A person compares what is on the screen with the paper document.
parts.answer: (i) Validation (ii) Verification (iii) Validation (iv) Verification
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A clerk is typing students' examination marks from paper mark sheets into a database. Explain why both validation and verification should be used.
parts.answer: Validation will reject marks that are impossible/unreasonable, e.g. 112 when the maximum is 100; but validation cannot detect a reasonable but wrong mark, e.g. 67 typed as 76; verification (double entry/visual check) compares the entry with the mark sheet so it finds these copying errors; but verification does not check the data is sensible – a mark copied correctly may still be impossible if the sheet is wrong; so together they reduce errors (although neither guarantees the data is correct).
parts.working: 1 mark per point, max 4. Must refer to both methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how double data entry is used to verify data.
parts.answer: The data is entered twice (often by two different people); the computer compares the two versions and flags/rejects any differences so they can be checked against the source.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of double data entry.
parts.answer: Takes twice as long/costs more in staff time; if both people make the same mistake it is not detected; it does not detect errors in the source document.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a visual check is carried out.
parts.answer: After data is entered, the person compares the data on the screen with the original source document, item by item, and corrects any differences.
parts.working: 1 mark for comparing with the source, 1 mark for correcting differences.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of a visual check.
parts.answer: The person may not notice errors (tiredness/boredom); slow for large amounts of data; the person who typed the data may make the same reading error again.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A Pakistani CNIC number has the form 12345-1234567-1 (five digits, a hyphen, seven digits, a hyphen, one digit). Name the most suitable validation check for this field and describe what it checks.
parts.answer: Format check; it checks that the characters are in the pattern 5 digits, '-', 7 digits, '-', 1 digit (15 characters in total).
parts.working: 1 mark for format check, 1 mark for description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a numeric type check would not be suitable for this field.
parts.answer: The CNIC contains hyphens, which are not numbers, so valid entries would be rejected (and a number field could not check the pattern).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a character check does. Give an example of a field where it could be used.
parts.answer: It checks that the data contains only allowed characters (e.g. letters, spaces, hyphens, apostrophes) and no invalid ones; e.g. a person's name field such as 'Bushra Al-Saud' should not contain digits.
parts.working: 1 mark for description, 1 mark for suitable example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a name that passes the character check may still be incorrect.
parts.answer: Validation only checks the characters are allowed, not that the name is spelt correctly, e.g. 'Busra' would pass.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A sports club database has a table MEMBERS. The field JoinDate stores the date the member joined. The field Surname must always be completed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a validation rule that prevents a JoinDate later than today's date.
parts.answer: <=Date() (accept <=Now())
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how you would make sure the Surname field is never left blank, and name this type of check.
parts.answer: Set the field's Required property to Yes (accept validation rule Is Not Null); presence check.
parts.working: 1 mark for both.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Contrast validation and verification.
parts.answer: Validation is carried out automatically by the computer, whereas verification is often done by a person (visual check) or by entering data twice; validation checks data is reasonable/follows rules, while verification checks data has been copied accurately from the source; validation can reject impossible values (e.g. 32/13/2026) but not correctly formatted wrong data, while verification can find copying mistakes but not errors in the source; validation uses checks such as range/presence/format, verification uses double entry/visual check.
parts.working: 1 mark per contrasting point, max 4. Points must refer to both methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Pakistani mobile numbers are entered as 11 digits starting with 03, for example 03214567890. Describe three validation checks that could be used on this field.
parts.answer: Length check – exactly 11 characters; format check – must start with '03'; type/character check – only the digits 0–9 allowed; presence check – the field must not be blank.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three appropriate checks with their purpose.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A clerk types 03214576890 instead of 03214567890. Explain why the validation checks will not find this error and name a method that would.
parts.answer: The wrong number is still 11 digits starting with 03, so it is valid; verification such as double data entry or a visual check against the original would find it.
parts.working: 1 mark: data is still valid / follows the rules; 1 mark: names visual check or double entry.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each item of data entered into a school database, name the validation check that would reject it.
(i) Quantity of books: −3 (must be between 1 and 20)
(ii) Surname: left empty
(iii) Mark: 'seventy' (must be a number)
(iv) Locker code: AB12 (must be exactly 6 characters)
parts.answer: (i) Range check (ii) Presence check (iii) Type check (iv) Length check
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An online registration form makes students choose their subjects from a drop-down list instead of typing them. Explain how this reduces errors.
parts.answer: Students can only choose from allowed subject names, so there are no spelling mistakes or invalid subjects; it is quicker and every entry is in the same form.
parts.working: 1 mark: only valid options can be chosen; 1 mark: no typing/spelling errors / consistent data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a student could still enter the wrong data.
parts.answer: The student could click the wrong subject in the list by mistake – the choice is valid but not the one intended.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A college's Student ID is two letters followed by four digits, for example KA2045. Explain why a length check alone is not enough for this field.
parts.answer: A length check only checks there are 6 characters, so values such as 123456 or KAB2X5 would be accepted although they are not in the correct pattern.
parts.working: 1 mark: only counts characters; 1 mark: invalid example would pass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the format check that should be used instead.
parts.answer: Check that characters 1–2 are letters and characters 3–6 are digits (e.g. an input mask LL0000).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A receptionist copies a patient's date of birth from a handwritten form and then checks the screen against the form. The form says 12/07/1985 but the patient actually wrote it wrongly; the correct date is 21/07/1985. Explain why the visual check did not find the error.
parts.answer: Verification only checks that the data on screen matches the source document; the copy was accurate, but the source document itself was wrong.
parts.working: 1 mark for what verification compares, 1 mark for source being wrong.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a range check would also not have found this error.
parts.answer: 12/07/1985 is a valid, reasonable date within any sensible range, so it passes validation.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest how the clinic could reduce this kind of error.
parts.answer: Ask the patient to check the details shown on screen/printout; check against an ID document such as a CNIC.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bank in Karachi employs staff to type customer details from paper application forms into its computer system. Explain how validation and verification can be used to reduce errors in the data. Include examples relevant to the bank.
parts.answer: Validation: checks done by the computer as data is entered; presence check that the customer's name and CNIC number are entered; format check on the CNIC number (5 digits-7 digits-1 digit); range check on date of birth so the customer is at least 18; lookup check on branch code/account type; type check that the phone number contains only digits. Verification: double data entry – two staff type each form and the computer compares the two copies, flagging differences; visual check – the clerk compares the screen with the paper form. Validation finds unreasonable data but not wrongly copied reasonable data; verification finds copying errors but not wrong source data; neither guarantees data is correct.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point with example, max 6. Max 4 if only one of validation/verification is covered.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When creating an account on an online learning website, a student must type a new password twice. Explain whether this is validation or verification.
parts.answer: Verification; it checks that the second entry matches the first, so the password has been typed accurately (it does not check whether the password is reasonable).
parts.working: 1 mark for verification, 1 mark for reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The website also rejects any password with fewer than 8 characters. Name this check and explain why the website uses it.
parts.answer: Length check (validation); short passwords are easier to guess/crack, so a minimum length makes accounts more secure.
parts.working: 1 mark for length check, 1 mark for reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each error made when typing data from a paper form, state whether it would be found by validation, by verification, or by both. Give the name of a suitable check or method for each.
(i) Age typed as 150.
(ii) Telephone number 03001234567 typed as 03001234576.
(iii) Surname field left blank by mistake.
(iv) Date of birth typed as 31/02/2010.
(v) Quantity 18 typed as 81 when quantities from 1 to 100 are allowed.
parts.answer:
(i) Validation (range check) – also found by verification
(ii) Verification only (double entry/visual check) – passes format and length checks
(iii) Validation (presence check) – also found by verification
(iv) Validation (type check – a Date field rejects 31/02 because it is not a real date; a simple dd/mm/yyyy format check alone would not) – also found by verification
(v) Verification only (double entry/visual check) – 81 is within range
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct answer with suitable check/method. Accept 'both' for (i), (iii), (iv).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A university in Doha asks applicants to type their email address twice, and also checks that it contains an @ symbol followed by a full stop later in the address. Explain what kind of error each of these two checks can detect.
parts.answer: Typing it twice (verification) detects a typing/copying slip where the two entries are different; the @ and full stop check (format check, validation) detects entries that cannot be email addresses, e.g. missing @.
parts.working: 1 mark for each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An applicant types ahmed.raza@gmial.com in both boxes. Explain why neither check detects the error and what effect this will have.
parts.answer: Both entries are identical so verification passes; the address has the correct format so validation passes; the university's emails will go to a non-existent/wrong address so the applicant will not receive them.
parts.working: 1 mark for why both checks pass, 1 mark for effect.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what a consistency check is. Give an example from a school database.
parts.answer: It checks that data in two (or more) fields agrees/makes sense together; e.g. if Title is 'Mrs' then Gender must be F; or LeavingDate must be after JoiningDate; or a student in Year 7 cannot have an age of 17.
parts.working: 1 mark for description, 1 mark for example.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a consistency check is different from a range check.
parts.answer: A range check compares one field with fixed upper and lower limits; a consistency check compares the value in one field with the value in another field.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why data that passes all validation and verification checks may still be wrong.
parts.answer: Checks only find data that is unreasonable or wrongly copied; the source data itself could be wrong (e.g. the person gave the wrong information).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A 13-digit book number uses a check digit. To find it, the first 12 digits are multiplied alternately by 1 and 3 (starting with 1), the results are added, and the check digit is the number that must be added to the total to reach the next multiple of 10 (0 if the total is already a multiple of 10). Calculate the check digit for 978969803421.
parts.working: Total = 9+21+8+27+6+27+8+0+3+12+2+3 = 126 (M1 for weights, A1 for 126); next multiple of 10 is 130, so check digit = 4 (A1).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A clerk types the number with the last two digits before the check digit swapped, 978969803412, followed by the check digit 4. Show that the computer will detect this error.
parts.answer: The weighted total for 978969803412 is 128, so the check digit should be 2, not 4; the numbers do not match and the entry is rejected.
parts.working: 1 mark: total 128 / correct check digit 2; 1 mark: mismatch with 4 so error detected.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State whether a check digit is a validation or a verification method.
parts.answer: Validation.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A river monitoring station records water levels automatically using a sensor; no person types the data. Explain why validation is still needed.
parts.answer: A faulty sensor or a transmission error can produce impossible values (e.g. a negative level or a sudden huge jump); a range check can detect and flag these readings before they are used.
parts.working: 1 mark: sensors/transmission can produce wrong data; 1 mark: validation (range) flags impossible values.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a visual check is not a practical form of verification for this data.
parts.answer: There is no paper source document to compare with, and readings are taken too often for a person to check them all.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cricket stadium's online booking form has the fields: Name, CNIC number, NumberOfTickets (1 to 6 per person) and MatchDate (must be one of the match dates in the season). For each field, name a suitable validation check and give the rule it applies.
parts.answer: Name – presence check: must not be blank (or character check: letters, spaces, hyphens only). CNIC – format check: 5 digits, hyphen, 7 digits, hyphen, 1 digit (or length check of 15 characters). NumberOfTickets – range check: >=1 And <=6 (also type check: whole number). MatchDate – look-up from a list / format check as a date and must be one of the season's dates (cannot be in the past).
parts.working: 1 mark for each field with a suitable check and rule.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The site asks the customer to type the email address twice. State why this is a verification method, not validation.
parts.answer: It checks the two copies match, i.e. that the data was entered as the customer intended, not that it is reasonable.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A database designer puts a presence check on the field MiddleName. Explain why this is a poor choice and what problem it causes.
parts.answer: Many people do not have a middle name, so the field must sometimes be empty; the check would force them to type something false (e.g. 'none' or a dot), giving incorrect data or stopping them registering.
parts.working: 1 mark: not everyone has a middle name; 1 mark: forces false data / user cannot submit.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A range check on DateOfBirth for a primary school allows any date between 01/01/2000 and 31/12/2030. Explain why this rule is poorly designed and suggest a better rule.
parts.answer: The range is far too wide – it accepts children who are adults or not yet born. A better rule relates to today's date and the age range of pupils, e.g. the pupil must be between 4 and 12 years old on the admission date.
parts.working: 1 mark: range too wide / allows impossible ages or future dates; 1 mark: rule linked to current date / realistic age range.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by proofreading a document.
parts.answer: Reading through a document carefully (by a person) to find and correct errors in spelling, grammar, punctuation, layout and content/consistency.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two types of error that a spell checker would not find.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. a correctly spelt word used in the wrong place (their/there, form/from); missing words; wrong facts/numbers; correctly spelt names typed incorrectly; layout errors such as inconsistent fonts.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before printing a word-processed report, a student proofreads the layout. Give three layout problems the student should check for.
parts.answer: Any three, e.g. blank pages; widows and orphans; tables split across pages/columns; headings separated from the text that follows; images overlapping text or outside margins; inconsistent styles, fonts or spacing; inconsistent bullet/numbering; text not aligned as required.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem:
A school office types this notice:
"the annual sports day will be held on on Friday 13 November at the Model town ground. Parents are welcome too attend. Refreshments will be avalable from 10:00"

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify five errors in the notice and state how each should be corrected.
parts.answer:
1. 'the' at the start should have a capital T.
2. 'on on' – remove the repeated word.
3. 'Model town' should be 'Model Town' (proper noun).
4. 'too' should be 'to'.
5. 'avalable' should be 'available'.
6. A full stop is missing at the end.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any five correctly identified and corrected errors.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Name the type of error in each case.
(i) 1965 is typed as 1956.
(ii) Islamabad is typed as Islambad.
(iii) 'the the meeting' – a word is typed twice.
(iv) 'from' is typed as 'form'.
parts.answer: (i) Transposition error (ii) Omission error (a letter left out) (iii) Repetition/duplication (iv) Real-word error (a wrong word that is spelt correctly)
parts.working: 1 mark each. Accept transposition for (iv) as letters swapped.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A small business called Zarvix Traders finds that its spell checker underlines its own name in every document. Describe how the spell checker can be made to accept the name.
parts.answer: Right-click the word (or use the spell-check dialogue) and choose 'Add to dictionary'; the name is stored in the custom dictionary and is no longer flagged.
parts.working: 1 mark: add to dictionary; 1 mark: custom/user dictionary stores it for future documents.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why staff should not simply click 'Ignore all' for every underlined word in a long report.
parts.answer: Some underlined words are genuine spelling mistakes, which would be left in the report.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A print shop in Gujranwala sends a customer a proof of her business card before printing 500 copies. Explain why.
parts.answer: So the customer can check the content and layout are correct before printing; errors found after printing would waste money, paper and time.
parts.working: 1 mark: check before printing; 1 mark: avoids wasting cost of reprinting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three things the customer should check on the proof.
parts.answer: Spelling of her name and job title; phone number and email address digit by digit; the logo and colours are correct; text is not too close to the edges; font size is readable.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A teacher has typed a table of exam results into a report. Give three things she should check when proofreading the table.
parts.answer: Every student is included and none is repeated; each mark matches the original mark sheet; column headings are correct and consistent; numbers are aligned (e.g. right-aligned) with the same number of decimal places; any totals or averages are correct; the table is not split badly across pages.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two problems with images that should be checked when proofreading a newsletter.
parts.answer: An image is stretched or squashed (aspect ratio not kept); an image overlaps or hides text; the image is blurred/pixelated; the wrong image or caption has been used; an image is cut off by the page margin.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the aspect ratio of a photograph should be kept when it is resized.
parts.answer: So the image is not distorted – people and objects keep their correct shape.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When proofreading a spreadsheet, Asad sees ##### in some cells. State what this means and how to correct it.
parts.answer: The column is too narrow to display the number/date; widen the column.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two other display problems he should check for in the spreadsheet.
parts.answer: Numbers stored as text (left-aligned, not used in calculations); inconsistent numbers of decimal places; missing currency symbols; text cut off by the next cell; formulas showing error values such as #DIV/0!
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: This sentence was typed into a newsletter: "The prize giving will be held in the mane hall on Mondey at 10 am, and all parents are invited to there celebration."

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the three spelling or word errors in the sentence and give the correct word for each.
parts.answer: mane → main; Mondey → Monday; there → their
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which of these errors a spell checker would detect and explain why the others would not be detected.
parts.answer: Only 'Mondey' would be detected because it is not in the dictionary; 'mane' and 'there' are real words, so the spell checker accepts them even though they are wrong in this context.
parts.working: 1 mark for Mondey, 1 mark for explanation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When proofreading a document you must make sure there are no widows or orphans. State what is meant by a widow and an orphan.
parts.answer: Widow: the last line of a paragraph appears on its own at the top of a new page/column. Orphan: the first line of a paragraph appears on its own at the bottom of a page/column.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one way to prevent widows and orphans in a word-processed document.
parts.answer: Turn on widow/orphan control in the paragraph settings (or insert a page/column break before the paragraph; keep lines together).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a visual check needs the original source document.
parts.answer: The data on screen must be compared with the original to see whether it has been copied accurately; without the source there is nothing to check it against, so only obvious errors could be spotted.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why it is better for a different person to carry out the visual check.
parts.answer: The person who typed the data may repeat the same misreading; a second person is more likely to spot mistakes.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two types of error that a grammar checker can detect.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. subject–verb agreement (they was); repeated words; missing capital at the start of a sentence; incorrect punctuation/spacing; sentence fragments; some wrong word choices (your/you're).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a user should not accept every suggestion made by a grammar checker.
parts.answer: The checker does not understand meaning/context and can suggest changes that make the sentence wrong or change its meaning (e.g. in technical terms or quotes).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A company has a corporate house style. While proofreading a report, an employee checks that all headings, body text and line spacing match the house style. Give two reasons why this consistency is important.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. gives a professional appearance; makes the company's documents instantly recognisable (brand identity); makes documents easier to read/navigate; staff do not need to make layout decisions/documents from different people match.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the autocorrect feature can introduce errors into a document.
parts.answer: It automatically changes words it thinks are misspelt, without asking; it can replace correct names or technical words (for example a surname or a medicine name) with a common word, and the writer may not notice.
parts.working: 1 mark: changes text automatically; 1 mark: correct but unusual words replaced with wrong ones.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a writer can reduce this problem.
parts.answer: Proofread carefully after typing; add the names to the dictionary/autocorrect exceptions; undo the change when it happens; turn off the autocorrect entries that cause trouble.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A clerk copies sales figures (in rupees) from a paper sheet into a spreadsheet.
Source sheet: Branch A 1,250; Branch B 3,475; Branch C 980; Branch D 12,600; Branch E 455
Typed data: Branch A 1,250; Branch B 3,745; Branch C 980; Branch D 1,260; Branch E 455
Identify each error and name the type of error.
parts.answer: Branch B: 3,475 typed as 3,745 – transposition error. Branch D: 12,600 typed as 1,260 – omission error (a digit left out).
parts.working: 1 mark for each branch identified; 1 mark for each correct error type.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the correct total of the five source figures.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The clerk's spreadsheet shows a total of 7,690. Explain how comparing totals helps to find copying errors.
parts.answer: If the total of the typed figures (7,690) does not equal the total from the source (18,760), at least one figure has been copied wrongly, so the data must be checked.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school newsletter contains these phrases: 'Sports day on 12 March 2026', 'Parents' evening on 03/04/2026', 'Prize giving on April 5th'; 'Fee Rs 500', 'Trip PKR 750', 'Uniform Rs.1,000'. Identify two types of inconsistency.
parts.answer: Dates are written in three different formats; currency is written in different ways (Rs, PKR, Rs.).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Rewrite all three dates and all three amounts in one consistent style.
parts.answer: Example: 12 March 2026, 3 April 2026, 5 April 2026; Rs 500, Rs 750, Rs 1,000.
parts.working: 1 mark for consistent dates (03/04 interpreted as 3 April, day/month); 1 mark for consistent amounts. Any single consistent style is accepted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three techniques that help a person proofread a long report more accurately.
parts.answer: Print it out and read it on paper; read slowly, one line at a time, using a ruler; read the text aloud; ask another person to read it; leave a gap of time before proofreading your own work; check one type of error at a time (e.g. numbers, then headings).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three described techniques.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A bar chart in a report is titled 'Rainfall in Karachi 2025'. The vertical axis has no title, the legend shows 'Series1' and the bars are labelled Jan to Dec, but the data was taken from a table headed 'Rainfall in Lahore 2025 (mm)'. Identify three errors that should be found by proofreading and state the correction for each.
parts.answer: Title names the wrong city – change to Lahore; vertical axis has no title/units – add 'Rainfall (mm)'; legend shows 'Series1' – rename the series or remove the legend since there is only one series.
parts.working: 1 mark for each error with a correction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A charity in Peshawar must enter 3,600 paper application forms. One typist enters 45 forms per hour and is paid Rs 700 per hour. Calculate the cost of entering the forms once.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The charity decides to use double data entry. Calculate the extra cost and explain what the extra cost buys.
parts.answer: Extra Rs 56,000. Each form is typed twice and the computer compares the two copies, so typing errors that would not be detected by validation are found.
parts.working: 1 mark: 56,000 (total 112,000); 1 mark: explanation of double entry benefit.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A database report lists customers of a courier company in Lahore. When proofreading it, Zara finds that long customer names are cut off, for example 'Muhammad Abdul Rehm', and that one column heading reads 'CustTelNo'. Explain the cause of each problem and how to correct it.
parts.answer: Names cut off: the column in the report is too narrow for the longest data – widen it (or reduce the font size) so all of the data shows. 'CustTelNo': the field name has been used as the label – edit the label to a clear heading such as 'Telephone number'.
parts.working: 1 mark for each cause and 1 mark for each correction.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student types a travel guide about Pakistan. The spell checker underlines the correctly spelt place names Peshawar, Hunza and Skardu. Explain what the student should do with each place name and why she should not choose 'Change' or 'Change All'.
parts.answer: Choose 'Ignore All' (or 'Add to dictionary' if the names will be used again); the names are correct but are not in the software's dictionary; 'Change'/'Change All' would replace the correct names with the suggested (wrong) words throughout the document.
parts.working: 1 mark for ignore/add, 1 mark for why flagged, 1 mark for danger of Change All.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The guide is written for a British publisher. State which dictionary language the student should set and why.
parts.answer: English (UK), so that British spellings such as 'colour' and 'centre' are accepted and US spellings are flagged.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A research organisation in Islamabad must enter the answers from 5000 paper survey forms. Compare double data entry and visual checking as methods of verifying the data.
parts.answer: Both compare the entered data with the source to find copying errors and neither finds errors in the source. Double entry is automatic in the comparison so it finds almost all differences, whereas a visual check relies on a person noticing errors and may miss some through tiredness; double entry needs each form typed twice so costs more staff time, while a visual check is a single re-read; for 5000 forms a visual check would be very tiring, so double entry is more reliable; double entry cannot detect the same mistake made twice.
parts.working: 1 mark per comparison point, max 4; at least one similarity for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A document is set out in two columns. After proofreading, a student notices that the subheading 'Visiting Lahore Fort' is the last line of the first column while its paragraph starts at the top of the second column. Explain why this is a problem and describe how to fix it.
parts.answer: A heading should stay with the text it introduces – the reader sees it separated from its content (unprofessional/harder to read); fix by setting 'Keep with next' on the heading/heading style or by inserting a column break before the subheading.
parts.working: 1 mark for problem, 2 marks for a correct method described.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A table in the same document is split across two pages. Describe two ways to make the table easier to read.
parts.answer: Any two, e.g. move the table/insert a page break so it is on one page; set table rows not to break across pages/keep with next; repeat the header row on the second page.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: After a long document is printed, the proofreader notices that page numbers on the contents page do not match the actual page numbers of the sections. Explain why this happened and how to correct it.
parts.answer: Text was added or removed after the table of contents was created, so the sections moved to different pages; update the table of contents (update field) before printing.
parts.working: 1 mark: contents created before later changes; 1 mark: update/refresh the table of contents.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one other automatically generated item that should be updated before printing.
parts.answer: Cross-references; index; captions/figure numbers; page count in a footer (Page x of y).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a report about computing, a writer uses Replace All to change every 'ICT' to 'Information and Communication Technology', with 'Match case' turned off. Explain what happens to the word 'dictionary' and why.
parts.answer: It becomes 'dInformation and Communication Technologyionary', because the letters 'ict' inside 'dictionary' match 'ICT' when case is ignored and the word is not checked as a whole word.
parts.working: 1 mark: the result; 1 mark: matching letters inside another word / case ignored.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two settings the writer should have used, and one other good practice when using Replace All.
parts.answer: Turn on 'Match case'; turn on 'Find whole words only'. Good practice: use Replace (one at a time) to review each change, or proofread/search the document afterwards; save a copy before replacing.
parts.working: 1 mark for each setting; 1 mark for good practice.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school uses mail merge to produce letters to parents. One letter begins 'Dear  Khan,' and another says 'Your child, , has been selected'. Explain the cause of each error.
parts.answer: The Title field (e.g. Mr/Mrs) is blank for that record, leaving two spaces before the surname; the child's name field is empty in the data source, so nothing is inserted between the commas.
parts.working: 1 mark for each cause linked to missing data in the source.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two checks that should be made before printing all the merged letters.
parts.answer: Preview the merged letters for several records, including unusual ones; check the data source for blank or wrongly entered fields; check spacing and punctuation around each merge field; check the right fields are inserted in the right places; print a test letter.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student's presentation includes a slide whose title is a picture of text, made in a graphics program, and a chart pasted as an image. Explain why the spell checker did not find the spelling mistake 'Enviroment' in the title.
parts.answer: The title is an image, not text; the spell checker can only check text characters, so the letters in the picture are not checked.
parts.working: 1 mark: it is an image; 1 mark: spell checker only checks text.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two other checks the student should make when proofreading the slides.
parts.answer: Fonts, sizes and colours consistent on every slide (use the master slide); text readable from the back of the room; no text running off the slide; transitions/animations consistent; slide numbers correct; images not distorted.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Before a school's new web page is published, it must be proofread. Describe four things, apart from spelling and grammar, that should be checked.
parts.answer: All hyperlinks work and go to the right pages (no broken links); images display (correct relative file paths) and have alt text; the page displays correctly in different browsers and on phones; text and headings use the same styles throughout (CSS applied); contact details and dates are correct; the page title is correct.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A spreadsheet of 400 student records prints on 9 pages. Only the first page shows the column headings, and the last column prints on separate pages by itself. Describe how to correct each problem.
parts.answer: Set the heading row to repeat at the top of every printed page (print titles); change the page orientation to landscape or set 'fit all columns on one page' / reduce the scaling.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correction.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one other item to check in the print preview before printing all the pages.
parts.answer: Page numbers in the header/footer; gridlines or borders as required; no blank pages; data not cut off at page breaks.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the three layers used in web development.
parts.answer: Content layer, presentation layer, behaviour layer.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which layer each of these belongs to: (i) a CSS file that sets the font colour of headings; (ii) a script that checks a form has been filled in before it is sent; (iii) the HTML table that holds the page text.
parts.answer: (i) presentation; (ii) behaviour; (iii) content.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the purpose of the head section and the body section of a web page.
parts.answer: The head contains information about the page that is not displayed in the page itself, such as the title, metatags and links to stylesheets; the body contains the content shown in the browser window, such as text, images, tables and links.
parts.working: 1 mark: head – page information/metadata/title/stylesheet links not displayed in the page. 1 mark: body – the visible content.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two items that are placed in the head section.
parts.answer: The page title; the link to an external stylesheet.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: title | meta tags (charset, keywords, description, author, viewport) | link to external CSS | internal <style> | base target | scripts.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what each of these HTML elements is used for: <tr>, <td>, <th>.
parts.answer: <tr> defines a table row; <td> defines a table data cell; <th> defines a table header cell (bold and centred by default).
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the attribute colspan="2" does to a table cell.
parts.answer: It makes the cell stretch across (merge) two columns.

practice.stem: You are creating a web page for a hiking club in Gilgit. The stylesheet hike.css is in the same folder as the page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the HTML to attach the stylesheet hike.css to the page.
parts.answer: <link rel="stylesheet" href="hike.css">
parts.working: 1 mark: <link rel="stylesheet" …>. 1 mark: href="hike.css" (relative path, exact file name).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State where in the HTML document this line must be placed.
parts.answer: In the head section (between <head> and </head>).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the HTML to make the page title, shown in the browser tab, 'Gilgit Hikers'.
parts.answer: <title>Gilgit Hikers</title>
parts.working: B1 exact text, in head.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the HTML for a hyperlink with the text 'Email us' that opens an email to info@hikersclub.org with the subject 'Membership'.
parts.answer: Email us
parts.working: 1 mark: mailto: with correct address. 1 mark: ?subject=Membership. 1 mark: anchor text Email us and closing .

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the HTML for a hyperlink with the text 'Route map' that opens the local file routes.html in a new window or tab.
parts.answer: Route map
parts.working: 1 mark: href="routes.html". 1 mark: target="_blank".

practice.stem: An image file falcon.jpg is stored in a folder called images, inside the folder that holds the web page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the HTML to place this image on the page with the alternative text 'Peregrine falcon' and a width of 300 pixels, keeping its aspect ratio.
parts.working: 1 mark: src="images/falcon.jpg" (relative path). 1 mark: alt="Peregrine falcon". 1 mark: width="300" only (height omitted so aspect ratio is kept, or correct calculated height).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the path images/falcon.jpg is used rather than C:\Users\Sara\website\images\falcon.jpg.
parts.answer: The relative path still works when the website is uploaded to a web server; the C: path only exists on the developer's computer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the CSS rule to set the background colour of the whole page to light yellow #FFFFE0.
parts.answer: body { background-color: #FFFFE0; }
parts.working: 1 mark: body selector. 1 mark: background-color: #FFFFE0;

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the CSS rule that makes all paragraphs 12 pt and fully justified.
parts.answer: p { font-size: 12pt; text-align: justify; }
parts.working: 1 mark each property.

practice.stem: A stylesheet called museum.css contains the rule h1 { color: red; font-size: 24px }.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the punctuation error in this rule and rewrite the rule correctly, giving the colour as the hex code for pure red.
parts.answer: The final declaration has no semicolon after 24px. Corrected rule: h1 { color: #FF0000; font-size: 24px; }
parts.working: 1 mark: missing semicolon after 24px identified. 1 mark: rewritten rule with color: #FF0000; and both semicolons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a CSS comment containing the text 'Heading styles'.
parts.answer: /* Heading styles */

practice.stem: A student must add a sound file called school_bell.mp3 (in the same folder as the page) with controls so that visitors can play it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the HTML to add the sound with controls.
parts.answer:
<audio controls>
  <source src="school_bell.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
</audio>
parts.working: 1 mark: <audio> … </audio>. 1 mark: controls attribute. 1 mark: source with src="school_bell.mp3" (accept src on the audio element).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the controls attribute is needed.
parts.answer: Without it no play/pause buttons are shown, so visitors could not start the sound.

practice.stem: A web page for a plant nursery in Multan is being prepared for search engines.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the meta tag that sets the keywords to: plants, nursery, Multan, gardening.
parts.answer: <meta name="keywords" content="plants, nursery, Multan, gardening">
parts.working: 1 mark: name="keywords". 1 mark: content with the four words exactly.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the meta tag that gives the author as Green Leaf Nursery.
parts.answer: <meta name="author" content="Green Leaf Nursery">

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write the meta tag that makes the page fit the width of the device it is viewed on.
parts.answer: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
parts.working: 1 mark: name="viewport". 1 mark: content="width=device-width…" (initial-scale optional).

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A website for a school canteen in Abbottabad is made from these parts. State which web development layer (content, presentation or behaviour) each part belongs to.
(i) A file menu.css that sets the background colour and fonts.
(ii) A table in the HTML that lists the meals and prices.
(iii) A script that shows a message 'Added to your order' when a button is clicked.
(iv) A list of opening times typed in the HTML body.
parts.answer: (i) presentation (ii) content (iii) behaviour (iv) content
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A web page contains Fruit Market Prices in its head section and

Today's Prices

in its body. State where each piece of text is displayed.
parts.answer: 'Fruit Market Prices' appears in the browser tab (title bar / bookmarks and search results); 'Today's Prices' appears on the page itself as the main heading.
parts.working: B1: title in browser tab/title bar (also used for bookmarks/search results); B1: h1 shown in the page body as the largest heading.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each of these elements belongs in the head section or the body section of a web page.
(i) <title>
(ii) <table>
(iii) <meta name="description" content="…">
(iv) <video>
(v) <link rel="stylesheet" href="site.css">
(vi) <h1>
parts.answer: Head: (i), (iii), (v). Body: (ii), (iv), (vi).
parts.working: 1 mark for each two correct (6 correct = 3 marks).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An HTML page contains: Book a tour State the purpose of each of these attributes: src, alt, href, controls.
parts.answer: src gives the file name/location of the image or video; alt gives text shown if the image cannot be displayed (and read by screen readers); href gives the address of the page the link goes to; controls shows the play, pause and volume buttons for the video.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the HTML to make the text 'Fee structure' a hyperlink to the page fees.html, stored in the same folder, opening in the same window.
parts.answer: Fee structure
parts.working: B1: with correct relative path; B1: text and closing . Accept target="_self".

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the HTML to make the image logo.png a hyperlink to index.html. The image must have the alternative text 'Home'.
parts.working: B1: img with src and alt inside the anchor; B1: anchor href="index.html" opened before and closed after the image.

parts.label: a
