parts.text: Explain why the title must be typed exactly as shown.
parts.answer: The capital letters, spelling and spaces must match the original so the text is accurate (any error means the text is wrong).
parts.working: B1 accuracy – capitals/spaces/spelling must match.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two ways of enhancing text in a heading, other than changing the font size.
parts.answer: Any two: bold; italic; underline; change font colour; change font face; highlight/shading; all capitals.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A student's report ends with a reference list. Each reference is one paragraph and runs over two or more lines.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the paragraph setting needed so that the second and later lines of each reference in a list are indented.
parts.answer: Hanging indent
parts.working: 1 mark: hanging indent (Paragraph dialog > Indentation > Special: Hanging).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the steps to apply this setting to the selected reference paragraphs.
parts.answer: Select the reference paragraphs; open the Paragraph settings (Indentation); in the Special list choose Hanging and enter the indent amount (e.g. 1.25 cm); confirm.
parts.working: 1 mark: select the paragraphs and open the Paragraph settings. 1 mark: choose Hanging in Special and set the amount.

practice.stem: The text area of an A4 page is 23.5 cm high after the top and bottom margins are set. Each line of body text takes 18 pt of vertical space. Use 1 cm = 28.35 pt.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of complete lines of text that fit in the text area. Give your answer as a whole number.
parts.answer: 37 lines
parts.working: M1: 23.5 cm × 28.35 pt/cm = 666.2 pt. M1: 666.2 ÷ 18 = 37.01. A1: 37 complete lines (the part line is not counted).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one feature of a typical page, other than the body text, that means fewer lines of text fit on the page than this calculation suggests.
parts.answer: Headings, paragraph spacing, images or a footer take up part of the height.
parts.working: 1 mark for any one valid feature that uses vertical space.

practice.stem: A table in a planning report lists the floor area of each room in square metres. A student has typed 12 m2 and the 2 is at normal height.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the formatting that should be applied to the 2 so that it appears above the line.
parts.answer: Superscript (Home tab, Font group: superscript button)
parts.working: 1 mark: superscript.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why typing a caret and a number, such as m^2, is not suitable in a formal document.
parts.answer: The caret and the 2 both show as text, so the document looks unprofessional; the proper formatting is not used.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid reason, e.g. it is not the correct formatting and the caret is shown literally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of font in which every character has the same width.
parts.answer: Monospaced (fixed-width) font, for example Courier New
parts.working: 1 mark: monospaced or fixed-width font.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one type of document in which this font is suitable.
parts.answer: A code listing, a programming example, or printed computer output in aligned columns.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid example in which characters must line up.

practice.stem: A report contains 2130 lines of text. Each printed page holds 45 lines.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of pages needed for the report. Show your working.
parts.answer: 48 pages
parts.working: M1: 2130 ÷ 45 = 47.33. A1: 48 pages (a partly used page still needs a whole sheet).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the answer must be rounded up, not to the nearest whole number.
parts.answer: The last 0.33 of a page still needs a whole page, so 47 pages would be too few.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid reason that the partly filled page is still a whole page.

practice.stem: A student has changed the font and colour of one sentence by hand, and the sentence no longer matches the rest of the document.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two ways to remove direct formatting from a selected piece of text so that it takes on the formatting of its paragraph style.
parts.answer: Use the Clear All Formatting button (Home tab); press Ctrl+Spacebar; or reapply the paragraph style.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid method, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the paragraph setting that stops a heading from being left at the bottom of a page when the paragraph it introduces starts on the next page.
parts.answer: Keep with next
parts.working: 1 mark: Keep with next.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the name of the built-in style that has this setting switched on by default.
parts.answer: Heading 1 (or any Heading style)
parts.working: 1 mark: a Heading style.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why body text of at least 11 pt is recommended for a printed leaflet for older readers.
parts.answer: Any two: larger text is easier to read; it reduces eye strain; it reduces the chance of misreading words.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid reason, up to 2.

practice.stem: A student's introduction has three paragraphs. The paragraphs contain 84, 117 and 96 words.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the average number of words per paragraph.
parts.answer: 99 words

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the feature on the Review tab that shows the number of words in a document.
parts.answer: Word Count
parts.working: 1 mark: Word Count.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what a soft return (Shift+Enter) does, compared with pressing Enter.
parts.answer: Shift+Enter starts a new line inside the same paragraph, so the paragraph formatting and spacing after it are not split; Enter starts a new paragraph.
parts.working: 1 mark: Shift+Enter starts a new line within the same paragraph. 1 mark: Enter starts a new paragraph (with its own spacing).

practice.stem: A report is set up on A4 paper (21.0 cm wide, 29.7 cm high) in portrait orientation. The left margin is 2.5 cm and the right margin is 2.0 cm. The body is to be set in two columns with 1.0 cm of spacing between the columns.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the width of the text area between the margins.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the width of each column if both columns are equal.

practice.stem: An image of the Faisal Mosque is 12.0 cm wide and 8.0 cm high. It must be resized to 9.0 cm wide with its aspect ratio maintained, then placed to the right of a paragraph with the text wrapping around it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the new height of the image.
parts.answer: 6.0 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what is meant by maintaining the aspect ratio.
parts.answer: The width and height are changed in the same proportion so the image is not stretched or squashed.
parts.working: B1 width and height kept in same ratio / not distorted.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Name a text-wrapping setting that lets the paragraph flow around the image.
parts.answer: Square (or tight) wrapping.
parts.working: B1 square / tight / through. Not 'in line with text'.

practice.stem: A café in Gilgit is typing a price list in a word processor. Each line has the item name at the left margin and the price, such as 85.50 or 1250.00, further along the line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of tab stop that should be used for the prices so that the decimal points line up.
parts.answer: Decimal tab.
parts.working: B1 decimal tab.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name two other types of tab stop and describe how text lines up at each.
parts.answer: Left tab – text starts at the tab position and runs to the right; right tab – text ends at the tab position (runs to the left); centre tab – text is centred on the tab position.
parts.working: Any two: B1 name + B1 correct description for each (left, right, centre).

practice.stem: A bank with branches across Pakistan insists that all its letters and leaflets follow a corporate house style.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain three reasons why the bank uses a corporate house style.
parts.answer: Any three: gives a consistent look across all documents/branches; makes the bank's documents instantly recognisable (brand image); looks professional; staff do not have to make layout decisions so saves time; reduces errors because settings are defined; new staff know exactly how documents must look.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three expanded points: consistency; brand recognition/identity; professional image; saves time / templates; fewer formatting mistakes; easier training.

practice.stem: A bibliography in a history project on the Mughal Empire uses a hanging indent, while the body paragraphs use a first-line indent of 1 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe a first-line indent.
parts.answer: Only the first line of the paragraph starts further in from the left margin than the other lines.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a hanging indent.
parts.answer: The first line starts at the left margin and all the following lines of the paragraph are indented further in.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: c
parts.text: Suggest why a hanging indent suits a bibliography.
parts.answer: The author's name at the start of each entry stands out, so entries are easy to scan alphabetically.
parts.working: B1 start of each entry stands out / easy to find each item.

practice.stem: A student's poster about dengue prevention uses seven different fonts, many colours, and underlines nearly every sentence.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems with this formatting.
parts.answer: Any two: too many fonts look unprofessional/inconsistent; the reader cannot tell which text is important because everything is emphasised; too many colours or underlining make text harder to read; distracts from the message.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two explained points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways the student could make the key message stand out while keeping the poster easy to read.
parts.answer: Any two: use one or two fonts only; make the key message larger and/or bold; use one contrasting colour for it; place it centrally with white space around it; use a heading style.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: Before printing a 12-page charity report, a student is told to check the layout of the whole document.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List four layout problems the student should look for and correct.
parts.answer: Any four: widows or orphans; blank pages; a table split across two pages; a heading at the bottom of a page separated from its text; inconsistent spacing between paragraphs; images overlapping text or margins; text running beyond the margins; inconsistent fonts/styles.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four.

practice.stem: A school timetable is laid out in a table with days in the first column and periods 1 to 7 across the top. On Friday, periods 6 and 7 are combined for Jumu'ah prayers and a sports session.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to make one cell span periods 6 and 7 for Friday.
parts.answer: Select the two Friday cells for periods 6 and 7, then use 'merge cells' so they become one cell.
parts.working: B1 select both cells. B1 merge.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the table gridlines should be shown (borders applied) when this timetable is printed.
parts.answer: So that the rows and columns are clearly separated on paper (gridlines that are not borders do not print).
parts.working: B1 easier to read / gridlines alone may not print.

practice.stem: A teacher asks students to hand in draft essays with double line spacing and wide margins.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why double line spacing and wide margins are useful on a draft.
parts.answer: They leave space between lines and at the edges for the teacher to write corrections and comments; the text is also easier to read and edit.
parts.working: B1 space for annotations/corrections. B1 easier to read/proofread.

practice.stem: A house style states: heading – 16 pt with 12 pt space before and 6 pt space after; body text – 11 pt with 0 pt before and 6 pt after.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A heading is followed directly by a body paragraph. State the space, in points, between the bottom of the heading and the top of the body text, assuming the larger of the two settings applies.
parts.answer: 6 pt (heading space after is 6 pt, body space before is 0 pt).
parts.working: B1 6 pt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A body paragraph is followed by a heading. Calculate the total space between them if both settings are added together.
parts.answer: 18 pt

practice.stem: A 25-page project report has its section headings formatted with the Heading 1 and Heading 2 styles.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to insert an automatic table of contents that uses the Heading 1 and Heading 2 styles.
parts.answer: Go to References > Table of Contents and choose an automatic style; the contents list is built from paragraphs formatted with the heading styles.
parts.working: 1 mark: References > Table of Contents. 1 mark: built from paragraphs in Heading 1 and Heading 2 styles (the headings must use the styles).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The author then changes the wording of a heading. State what must be done so the contents page is correct.
parts.answer: Right-click the table of contents and choose Update Field (or Update Table) so that the titles and page numbers are refreshed.
parts.working: 1 mark: update the table (Update Field / Update Table).

practice.stem: A guide has sections numbered 1, 2, 3 and so on. The numbers were typed by hand. The author inserts a new section between sections 2 and 3.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the numbers of the sections after the new section are now wrong and must all be retyped.
parts.answer: The section numbers were typed by hand, so Word does not change them when a section is added; each number after the new section has to be typed again.
parts.working: 1 mark: numbers are typed manually / not automatic. 1 mark: adding a section does not update the later typed numbers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how a multilevel list linked to the heading styles avoids this problem.
parts.answer: Apply the multilevel list to the headings so each heading's number is generated automatically; when a new heading is inserted, all later numbers update.
parts.working: 1 mark: numbering is automatic / generated by the list. 1 mark: numbers renumber when a heading is added or removed.

practice.stem: A dissertation has 1840 words of body text. Each body page holds 320 words. The dissertation also has a separate cover page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total number of pages, including the cover page. Show your working.
parts.answer: 7 pages
parts.working: M1: 1840 ÷ 320 = 5.75, so 6 pages of body text (round up). A1: 6 + 1 cover page = 7 pages.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the header and footer option that stops the cover page showing a page number.
parts.answer: Different First Page (Header & Footer tab)
parts.working: 1 mark: Different First Page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two problems with a student who presses the Enter key ten times to move the next chapter onto a new page.
parts.answer: Any two: the blank paragraphs move when text above is edited; the page may break in the wrong place if the text changes; the blank lines are hard to remove and can leave a blank page.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid problem, up to 2.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the feature that should be used instead to start the new chapter on a new page.
parts.answer: Page break (Insert > Page Break, or Ctrl+Enter)
parts.working: 1 mark: a page break.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the effect on the number of pages of changing the body text from 11 pt to 12 pt.
parts.answer: The text takes up more space, so the document usually becomes longer (more pages), and the line breaks change.
parts.working: 1 mark: more pages. 1 mark: larger text takes more space or the line breaks change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student should check the page layout after making this change.
parts.answer: Headings, images and page breaks may move to a different place and the layout may need correcting.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid reason that the layout changes.

practice.stem: A business letter uses four different fonts, one for each paragraph.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why a document should use only one or two fonts consistently.
parts.answer: Any two: it looks more professional; it is easier to read; the reader can recognise the document's style; it is consistent with the house style.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid reason, up to 2.

practice.stem: A student formats each heading in a 30-page company report by selecting it and changing the font and size by hand.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain one disadvantage of formatting every heading by hand, rather than using a heading style.
parts.answer: Each heading must be changed separately, so the headings may not match and it takes time.
parts.working: 1 mark: each heading has to be changed one at a time. 1 mark: headings can become inconsistent or it wastes time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain how a heading style would help when the company decides to change the heading font.
parts.answer: Changing the style once updates every heading that uses it.
parts.working: 1 mark: all headings using the style update automatically.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why text copied from a web page may bring unwanted formatting into a report.
parts.answer: The text keeps the fonts, colours, spacing and links of the web page, which do not match the report.
parts.working: 1 mark: copied text keeps its original formatting. 1 mark: this clashes with the report's house style.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one way to remove the unwanted formatting when the text is pasted.
parts.answer: Use Paste Special > Unformatted Text (or Keep Text Only), or select the text and use Clear All Formatting.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid method.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a style in a word processor.
parts.answer: A saved set of formatting settings that can be applied to text or paragraphs in one step.
parts.working: 1 mark: a saved group of formatting settings applied together.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two elements of formatting that a paragraph style can control.
parts.answer: Any two: font, font size, font colour, alignment, line spacing, paragraph spacing, indentation.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid element, up to 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why setting the line spacing to 'Exactly 12 pt' can cut off the tops of large characters.
parts.answer: Exactly spacing fixes the height of each line, so a line containing larger characters has less room than it needs and the tops are clipped.
parts.working: 1 mark: exact spacing fixes the line height. 1 mark: taller characters do not fit in that height and are cut off.

practice.stem: A school magazine page must show the title across the full width of the page in one column, and then the articles underneath in three columns. Later in the same document, one page holding a wide table must be landscape while the other pages stay portrait.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a section break (continuous) is needed after the title rather than a page break.
parts.answer: A continuous section break starts a new section on the same page, so the column setting can change from one to three columns below the title; a page break would push the articles onto a new page and cannot change the number of columns.
parts.working: B1 section break allows different layout (number of columns) in each section. B1 continuous keeps the text on the same page / page break moves text to new page.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the single landscape page can be created.
parts.answer: Insert a (next page) section break before and after the table page, then set the orientation of that section only to landscape.
parts.working: B1 section breaks before and after the page. B1 change orientation for that section only (apply to this section).

practice.stem: A travel brochure was written about Murree. The same text is to be reused for a brochure about Nathia Gali, so every occurrence of the word Murree must be replaced. The text also contains the word Murree's.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to make the change using find and replace.
parts.answer: Open find and replace, enter Murree in the 'find' box and Nathia Gali in the 'replace with' box, then select 'replace all' (checking the result).
parts.working: B1 enter search text Murree and replacement Nathia Gali. B1 use replace all / replace each in turn.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the options 'match case' and 'find whole words only' can be useful when replacing words in a document.
parts.answer: Match case only finds text with exactly the same capital letters, so words with different capitalisation are not changed by mistake; whole words only stops the search text being replaced when it is part of a longer word (e.g. replacing 'rain' would otherwise also change 'train' or 'drain').
parts.working: B1 match case – exact capitalisation only. B1 whole words – avoids changing the text inside longer words (example helps).

practice.stem: A newsletter page is A4 landscape (29.7 cm wide). The left and right margins are each 1.8 cm. The text is set in three equal columns with 0.9 cm spacing between adjacent columns.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the width of each column. Give your answer in cm correct to 2 decimal places.

practice.stem: A college in Peshawar prints its 40-page prospectus double-sided and binds it along the left edge of odd pages and the right edge of even pages.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what a gutter margin is and why one is needed here.
parts.answer: A gutter margin is extra margin space added on the binding edge; it stops text being hidden or hard to read where the pages are bound.
parts.working: B1 extra space on binding side. B1 text not lost in binding.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the page setting that makes the inside and outside margins swap on facing pages.
parts.answer: Mirror margins (book fold / facing pages).
parts.working: B1 mirror margins.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The page is 21.0 cm wide, the inside margin is 2.0 cm, the outside margin is 1.5 cm and the gutter is 1.0 cm. Calculate the width available for text.

practice.stem: A table in a document lists eight cricket grounds in Pakistan with three columns: Ground, City, Capacity. The first row holds the column headings.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to make the heading row stand out and repeat at the top of each page if the table splits.
parts.answer: Format the first row (e.g. bold and shaded/coloured background), and set it as a header row that repeats on each page.
parts.working: B1 format heading row – bold/shading/centre. B1 'repeat as header row' setting.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the alignment that should be used for the Capacity column and give a reason.
parts.answer: Right aligned, so that units, tens and thousands line up and numbers are easy to compare.
parts.working: B1 right (accept decimal). B1 digits line up.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A new ground must be added between rows 4 and 5. State how this is done.
parts.answer: Place the cursor in row 4 and insert a row below (or in row 5 and insert a row above).
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: One point (pt) is 1/72 of an inch, and one inch is 2.54 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the height in millimetres represented by a 36 pt heading. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A sign must be readable from a distance and the letters need to be at least 2.5 cm high. Calculate the smallest whole number of points that gives at least 2.5 cm.
parts.answer: 71 pt

practice.stem: In a long science report, a subheading 'Results of the pH tests' appears as the last line of page 5, and the table that belongs to it starts on page 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why this is a layout error.
parts.answer: The subheading is separated from the content it introduces, so the reader sees a heading with nothing under it.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two different ways of correcting it.
parts.answer: Apply 'keep with next' to the subheading so it always stays on the same page as the following paragraph/table; or insert a page break before the subheading so it moves to page 6.
parts.working: 1 mark each: keep with next; page break before heading; (accept adjusting spacing only if it moves the heading to page 6).

practice.stem: In a fully justified paragraph, the measurement '25 kg' is split so that '25' ends one line and 'kg' starts the next.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to stop the number and its unit being split across lines.
parts.answer: Replace the ordinary space with a non-breaking space between 25 and kg.
parts.working: B1 non-breaking space.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why fully justified text sometimes shows large gaps between words, and state one way to reduce them.
parts.answer: Extra space is added between words so each line reaches both margins; with long words or narrow columns the gaps become large. Reduce by using automatic hyphenation (or left alignment / a wider column).
parts.working: B1 explanation of spacing to fill line. B1 hyphenation / left align / wider column.

practice.stem: A poster designed on A4 paper (21.0 cm × 29.7 cm) is to be printed on A3 paper (29.7 cm × 42.0 cm) without changing its layout.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the scale factor applied to each side, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A heading was 40 pt on the A4 version. Calculate its new size, to the nearest whole point.
parts.answer: 57 pt

practice.stem: A small business in Sialkot that exports sports goods types every invoice and letter from a blank page, changing the margins, fonts and alignment each time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of a document template with preset page and text formatting for this business.
parts.answer: Benefits: consistent appearance on every document; saves time because margins, fonts, logo, alignment are already set; fewer formatting errors; staff need less training; professional image with overseas customers. Drawbacks: time and skill needed to design the template at first; may not suit every document type so several templates may be needed; staff may forget to use it or use an old version; changes to house style mean templates must be updated. Conclusion: benefits usually outweigh costs for a business producing many similar documents.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for benefits, up to 4 for drawbacks, max 5 if no reasoned conclusion. 1 mark per valid expanded point, total 6.

practice.stem: A notice is typed in Courier New 12 pt, a monospaced font. Each character has a width of 0.6 em, where 1 em equals the font size. 1 inch = 72 pt = 2.54 cm. The text area is 16.5 cm wide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the width of one character in cm, correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the maximum number of characters that fit on one line. Give a whole number.
parts.answer: 64 characters
parts.working: M1: 16.5 ÷ 0.254 = 64.96. A1: 64 characters (only whole characters fit).

practice.stem: A line of justified text is 16 cm wide. The 9 words on the line, without spaces, have a total width of 422.4 pt. There are 8 gaps between the words. Use 1 cm = 28.35 pt.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total width of the line, in pt.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the extra space added to each of the 8 gaps between words, in pt.
parts.answer: 3.9 pt
parts.working: M1: 453.6 − 422.4 = 31.2 pt of spare space. A1: 31.2 ÷ 8 = 3.9 pt per gap.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the spaces are wider on this line than on the lines above it, which are not justified.
parts.answer: The justified line is stretched to the full width, so the spaces between words are widened.
parts.working: 1 mark: justified text stretches spaces to fill the full line width.

practice.stem: A school newsletter has a text area 17 cm wide. It is set in two newspaper-style columns with a 0.8 cm gutter between them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the width of each of the two columns, in cm, when the gutter is 0.8 cm.
parts.answer: 8.1 cm
parts.working: M1: 17 − 0.8 = 16.2 cm left for the columns. A1: 16.2 ÷ 2 = 8.1 cm per column.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a gutter is needed between the two columns of text.
parts.answer: It separates the columns so the reader can tell where one ends and the next begins.
parts.working: 1 mark: keeps the columns visually separate for reading.

practice.stem: A publisher is preparing a textbook. Ten authors each write chapters in the same word-processed file.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss two advantages and one disadvantage of using Heading styles for a 200-page textbook written by ten authors.
parts.answer: Advantages: the same heading style applies to every chapter so the book looks consistent; a contents page and cross-references can be generated automatically; the style can be changed once and all headings update. Disadvantage: authors who do not use the styles, or who apply direct formatting, create inconsistencies that have to be found and corrected.
parts.working: Mark bands: 5–6 marks for two clear advantages and one reasoned disadvantage that refers to the 10 authors and the 200 pages. 3–4 marks for two advantages or one advantage and one disadvantage, stated with little reason. 1–2 marks for a generic answer about formatting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a font that is not installed on the printing computer can change the layout of a document.
parts.answer: Word replaces the missing font with a substitute font that may be wider or narrower, so the line breaks, page breaks and page count change.
parts.working: 1 mark: a substitute font is used. 1 mark: the substitute has different character widths. 1 mark: line breaks, page breaks or page count change.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one way to stop this happening when the document is sent to another computer.
parts.answer: Embed the fonts in the file when saving, or send the file as a PDF.
parts.working: 1 mark: embed fonts or save/send as PDF.

practice.stem: A report is set in 12 pt text with 1.5 line spacing. The text area is 25 cm high. Use 1 cm = 28.35 pt.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of complete lines that fit in the text area. Show your working.
parts.answer: 32 lines

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one assumption you have made about the height of a line.
parts.answer: The single-spaced line height is 1.2 times the font size.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid assumption about line height (1.2 × font size).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a hard page break and the 'Page break before' paragraph setting when a new paragraph is inserted in the middle of a chapter.
parts.answer: A hard page break stays at its fixed position, so the text after it may start on the wrong page when editing changes; 'Page break before' stays attached to the heading paragraph, so the heading always starts a new page.
parts.working: 1 mark: a hard break is fixed in position. 1 mark: 'Page break before' is a paragraph setting that moves with its paragraph. 1 mark: the effect on the layout when text is edited.

practice.stem: A school must print seven copies of a 300-page report. The printer uses double-sided printing. One ream contains 500 sheets of A4 paper.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of reams needed. Show your working.
parts.answer: 3 reams
parts.working: M1: 300 ÷ 2 = 150 sheets per copy (two pages per sheet side). M1: 7 × 150 = 1050 sheets. A1: 1050 ÷ 500 = 2.1, so 3 reams.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State why the printer should use double-sided printing for the copies.
parts.answer: It uses half as much paper, which reduces cost and waste.
parts.working: 1 mark: any valid reason such as less paper, lower cost or less storage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the layout problems that the printer would meet with a 40-page brochure that uses six fonts and different margins on each page. Suggest a correction for each problem.
parts.answer: Problems: six fonts make the brochure look unprofessional and harder to read; different margins make the pages misaligned when printed and folded; the layout may shift when printed on a different machine. Corrections: use two fonts at most, set one margin size in a master page or style, and embed the fonts or export as PDF.
parts.working: Mark bands: 5–6 marks for two or more layout problems each linked to the brochure, plus a suitable correction for each. 3–4 marks for problems with limited reasons or corrections. 1–2 marks for vague comments.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the advantages of using the Navigation pane and heading styles to move around a 60-page manual that several people edit.
parts.answer: Advantages: the Navigation pane shows the structure of the manual, so a reader or editor can jump straight to any heading; headings are consistent across editors, so the Navigation pane lists the same structure for everyone; sections can be moved by dragging headings; the contents page can be generated automatically and updated after edits.
parts.working: Mark bands: 5–6 marks for two clear advantages linked to a 60-page manual edited by several people and a reasoned point. 3–4 marks for two advantages with little reasoning. 1–2 marks for general comments about the Navigation pane.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a flat-file database.
parts.answer: A database that stores all its data in a single table, so data about different things (for example customers and their orders) is held together in one file.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: data held in one table/file | each record holds all the data / no links to other tables (data often repeated).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a relational database.
parts.answer: A database made of two or more tables that are linked by relationships using key fields (a primary key in one table matching a foreign key in another).
parts.working: 1 mark each for: data stored in more than one table | tables linked using common/key fields (primary key – foreign key).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two advantages of a relational database over a flat-file database.
parts.answer: Data is stored only once, so there is less duplication (redundancy) and less storage is used; updating data in one place keeps it consistent everywhere, so there are fewer errors.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: less data redundancy/duplication | less storage needed | data consistency/integrity – change once | fewer data entry errors | more complex queries/reports across tables | easier to add new types of data | better security – access to tables can be restricted.

practice.stem: A sports club in Sialkot stores these fields about each member: MemberID, FirstName, DateOfBirth, PhoneNumber, FeesPaid (whether this year's fees are paid), FeeAmount (in rupees, e.g. 3500.00).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the most suitable data type for each field: MemberID (e.g. M0451), DateOfBirth, PhoneNumber (e.g. 03001234567), FeesPaid, FeeAmount.
parts.answer: MemberID – text/alphanumeric; DateOfBirth – date/time; PhoneNumber – text/alphanumeric; FeesPaid – Boolean (logical, Yes/No); FeeAmount – currency (or numeric, 2 decimal places).
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct data type.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why PhoneNumber should not be stored as a numeric field.
parts.answer: A numeric field would remove the leading zero, and phone numbers are never used in calculations (they may also contain + or spaces).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: leading zero would be lost | no calculations are carried out on it | may contain symbols such as + or spaces/dashes | may be longer than some number formats allow.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by a primary key.
parts.answer: A field that holds a unique value for every record, so it can be used to identify each record.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: a field (key field) | unique value for each record / identifies each record. Cannot be empty.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A supermarket stores data about products with these fields: ProductName, Barcode, Category, Price, Supplier. Identify the most suitable primary key and explain why ProductName would not be suitable.
parts.answer: Barcode – every product has a different barcode number. ProductName is unsuitable because two products (e.g. different sizes) can share the same name.
parts.working: 1 mark: Barcode. 1 mark: two products (e.g. different sizes/brands) can have the same name, so ProductName is not unique.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A data entry form is used to add records to a database. Describe three features of a well-designed data entry form.
parts.answer: Clear labels or instructions next to each box; drop-down lists or option buttons for fields with fixed choices; validation that shows an error message when invalid data is entered.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: clear title | clear labels/instructions | fields in a logical order | appropriate size boxes / character boxes | drop-down menus / radio buttons / tick boxes | validation with helpful error messages | navigation buttons (next, previous, save, new record) | not cluttered – white space | consistent fonts/colours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage of using a drop-down list on a form for the field Province.
parts.answer: The user can only choose from valid options, so spelling mistakes are avoided and data entry is faster.
parts.working: B1: prevents spelling/typing errors | only valid entries | faster entry | consistent data for searching.

practice.stem:

PlantCode,CommonName,Height_cm,Price,Indoor,DateAdded

practice.stem: A teacher in Karachi keeps records of 400 students' marks in a spreadsheet. The school's IT manager suggests moving the records into a relational database.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare using a database with using a spreadsheet to store and process the student records.
parts.answer: Both store data in rows and columns and can sort and search it. A spreadsheet is better for calculations, what-if modelling and charts, whereas a database is better for storing large amounts of related data. A database can use validation and forms to control data entry more strongly and links several tables (students, subjects, marks) so data is stored once, whereas a spreadsheet often repeats data. A database is better for complex queries and reports and allows multiple users to edit records at the same time, while a spreadsheet is easier to set up and learn.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity (both rows/columns, sort, search, filter, charts/reports). Up to 5 marks for linked differences: database handles large volumes of related data vs spreadsheet better for numerical calculation/modelling | database tables linked – less redundancy vs spreadsheet data duplicated | database queries on multiple criteria/reports easier | database forms and validation control input | database supports many simultaneous users/access rights | spreadsheet quicker to set up/easier to learn | spreadsheet better for graphs/what-if. Each difference must refer to both.

B204 | 05/03/2026 | Faiza Khan | 03215550110 | Imran Ali | 03335550919

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two examples of data redundancy in this table.
parts.answer: Imran Ali's name and phone number are stored three times; Faiza Khan's name is stored three times (and her phone number twice).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two: driver Imran Ali + 03335550919 repeated | customer Faiza Khan repeated | Faiza Khan's phone repeated | date 03/03/2026 repeated (accept).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain the problem shown by booking B204.
parts.answer: Faiza Khan's phone number is different from the other two records (03215550110 instead of 03215550101), so the data is inconsistent – it is not clear which number is correct, probably caused by typing the repeated data again.
parts.working: 1 mark: identifies inconsistent phone number for the same customer. 1 mark: caused by re-entering duplicated data / impossible to know which is correct (data integrity problem).

parts.label: c

parts.answer: Split it into three tables: CUSTOMERS (CustomerID primary key, name, phone), DRIVERS (DriverID primary key, name, phone) and BOOKINGS (BookingID, Date, CustomerID, DriverID). CustomerID and DriverID are foreign keys in BOOKINGS, creating one-to-many relationships, so each customer's and driver's details are stored only once.
parts.working: 1 mark: separate CUSTOMERS and DRIVERS tables (and BOOKINGS). 1 mark: each with its own primary key (CustomerID, DriverID). 1 mark: BOOKINGS holds foreign keys / one-to-many relationships so details stored once.

practice.stem: A dental clinic in Hyderabad stores patient details and appointment history on paper record cards kept in filing cabinets. The owner is considering a computerised database.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate the use of a computerised database rather than paper record cards for the clinic.
parts.answer: A database lets staff search for a patient instantly, sort and produce reports such as all appointments for tomorrow, uses validation to reduce errors, can be backed up and needs less physical space, and access can be restricted with passwords. However it costs money for hardware, software and training, needs electricity (load-shedding is a problem), data could be hacked or lost if not backed up, and data protection rules apply. Conclusion: the database is better in the long term if backups and security are in place.
parts.working: Max 4 marks for one side; 1–2 marks for reasoned conclusion. Benefits: faster searching | easy sorting/queries/reports | validation reduces errors | backups possible – cards can be lost/destroyed by fire | less storage space | several staff can access at once | easier to update | password-protected. Drawbacks: initial cost of hardware/software | staff training | data entry of existing cards takes time | power cuts/system failure stop access | hacking/malware risk | must comply with data protection.

practice.stem: A school stores data about students and the clubs they join. A student can join many clubs and each club has many students. The designer proposes three tables: STUDENT (StudentID, Name, Class), CLUB (ClubID, ClubName, Teacher) and MEMBERSHIP (StudentID, ClubID, DateJoined).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the MEMBERSHIP table is needed.
parts.answer: The relationship between students and clubs is many-to-many, which cannot be linked directly. MEMBERSHIP holds one record for each student joining each club, linking StudentID and ClubID, so it turns the relationship into two one-to-many relationships (STUDENT to MEMBERSHIP and CLUB to MEMBERSHIP) without repeating student or club details.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: relationship is many-to-many | cannot be stored directly without repeating data | MEMBERSHIP has one record per student per club | contains StudentID and ClubID as foreign keys | creates two one-to-many relationships | stores data about the joining (DateJoined).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why StudentID alone cannot be the primary key of MEMBERSHIP, and suggest a suitable primary key.
parts.answer: A student who joins several clubs appears in several records, so StudentID is not unique; a composite key of StudentID and ClubID together (or a new MembershipID field) is unique.
parts.working: 1 mark: StudentID repeated – not unique. 1 mark: StudentID + ClubID combined (composite key) or a new unique MembershipID.

parts.answer: Link CustID in CUSTOMER (primary key) to CustID in SALE (foreign key); it is a one-to-many relationship because one customer can make many sales; enforce referential integrity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A query uses both tables and selects sales where City = "Lahore". State how many sales are found and their total amount.
parts.answer: 5 sales; total Rs 14,300.

practice.stem:
A student designed a query on a table of laptops (fields: Model, Brand, RAM_GB, Price, InStock). The task was: 'Select laptops made by Brand A or Brand B that have at least 8 GB of RAM and are in stock.' The student set these criteria:
Row 1: Brand = "Brand A", RAM_GB > 8, InStock = Yes
Row 2: Brand = "Brand B"

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify two errors in the student's criteria and explain the effect of each.
parts.answer: Error 1: RAM_GB > 8 should be >= 8 – laptops with exactly 8 GB of RAM are wrongly excluded. Error 2: the RAM and InStock criteria are missing from row 2 – every Brand B laptop is selected, even those with less than 8 GB RAM or out of stock.
parts.working: 1 mark for each error identified + 1 mark for each effect: > instead of >= excludes 8 GB laptops | row 2 has only Brand so all Brand B laptops are shown regardless of RAM/stock.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the corrected criteria.
parts.answer:
Row 1: Brand = "Brand A", RAM_GB >= 8, InStock = Yes
Row 2: Brand = "Brand B", RAM_GB >= 8, InStock = Yes
(or Brand: "Brand A" OR "Brand B" with RAM_GB >= 8 AND InStock = Yes on one row)
parts.working: 1 mark: >= 8 on both rows. 1 mark: InStock = Yes repeated on row 2 / single row with Brand A OR Brand B.

practice.stem:

E4 | Laiba | 30 | 800

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate WeeklyPay for each member of staff.
parts.answer: Rizwan Rs 27,300; Asma Rs 27,360; Jawad Rs 27,000; Laiba Rs 24,000; Fahad Rs 27,200.

parts.label: c

practice.stem:

practice.stem:
A hardware store in Mardan uses a relational database with two tables. Price is in rupees.
Table SUPPLIERS:
SupplierID | SupplierName | City
S1 | Khyber Tools | Peshawar
S2 | Indus Paints | Karachi
S3 | Ravi Fittings | Lahore
S4 | Margalla Electric | Islamabad
Table PRODUCTS:
ProductCode | Description | SupplierID | Price | StockLevel
H01 | Claw hammer | S1 | 1450 | 32
H02 | Wall paint 4 litre | S2 | 5200 | 14

H07 | PVC pipe 3 m | S3 | 950 | 40
H08 | Extension lead | S4 | 2300 | 12
H09 | Screwdriver set | S1 | 1800 | 25

parts.label: a
parts.text: A query uses both tables to find products from suppliers based in Peshawar that have fewer than 30 items in stock. State the criteria and the field each is entered in.
parts.answer: City (from SUPPLIERS): "Peshawar"; StockLevel (from PRODUCTS): <30.

parts.label: b
parts.text: List the ProductCodes and the SupplierName shown in the output.
parts.answer: H05, H09 – Khyber Tools
parts.working: H01 has 32, so it is not selected. 1 mark codes, 1 mark supplier name.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Referential integrity is enforced on the relationship. A clerk tries to add a new product with SupplierID S7. Explain what happens and why.
parts.answer: The record is rejected, because there is no supplier S7 in SUPPLIERS; referential integrity means every foreign key value must match an existing primary key value.
parts.working: 1 mark: rejected/error. 1 mark: no matching primary key in SUPPLIERS.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The clerk then tries to delete supplier S2 from SUPPLIERS. Explain what happens and why this protects the data.
parts.answer: The deletion is not allowed while products H02 and H06 still refer to S2; otherwise these products would be left with a supplier that does not exist (orphan records).
parts.working: 1 mark: deletion prevented. 1 mark: avoids orphan records / products with no supplier.

practice.stem:

Table PRODUCTS:

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a calculated field called StockValue that gives the total value of the stock of each product.
parts.answer: StockValue: [Price]*[StockLevel]
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total StockValue of all products supplied by Khyber Tools.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the products need to be linked to the SUPPLIERS table to answer the question 'total stock value from suppliers in Peshawar'.
parts.answer: The City of each supplier is stored only in SUPPLIERS, so the tables must be joined on SupplierID to know which products come from Peshawar.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a calculated field in a database query, and give two reasons why calculated fields are used instead of a spreadsheet for this calculation in a large database.
parts.answer: A calculated field is a new field in a query whose value is worked out from other fields (e.g. [Price]*[Quantity]) each time the query is run, and is not stored in the table. Reasons, e.g. the result is always up to date with the stored data; no need to export the data to a spreadsheet so no copies that become out of date; it can be combined with criteria and sorting in the same query and used in reports; it works on very large numbers of records easily.
parts.working: 1 mark: meaning (worked out from other fields when the query runs). 1 mark: not stored. 1 mark each for two reasons (max 2).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A newsletter for a cricket club in Sialkot contains a photograph that is 15 cm wide and 10 cm high. It must be resized so that it is 6 cm wide and the aspect ratio is maintained. Calculate the new height of the photograph.
parts.answer: 4 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the aspect ratio of the photograph should be maintained when it is resized.
parts.answer: So that the image is not distorted/stretched or squashed; the proportions of the people and objects stay correct so the image still looks realistic/professional.
parts.working: 1 mark: image not distorted (stretched/squashed). 1 mark: proportions (width to height) stay the same / people and objects keep their correct shape.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student is editing an image of a market stall for a school magazine. Describe the difference between cropping the image and resizing the image.
parts.answer: Cropping removes unwanted parts from the edges of the image, so some content is lost and the remaining part is unchanged in scale. Resizing changes the size/dimensions of the whole image but keeps all of its content.
parts.working: 1 mark: cropping cuts away/removes part of the image (from the edges). 1 mark: resizing makes the whole image bigger or smaller with all content kept.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why the student might crop the image.
parts.answer: e.g. to remove an unwanted person/object at the edge; to focus attention on the main subject (the stall); to change its shape to fit a space.
parts.working: 1 mark for one valid reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A word-processed leaflet for a dental clinic in Peshawar contains a paragraph about opening hours. Describe the steps needed to place the image clinic.jpg so that it is aligned with the right margin and the text of the paragraph wraps around it.
parts.answer: Place the cursor in the paragraph and insert the image from file (Insert → Picture → clinic.jpg); select the image and set text wrapping to square (or tight); drag/position the image so its right edge is aligned with the right margin (or set horizontal alignment: right, relative to margin).
parts.working: 1 mark: insert the picture from the file. 1 mark: set text wrapping to square/tight. 1 mark: align/position image to the right margin.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A travel agent in Lahore wants to reduce the file size of the photographs on her website. State three ways the file size of an image can be reduced.
parts.answer: Any three: reduce the resolution/number of pixels (resize it smaller); crop unwanted areas; reduce the colour depth; compress the image (e.g. save as a compressed .jpg at a lower quality).
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three distinct methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An image is 1080 pixels wide and 720 pixels high. It is rotated 90° clockwise. State the width and height of the rotated image.
parts.answer: 720 pixels wide and 1080 pixels high
parts.working: B1: width and height swap.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why an image taken with a phone might need to be rotated before it is used.
parts.answer: e.g. the phone was held sideways so the image appears on its side; to change it from landscape to portrait to fit a space.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The image fort.jpg is 900 pixels wide and 600 pixels high. On a web page it must be displayed 300 pixels wide with its aspect ratio kept. Calculate the height at which it must be displayed.
parts.answer: 200 pixels

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the HTML to display the image at this size, with the alternative text 'Lahore Fort'.
parts.working: 1 mark: img element with src="fort.jpg". 1 mark: width="300" and height="200" and alt="Lahore Fort". Accept the size given with a style attribute.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps needed to insert the image bus.png into a document so that it is exactly 5 cm wide, with its height in proportion, and placed at the top left of the first page below the header.
parts.answer: Position the cursor at the start of the document (top left, below the header) and insert the picture from the file bus.png; with aspect ratio locked, set the width to 5 cm (the height changes automatically); check the image is aligned with the left margin/top of the text area.
parts.working: 1 mark: insert picture from file at start of document. 1 mark: lock aspect ratio and set width to 5 cm. 1 mark: align to left margin at top of page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the aspect ratio of an image.
parts.answer: The ratio of the width of the image to its height.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: An image is 640 pixels wide and 480 pixels high. Give its aspect ratio in its simplest form.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A scanned map has been inserted into a sports day flyer upside down: the north arrow and the labels point towards the bottom of the page. Name the image edit, including the angle, that will correct it.
parts.answer: Rotate the image through 180°.
parts.working: 1 mark: rotate 180°. Do not accept flip/reflect vertically (this would leave the labels as a mirror image).

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other edit, apart from resizing and cropping, that can be applied to an image in a document.
parts.answer: e.g. rotate; change brightness; change contrast; change colour depth/recolour; apply text wrapping.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A photograph of a wedding was taken outdoors in strong sunlight and looks too light, with faded colours. State which adjustment should be made.
parts.answer: Decrease the brightness (accept: also increase the contrast).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why the original photograph should be kept before editing.
parts.answer: So the edits can be undone / the original can be used again if the edit is not suitable, because some edits cannot be reversed once saved.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: A photograph in a school newsletter is 1200 pixels wide and 800 pixels high.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the aspect ratio of the image in the form width : height, in its simplest form.
parts.working: 1 mark: 1200 : 800 = 3 : 2 (divide both by 400).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The photograph is resized to 600 pixels wide, keeping its aspect ratio. State its new height in pixels.
parts.answer: 400 pixels

practice.stem: A square profile picture in a club's member list is 500 pixels wide and 500 pixels high. It is resized to 200 pixels wide with the aspect ratio maintained.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the new height of the picture in pixels.
parts.answer: 200 pixels
parts.working: 1 mark. The picture is square, so the aspect ratio is 1 : 1 and the height must equal the width.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the picture keeps its shape when it is resized in this way.
parts.answer: The aspect ratio is kept, so the width and height are scaled by the same amount.
parts.working: 1 mark for stating that width and height are reduced by the same proportion (or that the aspect ratio is maintained).

practice.stem: A photograph of a school sports day has a stranger standing at the far right edge of the picture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps to remove the person at the far right edge of the photograph using the crop tool, so that everyone else stays in the picture.
parts.answer: Select the image; choose the crop tool; drag the right-hand crop handle inwards so that the stranger is outside the crop box but everyone else stays inside; apply the crop and check the picture.
parts.working: 1 mark for selecting the image and opening the crop tool. 1 mark for dragging the correct edge inwards so the stranger is excluded. 1 mark for applying the crop and checking the result.

practice.stem: A landscape photograph is 1600 pixels wide and 900 pixels high. It is rotated through 90° anticlockwise so that it becomes a portrait picture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the new width and height of the picture.
parts.answer: Width 900 pixels, height 1600 pixels
parts.working: 1 mark for width 900. 1 mark for height 1600. Swapping the two values is the effect of a 90° rotation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by the resolution of a digital image.
parts.answer: The number of pixels (or dots) used to make up the image. More pixels give more detail.
parts.working: 1 mark: the number of pixels or dots in the image. 1 mark: more pixels give more detail or a sharper image.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the type of image that is more suitable for a company logo that must be enlarged to a banner three metres wide without losing quality. Explain why.
parts.answer: Vector image. It is made of mathematical shapes, so it can be scaled to any size without losing quality.
parts.working: 1 mark for vector. 1 mark for the explanation: stored as shapes or paths, not a fixed grid of pixels.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the generic file format that stores a short animation of several frames that repeats on a web page, and state one limitation of this format.
parts.answer: GIF. Limitation: it supports only a limited palette of 256 colours, so photographs may lose quality.
parts.working: 1 mark for GIF. 1 mark for a valid limitation (256 colours or limited palette; not good for detailed photographs).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps to reduce the brightness of a photograph in a photo editor.
parts.answer: Select the image; open the brightness and contrast (or brightness) adjustment; drag the brightness control to the left or enter a lower value; preview the result and apply the change.
parts.working: 1 mark for opening the adjustment tool with the image selected. 1 mark for lowering the brightness setting. 1 mark for previewing and applying.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the number of different colours that can be shown with a colour depth of 2 bits.
parts.working: 1 mark: 2 bits gives 2² = 4 colours.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of different colours that can be shown with a colour depth of 4 bits.
parts.working: 1 mark: 4 bits gives 2⁴ = 16 colours.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the enlarged bitmap image looks blocky when it is made much bigger.
parts.answer: A bitmap has a fixed number of pixels; when it is enlarged, each pixel becomes a larger block of one colour, so the individual squares are visible and no new detail is created.
parts.working: 1 mark: pixels become larger blocks. 1 mark: a fixed number of pixels, so no new detail can be created.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A digital photograph of the Badshahi Mosque is 1600 pixels wide and 1200 pixels high. It is to be reduced to 480 pixels wide for a web page, keeping the aspect ratio. Calculate the new height in pixels.
parts.answer: 360 pixels

parts.label: b
parts.text: Each pixel is stored using 3 bytes and the image is not compressed. Calculate the file size, in bytes, of the original image and of the reduced image.
parts.answer: Original 5 760 000 bytes; reduced 518 400 bytes

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the reduced image is more suitable for the web page.
parts.answer: It has a much smaller file size so the page loads/downloads faster and uses less bandwidth.
parts.working: 1 mark: smaller file → faster loading.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An image of a horse facing right is placed in a document. Explain the difference between reflecting the image horizontally and rotating it through 180°.
parts.answer: Reflecting (flipping) horizontally makes a mirror image so the horse faces left but stays the right way up. Rotating through 180° turns the image so the horse faces left and is also upside down.
parts.working: 1 mark: reflect = mirror image, horse now faces left, still upright. 1 mark: rotate 180° = horse upside down (and facing left).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The horse must face towards the text on the left of the page. State which of the two edits should be used.
parts.answer: Reflect (flip) horizontally.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An image in a report is 9.3 cm wide and 12.4 cm high. It must be resized to exactly 8 cm high with the aspect ratio maintained. Calculate the new width, in centimetres.
parts.answer: 6 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how the student can make sure the aspect ratio is maintained when entering the new height in the software.
parts.answer: Tick/select the 'lock aspect ratio' (keep proportions) option before typing the new height, so the width changes automatically.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An image of the Karakoram mountains is 2000 pixels wide and 1500 pixels high. It is cropped by removing 250 pixels from the left and 250 pixels from the right, and 150 pixels from the top and 150 pixels from the bottom. Calculate the dimensions of the cropped image.
parts.answer: 1500 pixels wide × 1200 pixels high

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give the aspect ratio of the cropped image in its simplest form, width : height.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A document for a book club contains three images. For each image, name the most suitable text wrapping setting.
(i) A logo that must sit on its own line above the title, with no text on either side.
(ii) A photograph in the middle of a paragraph, with the text running down both sides close to the outline of an irregular-shaped object.
(iii) A small icon that must move with the words in a line of text as if it were a character.
parts.answer: (i) Top and bottom; (ii) Tight (or through); (iii) In line with text.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
A graphic designer is preparing images for a charity website. State the most suitable generic file format for each image and give a reason.
(i) A colour photograph of a flood relief camp.
(ii) A logo that must have a transparent background so the page colour shows through.
(iii) A small, simple animated 'Donate' banner.
parts.answer: (i) .jpg — compressed format suited to photographs with many colours (small file). (ii) .png — supports transparency (and lossless compression keeps sharp edges). (iii) .gif — supports simple animation (limited colours suit a simple banner).
parts.working: 1 mark each: correct format with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: In a poster for a science fair, a photograph of a student has been made wider without changing its height. The student's face now looks stretched. Explain why this has happened and describe how to correct it.
parts.answer: The aspect ratio was not maintained, so the width was increased by a different factor from the height. To correct it: reset the image size (or undo), lock the aspect ratio, then resize by dragging a corner handle (or changing one dimension) so both dimensions change in proportion.
parts.working: 1 mark: aspect ratio not maintained / width changed but not height. 1 mark: reset or undo the distortion. 1 mark: lock aspect ratio / use corner handle so width and height change proportionally.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A photograph is to be printed 6 inches wide and 4 inches high at 300 dots (pixels) per inch. Calculate the number of pixels needed across and down the image.
parts.answer: 1800 pixels across and 1200 pixels down

parts.label: b
parts.text: The photographer only has a version 900 pixels wide. Calculate the number of pixels per inch it would give if printed 6 inches wide, and explain the effect on the printed photograph.
parts.answer: 150 pixels per inch; the photograph would look less sharp/blurred or pixelated because each pixel is printed larger.
parts.working: B1: 900 ÷ 6 = 150. B1: less sharp / pixelated with reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A table in a recipe booklet has a column that is 4.5 cm wide. A picture of a mango, 7.5 cm wide and 5 cm high, must fit exactly across the width of one cell with its aspect ratio maintained. Calculate the height of the resized picture.
parts.answer: 3 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one reason why the picture should be resized in the document rather than stretched by dragging a side handle.
parts.answer: Dragging a side handle changes only one dimension so the picture is distorted; entering the size with the ratio locked keeps proportions and gives an exact width.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Complete the statements: the maximum number of different colours that can be represented with a colour depth of
(i) 1 bit
(ii) 4 bits
(iii) 8 bits
(iv) 16 bits.
parts.working: 2 marks for all four correct; 1 mark for two or three correct (2ⁿ).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a photograph stored with a colour depth of 24 bits has a larger file size than the same photograph stored with 8 bits.
parts.answer: Each pixel needs 24 bits instead of 8, so three times as much data is stored for the same number of pixels.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why images placed on web pages are usually compressed.
parts.answer: Compression reduces the file size so the image downloads faster and the web page loads more quickly; it also uses less bandwidth/storage on the server.
parts.working: 1 mark: smaller file size. 1 mark: faster loading / less bandwidth or storage.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the difference between lossy and lossless compression of an image.
parts.answer: Lossy compression permanently removes some image data (detail the eye may not notice), so the original cannot be fully restored but the file is much smaller. Lossless compression reduces the file size without losing any data, so the original image can be restored exactly.
parts.working: 1 mark: lossy removes data permanently. 1 mark: lossless — no data lost / original restored exactly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A page from an old school register has been scanned. The scanned image is tilted about 3° anticlockwise and has white triangles at its corners after it is straightened. Describe the two edits needed to produce a neat, straight rectangular image.
parts.answer: Rotate the image about 3° clockwise so the text lines are horizontal; then crop the image to remove the empty/white triangles at the corners.
parts.working: 1 mark: rotate 3° clockwise. 1 mark: crop to remove the corners/edges.

practice.stem: An uncompressed image is 1024 pixels wide and 768 pixels high. Its colour depth is 16 bits per pixel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the file size in bytes of the uncompressed image.
parts.answer: 1 572 864 bytes
parts.working: M1: 1024 × 768 × 16 bits. A1: 1 572 864 bytes (divide by 8 bits per byte).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the file size in kilobytes (1 KB = 1024 bytes).

practice.stem: A digital photograph is 3000 pixels wide and 2000 pixels high. It is printed at 300 pixels per inch. Use 1 inch = 2.54 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the printed width of the photograph in centimetres. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

practice.stem: An image 1000 pixels wide and 750 pixels high is cropped by removing 100 pixels from the left, 100 pixels from the right, 50 pixels from the top and 50 pixels from the bottom.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the new width and height of the image after cropping, in pixels.
parts.answer: Width 800 pixels, height 650 pixels
parts.working: 1 mark for width: 1000 − 100 − 100 = 800. 1 mark for height: 750 − 50 − 50 = 650.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the percentage of the original picture area that the crop removes. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
parts.answer: Original area = 750 000 pixels; new area = 520 000 pixels; removed = 230 000 pixels, which is 30.7% of the original area.

practice.stem: A photograph of 2000 × 1500 pixels is first cropped to 1600 × 1200 pixels. It is then resized so that its width is 400 pixels, keeping the aspect ratio.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the final height of the image in pixels after cropping and resizing.
parts.answer: 300 pixels
parts.working: M1: cropped image is 1600 × 1200 (aspect ratio 4 : 3). M1: scale factor 400 ÷ 1600 = 0.25. A1: height 1200 × 0.25 = 300 pixels.

practice.stem: A student repeatedly edits and saves a photograph as a JPEG file.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why quality is lost each time the photograph is saved again as a JPEG.
parts.answer: JPEG uses lossy compression, which removes some image data each time it is saved; the removed data cannot be recovered.
parts.working: 1 mark: JPEG is lossy compression. 1 mark: data is discarded each time and cannot be restored.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Name a lossless file format that can be used instead to avoid this loss.
parts.answer: PNG (or TIFF)
parts.working: 1 mark for PNG or TIFF.

practice.stem: An uncompressed image is 500 pixels wide and 400 pixels high. It has a colour depth of 8 bits per pixel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the file size in kilobytes (1 KB = 1024 bytes). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the HTML code to display the image sunset.jpg 480 pixels wide and 320 pixels high, with the alternative text 'Sunset over Gwadar'.
parts.working: 1 mark: img element with src="sunset.jpg". 1 mark: width="480" and height="320". 1 mark: alt attribute with the given text.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the image edit that reduces the number of colours in a poster image and describe its effect on the file size.
parts.answer: Reduce the colour depth (use fewer bits per pixel or a smaller colour palette). The file size becomes smaller because fewer bits are stored for each pixel.
parts.working: 1 mark for reducing colour depth or the number of colours. 1 mark for fewer bits per pixel. 1 mark for the smaller file size as a result.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what happens to the photograph when it is converted to greyscale.
parts.answer: Colour information is removed, so each pixel shows only a shade of grey between black and white.
parts.working: 1 mark for removing colour so only shades of grey remain.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why a school might convert a photograph to greyscale.
parts.answer: Any one: it reduces the file size; printing in black and white uses less ink; the photograph may suit a formal or historical look.
parts.working: 1 mark for a valid reason.

practice.stem: An image is 1280 pixels wide and 720 pixels high. It is to be displayed 400 pixels wide on a web page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the new height of the image in pixels, keeping the aspect ratio.
parts.answer: 225 pixels

parts.label: a
parts.text: An uncompressed image is 800 pixels wide and 600 pixels high. Its colour depth is 24 bits per pixel. Calculate its file size in bytes.
parts.answer: 1 440 000 bytes

parts.label: b
parts.text: The colour depth is reduced to 8 bits per pixel. Calculate the new file size in bytes and the number of different colours that can now be shown.
parts.answer: 480 000 bytes; 256 colours

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe one effect on the appearance of the image of reducing the colour depth.
parts.answer: Fewer colours are available so smooth changes of colour (e.g. a sky) appear as bands/blocks of colour and some detail/realism is lost.
parts.working: 1 mark: fewer colours → banding / less realistic / loss of quality.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A photograph taken inside a dimly lit museum looks dark and dull: the dark areas and light areas look very similar. Explain the difference between adjusting the brightness and adjusting the contrast of an image.
parts.answer: Brightness makes every pixel in the whole image lighter (or darker) by the same amount. Contrast changes the difference between the light and dark areas: increasing it makes light areas lighter and dark areas darker.
parts.working: 1 mark: brightness = whole image lighter/darker. 1 mark: contrast = difference between light and dark parts.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State which adjustments should be made to improve this photograph, giving a reason for each.
parts.answer: Increase the brightness so that the details in the dark image can be seen; increase the contrast so that the light and dark areas are more clearly different/the image looks less dull.
parts.working: 1 mark: increase brightness + reason. 1 mark: increase contrast + reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school in Multan is putting hundreds of photographs of school events on its website. The web designer plans to reduce the resolution of every photograph before uploading it. Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of reducing the resolution of the photographs.
parts.answer: Benefits: smaller file sizes so pages load faster, especially on mobile data; uses less storage space on the web server; uses less bandwidth so hosting may cost less; quicker to upload; less data used by visitors. Drawbacks: image quality/detail is lost; images may look pixelated if enlarged or viewed on large high-resolution screens; visitors cannot download good-quality versions to print; the reduction cannot be undone unless the originals are kept; it takes time to edit hundreds of photographs. Conclusion e.g. benefits outweigh drawbacks for a web page if originals are kept.
parts.working: Max 4 marks for one side only. 1 mark per expanded point from: faster loading; less server storage; less bandwidth/cost; faster upload; loss of detail; pixelation when enlarged; poor for printing; cannot undo/originals must be kept; time taken. 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion. Answers in prose comparing both sides needed for full marks.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An image 2400 pixels wide and 1800 pixels high is scaled to 35% of its width and 35% of its height. Calculate the new dimensions.
parts.answer: 840 pixels × 630 pixels

parts.label: b
parts.text: The image is uncompressed. Calculate the new file size as a percentage of the original file size.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student says 'scaling to 35% makes the file 35% of its original size'. Explain why the student is wrong.
parts.answer: Both the width and the height are reduced, so the number of pixels is multiplied by 0.35 twice (0.35 × 0.35), not once.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A profile photograph is 1200 pixels wide and 900 pixels high. It must become a square image 250 pixels wide for a membership card, showing the person's face in the centre. Describe, with dimensions, the two edits needed and the order in which they should be done.
parts.answer: First crop the image to a square 900 × 900 pixels by removing 150 pixels from each side (left and right), keeping the face central. Then resize the square image, with aspect ratio locked, to 250 × 250 pixels.
parts.working: 1 mark: crop to 900 × 900 (remove 300 pixels of width). 1 mark: 150 pixels from each side to keep face centred. 1 mark: then resize to 250 × 250 with aspect ratio kept.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why resizing the original image straight to 250 × 250 pixels would not be suitable.
parts.answer: The original is 4 : 3, not square, so forcing it to 250 × 250 would distort/squash the face.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: An uncompressed image uses 3 bytes per pixel and has an aspect ratio of 4 : 3. Its file size must be no more than 600 KB, where 1 KB = 1024 bytes. Its width must be a multiple of 4 pixels. Calculate the largest possible width and height, and the file size in bytes at that size.
parts.answer: Width 520 pixels, height 390 pixels, file size 608 400 bytes

parts.label: a
parts.text: A newsletter is set on A4 portrait paper (21 cm wide). The left and right margins are each 2 cm. The page has two columns of equal width with 1 cm spacing between them. Calculate the width of each column.
parts.answer: 8 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: An image 12 cm wide and 9 cm high must fill the full width of one column with its aspect ratio maintained. Calculate the new height.
parts.answer: 6 cm

parts.label: a
parts.answer: Squashed: reset the size and resize with the aspect ratio locked (drag a corner handle). Overlaps margin: reduce the width (in proportion) or move it so it fits within the column/margins. Empty spaces: change text wrapping from top and bottom to square/tight. Covers header: move the image down into the body of the page (below the header) / anchor it in the text.
parts.working: 1 mark per correct fix for each problem (4).

practice.stem: A 24-bit uncompressed image is 3840 pixels wide and 2160 pixels high. It is compressed so that the file is one tenth of its uncompressed size.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the compressed file size in MB (1 MB = 1 048 576 bytes). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

practice.stem: An image is 1200 pixels wide and 900 pixels high. It must fit inside a box that is 500 pixels wide and 400 pixels high, without distorting the picture.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the largest width and height, in whole pixels, that the image can have so that it fits inside the box and keeps its aspect ratio.
parts.answer: Width 500 pixels, height 375 pixels
parts.working: M1: scale to the box width: 500 ÷ 1200 = 0.4167; scale to the box height: 400 ÷ 900 = 0.4444. M1: use the smaller scale factor, 0.4167. A1: 500 × 375 pixels.

practice.stem: A 16-bit colour image is 2000 pixels wide and 1000 pixels high. The device has 3 MB of free storage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the uncompressed file size in bytes.
parts.answer: 4 000 000 bytes

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the file size in MB (1 MB = 1 048 576 bytes) and state whether the image can be stored in the 3 MB of free space without compression. Show your working.
parts.answer: 3.81 MB, which is larger than 3 MB, so it cannot be stored uncompressed.
parts.working: M1: 4 000 000 ÷ 1 048 576 = 3.81 MB. M1: compare with 3 MB. A1: it cannot be stored uncompressed; it must be compressed or resized.

practice.stem: A greeting card is to be printed 10 cm wide and 15 cm high at 200 pixels per inch. Use 1 inch = 2.54 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of pixels needed across and down the image. Round to the nearest whole pixel.
parts.answer: 787 pixels across and 1181 pixels down
parts.working: M1: 10 cm ÷ 2.54 = 3.937 inches; × 200 = 787.4, so 787. M1: 15 cm ÷ 2.54 = 5.906 inches; × 200 = 1181.1, so 1181. A1 and A1 for each correct value.
