practice.stem: A school in Multan is putting hundreds of photographs of its events on its website. The camera files are very large, and the school wants the gallery to load quickly on a phone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss how a school should prepare and store its photographs so that the gallery loads quickly on the website but the images still look good.
parts.answer: Sample points: resize each image to the display size needed (not the full camera size); use JPEG for photos and compress to a sensible quality level; keep the aspect ratio; crop unwanted edges; keep the original full-size photos in a separate archive for printing; test the page to check load speed; avoid compressing a photo so much that it looks blocky. Trade-offs: a lower resolution or higher compression gives smaller files and faster loading but less detail; keeping high resolution gives good quality but slower loading and more storage space.
parts.working: Up to 6 marks: 2 marks for preparing the images (resize, crop, aspect ratio); 2 marks for compression and file format with reasons; 2 marks for a balanced discussion of the trade-off between quality, file size and loading speed, with a link to the website.

practice.stem: A logo for a school website is a dark-blue shape on a plain white background. It must sit on a coloured page with no white box around it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the steps to make the white background of the logo transparent, and state the file format to save the logo in.
parts.answer: Select the background area with the select-by-colour (magic wand) tool or use a background removal tool; delete the selected background so it shows as a checkerboard; check the edges of the logo for any white halo and tidy them; save as a PNG file, which supports transparency.
parts.working: 1 mark: selecting the background (magic wand or select by colour). 1 mark: deleting it so it becomes transparent. 1 mark: checking and tidying the edges. 1 mark: saving as PNG (not JPEG, which has no transparency).

practice.stem: A 1920 × 1080 pixel image is placed on a 1024 × 768 pixel slide. The image must fit the full width of the slide and keep its aspect ratio.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the width and height the image occupies on the slide, in pixels, keeping the aspect ratio.
parts.answer: 1024 pixels wide and 576 pixels high
parts.working: M1: scale factor = 1024 ÷ 1920 = 0.5333 (height 768 ÷ 1080 = 0.7111, which is larger, so the width is the limit). M1: 1080 × 0.5333 = 576. A1: 1024 × 576.

practice.stem: An uncompressed image is 1000 × 1000 pixels with 8-bit colour depth. The colour depth is reduced to 4 bits per pixel.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the new file size in bytes and the percentage reduction in file size compared with the original.
parts.answer: New file size 500 000 bytes; the file is 50% smaller.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a CSS rule that sets the width of every image in the class 'gallery' to 300 pixels and keeps the aspect ratio by setting the height to adjust automatically.
parts.answer: .gallery { width: 300px; height: auto; }
parts.working: 1 mark for the selector .gallery (or img.gallery). 1 mark for width: 300px and height: auto.

practice.stem: A photographer saves 200 uncompressed photographs. Each photograph is 4000 pixels wide and 3000 pixels high, with 24-bit colour depth.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total storage needed for 200 photographs, in GB (1 GB = 1 073 741 824 bytes). Give your answer to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by software copyright.
parts.answer: The legal right of the creator/owner of software to control how it is copied, used, changed and distributed.
parts.working: B1 legal protection/ownership – others need permission to copy or distribute.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two actions that would break software copyright.
parts.answer: Any two: making copies of the software and giving or selling them to others; installing it on more computers than the licence allows; using parts of the code in your own program without permission; renting or lending it out without permission; removing or bypassing the copy protection / using a cracked key; modifying it and distributing it without permission.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what is meant by software piracy.
parts.answer: Illegally copying, distributing or using software without a valid licence / the copyright owner's permission.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why software piracy is harmful to software companies.
parts.answer: Any two: loss of sales income; less money to invest in developing new software and updates; jobs may be lost; harm to reputation if pirated copies contain malware or faults.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe three methods used by software producers to prevent their software being copied illegally.
parts.answer: Any three: a unique product/licence key must be entered during installation; online activation links the key to one device so it cannot be reused elsewhere; the user must accept a licence agreement before installing; holograms on packaging show it is genuine; a dongle (hardware key) must be plugged in for the software to run; the original disc/memory stick must be present to run it; the program code is encrypted and needs a key to run.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three described.

practice.stem: Zain bought a licensed copy of a video-editing program. His friend asks Zain to install it on the friend's laptop as well.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why Zain should not do this.
parts.answer: The licence usually allows use on one computer only, so installing it on another person's laptop is illegal copying/breaks copyright; the producer loses the income from a sale.
parts.working: B1 licence limits installations/is for Zain only. B1 breaks copyright law / illegal / unfair to producer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how a hologram on software packaging helps to protect copyright.
parts.answer: Holograms are difficult to copy, so they show buyers that the product is genuine; customers and shops can recognise counterfeit (pirated) copies that lack the hologram.
parts.working: B1 hard to copy. B1 identifies genuine copy / detects fakes.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why copyright laws are especially important for software.
parts.answer: Software can be copied quickly, easily and cheaply; every digital copy is identical to the original; copies can be distributed worldwide over the internet in seconds; developers invest a lot of time and money, so the law protects their income and encourages new software.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: When installing software, the user is asked to accept a licence agreement. Give three things the agreement is likely to state.
parts.answer: Any three: the number of devices/users the software may be installed on; that the software must not be copied or distributed; that it must not be modified or reverse engineered; whether it can be used for commercial purposes; that the user does not own the software, only a right to use it; the length of the licence; limits of the producer's responsibility.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A publisher sells ePublications that can only be opened on the buyer's registered devices. Describe how this protects the publisher's copyright.
parts.answer: The file is encrypted and linked to the buyer's account/devices, so if it is copied to another person's device it cannot be opened, stopping illegal sharing.
parts.working: B1 encrypted/locked to account or device. B1 copies cannot be read by others.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between a single-user licence and a multi-user licence.
parts.answer: A single-user licence allows the software to be installed/used by one user on one computer; a multi-user licence allows a set number of users or computers (e.g. in a network) to use it.
parts.working: B1 each.

practice.stem: A student in Islamabad writes a mobile game and uploads it to an app store.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two ways the student could protect the game from being copied.
parts.answer: Any two: include a licence agreement users must accept; require users to log in / activate with an account; encrypt or obfuscate the code; include a copyright notice; use the app store's licence-checking system.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one benefit to the student of copyright law.
parts.answer: It gives the student the legal right to control and earn money from the game, and to take action against anyone who copies it.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each statement is true or false.
(i) When you buy a program, you own the program code and may do what you like with it.
(ii) In most countries, copyright protects software automatically as soon as it is written.
(iii) Anyone who downloads freeware may sell copies of it.
(iv) The source code of open-source software is available for users to read and change.
parts.answer: (i) False (ii) True (iii) False (iv) True
parts.working: 1 mark each. (i) the buyer only gets a licence to use it; (iii) freeware is free to use but the author keeps the copyright.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the difference between buying a copy of a program and owning the program itself.
parts.answer: The buyer pays for a licence that gives permission to use the program under certain conditions; the copyright in the program (and the right to copy, change or sell it) stays with the company or person who wrote it.
parts.working: 1 mark: buyer gets a licence/permission to use; 1 mark: copyright/ownership stays with the author/company.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each program is freeware, shareware or free (open-source) software.
(i) A PDF reader that can be used free for ever, but its code cannot be seen or changed.
(ii) A video converter that can be used free for 30 days, after which the user must pay to continue.
(iii) An office suite whose code anyone may study, change and share.
parts.answer: (i) Freeware (ii) Shareware (iii) Free (open-source) software
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two reasons why some people use pirated software.
parts.answer: The genuine software is too expensive for them; pirated copies are easy to download; they think they will not be caught; they believe it does no harm.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two risks to the user of installing a pirated program.
parts.answer: Pirated copies often contain malware such as viruses or spyware; the user cannot get updates or security patches; no technical support; the user may be fined or prosecuted; the program may stop working when the copy is detected.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The 'About' screen of a program shows: '© 2026 Sabz Software Ltd. All rights reserved.' State what information this copyright notice gives.
parts.answer: The symbol © shows the program is protected by copyright; 2026 is the year of publication; Sabz Software Ltd is the copyright owner; 'All rights reserved' means no copying or other use is allowed without permission except as the licence allows.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why the company includes this notice even though copyright exists without it.
parts.answer: It warns users that the software is protected and who owns it, so people cannot claim they did not know.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
State whether each action is legal or illegal under normal software copyright.
(i) A school installs a program on all its computers under the site licence it has bought.
(ii) A student posts the licence key for a paid program on an online forum.
(iii) A user installs freeware that the author allows anyone to download free.
(iv) A shop sells laptops with copies of a paid program installed but without licences.
parts.answer: (i) Legal (ii) Illegal (iii) Legal (iv) Illegal
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Match each licence type to its description.
Licence types: A Single-user licence, B Site licence, C Concurrent-user (network) licence, D Subscription licence.
1 Allows the program to be used anywhere in one organisation's premises, on any number of computers.
2 Allows only a fixed number of people to use the program at the same time.
3 Allows one person to install and use the program.
4 Allows use for as long as regular payments are made.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Bushra sees a well-known paid program on sale very cheaply at a market stall. Give three signs that would help her decide whether a copy of software is genuine.
parts.answer: A hologram or certificate of authenticity on the packaging; sealed, professionally printed packaging; a realistic price; sold by an authorised dealer or the official website; a genuine licence key that activates online; an official receipt/invoice.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Hassan borrows a friend's game disc, plays it and returns it. Asad copies the same game from his friend's disc onto his own computer and returns the disc. Explain why Asad has broken copyright but Hassan has not.
parts.answer: Hassan used the one original licensed copy and gave it back, so no new copy was made. Asad made an extra copy without permission, so two people now have the game but only one licence was paid for.
parts.working: 1 mark: borrowing makes no new copy; 1 mark: copying creates an unauthorised copy.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some websites offer 'key generators' or 'cracks' that let paid software run without a licence. Describe two dangers of downloading these.
parts.answer: They often contain viruses, trojans or ransomware; they may install spyware that steals passwords or bank details; using them is illegal and can lead to fines; the cracked software may be unstable or damage files.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

practice.stem: A college in Peshawar has 120 computers. A design program is installed on all of them, but timetabling means that at most 30 students ever use the program at the same time.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what is meant by a concurrent-user licence.
parts.answer: A licence that allows a set maximum number of people to use the software at the same time, regardless of how many computers it is installed on.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the number of concurrent-user licences the college needs and explain why this may be cheaper than licensing every computer.
parts.answer: 30 licences; the college pays for 30 simultaneous users instead of 120 individual installations.
parts.working: B1 30. B1 fewer licences than computers.

practice.stem: A school in Lahore needs a mathematics program on 40 computers. Single-user licences cost Rs 4,500 each. A site licence for the whole school costs Rs 150,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of buying single-user licences for all 40 computers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate how much the school saves by buying the site licence.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give one other advantage of a site licence for the school.
parts.answer: More computers can be added later without buying extra licences (within the site); easier to manage one licence.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: A software audit at a logistics company in Karachi finds the accounts program installed on 75 computers, but the company owns only 60 licences. Each extra licence costs Rs 8,200.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the cost of buying enough licences so that all installations are legal.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other way the company could become legal.
parts.answer: Uninstall the program from the 15 unlicensed computers.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a dongle is used to protect software.
parts.answer: A dongle is a small hardware device plugged into a USB port; the software checks for the dongle and will only run while it is connected, so copies of the software are useless without it.
parts.working: B1 hardware device plugged into computer. B1 software only runs when it is present.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one disadvantage of this method for a legitimate user.
parts.answer: Any one: if the dongle is lost or damaged the software cannot be used; it takes up a USB port; it can only be used on one computer at a time.
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: A security program is sold in packs, each licensed for up to 5 devices. A family in Rawalpindi has 4 laptops, 6 smartphones and 2 tablets that all need protecting.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the smallest number of packs the family must buy.
parts.answer: 3 packs

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why installing the program from 2 packs on all 12 devices would be wrong.
parts.answer: Two packs cover only 10 devices; using it on 12 breaks the licence terms/copyright.
parts.working: B1

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how 'trial versions' of software help software producers sell their product while still protecting it.
parts.answer: Users can try the program free for a limited time or with limited features, which encourages them to buy; after the time ends the software stops working (or features stay locked) until a licence key is purchased; so the full program is not given away.
parts.working: B1 try before buying / advertising. B1 time-limited or feature-limited. B1 needs purchase/key to unlock full version.

practice.stem: A teacher in Gujranwala is making a presentation for 12-year-old students and wants to use photographs and music she found on the internet.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why she should check the copyright of the photographs and music before using them.
parts.answer: The material belongs to its creator and is protected by copyright; using it without permission (or outside its licence terms) may be illegal, so she must check whether it is free to use, needs permission, or must be credited.
parts.working: B1 protected by copyright / owned by creator. B1 need permission or licence / acknowledgement.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two ways she can use suitable images legally.
parts.answer: Any two: use images that are copyright-free or licensed for reuse (and follow the licence terms, e.g. credit the creator); ask the owner for permission; buy a licence from a stock image library; take her own photos.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: For a coursework project, a student copies large sections of program code from a website and submits it as his own work.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain two reasons why this is wrong.
parts.answer: It may break the copyright of the code's author if permission/licence terms are not followed; it is plagiarism – presenting someone else's work as your own, which is dishonest and breaks exam/school rules.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State what the student should have done if he wanted to use some of this code.
parts.answer: Check the licence allows reuse and acknowledge/credit the source clearly (or ask permission).
parts.working: B1

practice.stem: A school has a 50-computer licence for a science simulation program. The head teacher asks the IT technician to install it on the home laptops of the 12 science teachers as well.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what the technician should check before doing this.
parts.answer: Whether the licence terms allow home use / installation on staff devices, and whether the number of installations would exceed 50 (some licences count every installation).
parts.working: B1 licence terms on home/off-site use. B1 limit on number of installations.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the total number of installations if all school computers and all teachers' laptops have the program.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some older programs would only run if the original disc was in the drive. Explain how this protected the software and give one drawback for the user.
parts.answer: The program checked for a special code/feature on the original disc that ordinary copying could not reproduce; a copied installation would not run without the original disc. Drawback: the user had to keep the disc with them and could not run the software if it was lost or scratched / the computer had no disc drive.
parts.working: B1 check for original disc. B1 copies lack the feature so will not run. B1 drawback.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A university in Lahore buys concurrent-user licences for a statistics program. Over one week, the highest number of students using the program at the same time each day was: Monday 38, Tuesday 47, Wednesday 41, Thursday 44, Friday 29. Licences are sold in packs of 10 users for Rs 18,000 per pack. Calculate the number of packs needed so that every student in the busiest hour can use the program, and the total cost.
parts.answer: 5 packs; Rs 90,000

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain what happens when one more student tries to start the program after all the licences are in use.
parts.answer: The licence server refuses to open the program (or puts the student in a queue) until another user closes it.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A school has 20 teachers, each with a laptop, a tablet and a phone. A planning app costs Rs 2,000 per device with a per-device licence, or Rs 5,000 per teacher with a per-user licence that covers all of that teacher's devices. Calculate the cost of each option and state which is cheaper and by how much.
parts.answer: Per-device Rs 120,000; per-user Rs 100,000; per-user is cheaper by Rs 20,000.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A design company sells a student edition of its software at a large discount. The licence says it may not be used for commercial work. Explain why the company offers the student edition.
parts.answer: Students learn to use its software and are likely to buy the full version when they start work; it reduces the temptation for students to use pirated copies.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid reasons.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student who now works as a freelance designer uses his student edition to make paid logos for clients. Explain why this breaks the licence.
parts.answer: The work is commercial (he is being paid), which the student licence does not allow, so he must buy a commercial licence.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A photo-editing program is sold as a monthly subscription. Describe how the software can make sure it is used only while the subscription is paid.
parts.answer: The program connects to the company's server regularly to check the account's subscription status; if the payment has stopped, the licence is marked as expired; the program then stops working or allows only limited (e.g. view-only) use until the user renews.
parts.working: 1 mark each: regular online check; server records payment/licence status; program restricted when expired.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A graphic designer in Islamabad uses a font she downloaded for 'personal use only' in a logo for a paying client. Explain why this may break copyright.
parts.answer: Fonts are software protected by copyright and have their own licences; a personal-use licence does not cover commercial work, so she needs a commercial licence (or a font that allows commercial use).
parts.working: 1 mark: fonts are licensed/copyright software; 1 mark: personal-use licence does not allow commercial use.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one way she could avoid the problem.
parts.answer: Buy a commercial licence for the font, or choose a font whose licence allows free commercial use.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A new laptop comes with an operating system whose licence is tied to that laptop. When the laptop breaks, the owner wants to install the same operating system copy on a new desktop computer. Explain why the licence does not allow this.
parts.answer: The licence was sold with that particular laptop and is valid only on it; installing it on another computer would create an unlicensed copy, so a new licence must be bought.
parts.working: 1 mark: licence linked to the original hardware; 1 mark: new computer needs its own licence.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Another program's licence allows use on one computer at a time. Describe what the owner must do to move it legally to a new computer.
parts.answer: Deactivate/sign out of the licence on the old computer (or uninstall it), then install and activate it on the new computer, so it is never on two computers at once.
parts.working: 1 mark: deactivate/remove from old computer; 1 mark: activate on new one.

parts.label: a
parts.text: The IT manager of a company in Sialkot must make sure all software is properly licensed. Describe four steps the manager should take.
parts.answer: Keep a register of all licences bought and how many installations each allows; use software to list the programs installed on every computer; compare the installations with the licences; uninstall unlicensed copies or buy extra licences; stop users installing software without permission (admin rights); repeat the audit regularly; keep proof of purchase.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four steps.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A software company estimates that its accounting program is installed on 25,000 computers in a country, and that 40% of these copies are unlicensed. Each licence costs Rs 3,500. Calculate the income the company loses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give two reasons why the true loss may be lower than this figure.
parts.answer: Many people using pirated copies would not have bought the software at full price; some unlicensed copies may not be used much; the estimate of 40% may be inaccurate; some users may later buy licences.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A website offers a 'modded' version of a paid mobile app in which all paid features are unlocked free. Explain why downloading and installing it breaks copyright.
parts.answer: The app's code has been changed and redistributed without the owner's permission; it lets the user get paid features without paying for a licence.
parts.working: 1 mark: unauthorised modification/distribution of copyright code; 1 mark: avoids paying for licensed features.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one security risk of installing it.
parts.answer: It comes from an unofficial source and may contain malware that steals data from the phone.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why companies usually give software updates and security patches only to users with a registered, licensed copy.
parts.answer: It encourages people to buy licences, because unlicensed copies become out of date; checking the licence during updates also helps the company detect pirated copies.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two valid points.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a user of a pirated copy is at greater risk from hackers.
parts.answer: Without security patches, known weaknesses in the program are not fixed and can be exploited by hackers.
parts.working: 1 mark.

practice.stem: An architect's office in Islamabad can buy design software for a one-off payment of Rs 60,000 per user, or pay a subscription of Rs 1,500 per user per month.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the number of months after which the total subscription cost equals the one-off payment.
parts.answer: 40 months

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of the subscription for the office, apart from cost.
parts.answer: Advantage: updates/new versions and support are included; can easily reduce the number of users. Disadvantage: the software stops working if payments stop; often needs internet to check the licence; price may rise.
parts.working: B1 advantage. B1 disadvantage.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a product key on its own may not stop software piracy, and how online activation improves protection.
parts.answer: A product key can be copied and shared with others, so many people could install the software with the same key; it may also be generated by key-generating programs. Online activation sends the key (and details of the device) to the producer's server, which checks it has not already been used on more devices than allowed and ties it to that hardware, so a shared key will be rejected.
parts.working: B1 key can be shared. B1 or generated / no check of number of uses. B1 activation checks key with server. B1 linked to hardware/limits number of installs.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the differences between freeware, shareware and free (open source) software.
parts.answer: Freeware is free to use but is still protected by copyright, the source code is not available and users may not modify it. Shareware is free to try for a limited time or with limited features, after which the user must pay to continue. Free/open-source software is supplied with its source code, which users may study, modify and redistribute, subject to the conditions of its licence.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A student in Multan downloads a 'cracked' copy of an expensive photo-editing program from a file-sharing site, saying that the company is rich and will not miss the money.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the legal, ethical and practical issues of the student's action.
parts.answer: Legal: it breaks copyright law and the licence terms; the student could be fined or face legal action. Ethical: it is unfair to the developers who are not paid for their work; it is effectively theft; argument that the company is rich does not make it right. Practical: cracked copies often contain viruses/spyware that can steal data; no updates or technical support; may stop working; a free alternative or student discount could be used instead. Conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point; at least two of legal/ethical/practical needed for full marks; 6th mark for reasoned conclusion.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why software provided as an online (cloud-based) service is harder to pirate than software installed from a disc.
parts.answer: The program code runs on the company's servers rather than being copied onto the user's computer; users must log in to an account, so access is controlled and checked each time; a licence that is not paid for can be cancelled immediately.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A software house in Lahore needs an office program for 25 staff. An annual licence costs Rs 9,600 per user. A volume discount of 15% is given for 20 or more users.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the total annual cost for 25 staff after the discount.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Two staff leave, so only 23 licences are needed. Calculate the new annual cost.
parts.working: 23 × 9,600 × 0.85 = 187,680. B1 (still ≥ 20 users so discount applies).

practice.stem: A programmer buys a licensed app and changes its code so that it works in Urdu, then sells the new version online.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether this is allowed under normal software copyright.
parts.answer: Not allowed: the programmer bought only a licence to use the app, not ownership of the code; licences normally forbid modifying/reverse engineering the code; selling the changed version distributes the copyright owner's work without permission, so it is illegal (unless the licence, e.g. some open-source licences, specifically permits it).
parts.working: B1 licence = right to use, not to change. B1 modification/reverse engineering forbidden. B1 distribution/selling without permission illegal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Discuss the risks to a company of using unlicensed software on its computers.
parts.answer: Legal: fines, legal action and having to pay for all licences; possible criminal charges for managers. Security: unlicensed copies may contain malware, risking data theft. Operational: no updates or security patches; no technical support; software may stop working when detected. Reputation: customers and partners lose trust if it becomes public. Also: some may argue it saves money in the short term, but costs of being caught are greater. Conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point; max 5 without a conclusion; full marks need a range of risk types.

practice.stem: A start-up in Karachi plans to use open-source software for its office tasks instead of buying commercial software.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Evaluate this plan.
parts.answer: Benefits: usually no licence fee; source code available so it can be adapted; large user communities for help; no restriction on number of installations (depending on licence). Drawbacks: may have less official technical support; staff may need training if they are used to commercial programs; file compatibility with customers' software may be an issue; licence conditions still apply (e.g. changes may have to be shared if distributed); updates depend on the community. Conclusion.
parts.working: 1 mark per valid point; max 4 if one-sided; 6th mark for conclusion.

practice.stem: Three friends share one paid account for an online music-making program, each logging in from their own computer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain whether this is acceptable, and describe how the software company might detect and prevent it.
parts.answer: It is usually not acceptable: the subscription licence is for one user, so sharing breaks the terms and the company loses income. Detection/prevention (any two/three): limiting the number of devices or simultaneous logins on one account; checking the location/IP address of logins; requiring two-factor authentication to a single phone; device registration.
parts.working: B1 breaks licence/one-user terms. B1 unfair/loss of income. Up to 2 for detection/prevention methods.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Software companies use different kinds of trial version: a time-limited trial (full features for 14 days), a feature-limited trial (some features disabled) and a watermarked trial (output marked with the company's logo). For each product below, suggest the most suitable kind of trial and justify your choice.
(i) A video-editing program.
(ii) A tax-calculation program used once a year.
parts.answer: (i) Watermarked (possibly with time limit): users can try every feature, but finished videos carry a watermark, so they must buy to get usable results. (ii) Feature-limited (calculations work but saving or printing the return is disabled): a time-limited trial would let a once-a-year user complete the whole task free during the trial, so the restriction must be on features, not on time.
parts.working: For each product: 1 mark for a sensible trial type and 1 mark for a justification linked to how the product is used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Many software licences forbid users to decompile or reverse-engineer the program. Explain what this means and why software companies include this condition.
parts.answer: Decompiling/reverse-engineering means working back from the program to discover how it works or to obtain a version of its code. Companies forbid it so that competitors cannot copy their ideas and code; so that people cannot remove the copy-protection or licence checks; to protect years of investment in development.
parts.working: 1 mark: meaning; 1 mark each for two reasons (max 3).

parts.label: a
parts.text: A software house in Karachi uses an open-source code library in a product it sells. The library's licence allows anyone to use and change it, but says that if a changed version is distributed, its source code must also be made available under the same licence, with credit to the original authors. Explain what the software house must do if it changes the library and sells the product.
parts.answer: It must make the source code of its changed version of the library available to those who receive the product, under the same open-source licence; it must keep the original copyright notice and credit the original authors; it cannot claim the library as its own work or put it under a closed licence.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: share source of changes; same licence; credit/attribution kept.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why open-source software is still protected by copyright.
parts.answer: The authors still own the copyright; the open-source licence is how they grant permission and set the conditions for using it.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Compare public-domain software with open-source software.
parts.answer: Both can be used and copied free of charge, and in both the code may be available. Public-domain software has no copyright at all (the author has given up all rights), so there are no conditions. Open-source software is still copyrighted; it is licensed with conditions such as keeping credits or sharing changes under the same licence.
parts.working: 1 mark for a similarity; 2 marks for differences (copyright status; conditions on use).

parts.label: a
parts.text: An engineering firm can buy a perpetual licence for a design program for Rs 80,000, plus Rs 30,000 for each upgrade, which it would buy in year 3 and in year 5. Or it can pay a subscription of Rs 1,800 per month, which includes all upgrades. Calculate the total cost of each option over 5 years and state which is cheaper and by how much.
parts.answer: Perpetual Rs 140,000; subscription Rs 108,000; subscription is cheaper by Rs 32,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give one reason why the firm might still choose the perpetual licence.
parts.answer: With a perpetual licence it can keep using the program even if it stops paying; it does not depend on online licence checks; future subscription prices may rise.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Omar writes a stock-control program while employed by a company in Faisalabad. When he leaves for a job at a competitor, he takes a copy of the program's code and uses it there. Explain why this breaks copyright.
parts.answer: Software written as part of an employee's job normally belongs to the employer, who owns the copyright (unless the contract says otherwise); Omar has copied the code without the owner's permission; using it at the competitor is an unauthorised use and distribution of the company's work.
parts.working: 1 mark each: employer owns copyright of work done in employment; copying without permission; use at competitor unauthorised.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one other legal problem this may cause for Omar.
parts.answer: He may also break his employment contract / confidentiality agreement, as the code may contain trade secrets.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A science program is priced per licence by quantity: 1–9 licences Rs 6,000 each; 10–49 licences Rs 5,100 each; 50 or more licences Rs 4,500 each. A school needs 48 licences. Calculate the cost of buying 48 licences and the cost of buying 50, and state the saving from buying 50.
parts.answer: 48 licences Rs 244,800; 50 licences Rs 225,000; saving Rs 19,800.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain whether it is legal for the school to own more licences than the computers it installs the program on.
parts.answer: Yes – copyright is only broken by using more copies than are licensed; owning spare licences is allowed (and they can be used for new computers later).
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A college has 200 computers, but no more than 35 students ever use a CAD program at the same time. A per-computer licence costs Rs 2,500, and a concurrent-user licence costs Rs 12,000 per simultaneous user. Calculate the cost of each option and the saving from the cheaper option.
parts.answer: Per-computer Rs 500,000; concurrent Rs 420,000; concurrent saves Rs 80,000.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe one risk of choosing the concurrent-user option.
parts.answer: If more than 35 students need it at once (e.g. during an exam or coursework deadline), some will be refused access; it also needs a licence server that must always be running.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Some people argue that schools in low-income countries should be allowed to use expensive commercial software without paying. Discuss this view.
parts.answer: For: schools cannot afford licences, so students miss important skills; software companies lose little because the schools would not buy anyway; students who learn the software may become paying customers later; education benefits the whole society. Against: it is still illegal and breaks copyright; developers need income to pay staff and create new software; it encourages a culture of piracy; legal alternatives exist – free/open-source software, education discounts and donated licences; unlicensed copies lack updates and may contain malware. Conclusion: better solution is educational licensing or open-source software rather than ignoring copyright.
parts.working: Up to 4 marks for points for and up to 4 for points against (max 5 if one-sided); 1 mark for a reasoned conclusion. Max 6.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Zeeshan's licence for an accounting program says: 'The licensed user may install the software on one desktop and one laptop, both used by the licensed user, but may not use both at the same time.' For each situation, state whether it is allowed and explain why.
(i) Zeeshan installs it on his office desktop and his own laptop, and uses the laptop when travelling.
(ii) Zeeshan's assistant uses the program on the desktop while Zeeshan uses it on his laptop.
(iii) Zeeshan installs it on a third computer at home.
parts.answer: (i) Allowed – two installations, one user, not used at the same time. (ii) Not allowed – a second person is using it and both copies are in use at the same time. (iii) Not allowed – the licence permits only two installations.
parts.working: 1 mark each for the correct decision with a reason.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by a corporate house style.
parts.answer: A set of rules an organisation uses for all its documents and media, fixing items such as the logo, fonts, font sizes, colour scheme and layout, so that everything it produces looks the same.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: a standard/consistent style for all documents | set by the organisation | specifies fonts/sizes/colours/logo/layout/spacing | so all documents look the same / are recognisable.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Give three items that a corporate house style might specify.
parts.answer: The company logo and its position; the font type and sizes for headings and body text; the colour scheme.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: logo (size/position) | font/typeface | font sizes | colour scheme | margins | line spacing | paragraph spacing | text alignment | header/footer contents | page orientation/size | slogan/strapline.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give three reasons why a company uses a corporate house style.
parts.answer: Documents are consistent, so customers instantly recognise the brand; the company looks professional; staff save time because templates already have the styles set up.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any three of: consistency across all documents | brand identity/recognition | professional image | saves time – templates/styles reused | fewer formatting decisions/errors | easy for new staff to follow | builds customer trust.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the difference between a serif font and a sans-serif font.
parts.answer: A serif font has small extra strokes (serifs) at the ends of the letters; a sans-serif font has no such strokes, giving plain, clean letter ends.
parts.working: 1 mark each: serif has small lines/'feet'/tails on the ends of characters | sans-serif has none.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Tick the TWO statements that are true about corporate house style.
A It is only used for printed documents.
B It helps customers recognise an organisation.
C It means every document must have the same text.
D It can be applied using templates and styles.
E It allows each employee to choose their favourite font.
parts.answer: B and D.
parts.working: 1 mark each for B and D. Deduct for extra ticks (max 2).

practice.stem: You are told to create a new paragraph style called HL-body with these settings: sans-serif font, 11 point, left aligned, single line spacing, 0 pt space before and 6 pt space after.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to create this style in a word processor.
parts.answer: Open the Styles pane and choose New Style; name it HL-body and set the style type to paragraph; choose a sans-serif font and 11 pt; set alignment to left and, in Paragraph settings, line spacing single, spacing before 0 pt and after 6 pt; save the style.
parts.working: 1 mark: create new style and name it exactly HL-body. 1 mark: font sans-serif 11 pt. 1 mark: paragraph settings – left, single, 0 pt before, 6 pt after.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State how you would apply the style to all the body text in the document.
parts.answer: Select all the body text paragraphs and click HL-body in the styles list.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the style name must be typed exactly as given, including the capital letters and hyphen.
parts.answer: A style is identified by its name; a name spelt differently (e.g. HL Body or hl-body) is a different style, so the document would not match the house style and others could not find or apply the correct style.
parts.working: B1: styles identified by exact name / different spelling = different style, so house style not followed (accuracy).

practice.stem:
A house style for a school magazine is:
- Title: serif font, 28 pt, bold, centre aligned
- Subheading: sans-serif font, 16 pt, italic, left aligned
- Body: serif font, 12 pt, fully justified, 1.15 line spacing

parts.label: a
parts.text: A student's title is in a serif font, 28 pt, bold and left aligned. Identify the error and how to correct it.
parts.answer: The title is left aligned instead of centre aligned; apply/modify the Title style so the alignment is centre.
parts.working: 1 mark: error is alignment. 1 mark: change to centre (via style).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A subheading appears in a serif font, 16 pt, italic, left aligned. Identify the error.
parts.answer: The font should be sans-serif, not serif.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the alignment and line spacing for the body text.
parts.answer: Fully justified; 1.15 line spacing.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A table in a report must follow this house style: header row in a sans-serif font, 12 pt, bold, white text on a dark grey background, centre aligned; all other cells in 11 pt, left aligned; all borders visible.

parts.label: a
parts.text: List four formatting changes needed for the header row.
parts.answer: Set the font to sans-serif 12 pt; make it bold; set the text colour to white and the cell shading to dark grey; centre align the text.
parts.working: 1 mark each: sans-serif 12 pt | bold | white text + dark grey shading | centre aligned.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State one check to make after formatting the table.
parts.answer: Check that all borders are visible on every cell (and that no text has wrapped awkwardly or been cut off).
parts.working: B1: borders visible | text fits / no unwanted wrapping | body cells 11 pt left aligned | table fits within margins.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
For each description, state whether it describes a serif or a sans-serif font.
(i) Letters have plain ends with no small strokes.
(ii) Letters have small tails or feet at the ends of the strokes.
(iii) Often chosen for headings on posters to be read from a distance.
parts.answer: (i) sans-serif; (ii) serif; (iii) sans-serif.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A letter template for an engineering firm in Islamabad must use the house style: logo top left; firm name, address and phone number top right; body text 11 pt sans-serif; margins of 2.5 cm on all sides.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the firm saves the letter as a template.
parts.answer: Each new letter starts with the logo, header details, styles and margins already set, so staff save time and every letter follows the house style; the original template is not overwritten.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: settings already applied | consistency | saves time | original not overwritten / new file created each time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two ways to position the logo top left and the address top right on the same line.
parts.answer: Use a two-column table without borders in the header (logo in left cell, address in right cell, right aligned); or insert the logo with square wrapping at the left and right-align the address text.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: borderless table | text wrapping on the image + right aligned text | right tab stop | text box positioned at right.

practice.stem: A document contains two styles: Body-text (serif, 11 pt) and Caption (sans-serif, 9 pt, italic). The house style says every image must have a caption directly below it.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how a student should add a caption under an image so it follows the house style.
parts.answer: Type the caption text in a new paragraph directly below the image and apply the Caption style to it.
parts.working: 1 mark: caption placed directly below the image. 1 mark: Caption style applied.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two features of the Caption style that make it different from Body-text.
parts.answer: It is sans-serif rather than serif, and it is 9 pt italic rather than 11 pt.
parts.working: 1 mark each: font type | size/italic.

practice.stem: In a leaflet for a bakery in Hyderabad, the house style says the phrase 'freshly baked every morning' must be bold and italic wherever it appears in the body text, and the rest of the body text must have no enhancement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the two text enhancements required for the phrase.
parts.answer: Bold; italic.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student makes the whole paragraph containing the phrase bold and italic. Explain why this does not follow the house style.
parts.answer: Only the phrase itself should be enhanced; the rest of the body text must be plain, so the paragraph is now inconsistent with the other body text.
parts.working: 1 mark: enhancement applied to too much text. 1 mark: rest of body text must have no enhancement / inconsistent.

practice.stem: A house style says every page of a company report must show the logo and the page number in the same place.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the feature of a word processor that repeats the company logo and the page number on every page.
parts.answer: Header and footer
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the logo and page number should be placed in the header and footer rather than typed on each page.
parts.answer: They are set once and repeat automatically on every page, so no page is missed and the position stays the same if the document changes.
parts.working: 1 mark: they repeat on every page automatically. 1 mark: saves time and keeps the layout consistent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what a template is and how it helps a user follow a house style.
parts.answer: A template is a saved document with the house styles, page layout, logo and header and footer already set; a new document based on it starts with the house style applied.
parts.working: 1 mark: a saved document with styles and layout already set. 1 mark: new documents use the house style automatically, so the user does not need to set it again.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to apply the paragraph style Heading 2 to one paragraph in a word processor.
parts.answer: Click in or select the paragraph; open the styles gallery or styles pane; click Heading 2 (or choose it from the style list).
parts.working: 1 mark: select or place the cursor in the paragraph. 1 mark: open the styles gallery or pane. 1 mark: choose Heading 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the difference between a paragraph style and a character style.
parts.answer: A paragraph style formats the whole paragraph (for example font, alignment and spacing); a character style formats only the selected words or characters within a paragraph.
parts.working: 1 mark: paragraph style applies to the whole paragraph. 1 mark: character style applies only to selected text.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give two items that a corporate house style for an email signature might specify.
parts.answer: Any two: font and font size; colour of the company name; the logo and its size and position; the order of the name, job title and phone number; the disclaimer text.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid item.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a house style for a company's documents should specify the page margins.
parts.answer: Margins keep the layout the same on every document, so that the logo, text and footers appear in the same place and the documents look like one set.
parts.working: 1 mark: consistent layout across documents. 1 mark: the position of the text and images is the same, so documents look professional and match the printing area.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State how many points (pt) there are in one inch.
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the size of one point in centimetres, correct to 4 decimal places (1 inch = 2.54 cm).

parts.label: a
parts.text: State two things a house style for a government information leaflet should require so that it is easy to read for people with poor eyesight.
parts.answer: Any two: a larger font size (e.g. 12 pt or more); a sans-serif font; good contrast between the text and the background; left-aligned text, not justified; clear headings.
parts.working: 1 mark for each valid requirement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the purpose of a style guide written for the staff of a company.
parts.answer: A style guide sets out the house style rules (fonts, colours, layout and logos) so that all staff produce documents that look consistent and follow the company's identity.
parts.working: 1 mark: it sets out the rules for fonts, colours, layout or logos. 1 mark: it makes documents consistent across staff and the company's identity.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Name the indent setting that indents only the first line of each paragraph.
parts.answer: First line indent
parts.working: 1 mark.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how to set a first line indent of 1 cm in a body text paragraph style.
parts.answer: Open the paragraph dialogue for the style; in Indentation choose Special: First line; enter 1 cm; apply and update the style.
parts.working: 1 mark: open the paragraph settings for the style. 1 mark: first line indent of 1 cm set and applied.

practice.stem: A chain of pharmacies in Pakistan has 60 branches. Each branch manager currently designs their own posters and leaflets.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain the benefits to the chain of introducing a corporate house style for all branch posters and leaflets.
parts.answer: Customers will recognise any branch's material immediately because it looks the same everywhere, which strengthens the brand; it gives a professional, trustworthy image, important for a health business; managers save time by using ready-made templates with the styles built in; and errors such as wrong logos or colours are reduced.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four expanded points: brand recognition across all branches | consistent/professional image builds trust | templates save managers' time | less training needed | fewer mistakes with logo/colours | material from head office and branches matches | easier to update all documents when style changes.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe two drawbacks of introducing the house style.
parts.answer: It takes time and money to design the style and train all managers to use it; it limits managers' creativity and their ability to adapt posters for local customers.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: cost/time to design and set up templates | staff need training | less creative freedom | may not suit every type of document/local language | existing materials must be redone.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why using paragraph styles is better than formatting each paragraph by hand.
parts.answer: Every paragraph with the same style looks identical, so the document is consistent; if the house style changes, modifying the style updates every paragraph that uses it at once; applying a style in one click is faster than setting font, size, spacing and alignment each time; and heading styles can be used to build an automatic table of contents.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: consistency | changing a style updates all text using it | faster to apply | fewer errors/forgotten settings | can be saved in a template and shared | headings styles allow automatic contents/navigation pane | reduces file editing effort for long documents.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State two settings that can be stored in a paragraph style.
parts.answer: Font size and alignment.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: font/typeface | font size | font colour | bold/italic/underline | alignment | line spacing | space before/after | indentation | bullets/numbering.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe what is meant by each of these text alignments: left aligned, centre aligned, fully justified.
parts.answer: Left aligned: each line starts at the left margin and the right edge is uneven (ragged). Centre aligned: each line is centred between the margins. Fully justified: spacing between words is adjusted so lines are straight at both the left and right margins.
parts.working: 1 mark for each correct description.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Suggest why a newspaper house style uses fully justified text in columns.
parts.answer: Straight edges on both sides make narrow columns look neat and tidy and fit more text.
parts.working: B1: neat/straight edges on both sides / tidy columns / professional appearance.

practice.stem: A document already uses the style Heading 1 for twelve headings. The house style changes: Heading 1 must now be 20 pt, dark blue, with 18 pt space before and 6 pt space after.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe the most efficient way to update all twelve headings.
parts.answer: Modify the Heading 1 style itself (right-click the style → Modify) and change the size, colour and spacing; every heading using Heading 1 updates automatically.
parts.working: 1 mark: modify the style (not each heading). 1 mark: all headings using that style update automatically.

parts.label: b
parts.text: One heading did not change after the style was modified. Suggest a reason and how to fix it.
parts.answer: That heading had manual (direct) formatting applied, or a different style, which overrides the style; select it, clear the direct formatting and reapply Heading 1.
parts.working: 1 mark: direct/manual formatting or wrong style applied. 1 mark: clear formatting and reapply Heading 1.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why spacing is set in the style rather than by pressing Enter to add blank lines.
parts.answer: Blank lines are extra empty paragraphs that give inconsistent gaps and can cause blank pages or poor page breaks; style spacing gives exact, consistent gaps that change automatically if the style is changed.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: consistent exact spacing | no empty paragraphs/unwanted blank lines or pages | spacing updates when the style changes | easier to edit.

practice.stem: A house style states that the heading style Brand-H1 must have 36 pt space before and 18 pt space after. One point (pt) is 1/72 of an inch, and 1 inch = 2.54 cm.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the space before in centimetres, correct to 2 decimal places.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Calculate the space after in centimetres, correct to 3 decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the house style specifies spacing in points rather than as 'one blank line'.
parts.answer: A blank line's height depends on the font size used, so it varies; points are an exact measurement, so every document gets exactly the same spacing.
parts.working: 1 mark each: blank line size varies with font/size | points exact/consistent across documents.

practice.stem: You have been asked to create a style called Note-bullet based on the body text style. It must use the same font and size as the body text, be indented 1 cm from the left margin, and use a square bullet. Each paragraph must be followed by 3 pt space.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what 'based on the body text style' means and one benefit of this.
parts.answer: The new style inherits all the settings of the body text style and only the listed differences are changed; if the body text font or size is later modified, Note-bullet changes automatically too, keeping them consistent.
parts.working: 1 mark: inherits settings from the parent style. 1 mark: changes to the parent automatically carry through.

parts.label: b
parts.text: List the settings that must be changed in Note-bullet.
parts.answer: Left indent 1 cm; square bullet; space after 3 pt.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

practice.stem: A house style requires every document to have: the company name in the header, left aligned; the page number in the footer, right aligned; the file name and path in the footer, left aligned; all in the same font as the body text.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the page number and file name should be inserted as automated fields rather than typed.
parts.answer: Fields update automatically, so each page shows its correct number and the file name/path changes if the document is renamed or moved; typed text would be the same on every page and become wrong.
parts.working: 1 mark each: page numbers change automatically on each page | file name/path updates when the file is saved/moved/renamed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how to place the file name on the left and the page number on the right of the same footer line.
parts.answer: Insert the file name field at the left of the footer, then use the right-aligned tab stop (at the right margin) or press Tab to move to the right and insert the page number field.
parts.working: 1 mark: file name field at left. 1 mark: right tab stop aligned with right margin used for page number.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State why the header and footer must align with the page margins.
parts.answer: So that they line up with the body text and look consistent and professional, as the house style requires.

practice.stem: A presentation for a cricket academy in Karachi must follow the academy's house style: dark blue background, logo in the bottom right corner of every slide, titles in a white sans-serif font, 40 pt, and slide numbers on every slide except the title slide.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the logo and colours should be set on the master slide.
parts.answer: Items on the master slide appear on every slide automatically in exactly the same position, so the house style is consistent and the logo does not have to be added and positioned on each slide.
parts.working: 1 mark each: appears on all slides | consistent position/format | saves time | changes in one place update all slides.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe how to show slide numbers on every slide except the title slide.
parts.answer: In Header and Footer settings, tick slide number and tick 'Don't show on title slide', then apply to all slides.
parts.working: 1 mark: turn on slide numbers for all slides. 1 mark: option to hide on title slide.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one setting in the house style that would be hard to read if the background were changed to white.
parts.answer: The white title text would be invisible against a white background.

practice.stem: A charity's house style says all bulleted lists must use: round bullet, bullet at 0.6 cm, text indented to 1.2 cm, 3 pt space after each item, and the last item followed by 12 pt space.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the last item is treated differently and how this could be achieved.
parts.answer: Extra space after the last item separates the list from the next paragraph; it can be done by modifying the spacing after for the final item only, or by setting the next paragraph's space before.
parts.working: 1 mark: separates the list from following text. 1 mark: set 12 pt after on the last item (or space before next paragraph).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A student changes a numbered list into a bulleted list. State two ways the student can check that the list now matches the house style.
parts.answer: Look at the bullet character and indent markers on the ruler; open the paragraph settings for an item to check the indents and spacing values.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: visual check of bullet shape | ruler indent markers at 0.6/1.2 cm | paragraph dialog values | show formatting/reveal formatting pane | compare with a correct example.

practice.stem: A student must apply this house style to the title 'Annual Science Fair 2026': sans-serif, 24 pt, bold, centre aligned, all text in capital letters.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the title exactly as it should appear after formatting.
parts.answer: ANNUAL SCIENCE FAIR 2026
parts.working: B1 exact, including the year and spaces.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain one advantage of using the 'All caps' font effect rather than retyping the title in capitals.
parts.answer: The original text and spelling are kept, so there is less risk of typing errors, and if the style changes the text can be shown in normal case without retyping.
parts.working: 1 mark: no retyping so no new errors. 1 mark: effect can be removed/changed in the style.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the team should create a paragraph style for footnote text rather than format each footnote by hand. Give two reasons.
parts.answer: A style gives every footnote the same font, size and spacing automatically; changing the style later updates all footnotes at once.
parts.working: 1 mark for each reason: consistent formatting for all footnotes; one change updates all footnotes.

practice.stem: A house style gives the space after a heading as 24 pt.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert the space after a heading into centimetres. Give your answer to 2 decimal places (1 inch = 72 pt and 1 inch = 2.54 cm).

practice.stem: A newsletter has a text width of 17.0 cm. The text is set in three equal columns with a gap of 0.5 cm between each pair of columns.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the width of each column in centimetres, correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.working: M1: the gaps between columns total 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 cm. M1: 17.0 − 1.0 = 16.0 cm shared between 3 columns. A1: 16.0 ÷ 3 = 5.33 cm.

practice.stem: The brand colour of a company is red 0, green 102, blue 51.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the six-digit hexadecimal code for this brand colour.

practice.stem: A house style sets the Title style to 28 pt. The Subheading style must be 70% of the Title size.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the font size of the subheading in points.

practice.stem: A café menu in Lahore lists each dish name on the left and its price on the right of each line.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to set a right tab stop at 15 cm so that the price in each menu line is aligned at the right edge of the text.
parts.answer: Open the Tabs dialogue (from the paragraph settings for the style); enter 15 cm as the tab position; choose Right alignment; set; then press Tab before each price and update the style so every paragraph using it has the tab.
parts.working: 1 mark: open the tab settings. 1 mark: position 15 cm with right alignment. 1 mark: press Tab before the price, and store it in the style so it applies to all menu lines.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain what happens to the sub-style Note-text (based on Body-text) when the font of Body-text is changed, if Note-text has no font set of its own.
parts.answer: Note-text takes the new font from Body-text because it is based on it, so the change is passed on to it automatically.
parts.working: 1 mark: it inherits the change from the style it is based on. 1 mark: no separate change is needed for each paragraph.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Describe how to insert an automatic page number field in the footer, so that it shows Page 3 on the third page and updates if pages are added.
parts.answer: Double-click the footer; choose Insert Page Number (or Insert Field and then Page); select the position; close the footer to return to the body text.
parts.working: 1 mark: open the footer for editing. 1 mark: insert a page number field from the menu. 1 mark: the number is a field, so it updates on every page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the page size and margins should be set in the page setup, not in a paragraph style.
parts.answer: Page size and margins apply to the whole document or section, not to individual paragraphs; a paragraph style controls only the text within a paragraph.
parts.working: 1 mark: page setup applies to the whole document or section. 1 mark: a paragraph style only affects text in paragraphs.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
Which of these is NOT normally stored as part of a paragraph style?
A font size
B line spacing
C page size
D indentation
parts.answer: C page size
parts.working: Page size is a page setup setting for the whole document or section, not a paragraph property. Font size, line spacing and indentation are all paragraph formatting that a paragraph style normally stores. The main distractor is D, which is a normal paragraph setting.

practice.stem: A university in Islamabad publishes a prospectus, a website and slide presentations. Its house style says: logo top right; headings in a sans-serif font, dark green; body text in a serif font, 11 pt, black; all pages have the university name in the footer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the university can make sure that staff follow the house style in documents, presentations and web pages.
parts.answer: Provide word-processing templates with the paragraph styles and footer already set up; provide a master slide for presentations containing the logo, fonts and colours; use one external stylesheet (CSS) for all web pages so every page uses the same fonts and colours; and train staff and check documents before they are published.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any four of: document templates with styles | locked/predefined styles | master slide for presentations | external CSS stylesheet for all web pages | style guide document | staff training | proofreading/approval before publication | logo provided as a fixed image file in the templates.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Discuss whether a serif font or a sans-serif font is more suitable for the body text on the university's website.
parts.answer: Sans-serif fonts are usually clearer on screens because the plain letter shapes display well at low resolution, whereas serif fonts are traditionally easier to read in long printed text; so the website may use sans-serif body text even though the printed prospectus uses serif, but this breaks consistency with the house style unless the house style allows it.
parts.working: 1 mark: sans-serif clearer on screen / serif better for long printed text. 1 mark: conclusion weighing readability against consistency with the house style.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A designer says: 'A house style should use no more than two fonts.' Explain why.
parts.answer: Too many fonts make a document look cluttered and unprofessional and harder to read; limiting fonts keeps documents consistent and recognisable.
parts.working: 1 mark each for: many fonts look messy/unprofessional/distracting | two fonts (e.g. one for headings, one for body) give consistency/readability/brand identity.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a house style might specify colours as exact codes (such as #1B5E20) rather than names such as 'dark green'.
parts.answer: 'Dark green' can be interpreted differently by different people and software, giving many slightly different greens; an exact code gives exactly the same colour in every document, slide and web page, protecting brand consistency.
parts.working: 1 mark: names are vague/different shades. 1 mark: code gives an identical colour everywhere / consistency of brand.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two reasons why a corporate logo is usually supplied as a file rather than recreated by staff.
parts.answer: Recreated logos would vary in shape, proportion and colour; supplying a fixed file ensures every document shows the identical, correctly proportioned logo and saves staff time.
parts.working: 1 mark each for any two of: consistency | correct colours/proportions | prevents distortion | saves time | protects trademark/brand.

practice.stem: A company's house style for newsletters states: A4 portrait page 21.0 cm wide; left and right margins 2.0 cm each; body text in two equal columns with 1.0 cm spacing between them.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the width of each column.
parts.answer: 8.0 cm

parts.label: b
parts.text: The title of the newsletter must stretch across the full page width above the two columns. Describe how this is done.
parts.answer: Keep the title in a single column and insert a continuous section break after it; set the section below the break to two columns, so the title section stays one column wide.
parts.working: 1 mark: continuous section break after the title. 1 mark: two columns applied only to the section after the break.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The left margin is changed to 2.5 cm but the right margin stays at 2.0 cm. Calculate the new column width.

practice.stem:
Part of a corporate style sheet for a travel company in Lahore is:
TT-Title: sans-serif, 26 pt, bold, centre, 0 pt before, 12 pt after
TT-Sub: sans-serif, 14 pt, bold, italic, left, 12 pt before, 6 pt after
TT-Body: serif, 11 pt, fully justified, 0 pt before, 6 pt after, single spacing
A student's document shows:
Paragraph 1 (TT-Title): sans-serif, 26 pt, bold, centre, 12 pt before, 12 pt after
Paragraph 2 (TT-Sub): sans-serif, 14 pt, bold, left, 12 pt before, 6 pt after
Paragraph 3 (TT-Body): serif, 11 pt, left aligned, 0 pt before, 6 pt after, single spacing

parts.label: a
parts.text: Identify the three errors in the student's document.
parts.answer: TT-Title has 12 pt space before instead of 0 pt; TT-Sub is not italic; TT-Body is left aligned instead of fully justified.
parts.working: 1 mark each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why the student should correct these errors by modifying the styles rather than the individual paragraphs.
parts.answer: Every paragraph that uses the style is then corrected at once, and any paragraphs added later automatically have the correct settings, keeping the whole document consistent.
parts.working: 1 mark each: all paragraphs with that style fixed together | future text consistent / no direct formatting overrides.

practice.stem: A student is told: 'Create a style called Quote-box: serif, 12 pt, italic, centre aligned, 1 cm indent from both left and right margins, a 1 pt black border around the paragraph, 6 pt space before and after. Apply this style to the paragraph beginning "Our mission".'

parts.label: a
parts.text: List the settings that are paragraph settings and those that are font (character) settings.
parts.answer: Font settings: serif, 12 pt, italic. Paragraph settings: centre alignment, 1 cm left and right indents, 1 pt black border, 6 pt space before and after.
parts.working: 2 marks for all font settings correctly listed (1 mark if one wrong/missing); 2 marks for all paragraph settings (1 mark if one wrong/missing).

parts.label: b
parts.text: After applying the style, the border appears around two paragraphs. Explain the likely cause.
parts.answer: The student selected (or placed the cursor across) two paragraphs when applying the style, or the next paragraph's style is also Quote-box because 'style for following paragraph' was set to Quote-box; borders on adjacent paragraphs with identical settings merge into one box.
parts.working: 1 mark: two paragraphs selected / following paragraph also uses the style. 1 mark: identical adjacent bordered paragraphs are joined in one box.

practice.stem: A long report (60 pages) for a water research institute uses the styles Report-H1, Report-H2 and Report-body. The director asks for a table of contents and wants all Report-H2 headings to start on a new page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain how the heading styles make it possible to create the table of contents automatically.
parts.answer: The table of contents tool finds every paragraph using the heading styles (set as outline levels 1 and 2) and lists them with their page numbers; it can be updated if headings or pages change.
parts.working: 1 mark: TOC built from paragraphs with heading styles/outline levels. 1 mark: page numbers added automatically / can be updated.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the most efficient way to make every Report-H2 heading start on a new page.
parts.answer: Modify the Report-H2 style and turn on 'page break before' in its line and page break settings; every Report-H2 heading then moves to the top of a new page.
parts.working: 1 mark: modify the style (not insert breaks manually). 1 mark: page break before option.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Give two settings in the heading styles that help avoid a heading being left alone at the bottom of a page.
parts.answer: 'Keep with next' so the heading stays on the same page as the following paragraph; 'keep lines together' so a multi-line heading is not split.
parts.working: 1 mark each: keep with next | keep lines together (accept widow/orphan control).

practice.stem: A company's corporate colours are dark red (red 139, green 0, blue 0) and gold (red 255, green 204, blue 0). Its house style also requires all body text to be dark grey (red 64, green 64, blue 64).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Convert each colour to a six-digit hexadecimal colour code.
parts.answer: Dark red #8B0000; gold #FFCC00; dark grey #404040.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why dark grey body text on a white page is still readable.
parts.answer: There is a strong contrast between the dark grey text and the white background.

practice.stem: A 40-page annual report for a textile company in Faisalabad mentions the company name 'Indus Weave' 85 times. The new house style says the company name must always appear in bold, dark green, small capitals, but the surrounding text must keep its own paragraph style.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a character style is more suitable than a paragraph style for this requirement.
parts.answer: A character style applies only to the selected words, so the paragraph keeps its own style (spacing, alignment, font for other text); a paragraph style would change the whole paragraph.
parts.working: 1 mark: character style affects only selected text. 1 mark: paragraph style would reformat the entire paragraph.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe an efficient way to apply the style to all 85 occurrences.
parts.answer: Create a character style (e.g. Company-name) and use Find and Replace: find 'Indus Weave', replace with the same text but with the Company-name style as replacement formatting, then Replace All.
parts.working: 1 mark: Find and Replace (Replace All). 1 mark: replacement formatting set to the character style.
